Good morning. The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments on Wednesday in King v. Burwell, the latest challenge to the Affordable Care Act, the WSJ's Anna Wilde Mathews reports. If conservatives have their way, the court will decide that a few words in the law mean that federal subsidies to consumers in 37 states are unlawful, and effectively unravel marketplaces there. Such a decision could knock Obamacare into a "death spiral" of a shrinking pool of insured Americans and higher premiums for those who keep coverage through federal exchanges in those states.

But such a move is far from certain, and even if the court does rule against the federal subsidies that make plans in the affected states affordable to lower-income residents, Obamacare requirements on businesses will remain the law of the land--even if some commentators hope that such a ruling would be the beginning of the end for the law.

The case has put a cloud of uncertainty over insurers that are putting the final touches on their products and prices for 2016. "We're hedging our bets right now," says Ferris W. Taylor, chief strategy officer of Utah's Arches Health Plan. That insurer may propose an array of product designs this spring, then drop some of them before they're finalized, depending on what the court decides.

CFO JOURNAL TODAY

Almost half of global audits have problems. Nearly half of global audits inspected last year were deficient in some way, an international accounting consortium said Tuesday, CFO Journal's Maxwell Murphy reports. Top concerns included internal controls testing, measuring fair value of assets, and revenue recognition, according to the International Forum of Independent Audit Regulators. The organization examined almost 950 reports from 29 countries.

THE DAY AHEAD

The ADP private-employment report for February releases at 8:15 a.m., and analysts are expecting 220,000 new jobs, up somewhat from January's 213,000. Then, at 2 p.m., the Federal Reserve releases its Beige Book of economic activity, giving investors a peek at a key indicator ahead of the central bank's next policy meeting.

Smells like teen dispirit. Investors are bracing for more teen angst when Abercrombie & Fitch Co. and American Eagle Outfitters Inc. report fiscal full-year results on Wednesday, Ahead of the Tape's Spencer Jakab reports. The apparel retailers have suffered an almost unbroken string of sales declines lately.

CORPORATE NEWS

Tech firms buy up property. Some of Silicon Valley's biggest companies are on a real-estate buying binge, paying premium prices to make sure they have enough space for future expansion. Facebook Inc. agreed last month to spend $395 million for Menlo Science and Technology Park, a jumble of 21 low-slung warehouses and office buildings 30 miles southeast of San Francisco. Google Inc. spent more than $1 billion last year on at least 19 properties in Silicon Valley. The purchases, known as land banking, are being done in part to give the companies breathing room as they add employees. But it also a hedge against future real-estate price increases and helps fend off rivals from planting flags in their backyards.

GE CEO Jeff Immelt's crude problem. General Electric Co.'s CEO already had problems convincing investors he was moving fast enough to remake the conglomerate into a simpler industrial machine, and now there's this oil business. Mr. Immelt spent $14 billion on companies that help oil and gas drillers pump and transport. GE was touting the business as recently as September, but Mr. Immelt's annual investor meeting in December included a warning on oil and gas.

Best Buy rewards shareholders. Best Buy Co. unveiled plans to buy back shares for the first time since 2012 and boosted its dividend by 21%, as the electronics retailer posted better-than-expected profit in its holiday quarter. The chain said it would repurchase $1 billion in shares over three years as part of an existing $5 billion authorization. It also announced a 21% increase to its quarterly dividend and a special dividend of 51 cents a share.

Actavis sells $21 billion of bonds. Actavis PLC sold the second-biggest corporate-bond offering in history, with a $21 billion deal fueled by investors' desire for returns amid low interest rates. The sale comes as highly rated firms this year are selling debt at the fastest pace on record.

Vanguard and BlackRock are raising their voices. Vanguard Group and BlackRock Inc., giant fund managers once known for quiet relationships with the companies in which they invest, say they are getting more assertive. Vanguard is urging boards to be "substantially independent of management," and BlackRock, in newly revised voting guidelines, signaled for the first time that it may oppose U.S. board members' re-election.

Citi deal shrinks the bank's umbrella. Citigroup Inc.'s move to sell its U.S. subprime-lending business to Springleaf Holdings Inc. is emblematic of postcrisis regulations forcing banks out of their old mind-set of trying to serve as many customers as possible under one roof.

J.P. Morgan treasurer to step down. J.P. Morgan Chase & Co.'s treasurer, Craig Delany, is planning to leave the bank but will stay on until a successor is onboard. Mr. Delaney, who is in his mid-40s, will retire in the coming months to spend more time with his family, people familiar with the matter said. He also oversees the bank's Chief Investment Office, a role he assumed following the "London whale" trading fiasco.

Barclays hit by forex charge. Barclays PLC raised its provision for potential foreign-exchange settlements to $1.92 billion, leading it to report a full-year net loss, but said an effort to shrink and restructure its business is starting to pay off. Barclays cut around 5% of its workforce last year. More than 2,000 of the cuts were in its investment bank, and a further 5,000 of the remaining 20,500 investment-banking jobs are set to go over the next two years.

The next marketing frontier: your medical records. Practice Fusion Inc. is pioneering a new type of data-driven health care. Its software alerts doctors when a medical record indicates that a patient needs a particular treatment. Some of those alerts are sponsored by drug companies. Practice Fusion gives its software to clinics free of charge. It crunches 100 million patient records it has stored remotely in an online database to alert providers when treatments or tests might be needed. Some worry the sponsored alerts blur the line between promoting health and marketing medicines.

Investors balk at deals for specialty retailers. The recent collapse of private-equity buyouts of Chico's FAS Inc. and Express Inc. signal that investors and lenders are growing increasingly wary of specialty retailers. The sector has seen a rash of bankruptcies, and banks have been hit by losses as they struggled to resell loans backing earlier deals.

The driverless car, officially, is a risk. Three insurance companies and an auto-parts maker warned in their most recent annual reports that driverless cars and the technology behind them could one day disrupt the way they do business. The investor warnings aren't meant to spell out an imminent threat. But their inclusion in the catch all "Risk Factors" section of corporate filings indicates that driverless cars are now close enough to reality that companies feel they need to flag the risks to their investors.

SUV sales plow through February. Poor weather modestly dented the pace of U.S. auto sales in February, but did little to stem America's increasing thirst for pricey trucks and SUVs. Meanwhile, old-school auto makers are gearing up to take on the threat posed by emerging competitors Google and Apple Inc. in a technological and financial gunfight.

Target to cut several thousand jobs. Target Corp. plans to lay off several thousand employees at its Minneapolis headquarters and elsewhere as CEO Brian Cornell looks to get the retailer back on track and shoppers back in its stores.

For tech's highfliers, Fab is a cautionary tale. Fab.com had early traction and blue-ribbon backers, but instead of becoming a billion-dollar e-commerce juggernaut, it's a cautionary tale for startups. PCH, an Irish electronics contract manufacturer, on Tuesday said it had acquired the Fab.com website and two offices in New York and India. Fab co-founder Jason Goldberg and PCH founder Liam Casey declined to comment on the final price, but people with knowledge of the matter said the two sides were negotiating for a price in the low tens of millions. Fab was valued at close to $1 billion two years ago.

Sharp to ask lenders for new support. Sharp Corp.'s president plans to meet with the troubled electronics company's two main lenders to ask for a new round of financial support, less than three years after its last bailout. A turnaround plan is expected to be presented to the core banking units of Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group Inc. and Mizuho Financial Group Inc., which together hold more than $3.3 billion in Sharp debt.

Fraud comes to Apple Pay . A payments expert tells the WSJ that it's not an anomaly to see fraud accounting for about 6% of Apple Pay transactions, compared to about 0.1% of transactions using a plastic card to swipe. The reason for the high number lies with some banks that make it too easy for customers to be approved because they wanted to reduce the friction of adding their cards to Apple Pay. An Apple spokeswoman says Apple Pay is "designed to be extremely secure and protect a user's personal information." She added that "banks are always reviewing and improving their approval process, which varies by bank."

4 Mar 2015 06:39 ET  The Morning Ledger: Could Obamacare Be Undone? -2-

Samsung bets on its chips in Galaxy S6 . The Exynos chips powering Samsung Electronic Co.'s new Galaxy S6 phones are the product of a multiyear effort to improve the company's chip design and manufacturing process. Since 2010, Samsung has been spending at least $10 billion each year to upgrade and expand its chip facilities, including plants that make memory chips. The investment frees from having to rely on Qualcomm Inc. chips for its devices and, in the long run, help boost Samsung's logic-chip division.

NBCU plans to launch comedy video service. Comcast Corp.'s NBCUniversal is aiming to launch a comedy-focused subscription Web video service later this year, as interest grows in reaching young online viewers who don't watch traditional TV. NBCU is considering various possible price points--one range under considerations is $2.50 to $3.50 a month. It is the latest media giant to venture beyond the cable-TV bundle to target people who are "cutting the cord," as well as "cord nevers" who have never paid for traditional TV.

REGULATION

Yellen scolds Wall Street on culture, ethics. Federal Reserve Chairwoman Janet Yellen raised concerns about the state of Wall Street's culture and ethics, echoing similar comments from other regulatory officials and increasing pressure on the biggest U.S. banks to improve.

Crackdown deals Macau a rough hand. Macau gambling revenue remained in a free fall in February, sinking 49% from a year earlier amid China's crackdown on corruption. The drop marks the ninth-straight month of shrinking revenue in the Chinese territory. February's slide eclipsed a previous record drop in December, when it fell 30%.

J.P. Morgan settles robo-signing charges. A J.P. Morgan Chase & Co. unit struck a $50 million deal with regulators who accused the bank of filing "robo-signed" mortgage documents to bankruptcy courts across the country. The bank will make payments to more than 25,000 homeowners, including some who weren't properly notified that their mortgage payments increased after they filed for bankruptcy protection.

ECONOMY

Inflation in developed economies halved in January. The annual rate of inflation across the world's developed economies more than halved in January, reaching its lowest level since the recession that followed the global financial crisis. That widespread disinflation is likely to prompt further cuts in benchmark interest rates or other easing measures by central banks around the world.

Seoul swallows tough medicine for economy. Government's push for telemedicine, now available only on remote islands, is a test case for a broader effort to reduce the country's dependence on exports by developing its weak service industries. Economists see the process as essential for South Korea's long-term prospects.

Denmark intervenes in currency market in a big way. The central bank bought a record amount of foreign currency last month in a bid to protect the krone's peg to the euro, underscoring the fallout from the European Central Bank's efforts to boost economic growth.

CFO MOVES

KKR Financial Holdings LLC, which New York-based financial-services company KKR & Co. LP acquired last year, named Thomas Murphy chief financial officer, according to a regulatory filing. He succeeds Michael McFerran, who resigned.

FLIR Systems Inc., a Wilsonville, Ore.-based sensor-systems company, named Dave Muessle interim CFO. Mr. Muessle is vice president, corporate controller and principal accounting officer at the company. CFO Tony Trunzo resigned effective March 27. Mr. Trunzo received compensation valued at $3.4 million in 2013, according to a proxy filing.

Brinker International Inc., a Dallas-based casual-dining restaurant company, named Thomas Edwards Jr. CFO, effective March 16. Mr. Edwards was CFO at Wyndham Hotel Group. He will succeed Guy Constant, who left the company last March and whose duties have since been handled by interim CFO Marie Perry, the company's treasurer and controller, a company spokeswoman told CFO Journal. Mr. Constant received compensation valued at $2.6 million during the company's 2014 fiscal year, according to a proxy filing.

Herman Miller Inc., a Zeeland, Mich.-based interior-furnishings company, named Jeff Stutz CFO. Mr. Stutz was treasurer and chief accounting officer at the company. He succeeds Greg Bylsma, whom the company made chief operating officer for a North American division, a company spokesman told CFO Journal. Mr. Bylsma received compensation valued at $1.1 million during the company's fiscal year ended in 2014, according to a proxy filing.

text:
* Rupiah firms; month-end corporate dollar bids limits gains
    * Won up more than 1 pct on exporters, stop-loss dlr selling
    * Taiwan dollar rises on exporters, stock inflows

 (Adds text, updates prices)
    By Jongwoo Cheon
    SINGAPORE, Feb 25 (Reuters) - Most emerging Asian currencies
rose on Wednesday after Federal Reserve Chair Janet Yellen
suggested the U.S. central bank will not rush into raising
interest rates, while Indonesia's rupiah hovered near 17-year
lows.
    Regional currencies gained as better-than-expected Chinese
manufacturing activity eased some concerns over a slowdown in
the world's second-largest economy.
    The South Korean won and the Taiwan dollar
 advanced on exporter demand for month-end settlements.
Malaysia's ringgit gained on short-covering.
    Yellen said before the U.S. Senate Banking Committee on
Tuesday that any modification of the Fed's forward guidance
should not be read as an indication of interest rate hikes in a
couple of meetings. 
    The comments defied expectations that she would provide a
more specific time frame to revive prospects for higher U.S.
borrowing costs as early as mid-year. Such expectations hurt
most emerging Asian currencies earlier this week.
    Adding to support for regional currencies, the flash
HSBC/Markit Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) for China inched up
to a four-month high of 50.1 in February, beating market
expectations. 
    "Asia FX could see some slight positives for a short term on
the back of dollar reprieve from Yellen's comments and commodity
currencies could see some upmove from the positive HSBC flash
PMI," said Saktiandi Supaat, head of FX research for Maybank in
Singapore.
    Still, he had doubts about appreciation in the long term,
saying "the dollar will continue to mildly go up ahead of the
next FOMC."
    The Chinese yuan failed to join the regional
appreciation trend as the central bank fixed its daily mid-point
weaker on the first trading day after the week-long Lunar New
Year holidays. 
    
    RUPIAH
    The rupiah started the day up 0.4 percent at a
session high of 12,850 per dollar, tracking gains in regional
peers, before retreating.
    Foreign ownership of rupiah-denominated bonds rose to a
record high in nominal terms this week, the finance ministry
said. 
    The Indonesian currency gave up most of its earlier gains on
increasing dollar demand from local companies for month-end
payments.
    The official Jakarta Interbank Spot Dollar Rate,
which the central bank introduced in 2013 to manage exchange
rate fluctuations, was fixed at 12,887 rupiah per dollar, weaker
than the previous session's 12,866.
    On Tuesday, the rupiah fell to 12,897 per dollar, the
weakest since Dec. 16 when it hit 12,930, the lowest since
August 1998.
    
    WON
    The won rose more than 1 percent as demand from exporters
caused traders to dump dollar holdings to stop losses.
    Traders had added long dollar positions earlier as importers
bought the greenback and amid caution over possible intervention
by South Korea's foreign exchange authorities to curb the won's
strength.
    
    TAIWAN DOLLAR
    The Taiwan dollar gained as sustained stock inflows lifted
local shares.
    The central bank was spotted intervening to limit the
currency's upside, traders said.
    Foreign investors bought a combined net T$73.1 billion ($2.3
billion) worth of shares in February by Tuesday, Taiwan Stock
Exchange data showed. They were net buyers in the stock market
in all trading days this month, the data showed.

title: INTERVIEW-S.Korea  fx  rate seen market determined in recent months -IMF
text:
SEOUL, Feb 13 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund, which has previously urged South Korea against intervening in the currency market, says the won has moved in line with market trends in the past six months, suggesting authorities refrained from forceful intervention.

Recent central bank data shows foreign exchange reserves have inched down over several months, a sign that authorities in the export-reliant economy have veered away from the aggressive dollar buying of the past when the won rose sharply.

"From the data that are available, the exchange rate has been market-determined for the last six months I think, so the government is pursuing their policy of exchange rate flexibility at the moment. We think that's the right thing to do," said IMF division chief Brian Aitken in an interview with Reuters.

South Korean foreign exchange authorities are known to step into the market in times of volatility, usually to weaken the won against the dollar in order to support exporters, according to traders and analysts.

That has sparked complaints from the United States and IMF in the past, with the IMF's report last year saying there is no need for further accumulation of foreign exchange reserves through intervention.

Local policymakers in recent months have said that although they engage in smoothing operations to lessen fluctuations, they refrain from fighting against the tide.

While the won reached five-year highs last year, the dollar began strengthening dramatically in November, pressuring the won and other Asian currecies.

Aitken also said South Korea's household debt burden does not pose an imminent threat to the financial sector.

"One of the very interesting things about Korean households too, is that while debt is rising as share of income, so are assets. So they're not borrowing to spend," he said.

Earlier on Friday, data showed South Korean households' disposable income growth picked up in the October-December quarter from the previous quarter, brightening prospects for private consumption.

Aitken's comments came during the IMF's yearly visit to South Korea to discuss economic developments and policies. (Reporting by Christine Kim; Editing by Tony Munroe and Simon Cameron-Moore)

title: UPDATE 1-S.Korea economy faces risks from global uncertainties, oil to help -IMF
text:
* S.Korea 2015 outlook faces uncertainties               

* S.Korea to benefit from low oil prices               

* Won has moved in line with other currencies recently   (Adds more IMF comments from press conference)               

By Christine Kim               

SEOUL, Feb 13 (Reuters) - The South Korean economy faces uncertainties this year due to global weakness, the International Monetary Fund said on Friday, but expects it will benefit from low oil prices and doesn't see  an imminent risk from rising household debt.               

Given the backdrop of an improving U.S. economy and ongoing concerns over the outlook for China, Japan and the E.U., South Korea faces a risk that a "self-reinforcing downside dynamic" of weak growth and inflation could take hold, the IMF said.               

However, Asia's fourth-largest economy is better placed  compared to other emerging economies, it said.               

"Weakness in the global economy is the biggest risk but South Korea is in a very good position to (withstand) that weakness. Korea is well-placed to face any kind of shocks that may be coming," said Kalpana Kochhar, deputy director of the Asia and Pacific Department at the IMF.               

South Korea has enhanced external buffers that would help limit the impact of any renewed global financial volatility, the mission said, while South Korea's household debt does not pose a financial or systemic risk because debt and assets are both rising.               

The IMF also noted that South Korea has monetary and fiscal policy space to respond if needed, although it advised the government to take timely action should the situation warrant it. The mission also recommended far-reaching reforms to underpin long-run growth.               

Kochhar said it is too early to assess whether South Korea's economic weakness will persist or whether it has already bottomed out.               

The IMF, which has previously urged South Korea against intervening in the currency market, also said the won has moved in line with market trends in the past six months, suggesting authorities refrain from forceful intervention.               

Recent central bank data shows foreign exchange reserves have inched down over several months, a sign that authorities in the export-reliant economy have veered away from the aggressive dollar buying of the past when the won rose sharply.               

"From the data that are available, the exchange rate has been market-determined for the last six months I think, so the government is pursuing their policy of exchange rate flexibility at the moment. We think that's the right thing to do," said IMF division chief Brian Aitken in an interview with Reuters earlier this week.

    By Jongwoo Cheon
    SEOUL, Dec 31 (Reuters) - Emerging Asian currencies fell in
2014, led by the Malaysian ringgit, and regional units are
expected to stay under pressure in the new year due to
expectations the U.S. Federal Reserve will hike interest rates
and China's economy will stay sluggish.
    Regional currencies on Wednesday rose as the yen

year-end.

in emerging Asian currencies in 2015 as a solid U.S. economy is
likely to drive the Fed to raise interest rates.
    China's economy continues to slow down. Activity in the

months in December, according to a private survey.

given possibilities of U.S. rate hikes," said Jeong My-young,
Samsung Futures' research head in Seoul.
    "Southeast Asian units may suffer more as they are more
sensitive to the Chinese economy and oil prices, while Northeast
Asia peers may find some support from the U.S. recovery," Jeong
added.
    The dollar was on course to end 2014 with a 12 percent gain
against a basket of major currencies, its largest advance since
2005.
    The greenback is seen strengthening further as a U.S. rate
hike will boost its appeal when the Bank of Japan and the
European Central Bank are easing monetary policies.

partially due to expectations that the Federal Reserve may raise
interest rates in 2015, prompting investors to withdraw funds
from emerging markets and channel them back to the United
States.
    Trading was thin across Asia ahead of the New Year's holiday
and as many investors have already closed out their positions
for 2014.

text:
* S.Korea intervention caution up as won at 6-yr high vs yen
    * Rupiah at 6-year low, JISDOR record low
    * Indonesia c.bank spotted around 12,320/dlr-traders

 (Adds text, updates prices)
    By Jongwoo Cheon
    SINGAPORE, Dec 4 (Reuters) - Most emerging Asian currencies
slid on Thursday as the dollar stayed at multi-year highs
against major currencies on solid U.S. jobs data and ahead of an
European Central Bank policy meeting later in the day.
    South Korea's won underperformed regional peers
as the yen plumbed seven-year lows against the dollar,
heading towards the 120 per dollar level.
    The Indonesian rupiah hit a six-year low on dollar
demand from local corporates. The country's second biggest party
on Wednesday re-elected tycoon Aburizal Bakrie as its chief for
the next five years, dimming hopes that the opposition party
would join President Joko Widodo's minority coalition.
    
    The dollar index, the greenback's performance against
six major currencies, hovered around its highest since March
2009.
    U.S. private companies added workers at a fairly brisk pace
in November and the service sector expanded strongly, indicating
the world's top economy holds growth momentum. 
    By contrast, the euro zone economy may be on the verge of
another contraction, prompting some expectations that the ECB
may be preparing to add more stimulus, although a full-blown
quantitative easing programme is seen as unlikely at the policy
review later in the day.
    "If the ECB signals another easing, the dollar will gain
momentum further and Asia FX will weaken," said Yuna Park, a
currency and bond analyst at Dongbu Securities in Seoul.
    "A less dovish ECB may help the euro rebound and Asian
currencies may follow that, but that would be only temporary."
    
    WON
    The won slid against the dollar on caution that South
Korea's foreign exchange authorities may intervene to check
their currency's strength against the yen.
    The won hit 9.2872 to the Japanese unit, its strongest since
August 2008. Two countries compete in exports markets for
various products such as cars.
    The won has a chart resistance area between 9.2000-9.3000,
levels struck July and August 2008 during the early stages of
the global financial crisis, analysts said.
    
    RUPIAH
    The rupiah eased 0.2 percent to 12,319 per dollar, its
weakest since November 2008. 
    The official Jakarta Interbank Spot Dollar Rate (JISDOR),
which the central bank introduced last year in an effort to
manage exchange rate fluctuations, was fixed at 12,318 rupiah
per dollar, the weakest since the launch.
    Foreign banks sold the rupiah, and most government bond
prices fell.
    The rupiah, however, pared some of its earlier losses as the
central bank was spotted intervening around 12,320 via state-run
banks to limit the currency's decline, traders said.
    "It is possible to test 12,350 in a near term, but the
12,320 is capped for now with unlimited offers there," said a
Jakarta-based currency trader, referring to dollar selling by
state-run banks.

skidded lower on Wednesday as the dollar climbed to a seven-year
high against the yen, buoyed by higher U.S. Treasury yields on a
more bullish outlook for the world's top economy.
    Malaysia's ringgit hit a near five-year low as a
rebound in oil failed to ease concerns over the impact of lower
crude prices on the country, a net oil exporter and major palm
oil producer.

its weakest since December 2008, amid the global financial
crisis, on local corporate dollar demand.
    South Korea's won tracked the yen's slide.

performance against six major currencies, stayed around 4-1/2-
year high, on stronger U.S. bond yields.
    The dollar was supported by comments earlier this week from
New York Fed President William Dudley and Vice Chair Stanley
Fischer who both provided a mostly rosy outlook for the U.S.
economy. 
    "Asia FX will stay weaker as everybody agrees on a strong
dollar trend," said Jeong My-young, Samsung Futures' research
head in Seoul.
    "We may see some profit-taking from the dollar, but it is
hard to reverse the trend unless U.S. economic data is bad or
other economies show a solid picture of health."
    
    RINGGIT
    The ringgit lost as much as 0.5 percent to 3.4420 per
dollar, its weakest since February 2010. Kuala Lumpur stocks
 lost 0.8 percent, well underperforming other Southeast
Asian peers.
    The Malaysian currency pared some of its earlier losses as
the central bank was suspected of intervening to limit its
downside, traders said.

January rising to $67.97 a barrel earlier in the day, but
investors stayed concerned about Malaysia's weakening growth due
to lower oil prices.

be lower than the bank's forecast of 4.8 percent and next year's
budget deficit target of 3 percent could be more difficult to
achieve if oil price were to stay at $70.

past 3.55-3.60 before it represents a bigger risk to BNM's
inflation outlook," Credit Suisse said in a client note,
referring to Malaysia's central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia.

possible intervention by South Korea's foreign exchange
authorities to stem the currency strength against the Japanese
unit.
    Against the yen, the won advanced to 9.3231, a notch weaker

title: OPEC Meeting in Focus for USD/JPY -- Market Talk
text:
0147 GMT [Dow Jones] The OPEC meeting later today will be crucial to provide clues regarding future crude oil prices especially before the year-end big shopping season in the U.S., says Nomura Securities chief FX strategist Yunosuke Ikeda in a morning note. OPEC members are facing an impasse to iron out differences in opinions and remain cautious about output reduction until getting a detailed understanding about U.S. shale oil supplies. Mr. Ikeda says whether WTI oil prices fall to $70 for now (now at $72.60) will be closely monitored. Lower crude oil prices will work its way through to a higher USD/JPY by pushing up the U.S. economy and Treasury yields. (hiroyuki.kachi@wsj.com) 


 
Editor SXS 
 

0129 GMT [Dow Jones] Australia's equities market is in positive territory despite weaker energy and mining shares, echoing the small gains seen on Wall Street overnight. The ASX 200 is ahead 0.2% at 5404.3, helped by gains in banks. NAB (NAB.AU) is up 1.3% while Commonwealth Bank (CBA.AU), Westpac (WBC.AU) and ANZ (ANZ.AU) are up between 0.1% and 0.3%. Tristan K'Nell, head of trading at Quay Equities, notes the market bounced higher after the release of capital expenditure data which should offer some comfort to the central bank that some businesses outside mining will increase spending into next year. Despite a further fall in the price of iron ore, Fortescue (FMG.AU) is 1.1% higher, but BHP Billiton (BHP.AU) is down 1% and Rio Tinto (RIO.AU) is off 0.2%. A confirmation of the downtrend channel coming into play--contingent on a Thursday close below 44.880--would weigh the dollar further.     SINGAPORE, Nov 21 (Reuters) - Emerging Asian currencies rose
on Friday as the yen rebounded after Japan's Finance Minister
Taro Aso warned against the currency's recent swift fall,
although most regional units were set for another week of
losses.
    The yen gained as Aso earlier described the
currency's weakening as "too rapid," but ruled out intervention
to halt the slide. 
    The rebound caused investors to cover short positions in
emerging Asian currencies.
    Still, most regional units were poised to post weekly
losses, led by the South Korean won, as the yen hit a
seven-year low against the dollar on Thursday.

its fourth week of declines, according to Thomson Reuters data.
That was the longest streak of weekly losses since May 2013.
    South Korea's foreign exchange authorities were suspected of
intervening to check the won's strength against the yen
 on concerns it would erode the competitiveness of
exporters against their Japanese rivals.
    The Taiwan dollar fell 0.8 percent with the
island's exporters also seen vulnerable to weakness in the yen
and the won. The Indian rupee has eased 0.2 percent so
far this week.
    Malaysia's ringgit has slid 0.1 percent, while the
Philippine peso closed the week down 0.1 percent.
    The Indonesian rupiah stood firm in the face of
falls in regional peers, having risen 0.7 percent.
    Indonesia's President Joko Widodo on Monday announced a
long-awaited decision to raise fuel prices and free up funds to
rejuvenate Southeast Asia's biggest economy. The central bank on
Tuesday hiked interest rates to temper an expected upsurge in
inflation following the fuel price hike.
    China's yuan has gained 0.1 percent on
expectations of inflows due to a new link between the Hong Kong

title: S.Korean won down as bank worries rock shares
text:
* Won down as economy, financial sector woes hit stocks

* Further falls seen on risk aversion

* Intervention caution growing (Updates to domestic close)

By Cheon Jong-woo

SEOUL, Jan 20 (Reuters) - The South Korean won fell against the dollar on Tuesday as fresh worries about the health of global banks and the spreading impact of a worldwide recession on Asia's fourth-largest economy hit Seoul shares.

The won <KRW=> came under further pressure from expected dollar demand from overseas investors seen pulling out money deposited for a new share issue by Hynix Semiconductor after many failed to buy the chipmaker's stocks.

The local currency is expected to remain weak as more investors are seeking safer assets on persistent worries about grim corporate earnings amid a global recession, analysts said.

"The won is more likely to weaken past the support line of 1,380 and probably to 1,400 (versus the dollar) soon, as stock markets in the world may fall further on risk aversion," said Jeong My-young, a currency strategist at Samsung Futures Inc.

The South Korean currency was quoted at 1,374.4/4.6 per dollar as of 0600 GMT, compared with Monday's domestic close <KRW=KFTC> of 1,362.5.

Seoul shares <.KS11> ended down 2.07 percent as foreign investors sold a net 72.1 billion won worth of stocks in the country's main exchange.

Adding to evidence of a slowdown in the South Korean economy, data showed the country's exports to China, its biggest export market, and the European Union fell by more than a third each in December from a year ago. [IDnSEO337548]

With growing expectations for the won's further fall, market players saw more possibility for dollar-selling intervention by South Korea's foreign exchange authorities to prop up the currency.

"If the won breaks through the 1,400 line, it will go to 1,500 soon. That will make it difficult for the central bank to cut interest rates to boost the economy," said an analyst at a local futures firm, asking not to be identified as he was not authorised to speak to the press.

A weaker won usually lifts import prices, eventually boosting consumer inflation, which is seen denting already ailing domestic demand.

Earlier this month, the Bank of Korea cut interest rates to a new low and suggested more cuts to help fend off a recession.

Meanwhile, the won may find some support from demand related to LG Display's supply deal with Apple Inc , dealers said.

Earlier this month, LG Display said it had a signed a contract to supply LCD panels to Apple for five years and it would receive a $500 million advance in January.[ID:nPEK176050]

Earlier, central bank data showed South Korea's foreign exchange reserves rose in December for the first time in nine months as investment gains and rises in non-dollar assets more than offset intervention. [ID:nSEO359371]

title: Emerging  FX -Singapore dollar, won weighed down by econ fears
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 2 (Reuters) - The South Korean won and Singapore dollar slid on Friday on concerns about the countries' growth outlooks as the global downturn looked set to further hit Asia's export-dependent economies.

In 2008, many Asian currencies had their worst year in a decade, hit by waves of sell-offs in regional stock and bonds as the global financial crisis spooked investors to flee to safer assets.

The won <KRW=> lost more than 5 percent on Friday to 1,330.9 per dollar, its weakness since Dec. 24, on the government's grim export forecast for 2009 and as the market expected the authorities to cut dollar-selling intervention to boost exports.

South Korea's December exports slid a worse-than-expected 17.4 percent from a year earlier and the government said 2009 exports would probably grow only one percent, marking the weakest pace in eight years. [ID:nL179089]

The data fuelled market expectations of another interest rate cut when the Bank of Korea reviews monetary policy on Jan. 9.

Most Asian markets were closed on Thursday for the New Year holiday and those in China, Taiwan, Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines remained shut on Friday.

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> fell as far as 1.4555 per U.S. dollar, down almost 1.5 percent from Wednesday's close, after the government cut its economic outlook for 2009 to between a decline of 2 percent and growth of 1 percent. [ID:nSIN411254].

"The figures should help weaken the Singapore dollar," said a Singapore-based trader, who reckoned investors were buying back the U.S. dollar on the belief that the Singapore dollar is near the strong end of its trading band managed by the central bank.

Singapore's central bank steers monetary policy by managing the currency within an undisclosed traded-weighted band against a basket of currencies, rather than adjusting interest rates.

Kit Wei Zheng, an economist at Citigroup, expects Singapore's economy to contract an annual 2.8 percent in 2009, the most severe recession in city-state's history.

In response, the government is likely to unveil an aggressive fiscal stimulus later this month while the central bank would probably let the Singapore dollar weaken by re-centring its trading band downward in April, when it reviews policy, Kit said in a note.

"Although the current recession is due to a contraction in demand, a modest weakening of the Singapore dollar's nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) could still provide some relief for exporters," Kit said.

Meanwhile, the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> fell 0.6 percent to 3.4725 per dollar, taking its cue from the Singapore dollar.

title: UPDATE 1-Japan to up  FX  swaps with S.Korea to $30 bln-media
text:
(For more stories on the financial crisis click [ID:nCRISIS]) (Adds comments, details)

TOKYO, Dec 11 (Reuters) - Japan plans to expand its currency swap lines with South Korea, which has been hit by sharp falls in the won, to about $30 billion from the current $13 billion, Japanese business daily Nikkei reported on Thursday.

Japanese Finance Minister Shoichi Nakagawa said Tokyo is negotiating with Seoul to reach an agreement during a meeting of leaders from the two countries and China on Saturday in the southern Japanese city of Dazaifu.

"We are aiming to obtain good results at the summit meeting," Nakagawa said at a parliamentary committee.

But neither the minister nor senior officials from the Ministry of Finance elaborated on the amount.

The reported step would be in line with an agreement by finance ministers from Japan, China and South Korea to consider expanding the size of currency swap arrangements between their countries. [ID:nN14458729]

The South Korean won <KRW=> has been depreciating amid worries about the effect of fallout from the global recession on its export-driven economy, and Seoul has been keen to boost a regional web of bilateral currency swap deals, called the Chiang Mai Initiative (CMI).

Currently, Tokyo has two types of currency swap lines with Seoul -- dollar-won and yen-won swap arrangements -- in line with the CMI.

Under those arrangements, Japan can provide U.S. dollars worth up to $10 billion and Japanese yen worth up $3 billion to South Korea.

In theory, one possibility that may arise from the use of the yen-won swap pact is that South Korea could sell the yen it borrows from Japan to buy dollars in the market, and then use those dollars to conduct won-buying intervention.

Data last week showed that South Korea's foreign reserves fell again by $11.7 billion to $200.5 billion in November, the lowest level in almost four years.

Bahk Byoung-won, South Korea's senior presidential secretary, said last week that South Korean authorities would make only make marginal interventions in the foreign exchange market due to a rapid depletion of the country's foreign currency reserves. [ID:nSEO278114]

China is also negotiating with South Korea to expand their yuan-won swap facility, and they are expected to officially approve new details during the summit. (Reporting by Yoko Nishikawa and Tetsushi Kajimoto; Editing by Michael Watson)

title: WRAPUP 2-South Korea c.bank rushes to give banks more help
text:
* Central bank hold emergency meeting, to boost liquidity

* Presidential adviser sees no value in FX intervention

* Presidential adviser accepts 2009 growth to hit decade low

* Forex reserves in November drop to near four-year low (Recasts with central bank announcement)

By Cheon Jong-woo and Seo Eun-kyung

SEOUL, Dec 3 (Reuters) - South Korea's central bank promised at an emergency meeting on Wednesday to pump more funds into its cash-short financial system, as a top official accepted the economy is heading for much lower-than-expected growth in 2009.

The president's top economic adviser concurred with increasingly gloomy economic forecasts that growth in 2009 would be its weakest since the Asian financial crisis a decade ago and said it was pointless to squander the country's falling foreign exchange reserves to try to lift the weak won.

The comments followed news that currency reserves dropped to a near 4-year low in November, increasing pressure on the central bank to do more to help lift Asia's fourth-biggest economy as it confronts a global crisis that has already tipped some of its top export customers, including the United States, Japan and the euro zone, into recession.

"The presidential secretary is trying to pressure the central bank for more drastic action by highlighting a bleak economic outlook," said Kong Dong-rak, a fixed-income analyst at Hana Daetoo Securities.

The central bank's monetary policy committee agreed to provide additional support for financial institutions, including paying interest on local bank cash reserves totalling about 500 billion won ($341.8 million).

It will also purchase more bonds from local banks and actively supply liquidity to stabilise markets.

"These measures are aimed at reinforcing banks' lending capability," the central bank said in a statement.

But it made no mention of interest rates, which it has cut three times since the global crisis took a turn for the worse in September with the collapse of Lehman Brothers investment bank.

Still, financial markets expect the central bank to cut its base rate, currently a two-year low of 4.0 percent after cuts amounting to 1.25 percentage point since Oct. 9, at its next monthly rate review on Dec. 11.

WEAKER GROWTH

"Overall, there is a consensus forecast for growth of some 2-3 percent (next year). I do not disagree with that," senior presidential economic secretary, Bahk Byoung-won, told reporters.

The government is expected later this month to revise its 4 percent economic growth forecast for next year. GDP growth this year is expected to be 4.7 percent.

Growth of 2-3 percent would be the lowest since 1998, when the economy contracted 6.9 percent at the height of the Asian financial crisis.

In fact, some investment banks have predicted the economy will shrink in 2009 as much as 3 percent as the global recession drains export demand, long the country's main growth driver, and as domestic demand wilts.

Exports last month fell more than 18 percent, their biggest drop in seven years, with one official saying the economy was slowing more than expected.

Reserves last month dropped $11.7 billion, hitting their lowest in almost four years at $200.5 billion and following on from a record $27.4 billion decline in October.

NOT ENOUGH TO HELP

Even though Korea's reserves were the world's sixth largest at the end of October, Bahk said that they were not big enough to lift the won which has lost nearly 40 percent of its value this year against the dollar.

"South Korea does not have enough capacity for massive forex intervention. We will carry out smoothing operations in forex markets when necessary," presidential adviser Bahk said.

Since the Asian financial crisis, Asia countries have built up massive foreign exchange reserves to protect themselves against capital flight. Asian reserves are around $4 trillion.

But confidence in the cash pile has been severely tested by the global crisis. Worry that the nation's foreign exchange reserves might dip below $200 billion have been fanning investor concerns over a fresh currency crisis.

The government and central bank have been forced to pump foreign currency into the financial system after banks suddenly found themselves unable to raise dollars through normal banking channels as global credit conditions tightened.

South Korean banks have looked especially vulnerable to the crisis partly due to their high level of short-term foreign currency loans used to fund the country's exporters.

"The foreign exchange authorities steadily injected foreign currency liquidity to ease uncertainty in the local foreign currency money market due to a persistent global credit crunch," the Bank of Korea said.

Officials said they did not expect reserves to fall much further, a prediction echoed by a number of analysts, given an improvement in the current account, a $30 billion dollar credit line at the U.S. Federal Reserves and liquidity injections by other central banks. (Writing by Jonathan Thatcher; Editing By Keiron Henderson)

title: UPDATE 2-S.Korea c.bank buys US T.bills from pension service
text:
(Recasts)

SEOUL, Nov 28 (Reuters) - The Bank of Korea bought U.S. Treasuries from South Korea's National Pension Service on Friday, looking for ways to conserve its dwindling foreign exchange reserves as it battles to defend the sagging won.

Worry that the nation's once-impressive foreign exchange reserves may have already fallen below $200 billion this month have been fanning investor concerns over a new currency crisis similar to the one that rocked South Korea over a decade ago.

The NPS said it would sell $1.1 billion of U.S. Treasuries to the central bank in a bid to boost the country's foreign currency reserves, which have been run down by months of dollar sales in fruitless intervention to support the won.

South Korea's won is Asia's weakest currency this year, having slumped nearly 40 percent as foreign investors liquidated risky emerging economy assets, scrambling to salvage what wealth they can from the credit crunch and global market meltdown.

"Although the dollar supply from the pension fund is not an avalanche, it's better than nothing," said Song Jae-hyeok, an economist at SK Securities, adding the Bank of Korea's scramble for dollars was evidence of its current bind.

"The Bank of Korea is in the position where it has to decide between intervening to defend the won and conserving its forex reserves. If it intervenes those reserves will go down."

Further signs of the pressures on Asia's fourth-largest economy came on Friday as industrial output fell the most in two years in October suggesting the economy is slipping closer to its first recession since the Asian financial crisis a decade ago.

Factory output skidded a seasonally adjusted 2.3 percent in October from September, widely missing market expectations for a 1.3 percent rise and adding pressure on authorities for action to support the sagging economy.

"The output data is really disappointing, signalling that the economy is slipping into a recession, a deep and long one," said Lee Sang-jae, an economist at Hyundai Securities.

"I believe the Bank of Korea has realised how serious the economic conditions are. It might move to cut rates further in December, possibly by 50 basis points."

The Bank of Korea is next scheduled to review interest rates on Dec. 11. It has already cut its benchmark base rate by 1.25 percentage points to 4.0 percent, in an unprecedented series of three moves since early October.

MODEST BOOST

Earlier, Finance Minister Kang Man-soo gave markets a modest boost by saying South Korea's current account was expected to swing into surplus next year from a projected deficit in 2008 of around $10 billion.

But analysts weren't so sanguine about the forecast.

"The current account will post a surplus next year, not because of better exports, but because of reduced imports. The won will continue to remain weak, and this will further pressure imports," said Lee Dong-su, an economist at Tong Yang Securities.

On Thursday, data showed that the capital account in October posted a $25.5 billion deficit, the biggest monthly deficit in history, compared with a $4.78 billion shortfall in the prior month, hit by more outflow related to derivatives.

Friday's BOK purchases show the central bank's determination to squeeze out dollar liquidity from as many sources as it can and follow news on Thursday South Korea would tap a $30 billion swap line with the U.S. Federal reserve to bring in dollars.

The latest official data showed that South Korea's foreign reserves fell by a record $27.4 billion to $212.25 billion at the end of October from September, the lowest level in almost three years as the country injected billions of dollars into the banking system amid the financial crisis.

The foreign reserve declined by a combined $52 billion since the end of March till October as the central bank struggled with a falling won.

South Korea's last recession came during the Asian financial crisis when it went through three straight quarters of negative growth between 1997 and 1998. Since then South Korea has experienced single quarters of negative growth on two occasions earlier this decade.

"With the painful experience of the Asian financial crisis still haunting them, many Koreans are very sensitive to the nation's foreign currency reserve," Song said. (Additional reporting by Kim Yeon-hee and Cheon Jong-woo, Writing by Keiron Henderson, editing by Jonathan Thatcher)

title: WSJA: Asian Shares Drop,  Currencies  Sharply Lower
text:
OF THE WALL STREET JOURNAL ASIA 
 

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Asian stocks were sold off heavily Thursday, knocking many of the region's currencies sharply lower and prompting governments to intervene.

Markets in Tokyo, Hong Kong and South Korea fell in response to a broad selloff overnight in the U.S. Tokyo's benchmark index fell 6.9%, while Hong Kong and Seoul were down 4% and 6.7% respectively. Australia's major benchmark dropped 4.2% and Shanghai fell 1.7%. Mumbai and Singapore were down 4.1% and 2.8% late Thursday. Jakarta was down 2.8% late.

The selling continued in Europe, where the DJ Stoxx 600 index was 3% lower. U.S. stock futures were down 1% to 1.5% in screen trade.

The stock hits reflect fears of deflation in the U.S., a major market for Asia-made goods, and the impact of a slowdown on commodity-rich nations like Australia and Indonesia.

That has led to a flight to safer investments typically denominated in U.S. dollars and the Japanese yen, taking money out of Asian markets and contributing to a drop in local currencies.

"It's part of the wholesale destruction of wealth across the planet," said Patrick Bennett, a strategist with Societe Generale in Hong Kong. "With asset and equity prices tumbling, investors are being encouraged to cut exposure completely."

Weaker currencies can boost big exporting nations because it makes their goods cheaper to sell in other markets. But declining currencies also hit countries with extensive foreign borrowing needs, can drive up inflation by making imports more expensive and can scare off foreign investment.

Among the hardest hit, Indonesia's rupiah and South Korea's won fell to their lowest level against the U.S. dollar since the Asian financial crisis a decade ago.

Thailand's baht fell to its weakest level since March 2007, while Taiwan's dollar hit a three-week low and the New Zealand and Australian dollars also weakened further.

The central banks of South Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines, Indonesia, Singapore and India intervened to defend their currencies, local traders said. Australia's central bank issued data that showed it plowed A$3.15 billion into currency markets last month to defend the Australian dollar against a sharp decline.

Japan and Hong Kong have defied the trend, the former because its currency is seen as a safe haven and the latter because it is pegged to the value of the appreciating U.S. dollar. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the city's de facto central bank, put roughly HK$15 billion into the market Thursday to bring the currency's value within its trading band with the U.S. dollar.

Economists cautioned that the current environment hasn't reached the point of the Asian currency crisis, when domestic funds followed foreign investors as they ran for the exits. Most governments have moved to back bank deposits to reassure consumers. Regional financial institutions have cleaner balance sheets than a decade ago, and bad loans have so far had only a minor effect on regional banks.

Still, continuing hits to currencies continue could erode consumer confidence, leading locals to consider moving their money elsewhere. "The impact on confidence could become a much bigger problem," said Sim Moh Siong, an economist at Citigroup in Singapore. "If this goes beyond how much money foreigners remove from Asia, the situation could broaden out."

In Tokyo, the Nikkei Stock Average of 225 companies ended down 6.9% at 7703.04. Shares of major banks and brokerages were hammered, with Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group tumbling 10% to Y281,500 and Nomura Holdings ending down 11% at Y666.

Shares of nonlife insurers dropped after sector companies reported dismal fiscal first half results Wednesday and sharply reduced their earnings forecasts for the full fiscal year ending March.

Although most of the bad news had already been factored in by investors, forecast revisions confirmed the grim outlook. Tokio Marine Holdings went limit-down at Y2,220, and Mitsui Sumitomo Insurance Group Holdings also went limit-down at Y2,035.

Real estate stocks also sank, dogged by credit concerns, with Mitsui Fudosan skidding 14% to Y1,070, and Mitsubishi Estate falling 13% to Y1,077.

In Seoul, the Korea Composite Stock Price Index, or Kospi, finished down 68.13 points, or 6.7%, at 948.69, based on skepticism over conditions in the U.S., particularly among financials.

Shinhan Financial Group declined 9.7% to KRW26,400, and KB Financial Group plunged by the daily limit of 15% to KRW24,550. Among builders, Hyundai Engineering & Construction and GS Engineering & Construction both dropped by the daily 15% limit to KRW42,100 and KRW45,200, respectively.

In Shanghai, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index, which tracks both A and B shares, ended down 1.7%, or 33.71 points, at 1983.76. Railway companies and insurance companies fell on profit-taking.

China Railway Group Ltd. dropped 4.1% to CNY5.82 after gaining 4.7% Wednesday, while China Life Insurance Co. fell 4.0% to CNY20.24 after rising 6.1% in the previous session.

-By Carlos Tejada, The Wall Street Journal; carlos. tejada@wsj.com

(Takashi Mochizuki and Takashi Nakamichi in Tokyo and Rosalind Mathieson in Singapore also contributed to this article.) [ 20-11-08 0946GMT ]

title: UPDATE 4-South Korean slowdown raises pressure for rate cuts
text:
(Recasts with market close)

SEOUL, Oct 24 (Reuters) - South Korean growth hit a four-year low and stocks ended their worst week on record on fears that a global recession will hit its export-dependent manufacturers, adding pressure on the central bank to prevent more damage by cutting rates.

The main index for Seoul shares plunged more than 20 percent for the week to its lowest close since May 2005 with investors pricing in a sharp drop-off in demand for goods as major overseas markets slip toward recession.

Underlining the problems facing Asia's fourth-biggest economy, its largest firm Samsung Electronics Co Ltd posted a 44 percent drop in third-quarter profit and forecast tough times ahead as consumers around the world feel the pinch.

"Oh, don't even bring up that stocks thing," said Son Kyung-hwan, an South Korean insurance agent and investor. "I am never going to dabble in the stock market again in my life. I even had to pay taxes to sell my stocks."

The government has announced a raft of measures this week to try to restore investor confidence and steady the wobbling economy, including providing $130 billion to dollar-starved banks and $4 billion to debt-laden builders.

The central bank added another just as the stock market closed, saying it would inject emergency liquidity of 2 trillion won ($1.4 billion) via 28-day repurchase agreements.

The Korean Composite Stock Index ended down 10.6 percent, dipping below the 1,000 mark for the first time since May 2005.

The economic downturn cast a cloud over investors in the streets of Seoul.

"Stocks? What do you expect, I'm doomed," said Seol Jae-woo, an education industry worker and investor.

SAMSUNG WOES

Samsung, which fell almost 14 percent to its lowest since December 2004, and other exporters weighed on the index despite a bounce on Wall Street on Thursday.

Samsung is facing a lengthy downturn in the once-reliable memory chip market, a rapid margin deterioration in the flat-screen sector and slowing demand for consumer electronics.

"We foresee the coming months to be an even more challenging period," said Chu Woo-sik, Samsung's executive vice president in charge of investor relations.

South Korea's economy expanded a seasonally adjusted 0.6 percent in the third quarter from the previous three months -- the slowest pace in four years. Facing the headwinds of the global financial crisis, economic prospects are grim.

"GDP growth will slow going forward. It is important for the Bank of Korea to not only cut rates but to show a strong commitment to support the economy and join international stimulus effort," said Kim Jae-hong, a Shinyoung Securities economist.

UNLIKELY TO MEET FORECAST

South Korea was unlikely to meet the central bank's growth forecast of 4.6 percent in 2008 after it grew by 5.0 percent in 2007, a senior central bank official said.

A Reuters poll this week forecast 2008 growth of 4.3 percent and 2009 growth of 3.5 percent.

The economy grew 3.9 percent over a year earlier in the third quarter, sharply down from 4.8 percent in the second quarter and marking its weakest annual performance since mid-2005.

Earlier this month, the Bank of Korea cut its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 5 percent, the first reduction since late 2004. The cut was announced a day after key central banks joined forces in trimming rates to try to restore investor confidence to financial markets.

A battered won down about 17 percent over the past month and more than a third so far this year, was likely to face more pressure from a central bank rate cut. It ended local trade down almost 4 percent against the dollar, though suspected intervention cut some of the losses.

South Korea's presidential Blue House said a three-way summit that includes Japan and China is set for mid-December to coordinate plans to boost the regional economy.

President Lee Myung-bak, at an Asian-Europe summit in Beijing, has said he also wants to form a new global agency to manage the credit crunch.

East Asian leaders said in Beijing they will move to form an $80 billion currency swap scheme by the the middle of next year to help cushion the crisis' blow on economies.

Lee has warned the global crisis threatened to be more severe than the Asian financial meltdown a decade ago that almost derailed South Korea's economy. At that time, the country was bailed out of its troubles by a rescue package led by the International Monetary Fund worth close to $60 billion.

 The won <KRW=> also came under pressure from weaker stocks and on dollar demand from importers, despite measures from the country, the second bailout package this week, to help ailing construction sectors and to stabilise financial markets.

 The local unit recovered some of its earlier losses as the country's foreign exchange authorities were spotted selling dollars to cut the local currency's falls, but the move failed to lift it as trading was too thin, analysts said.

 The South Korean currency is expected to remain under pressure from lingering worries about a slowdown in the global economy, although eased concerns over the credit crisis after Sunday's $130 billion South Korean financial rescue package may give some relief to the won, analysts said.

 "Concerted actions by the global authorities have relieved investors a bit, but nobody thinks the world is free from the sluggish economy and the credit crunch," said Jeong My-young, an analyst at Samsung Futures Inc.

 "The won is seen moving around the 1,300 (per dollar) for a while, but it is more likely to weaken further than to rebound," she added.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia slides as stocks pounded, won trades wildly
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 10 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were battered on Friday as investors dumped stocks amid the financial turmoil despite a round of global interest rate cuts, prompting dollar-selling intervention in South Korea, Indonesia and India.

 The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> fell as far as 9,750 per dollar, down about 1.6 percent from Thursday's close, as trader cited dollar-selling intervention by the central bank to support the local currency.

 "The action keeps players sidelined," said a trader in Jakarta.

 The South Korean won <KRW=> moved wildly, gaining over 12 percent to 1,224.9 per dollar at one point after falling sharply earlier, as the authorities were seen selling dollars to defend the won, which has lost 27 percent against the dollar this year.

 A wave of selling pounded Asian shares amid growing fears of the financial turmoil, with the MSCI index of Asia-Pacific stocks excluding Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> falling 7.7 percent to its lowest since January 2005.

 The Indian rupee <INR=IN> hit a record low at 49.25 per dollar, as the central bank said it would cut bank's cash reserve requirements to 7.5 percent to ease a liquidity crunch. [ID:nBOM357479]

 Meanwhile, the Singapore dollar <SGD=> fell to 1.4865 per U.S dollar, giving up its early gains as investors turned bearish on data showing the economy is in recession.

 "It's due to the GDP figure," said a trader in Singapore.

 The Sing dollar briefly rose to 1.4724 immediately after the central bank announced an easing in monetary policy.

 Some traders said suspected official intervention helped the local unit.

 Singapore's central bank, which sets policy by managing the Singapore dollar in a secret trade-weighted band against a basket of currencies, eased monetary policy for the first time in five years after its economy sank into recession [ID:nSIN389047]

 The central bank said on Friday it was shifting policy from a gradual appreciation bias to a neutral zero-appreciation bias for the trade-weighted currency, in response to slowing growth and expected easing in inflation.

 The central bank maintained the width of the secretive band.

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> lost almost 0.9 percent to 47.8 per dollar, while the Thai baht <THB=TH> was down 0.4 percent to 34.48 per dollar.

 "We see some interest selling from exporters and some from offshore," said a trader in Bangkok. "The bias is that the dollar should go up against the baht, like dollar/regionals."

 Markets in Taiwan are closed for a holiday.

 Meanwhile, the cost of dollar funding remained elevated in Asia on Friday, with overnight dollar funds <USDOND=> quoted between 4 and 7 percent in Singapore, 4.5-5.8 percent in Bangkok and 4-5 percent in Jakarta, traders said.

 The levels held largely steady from Thursday, when several Asian central banks joined a worldwide rate-cutting campaign to contain the global financial crisis that has forced commercial banks to hoard cash, rather than lend to each other.  CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR  Change on the day at 0556 GMT

title: UPDATE: BOJ, RBA, MAS Inject Cash; Officials Soothe Markets
text:
(Adds further injections by BOJ, MAS)

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Central banks and other officials around Asia leapt into action Tuesday with either cash or soothing words to reassure the short-term borrowing and othermarkets after the U.S. House of Representatives voted down a key US$700-billion U.S. financial sector bailout package.

That decision sent the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbling 7% overnight, taking Asian bourses and manyof the region's currencies with it Tuesday.

The Bank of Japan injected Y3.0trillion into the short-term money market in two batchesto tackle an overnight call rate that was as high as 0.80%. The central bank's target rate is 0.50%.

The BOJ has now injected Y21.1 trillion into the money market over the 10 consecutive business days since U.S. investment bank Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc. filed for bankruptcy protection.

The Reserve Bank of Australia made a much smaller net injection of A$75 million in its daily operations.

Still, that will keep the level of commercial banks' exchange settlement accounts at the central bank around A$10.7 billion, the highest since the U.S. subprime-inspired market turmoil began making the headlines in mid-2007.

Money market rates in Australia were relatively steady, with the three-month bank bill swap rate fixed Tuesday at 7.32%, unchanged from Monday. The one-month rate is down 2 basis points at 7.38%. Traders said the Monetary Authority of Singapore Tuesday injected S$1.3 billion Tuesday to tackle an overnight rate of over 1.8%. The action pushed the rate down to around 1.375% and followed an injection of an estimated S$2.5 billion Monday.

Meanwhile, others used verbal intervention to calm the local markets.

Hong Kong Monetary Authority chief Joseph Yam said he expected the interbank funding market and the foreign exchange markets to be tense after the bailout was rejected but vowed to provide liquidity to the market and to banks if necessary.

A spokesman at the Reserve Bank of New Zealand said it "has the systems in place" to cope with the current global market shakeout, although that didn't stop some analysts from speculating that the RBNZ may have to continue with aggressive rate cuts, and possibly even an emergency easing, to prevent the country from sliding into a steep recession.

And in South Korea, the Bank of Korea said it had been intervening in the swap market for a week to calm the markets and would continue to do so until the market stabilizes.

Regulators and government leaders also felt the need to weigh in, expressing dismay over the failed package and hope that there would be a rethink.

Australian Treasurer Wayne Swan said he was "disappointed" that the U.S. package failed to pass, but nevertheless emphasized the differences between the struggling U.S. financial system and Australia's system.

"Our regulators...are in constant contact with all of our deposit-taking institutions," Swan said. "The advice that we are receiving is that (the system) is in good shape."

Australian Prime Minister Kevin Rudd Tuesday urged U.S. lawmakers to reconsider the package and said friends and allies of the U.S. would push the U.S. Congress to pass the package, or similar measures later this week.

Hong Kong Financial Secretary John Tsang was more positive, saying he believed in the U.S. Congress's resolve to approve the plan, adding the rejection would severely damage global economies.

Overnight, eight central banks around the world, including the Bank of Japan, Reserve Bank of Australia and the European Central Bank, announced they were more than doubling the dollar-swap facility with the Federal Reserve to US$620 billion from US$290 billion to unclog markets scrambling to meet dollar-funding needs ahead of the quarter-end.

Japan doubled the size its swap facility with the Fed to US$120 billion while Australia tripled its facility to US$30 billion.

"A dollar-liquidity problem has been intensifying in Japan, and we need to make every effort to ease" the issue, Bank of Japan Governor Masaaki Shirakawa at a press conference overnight.

The RBA said Tuesday that it would announce in the next few days another U.S. dollar repurchase agreement operation to inject U.S. dollars into the financial system as part of the swap line expansion.

-By Karen Lane, Dow Jones Newswires; 65 6415 4043; karen.lane@dowjones.com

(Iain McDonald and Enda Curran in Sydney, Jin-Young Yook in Seoul, Ben Garvey in Tokyo and Jackie Cheung in Hong Kong contributed to this story.) [ 30-09-08 0858GMT ]

title: S.Korea won down, jittery over Wall Street outlook
text:
(Updates to close)

 SEOUL, Sept 24 (Reuters) - The won fell against the dollar on Wednesday, as doubts about an early stabilisation of Wall Street markets persuaded international traders to keep away from riskier assets such as the South Korean currency.

 But the won managed to cut losses, with support from gains in local stock prices on the country's move to tighten supervision on short-selling and after local authorities pledged to help ease shortages in dollar funding in the local swap market.

 The won <KRW=> ended local trade at 1,154.0/4.6 per dollar, down from Tuesday's domestic close <KRW=KFTC> of 1,149.0 but above a session low of 1,157.9 set earlier in the day.

 "The market changed little for most of the day after the won's drop at the start of the session due to the volatile U.S. markets, but basis swaps narrowed in the afternoon after intervention by the authorities," said a foreign bank dealer.

South Korea's Finance Ministry and central bank officials said separately that they would inject sufficient liquidity into the local swap market, which has been struggling with shortages in dollar funding. [ID:nSEO166746] [ID:nSEO134879]

 Dollar/won basis swaps, which show how much additional costs investors have to pay to secure dollars, narrowed slightly to around -310 basis points from around -360 basis points on Tuesday, dealers said.

 South Korean financial institutions have been struggling to secure short-term dollar funding as the prolonged turbulence in the U.S. financial sector has raised risk aversion among international traders.

 The Seoul stock market's benchmark KOSPI <.KS11> index rose 1 percent, as foreign investors were net buyers of 542 billion won worth of local stocks.

 Regulatory officials have recently said they would draw up measures to tighten supervision on short-selling of stocks in the local market.

 The Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) said after trading ended that it had discovered many institutional investors had violated the ban on uncovered short-selling, in which investors sell shares that they do not actually own.

 The FSS said in a statement that it would recommend the Financial Services Commission, the policy-making agency that governs it, tighten regulatory guidelines.

 South Korea allows only covered short-selling, in which investors can sell borrowed stocks in the hope of buying them back at a lower price later to make a profit.

title: WRAPUP 3- South Korea intervenes , moves to speed won rebound
text:
* Won rallies after traders report government dollar sales

* Korea to scrap ceiling on foreign buying in offshore market

* Central bank predicts modest growth slowdown (Adds fresh central bank remarks, updates markets)

By Yoo Choonsik and Jonathan Thatcher

SEOUL, Sept 4 (Reuters) - South Korea intervened to support the battered won for a second day on Thursday, helping give the currency its biggest boost since early July just before it began its tumble to four year-lows on fears of capital flight.

An official said South Korea would also relax rules to help accelerate any recovery in the won which has lost 17 percent on the dollar this year and nearly 6 percent in a four-day sell-off triggered by worries foreign holders of about $7 billion of bonds maturing next week would take their money out of South Korea.

The selling turned to a frenzy on Tuesday when the Bank of Korea and finance ministry stood by and allowed the won to slide to its lowest level in four years instead of springing to the currency's defence as they have done for much of the year.

The won is Asia's worst-performing currency this year and has slumped as the economy, heavily reliant on imports of commodities, felt the full brunt of soaring prices for raw materials and food.

The currency began rebounding on Wednesday after traders reported the first dollar sales from authorities in more than a week, and extended gains on Thursday after another bout of intervention was spotted.

The won <KRW=> was quoted up 1.8 percent at 1,128.0 per dollar at 0714 GMT, its biggest daily percentage gain since early July, up from around 1,148 earlier in the day. Wednesday's domestic close was 1,148.5 per dollar.

NO SYSTEMIC RISKS

Currency dealers declined to estimate how much authorities had spent on the intervention and central bank governor, Lee Seong-tae, also declined to comment in parliament when asked about the intervention reports.

South Korea's finance ministry is in charge of foreign exchange policy, including intervention in currency markets. The central bank usually conducts the buying or selling.

Analysts, including those polled by Reuters on Wednesday, forecast more won weakness this year, although many said comparisons to the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis were overblown.

"While we retain the view that fundamentals are aligned for won weakness, speculative fervour surrounding recent moves appear stretched," JPMorgan Chase said in a note to clients.

In addition, analysts said the $7 billion in bonds that mature next week did not pose a risk to the country's financial system, even if foreign holders repatriate the proceeds.

In fact, foreign investors turned net buyers of domestic bonds in August after being sellers the previous two months, data from the country's main securities industry association show.

"All the data shows that we have no systemic risk in the financial sector," Rhee Chang-yong, deputy chairman of the Financial Services Commission, told Reuters in an interview.

Governor Lee dismissed talk of crisis, saying South Korea was not confronting problems more serious than those facing many other countries.

In a report to parliament, he said sluggish domestic demand will drag on the economy but strong exports will keep the slowdown modest while inflation should start to ease by the end of the year.

The current account, which has slipped into deficit as commodities prices soared, should also improve with the help of falling raw materials prices.

Putting a brave face on the turmoil, the government said it would next week meet investors to sell around $1 billion in government bonds, its first sovereign offering in two years.

Still, the mere mention of a capital flight from the bond market has touched a nerve in South Korea, stirring memories of the financial crisis a decade ago when foreign investors dumped assets across Asia.

ANCHOR OF STABILITY

Its timing could not have been worse either. South Korea is about to run its first annual current account deficit since that crisis. Foreign selling of Korean stocks is at a record this year.

Analysts polled by Reuters on Wednesday expect the won to fall another 4.3 percent before recovering in the fourth quarter.

Goldman Sachs economist Goohoon Kwon said the won may be rising under its own steam rather than intervention, adding holders of dollars appear to have already taken profits against the won while there is no further large dollar demand from Korean corporates.

South Korea's foreign exchange reserves are the world's sixth largest at $243 billion and have served as an anchor of financial stability since the Asian financial crisis.

Authorities have spent an estimated $30 billion this year to support the won, but moved to the sidelines last month, firing market speculation they were unwilling or unable to defend the currency. Instead, authorities tried to talk up the currency.

They plan to scrap the ceiling on the amount of dollar/won non-deliverable forward sales each bank can take from customers, an official from the foreign exchange authorities told Reuters on Thursday, speaking on the customary condition of anonymity.

The move would buy little in the way of immediate support for the won, analysts said.

"Foreign appetite to be short dollar/won NDFs is already low, so allowing them to do so does not change the overall sentiment, which remains to be long dollar/won," said Yen Ping Ho, a strategist at JPMorgan Chase. (Additional reporting Vidya Ranganathan in Singapore and Rafael Nam in Hong Kong, Writing by Dayan Candappa, Editing by Neil Fullick)
