title: CORRECTED - CORRECTED-S.Korea won at 4-yr low despite warning
text:
(Corrects story to make clear the intervention was minor and a regular market smoothing operation by the central bank and that some dealers said they had not detected such sales)

SEOUL, Sept 2 (Reuters) - The South Korean won fell 1.6 percent to hit a nearly four-year low against the dollar on Tuesday, despite official warnings of stern measures in the currency market.

Some dealers said the authorities were seen selling a small amount of dollars, but this was seen as a regular market smoothing operation rather than an attempt to affect currency levels.

The reported dollar-selling, which other dealers said they had not detected, was too weak anyhow to absorb dollar bids from importers and foreign investors who kept selling Seoul shares with the local stock hitting a 18-month low.

The won <KRW=> is expected to slide further, despite possible intervention by the authorities, on lingering concerns over capital outflow from the country and a slowdown in Asia's fourth-largest economy, analysts said.

"It is a matter of time for the won to weaken to 1,140 (per dollar) and it may fall further to 1,200. Some expect the won to rebound once concerns over the September financial crisis get resolved, but even after that, we will still have bearish factors such as global credit crunch and economic slowdown," said Jeong My-young, an analyst at Samsung Futures Inc.

The authorities have few other options but to resume massive dollar-selling intervention to prop up the won, but then that could fuel concerns about foreign exchange reserves, she added.

Dollar-selling intervention usually results in lower foreign exchange reserves. South Korea's foreign exchange reserves fell $4.32 billion in August after suffering a record loss in the previous month, central bank data showed earlier.

The South Korean currency was quoted at 1,133.4/4.1 per dollar as of 0600 GMT, compared with Monday's domestic close of 1,116 <KRW=KFTC>.

The won fell to as low as 1,133.9, the weakest since Oct. 26, 2004, just before the local market closed.

Earlier, it rose to as high as 1,108.3 after Vice Finance Minister Kim Dong-soo said the country had both the will and the ability to deal with one-way bets against the won, and called for calm a day after local financial markets tumbled on fears of massive capital flight out of the country. [ID:nSEO66739]

Investors have been worried that a huge amount of domestic bonds coming due next week would spur capital outflows.

South Korean shares <.KS11> ended at their lowest close in 18 months as foreign investors sold a net 264.1 billion won worth of stocks in the country's main exchange.

They unloaded a combined net 2.26 trillion won during the previous 10 consecutive sessions.

title: South Korean won rises on stocks, exporter deals
text:
(Updates to domestic close)

SEOUL, Aug 6 (Reuters) - The South Korean won rose against the dollar on Wednesday as domestic stocks jumped after the U.S. Federal Reserve signalled it would not rush to raise interest rates, and was helped further by exporter demand for settlements.

The won <KRW=> also found support from softer oil prices and as investors remained wary of possible dollar-selling intervention by South Korea's foreign exchange authorities.

However, the local currency is unlikely to rise further as foreign investors kept selling Seoul shares and concerns persist over a slowdown in Asia's fourth-largest economy amid higher inflation, analysts said.

"Despite various bullish factors, the won's gains were limited. I do not expect U.S. stocks to rise further due to lingering worries about the economy. That will push down shares here and the won," said Lee Tark-koo, a currency analyst at KB Futures Co Ltd.

The South Korean unit was quoted at 1,015.7/6.0 per dollar as of 0600 GMT, compared to Tuesday's local close of 1,017.9 <KRW=KFTC>.

Seoul shares <.KS11> ended up 2.81 percent after the Fed held U.S. interest rates steady on Tuesday, expressing concerns about both economic growth and inflation and indicating it was in no rush to push borrowing costs higher.

But foreign investors sold a net 42 billion won worth of shares in South Korea's main exchange after unloading a combined net 784.3 billion won during the previous three consecutive sessions.

Investors are keeping an eye on the South Korean central bank's monetary policy meeting on Thursday, when the Bank of Korea is expected to raise interest rates to a 7-½ year high to tackle inflation.

Oil fell further on Wednesday in Asia to stay around a three-month low as concerns over a weak U.S. economy continued to weigh on demand.

title: UPDATE 2-S.Korea sells dollars after biggest fall in reserves
text:
(Updates with intervention, more analysts, agencies, markets)

SEOUL, Aug 4 (Reuters) - South Korea's foreign exchange reserves suffered their biggest-ever monthly drop in July, when the authorities reportedly spent some $15 billion propping up the won, using the currency as their main tool to fight inflation.

Traders said the authorities sold an estimated $300 million on Monday to further support the won, demonstrating a preference for a firmer currency despite the sharp fall in reserves.

Asia's fourth-largest economy is expected to keep bolstering the currency <KRW=> to tackle imported inflation, but intervention is unlikely to be as strong as in July due to weaker oil prices and a slowing economy, analysts said.

"As oil prices fell from July, the burden of inflation on the government has been eased," said Kim Jae-eun, an economist at Hana Daetoo Securities. "The authorities will not reverse the market trend of a weaker won although they will slow down the speed of the unit's fall."

Oil prices <CLc1> hovered just below $126 a barrel on Monday, much lower than the record high of $147.27 in July.

Monday's intervention was small compared with money market operations in July, when the authorities spent an estimated $5 billion on one day itself to support the ailing local currency.

Before local financial markets opened on Monday, the Bank of Korea said the country's foreign reserves fell $10.58 billion to $247.52 billion by the end of July from a month earlier, citing "efforts aimed at stabilising the foreign exchange market".

It was the biggest monthly decline since the central bank started compiling foreign reserves figures in 1971.

The sharp fall in reserves heightened concerns South Korea could be confronted with an economic crisis similar to the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis, and raised expectations the authorities might intervene less, losing their grip on the won.

But senior officials at two of the world's top credit rating agencies told Reuters that there was no problem with the country's external payment capability despite the drop. [ID:nSEO256291]

NO CHANGE IN FX POLICY

A senior foreign exchange official also told Reuters the authorities saw no reason to change their policy of defending the local currency as one of the main tools to contain inflation.

"The authorities will consider falls in foreign exchange reserves when we manage currency policies, but there is no reason for falls to change the policies," said the official, who declined to be name.

He added that concerns over the drop in reserves had been misplaced.

The remarks, along with actual dollar-selling intervention, helped the won limit its falls, but could not prevent the currency from shedding 0.26 percent against the dollar during the local session.

Analysts agreed with the rating agencies' assessment, saying South Korea's overall external payment capability remained strong.

"The authorities have sufficient ammunition. The reserves' fall in July was smaller than expected, which indicates they have not only the reserves but also other means for intervention," said Lee Tark-koo, a currency analyst at KB Futures Co Ltd.

July's intervention helped lift the won by almost 4 percent against the dollar for the month. The currency had fallen 11 percent for the January-June period.

The authorities were also seen reducing their long-positions on dollar non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) and using dollar sell and buy swaps; selling dollar spots on certain days and later buying dollar futures.

The central bank did not provide the exact number of dollars it and the Finance Ministry sold during the month as they tried to prevent the sliding won from exacerbating high inflation, which has been led by imported commodities.

"We intervened in the market last month to correct mounting speculative trades, but the market usually overstates the intervention size," a Bank of Korea official, who declined to be named, said by telephone without giving the exact value.

But it was unusual for the South Korean central bank, which also attributed some of the decline to losses in dollar terms from non-dollar assets, to admit currency intervention.

Consumer-price inflation climbed to a near 10-year high of 5.9 percent in July, up from 5.5 percent in June.

South Korean authorities are worried accelerating inflation will cut the disposable income of consumers at a time when a slump in domestic demand is expected to dent growth this year. (Additional reporting by Yoo Choonsik and Lee Shin-hyung, Editing by Jonathan Hopfner and Jacqueline Wong)

title: ANALYSIS-S.Korea in high-stakes policy game with won battle
text:
SINGAPORE/SEOUL, July 11 (Reuters) - For all their talk of free markets, the South Korean authorities left investors in no doubt this week about who should control their currency, the won.

Using 5 percent of Korea's huge pile of foreign reserves, the Bank of Korea relentlessly pounded markets, selling dollars and pushing the won up 5 percent to what it regards as an appropriate level to fight imported inflation, near 1,000 per dollar.

By Friday, the bears had backed off and the authorities appeared to have won the first battle hands down.

The won <KRW=KFTC> was steady, just on the weaker side of 1,000 per dollar at 1,002.20/30.

"Perhaps the range on dollar/won is 980-1,025 multi-week rather than 1,015-1,060," said Westpac Bank's Sean Callow, the latter range being what investors had previously expected.

But analysts are worried. By using force to strengthen the won and deferring interest rate rises, the authorities may find themselves caught in a prolonged war as they fight against deteriorating economic fundamentals, a loss of confidence in the economy and damage to their inflation-fighting credibility.

An immediate risk is that they will have to keep expending their currency reserves to defend that line in the sand until all the speculators concede defeat.

ING economist Tim Condon said that if South Koreans began to doubt the authorities could win, they would hedge against their exposure. "Currency depreciation then becomes self-reinforcing."

South Korea can easily afford the intervention, with the world's sixth-largest stockpile of reserves at $258 billion.

What it probably cannot afford is the damage this policy gamble does to its reputation as an inflation-fighting central bank committed to liberal markets.

"They can hold the fort for the third quarter," said JPMorgan Chase strategist Claudio Piron.

"But the won intervention could build problems later on as the credibility gap widens," he added, interpreting comments by the central bank governor after a policy meeting on Thursday as being dovish on interest rates.

"It seems like the targeting of the foreign exchange rate may conflict with the Bank of Korea's mandate to establish price stability with interest rate policy."

NO OPTION?

But what if the Bank of Korea was left with no choice but to intervene on the won?

Market participants are not discounting the possibility that Korea's presidential Blue House has seized the monetary policy reins, eager to shore up the economy after conceding growth would probably be far lower than the lofty levels promised by President Lee Myung-bak before his landslide election victory in December.

This week the central bank left its policy rate unchanged for the eleventh month in a row, even though annual inflation at 5.5 percent is above the 5 percent base rate.

Placing the onus entirely on the currency is dangerous.

"If the intervention policy fails, the country could face an economic crisis, although the chances are not big," said Lee Tark-koo, a currency analyst at Kookmin Futures.

"The won will probably drop sharply when the authorities lose the game; that will boost inflation and interest rates, and in turn prompt foreign investors to sell local bonds, which again will push up interest rates and the debt burden on households."

In the longer term, the won will remain under pressure from a rising oil import bill and a falling stock market.

South Korea's current account could be in deficit in 2008 for the first time in 11 years and the country could soon be a net borrower from external markets for the first time in eight years.

Short-term external debt stood at $176.5 billion, or 67 percent of the total foreign exchange reserves, at the end of March, the highest ratio since the end of March 1999.

Raising interest rates carries its own risks. Besides hurting borrowers, it could spur businesses to access cheaper foreign money, potentially setting the country up for short-term debt problems of the kind that triggered the 1997/98 financial crisis.

A rate rise could rein in bank lending, which is expanding at a worrying pace of over 15 percent, far higher than the nominal economic growth rate. At the same time, a bigger interest burden could spell danger for over-leveraged banks and consumers, and risk a downgrade for the A-rated economy.

KEEPING FOREIGNERS SWEET

ING's Condon believes investor confidence is as important a factor as fundamentals in deciding the won's trajectory.

Having changed tack on their earlier preference for a weak won to help exporters, South Korea's game plan now, he reckons, is to ensure the economy remains attractive to foreigners.

Economic growth and strong corporate earnings then become as important as price stability in terms of policy objectives, which makes a strong won and steady interest rates an ideal policy mix.

"Korea is a nation of risk takers," said Condon, reckoning the country had the capacity to carry huge debt and run a current account deficit. "The pressure on the authorities is to maintain an attractive environment for investment." So far, the plan is working, and intervention seems to have steadied the won, which at its weakest point this month had shed 10 percent of its value against the dollar in just six months.

"At least, Korea's current intervention is consistent with keeping a tight monetary policy, whereas in 2005-2007 they were trying to weaken the won even as they hiked rates," said Westpac's Callow. (For a factbox on recent intervention click [ID:nSEO7888]) (Editing by Alan Raybould)

title: INTERVIEW-S&P sceptical S.Korea  FX intervention  will work
text:
SEOUL, July 8 (Reuters) - South Korea's decision this week to step up dollar-selling intervention to defend the won was probably politically motivated, and its effect is very questionable, an S&P official told Reuters on Tuesday.

South Korea had better raise interest rates as a means to contain inflation because the dollar-selling policy could only provide traders with chances to increase their sales of the won <KRW=>, he said in an interview.

"It's impossible to resist the market force for a long period of time, because the size of the international money, either for speculation or investment, is much much bigger than the foreign currency reserves can withstand," said Takahira Ogawa, director of sovereign ratings at Standard & Poor's.

The comments came hours after dealers reported the South Korean authorities had sold up to an estimated $2 billion to prop up the won to cushion imported inflation. The won ended local trade up 1 percent on the day on Tuesday.

"The result of (the intervention), the effectiveness of that is very questionable," Singapore-based Ogawa said while visiting Seoul for a seminar.

Analysts were also sceptical South Korea, which had already drawn some $10 billion this year on its nearly $260 billion foreign reserves to defend its currency, had slim chances of winning the game against the market.

"Both the government and the Bank of Korea need to be very careful because if they send a wrong signal to the market, then (investors) may take this as an advantage to sell the Korean won further because the government and the central bank are buying," Ogawa said.

The won had fallen 10 percent against the dollar this year until Monday, dragged down by expectations that the country's current account will swing into the first annual deficit in 11 years and by the increasing demand for dollars to buy oil.

The weakening won has contributed significantly to pushing up the country's annual consumer-price inflation to a near 10-year high of 5.5 percent in June.

"I suspect this (was) a politically motivated decision. Politics is irrational. So in one sense, even knowing the negative implication, they may have to choose this," he said.

When asked whether South Korea should have raised interest rates instead of using the intervention policy, he agreed: "I think (that's) more orthodox."

The Bank of Korea has held the policy interest rate steady at 5.0 percent for the past 10 months in the face of conflicting risks from high inflation and slow economic growth, and is widely expected to keep the rate unchanged again on Thursday. (Editing by Gerrard Raven)

title: Emerging  FX -Asia rangebound; c.banks shore up won, rupiah
text:
SINGAPORE, July 8 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies moved in tight ranges on Tuesday with investor sentiment torn between falling oil prices and renewed credit fears, while authorities in South Korea and Indonesia intervened to prop up their currencies.

 The won <KRW=> hit a two-week high at 1,025.3 per dollar, up 1.7 percent from Monday's domestic close of 1,042.9, as dealers said authorities sold up to $2 billion to boost the local unit.

 Meanwhile, traders also cited dollar-intervention by Indonesia's central bank to try to support the rupiah <IDR=>.

 "Bank Indonesia is still on the offer side," said a trader in Jakarta. "It seems that they are trying to push the dollar below 9,200."

 A second trader said the central bank's intervention was aimed at keeping the rupiah in tight ranges.

 The intervention pushed the rupiah <IDR=> as high as 9,190 per dollar before it edged back to around 9,205.

 The currency has gained about 1 percent against the dollar in the past month, benefiting from the central bank's three successive interest rate rises since early May, which took the benchmark rate to 8.75 percent, among the highest in Asia.

 Standard Chartered expects the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> to trade near 9,200 per dollar at the end of September before rising to 9,150 by the end of 2008, analysts at the bank said in a note, raising their forecast from 9,250 and 9,200, respectively.

 "Bank Indonesia is committed to raise interest rates gradually which should mitigate capital outflows," the analysts said, adding that the rupiah could hit 9,100 by end-March 2009 and 9,000 by end-June.

 Several authorities in Asia have been intervening regularly in recent months to support their currencies as part of efforts to cushion rising import prices from the likes of surging oil.

 WEAKER PESO

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> pulled back to 45.88 per dollar, down a third of a percent from Monday's close to its weakness level since September, after briefly hitting as high as 45.63.

 Traders said buying interest in the peso was undermined by concerns about high oil prices and the global credit crisis.

 "The bullish sentiment (on the dollar versus the peso) is still intact, it seems a test of the 46 level is just around the corner," said a trader in Manila.

 A second trader added: "Oil prices are still above $140 and (domestic) inflation is getting higher and higher."

 Oil prices <CLc1> held largely steady on Tuesday after dropping close to $4 on Monday, backing off last week's record high of $145.85.

 On Monday, a Lehman Brothers report said a pending accounting change could force Fannie Mae  and Freddie Mac , the top U.S. mortgage funders, to raise a combined $75 billion in capital at a tough time. [ID:nN07435475]

 Elsewhere, the Pakistani rupee was 2.9 percent weaker at a record low of 73 to the dollar <PKR=PK> because of worries about inflation, widening current and budget account deficits and security, dealers said.

 The rupee had closed at 71.00/05 to the dollar on Monday.

 The rupee has lost more than 18 percent against the dollar this year as annual inflation accelerated to a three-decade high of 19.27 percent in May and fiscal and current account deficits widened.  CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: WRAPUP 2-S.Korea gears up for  currency  fight, sells $5 bln
text:
(Updates with central bank comments)

SEOUL, July 9 (Reuters) - South Korea geared up for a fight with the currency market, warning on Wednesday it would not let the won weaken beyond 1,000 per dollar after its biggest one-day sale of dollars on record.

Dealers estimated South Korea dumped around $5 billion on the foreign exchange market on Wednesday alone, propelling the won to its strongest intraday rise in a decade as part of a strategy to prevent the weakness seen in the currency so far this year from fuelling inflation.

A senior central bank official said after the intervention that authorities would not allow the won to weaken beyond 1,000 per dollar.

The currency fell 10.5 percent against the U.S. currency in the first half of the year, exacerbating the impact on domestic inflation of rising imports costs for oil and other raw materials.

"The won can't be said to be at a 'balanced level' when it is traded at a four-digit rate per dollar," Rhee Gwang-ju, a deputy governor at the Bank of Korea, told Reuters in a telephone interview.

"(The authorities) have no reason to intervene even if the won strengthens to a three-digit rate."

Dealers estimate that South Korean authorities have now sold about $17 billion this year to prop up the won, which has ranged between 1,057 per dollar and 930 per dollar so far in 2008.

Dollar-selling intervention aimed at offsetting imported inflation has persuaded economists that the Bank of Korea will refrain from raising rates when it meets on Thursday and will instead keep them on hold for the 11th consecutive month.

BIGGEST ONE-DAY GAIN IN DECADE

The won rose as much as 3.7 percent on the day, its biggest intraday gain against the dollar since March 23, 1998, as dealers reported the authorities sold dollars for won right after an official issued a fresh warning against betting on a weaker unit.

The surge in the won <KRW=> <KRW=KFTC> sent bond futures prices sharply higher as traders became more convinced monetary authorities would stick to using the currency as its main tool to rein in inflation, rather than interest rates.

The won rose to as high as 996.0 per dollar, the strongest bid since 991.75 on April 29, helping to drive September treasury bond futures <KTBc1> up by as much as 38 ticks on the day.

But concern a stronger won will reduce the country's exports potential hit share prices in electronics makers. The sector's index <.KS41> fell 2.65 percent.

The reported dollar sales came right after a foreign exchange official warned against those who doubt South Korea's capability to dominate what they call speculative traders.

"Efforts by the government and the Bank of Korea to stabilise the foreign exchange rate don't stop here," said the official, who declined to be identified.

Central bank data backs up an estimate by dealers that South Korea has drawn down billions of dollars for intervention from its foreign currency reserves, a war chest amounting to nearly $260 billion.

IMPACT ON EXPORTERS

South Korea's annual consumer inflation hit a near 10-year high of 5.5 percent in June and producer inflation data released on Wednesday indicated there was further inflationary pressure in the pipeline.

The producer price index grew 10.5 percent in June over a year earlier, the fastest annual gain since November 1998, data from the central bank showed.

For a graphic on South Korean inflation data, click: https://customers.reuters.com/d/graphics/KR_PPI0708.gif("https://customers.reuters.com/d/graphics/KR_PPI0708.gif")

Reflecting pressure on the won, the government expects the country to record its first trade deficit this year since the 1997 Asian financial crisis because of the rising cost of imports.

But the falling share prices of Samsung Electronics and other electronics makers in response to the won's jump underscored how easily a policy can damage another part of Asia's fourth-largest economy.

The foreign exchange intervention came just hours after senior officials from the government, central bank and financial regulator held a hastily arranged meeting and called on stock investors not to panic.

"The government has (treated) the major economic problems facing Korea with a succession of short-term band-aid solutions that haven't amounted to much at all," said Daniel Melser, an economist at Moody's Economy.com.

"The lack of a consistent and cohesive approach to macroeconomic policy has eroded confidence in the administration and the country," he added. SEOUL, July 7 (Reuters) - South Korea's finance ministry and central bank warned on Monday they would carry out strong concerted intervention in the local currency market if necessary to support the won and cushion imported inflation.

Following are key remarks in the joint statement from the Ministry of Strategy and Finance and the Bank of Korea and their separate news conferences, translated and compiled by Reuters:

STATEMENT

"The government and the Bank of Korea are of the same opinion that stabilising the foreign exchange market was necessary and agreed to aggressively take concerted action toward it."

"The foreign exchange authorities are worried about a herd behaviour in the foreign exchange market and believe it is most desirable for such a phenomenon to be resolved by itself in the market."

"The authorities will closely watch trends in foreign exchange supply and demand and in the foreign exchange rates, and will take strong measures if there are excessive imbalances."

CHOI JONG-KU, DIRECTOR-GENERAL, INTERNATIONAL FINANCE BUREAU, MINISTRY OF STRATEGY AND FINANCE

"The authorities will use foreign exchange reserves if necessary to stabilise the foreign exchange market."

"The most important thing at this moment is price stability. Foreign exchange policy has to be managed toward it."

"We have foreign exchange reserves sufficient to stabilise the foreign exchange market."

"We are also looking for ways to stabilise the foreign exchange market without using foreign exchange reserves."

AHN BYUNG-CHAN, DIRECTOR, INTERNATIONAL DEPARTMENT, BANK OF KOREA

"The dollar/won rate had no reason to rise this much if not for psychological factors betting on the pair's rise."

"I believe market players are well aware (of the fair level for the won)."

"I don't see any side-effects (from strong intervention) because the market will get stabilised if the sentiment for stronger dollar/won is removed." (Reporting by Cheon Jong-woo, Lee Jin-joo, Yoo Choonsik; Editing by Keiron Henderson)

title: RPT-POLL-South Korea June inflation seen at near 10-yr high
text:
(This is a repeat of an earlier story ahead of Tuesday's data release)

* What: South Korea's June consumer price index

* When: Tuesday, July 1, at 1:30 p.m. (0430 GMT)

* Annual consumer inflation seen at near decade high in June

By Lee Jin-joo

SEOUL, June 27 (Reuters) - South Korea's annual consumer inflation is seen hitting a near decade-high in June, fuelled by high oil prices and a weaker won <KRW=> despite government efforts to boost the local currency, a poll showed on Friday.

The median forecast of economists polled by Reuters was for the consumer price index in June to rise 5.4 percent from a year earlier, compared with a 4.9 percent rise in May.

The forecast for June marks the strongest growth since consumer prices rose 6.8 percent in November 1998, and breaches the central bank's target range of 2.5-3.5 percent for the seventh consecutive month.

The median forecast of economists was for the CPI to rise a non-seasonally adjusted 0.5 percent in June from a month earlier, lower than 0.8 percent in May, although investors generally look to the annual rate as the key inflation gauge.

"Despite the government's efforts to abandon its previous stance of a softer local currency and boost the won's strength to stabilise inflation, the won is staying at a low level due to global credit woes while oil prices are staying at record highs," said Kim Jong-su, economist at NH Investment and Securities.

South Korea's financial authorities intervened in currency markets to strengthen the won earlier this month to contain soaring import costs.

A weaker currency usually exacerbates inflation by effectively making imported oil and raw materials even more expensive.

Industrial goods, including oil products, contribute 34 percent to South Korea's consumer inflation, according to data from the statistics agency.

"Inflation risks remain, but the government won't be able to keep up efforts to boost the won if the country's trade balance continues to post deficits," said Cheon Min-kyu, economist at Korea Investment and Securities.

South Korea's trade balance has remained in the red for all but one month since December last year due to higher raw material prices.

Swelling inflation pressure amid downside risks from a slowdown in the global economy also has the Bank of Korea caught between a rock and a hard place.

The central bank held interest rates steady for the 10th consecutive month at 5.00 percent in June, after raising them by a quarter percentage point each in July and August 2007.

title: UPDATE 4-S.Korea May c/a deficit dents inflation fight
text:
(Adds value of intervention in paragraphs 3, 12, 13)

SEOUL, June 27 (Reuters) - South Korea's current account swung to a deficit in May on the back of soaring oil prices, the third monthly gap this year which could undermine the already weak local currency and add to inflationary pressures.

South Korea's current account produced a seasonally adjusted $1 billion deficit in May after a revised $2.73 billion surplus in April, central bank data showed on Friday.

The won <KRW=> <KRW=KFTC> fell more than 1 percent to a 1-month low of 1,048.0 per dollar as record high oil prices heralded more current account pressure, before bouncing back sharply when authorities sold $1 billion to support the currency.

Analysts said South Korea's current account in the rest of the year would largely be shaped by global prices for oil and other raw materials, almost all of which are imported by Asia's fourth-largest economy.

"Our view is that the current account will show a surplus for the second half of the year, but this is on the assumption that oil prices don't rise much from the current level," said Lim Ji-won, an economist at JPMorgan Chase.

In the first five months of the year, South Korea recorded a seasonally adjusted current account deficit of $1.89 billion, compared with a $2.74 billion surplus for the same period in 2007, the Bank of Korea said.

For a graphic on the current account figures, click here: https://customers.reuters.com/d/graphics/KR_CURAC0608.gif("https://customers.reuters.com/d/graphics/KR_CURAC0608.gif")

A central bank official told reporters almost all of the $7.17 billion unadjusted January-May current account deficit was a result of soaring oil prices.

U.S. crude oil <CLc1> has jumped 46 percent this year, reaching a record above $140 a barrel on Thursday.

REGULAR CURRENCY INTERVENTION

The current account figures added to the selling pressure on the won, which has lost about 10 percent so far this year against the dollar.

The won's weakness, which exacerbates price pressures by making imports more expensive, comes at a time when the country is already grappling with high inflation led by skyrocketing commodities prices.

The won ended local trade down half a percent on the day at 1,041.5 per dollar, having briefly recovered to positive territory after the reported dollar-selling intervention, estimated by three dealers at up to $1 billion.

Friday marks the third day of reported dollar selling to prop up the local currency by South Korean authorities in less than two weeks, selling as much as $3 billion over the period,

according to estimates by dealers.

The Bank of Korea forecast late last year that the country would post a current account deficit of $3 billion this year for the first time in 11 years, but has recently said the shortfall could be bigger due to higher oil prices.

South Korea's young government under President Lee Myung-bak has recently shifted its economic policy goal from lifting economic growth sharply above market expectations to fighting inflation, which is running at a seven-year high of 4.9 percent.

The finance ministry has said it expects annual inflation to pass the 5 percent mark this month.

Friday's data also showed that South Korea's overseas borrowing fell by a net $4.77 billion in May after a net drop of $0.18 billion in April.

International credit rating agencies have expressed concerns about a jump in South Korea's short-term external debt in recent years, led by banks to fund robust lending and dollar forward deals at home.

The rupee <INR=IN> hit a two-week high of 42.782 per dollar after India's central bank raised its lending rate to its highest in six years and increased banks' reserve requirements. [ID:nBOM196971].

One rupee trader in Singapore said the rise in India's call money rates made it more expensive to hold dollars, and foreigners were also buying Indian debt.

"Nine percent yield is good enough yield and that, too, with this level of dollar/rupee," he said.

But most analysts remain bearish on the rupee, one of Asia's worst performers with a drop of 8 percent versus the dollar this year, just behind the Korean won's fall of nearly 10 percent.

"Given India's increasing current account deficit, high dependence on oil imports and inflationary concerns, we expect the rupee to continue to weaken," analysts at Goldman Sachs said in a note.

Goldman expects it to fall to 43.9 per dollar, then 44.1 before rebounding to 42.2 in three, six and 12 months' time respectively.

WAIT AND SEE

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> gained a fifth of a percent to 30.377 per U.S. dollar ahead of a policy review by the central bank, which is expected to raise interest rates on Thursday by another 12.5 basis points at least to tackle inflation.

The Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> inched up to a post-revaluation high of 6.8655 per dollar, but it was less than a tenth of a percent stronger than Tuesday's close at 6.8699.

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> was shackled between 1.3672 and 1.3690 per U.S. dollar, while the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> traded within a narrow range of 3.2535 and 3.2660 per dollar.

"The market seems in a wait-and-see mode ahead of the FOMC decision," said Christy Tan, a currency strategist at Bank of America, referring to the Fed's policy committee.

The Fed is widely expected to hold interest rates steady but investors will scrutinise the statement accompanying its decision for clues on the future course of monetary policy.

It is facing a dilemma, since increasing borrowing costs to quell inflation would put a further brake on the weak economy.

The Thai baht <THB=TH> fell to a six-month low of 33.60 per dollar as political tensions weighed on the unit.

Thai Prime Minister Samak Sundaravej's office remains under siege from hundreds of protesters and the opposition has launched a no-confidence motion against his five-month-old coalition, although the move is largely symbolic. [ID:nBKK149866].

text:

SEOUL, June 11 (Reuters) - The South Korean won slid against the dollar on Wednesday as foreign investors continued to sell domestic shares and following comments from U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke on inflation.

Investors remained cautious over possible dollar-selling intervention by South Korea to check inflation, but the authorities were not spotted of selling the U.S. currency.

The local unit is expected to remain under pressure as fears of inflation are likely to prevent investors from buying riskier assets although the government will step in to curb its sharp falls, analysts said.

"Globally, all investors are concerned over inflation amid weak economic growth and their appetite for riskier assets is getting weaker," said Lee Tark-koo, a currency analyst at KB Futures Co Ltd.

"The won may rebound a bit when the authorities take measures, but its falling trend is intact," he added.

The won <KRW=> was quoted at 1,029.75/30.25 per dollar as of 0600 GMT, compared to its previous domestic closing bid of 1,025.3.

The South Korean currency strengthened to as high as 1,022.8, helped by demand from exporters for settlements, which looked like the government's intervention.

"Sudden dollar sales caused market players to suspect intervention, but they were exporter deals," said a foreign bank dealer.

On Tuesday, the local currency jumped on suspected government intervention, which came after data showed annual producer price inflation in May hit a near 10-year high led by energy prices.

Finance Minister Kang Man-soo said on Wednesday that the government, faced with slowing domestic demand and high inflation, would focus on stabilising the economy, a local news website reported. [ID:nSEO327566]

Foreign investors sold a net 294.1 billion won worth of shares in South Korea's main stock market after dumping a combined 437 billion won during the previous two sessions.

Investors are keeping an eye on South Korea's central bank's interest rate setting meeting on Thursday.

title: UPDATE 2-S.Korea leader warns of resource crisis
text:
(Recasts with producer inflation, details, markets)

SEOUL, June 10 (Reuters) - South Korea's president warned on Tuesday that the country faced a "resource crisis", comments underlined by data showing that producer inflation shot to it highest level since the Asia financial crisis a decade ago.

Bond prices fell and the won rose as financial markets saw the comments and data as raising pressure on the central bank to tighten monetary policy when it reviews interest rates on Thursday.

The firmer currency also reflected the market view that authorities might allow the won to appreciate to offset the impact of rising imports costs as raw materials prices shoot higher globally.

"International crude oil prices have doubled over a year and grains and raw materials prices are also rising sharply. Accordingly, our economy is faced with a serious difficulty, with prices rising and the economy gradually slowing," President Lee Myung-bak said.

"We are faced with a 'resources crisis' coming next only to the oil crisis in the 1970s and the financial crisis in the 1990s," he said in a speech at a ceremony to mark the 21st anniversary of a pro-democracy protest rally.

After his comments, the central bank said its producer price index in May rose 11.6 percent over a year earlier, the highest annual growth since an 11.7 percent gain in October 1998 and up sharply from a 9.7 percent gain in April.

That suggested more price pressure in the pipeline for consumer inflation, already running at a 7-year high close to 5 percent, in Asia's fourth-biggest economy.

The data came shortly after Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke said the U.S. central bank would resist rising inflation, which weighed on bond prices globally as investors factored in the chance of a U.S. rate rise. [ID:nN09303720]

The Bank of Korea holds a policy meeting on Thursday. It has held its key rate steady at 5.0 percent for the past nine consecutive months, after raising it by a combined 1.75 percentage points since October 2005.

CABINET OFFERS TO RESIGN

June treasury bond futures <KTBc1> tumbled to 5 month lows. Futures fell as much as 43 ticks to 105.67, the lowest since the then front-end contract hit 105.51 on Jan. 10.

The won <KRW=> rose to 1,021 per dollar from Monday's domestic close of 1,031.25, partly helped by suspected central bank intervention. Stocks <.KS11> tumbled 2 percent.

South Korea relies almost wholly on imports of most energy, food and raw materials supplies, making it especially vulnerable to current skyrocketing prices around the world.

A labour union representing 13,000 truckers and transport workers voted on Monday to strike over high oil prices, threatening to halt much of the transportation of export cargoes to ports.

The vote came despite a government announcement on Sunday of a $10.2 billion package to help the poor, small businesses and truckers to cope with rising energy bills.

Lee, who swept to office on a high economic growth policy, also faces mounting pressure over his handling of opposition to sensitive beef imports from the United States.

Prime Minister Han Seung-soo and the other members of the country's three months-old cabinet offered to resign early on Tuesday after massive street protests sparked by an unpopular deal to open the market wider to U.S. beef imports.

South Korea's annual consumer price inflation shot up to a 7-year high of 4.9 percent in May, and the finance ministry is widely expected to lower this year's economic growth target, set at 6 percent, next month.

The Bank of Korea's chief said last month the country's economy would be lucky if it could achieve growth of 4.5 percent, having expanded 5 percent last year and 5.1 percent in 2006.

President Lee won December's election with a pledge to lift economic growth sharply but has seen his approval rating dive to 20 percent after his first 100 days in office. (Additional reporting by Rhee So-eui, Editing by Keiron Henderson and Neil Fullick)

title: UPDATE 2-S.Korea spends nearly $2 bln to prop up ailing won
text:
(Recasts with fresh intervention, economist, markets)

SEOUL, May 27 (Reuters) - South Korea intervened three times to support the sliding won on Tuesday and warned the currency may have fallen too far, as it wrestled with the problem of containing inflation without choking off economic growth.

The Bank of Korea is under political pressure to cut rates to help spur growth in Asia's fourth-largest economy, and minutes from an April policy review showed two of the six board members favoured a rate cut for the first time since November 2004.

The central bank is resisting that pressure because inflation is at a four-year high, partly due to a surge in oil prices and won weakness, which is making imports more expensive.

The currency, Asia's second-worst performer this year, may have fallen too far, Choi Jong-ku, head of the finance ministry's international bureau, told Reuters as news of the interventions began surfacing and pushed the won to a one-week high.

The foreign exchange authorities were seen selling almost $1 billion on Tuesday afternoon for won after dumping up to $800 million during the morning session, traders said.

The won's rise on Tuesday revived expectations among investors that the central bank would have more room to cut interest rates at its next review on June 12.

Others said the Bank of Korea, hemmed in between rising inflation and the wishes of a growth-hungry new government, would want to avoid cutting rates for fear of stoking inflation.

"The Bank of Korea's governor implied at his post-meeting comments in May that as long as the won turns weaker, it would be impossible for an interest rate cut in the near future," said Park Jong-yeon, fixed-income analyst at Woori Investment.

Annual inflation at 4.1 percent in April was above the central bank's 2.5 percent to 3.5 percent target range for a fifth straight month.

"The won fell as oil prices jumped but we are worried that the won's fall might be excessive," Choi told Reuters.

He also said the government was worried the won's fall was due to excessive herd behaviour in the currency market.

The intervention on Tuesday marks the second attempt to shore up the won in under a week. That pushed up the won <KRW=> to a session high of 1,034.9, matching the high on May 19, which was the strongest since May 8.

The South Korean authorities spent an estimated $500 million last Wednesday when the won weakened past 1,050 per dollar to a 2-1/2-year low.

South Korea's June Treasury bond futures <KTBc1> ended 21 ticks higher on Tuesday.

CENTRAL BANK MINUTES

Some board members of the Bank of Korea had said at the April rate meeting that a weaker won had more of a negative than positive impact on macroeconomic management, minutes of the meeting showed, reducing the case for a rate cut.

Analysts say massive intervention indicates the government is more concerned about inflation than growth but it still likely wants a relatively weak currency to support exports to help meet an ambitious economic growth target of 6 percent this year.

The government has repeatedly backed a weaker won to help boost growth in the export-focused economy, but analysts say fears that it will also lift inflation at home means the authorities will likely step in to prevent any nosedive.

"The comment (by Choi) comes as the government needs to show action as a weaker won boosts the impact of surging oil prices on domestic demand," said Jeong My-young, an analyst at Samsung Futures Inc.

"But the authorities will never allow the won to strengthen past the 1,000 (per dollar) again," she added.

Inflation -- which touched a four-year high of 4.1 percent in April -- has been a major factor keeping the central bank from cutting interest rates. (Additional reporting by Lee Soo-jung and Lee Jin-joo; Editing by Keiron Henderson and Jacqueline Wong)

title: UPDATE 3-S.Korea props up won as economic problems pile up
text:
(Updates with more details, markets closing)

SEOUL, May 21 (Reuters) - South Korea intervened to support the won on Wednesday after the currency dropped to a 2-1/2-year low as the government grappled with rising foreign debt, accelerating inflation and slowing economic growth.

The first intervention in two months followed news that the government was looking to check foreign borrowing that has doubled the country's external debt since 2005. Any curbs would shrink the supply of dollars converted to won.

The won is already Asia's second worst peforming currency this year and a Bank of Korea official was quoted as saying that further declines would fuel inflation, running above the central bank's target.

Tim Condon, head of Asia research at ING, said in a note that the flurry of comments about the rapid build-up of external debt might be due to worries about a possible credit rating downgrade.

"The Moody's sovereign analyst was recently in Korea for the annual review and we think the agency signalled the obvious, namely that its A2 sovereign rating could be jeopardised if the growth of short-term external debt does not slow," he wrote.

The won rose as much as 1 percent to 1,039.5 per dollar <KRW=> after purchases that dealers believed were made on behalf of the authorities. It earlier hit a low of 1,057.2, the weakest since October 2005, against Tuesday's close of 1,050.3.

"A sharp fall in the won lifts the risk of higher inflation while it does not create many jobs," the unnamed Bank of Korea official told online media outlet NewsPim.

The government, which is pressing the central bank not to raise interest rates, may have to cut its target for economic growth this year, a finance ministry official said.

"We have consumption, investment and employment indicators showing the economy is entering a slowing phase," Yim Jong-yong, head of the ministry's economic policy bureau, told reporters after a scheduled meeting on the financial market situation.

"(The government) may revise this year's economic growth and consumer price growth forecasts when it announces economic policy direction in the second half."

As current account and inflation problems grow, officials have already said it would be hard for the government to achieve its 6 percent economic growth target, far above a central bank forecast of 4.7 percent and dismissed as unrealistic by analysts.

Local financial markets are suffering, with the won falling 3.7 percent against the dollar this month, Dubai crude prices in won terms rising 13 percent and the benchmark five-year treasury bond yield <KR5YT=KSDA> up half a point.

Five dealers estimated the authorities sold $500 million to $700 million to prop up the won on Wednesday. Two dealers had initially placed the intervention at about $1 billion.

BONDS RATTLED

Government bond prices fell despite the warnings on slower growth. June bond futures <KTBc1> fell 20 ticks to 106.87.

Oil price increases and the weakness in the won could push up inflation further -- it hit a four-year high of 4.1 percent in April -- and prevent the central bank from cutting interest rates soon, or even force it to raise them.

On top of that, bond investors are worried about possible government measures to curb overseas borrowing by banks, which could prompt banks to unload their bond holdings to obtain cash. Converting that into dollars could further depress the won.

Vice Finance Minister Choi Joong-kyung reaffirmed that his ministry was studying ways to reduce overseas borrowing but had not yet decided on a course of action.

South Korea's overseas liabilities more than doubled to $381 billion at the end of 2007 from $188 billion two years before.

Banks have been borrowing to fund forward deals with local exporters, to swap dollars for won and lend the proceeds on, or to invest in higher-yielding Korean bonds.

The interest rate gap encourages such borrowing. A bank could borrow one-year dollars on Wednesday and swap them into won at an effective rate of just 2.5 percent. That compares with Korean interbank rates <KIKRW> of 5.57 percent.

Overseas borrowing, if unchecked, could dent the country's balance of payments and hurt its credit ratings. Standard & Poor's Ratings Service warned of the problem in October last year.

Analysts said the government had few options, other than to issue warnings to banks or limit the amount each bank can borrow. (Additional reporting by Cheon Jong-woo; Writing by Yoo Choonsik; Editing by Jonathan Hopfner and Alan Raybould)

title: UPDATE 1-S.Korea sold dollars to calm markets-dealers
text:
(Recasts throughout)   

SEOUL, March 18 (Reuters) - South Korea sold about $1 billion for won on Tuesday, dealers said, stemming losses of 8.5 percent in the past 12 sessions as the new government strives to keep its economic policy on track ahead of key elections next month.   

The won <KRW=> ended local trade up 1 percent against the dollar as dealers detected the intervention by authorities.   

Analysts said the won's drop against major currencies, including even the weakening dollar, was in reaction to its excessive rally in 2004-2006 and would deal an especially serious blow to South Korea grappling with already-high inflation.   

"In part, the intervention appears aimed at next month's elections because a weakening won definitely pushes up inflation at a time when raw materials prices are already rising," said Kim Jae-eun, an economist at Hana Daetoo Securities.   

The falling won and the resultant spike in inflation are not welcome developments for the growth-centred new government, installed only last month, especially as it gears up to consolidate power in parliamentary elections on April 9.   

The reported dollar purchases marked the first such major intervention aimed at propping up the won since early 2002.   

A foreign exchange official at the central bank, which can buy or sell dollars on behalf of the government when the won moves sharply, declined to comment on the talk of intervention.   

Since touching a decade high against the dollar on Oct. 31, 2007, the won has lost 11 percent against the dollar, 25 percent against the yen <JPYKRW=R>, 18 percent against the euro <EURKRW=R> and 16 percent against the yuan <CNYKRW=R>.   

ORDERLY DECLINE   

As the falling won is unnerving investors, the Finance Ministry said late on Tuesday that senior officials from the ministry, the central bank and other government agencies would meet early on Wednesday to check financial market movements.   

Prime Minister Han Seung-soo also told a cabinet meeting on Tuesday to draw up measures to stabilise domestic prices, a government spokesman said.   

Central bank data showed on Sunday import prices measured in won terms rose a whopping 22.2 percent in February from a year earlier, the fastest annual gain since October 1998.   

Analysts said South Korea's reported intervention was not seen as a concerted action with other countries, and added it appeared aimed at smoothing the won's decline rather than turning the currency around.   

"I think they do not want a disorderly decline like yesterday's 3 percent move," said Tim Condon, head of Asia research at investment bank ING, referring to the won's 3.3 percent peak-to-peak movement on Monday.   

"However, the Korean won was among Asia's top-performing currencies in 2004-2006 and I am beginning to think the authorities would like to see it retrace the gains of those years, which would put it above 1,100 against the U.S. dollar and above 11 against the Japanese yen."

SEOUL (Dow Jones)--A senior Bank of Korea official said Tuesday that the dollar's recent surge against the won seems "too sharp," and that the country's current account is likely to remain in a deficit until April, indicating that the dollar might continue to rise in the weeks ahead.   

Ahn Byung-Chan, director-general of the Bank of Korea's international department, said that the dollar's gains will likely persist in the first half, but that trend could reverse in the second half of the year.   

He also said that the central bank is watching the market closely, suggesting that it could intervene in the foreign exchange market by selling the dollar.   

Late last month, Kang Man-Soo, speaking at a National Assembly committee hearing prior to his appointment as finance minister, said that the central bank deemed that foreign exchange reserves of $250 billion are adequate, based on the country's foreign currency debt and foreigners' holding of local shares.   

His statement suggested that the Bank of Korea has the means to intervene in the market by unloading dollars.   

South Korea's foreign exchange reserves totaled $262.36 billion at the end of February.   

The dollar opened sharply higher against the won Tuesday, hitting a two-year intraday high of KRW974.51 at 0023 GMT.That was its highest level since March 31, 2006, when it had risen to an intraday high of KRW977.04.

title: UPDATE: Korea Oct Exports Jump;BOK Suspected Buying USD Again
text:
(Adds detail on trade and inflation data, foreign exchange intervention.)   

SEOUL (Dow Jones)--South Korean exports rebounded in October after September's drop but the government warned that the strong won could hurt overseas sales in coming months.   

Along with most other Asian currencies, the South Korean won has been rising against the U.S. dollar of late, prompting suspected intervention by the Bank of Korea again Thursday to keep the U.S. currency above KRW900.   

Traders estimate that the central bank bought $100 million to $200 million Thursday after three suspected rounds of intervention Wednesday totaling around $700 million.   

Last month, South Korea's exports jumped 24.2% from a year earlier to a total $34.79 billion while imports increased by 27.2% to $32.59 billion, the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Energy said Thursday.   

Growth in both was faster than economists had anticipated, although most had forecast a jump because the three-day Chusok holiday, which fell in September this year, pushed down that month's exports and imports.   

The end of the Chusok holiday also helped to stem price rises with the October consumer price index up a smaller 0.2% on month, although it was up a sharper 3.0% on year. In September, prices were up 0.6% on month and 2.3% on year.   

The impact of the strong won will likely start to show in export figures for December, a senior official at the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Energy said following the release of the data.   

At 0500 GMT, the dollar was at KRW902.50 after closing Wednesday at KRW900.70, its lowest closing level since KRW900.50 on Aug. 26, 1997.   

"Some say that the current forex level is endurable, while others say that companies are suffering greatly, but (exporters) will likely see answers from December," said Oh Jung-Kyu, director general for Trade & Investment Promotion at the commerce ministry.   

But he indicated that exports would likely maintain double-digit growth into the early part of 2008. Double-digit growth figures are usually taken to mean growth of between 10% and 20%.   

The commerce ministry said it will meet with a group of exporting companies later this month to discuss their difficulties in coping with the strong won.   

Minister of Finance and Economy Kwon Okyu though was quick to calm politicians about the potential damage of a strong won, telling a parliamentary audit Thursday that the government expects local companies to cope with the current exchange rate.   

Ahn Byung Chan, a director-general of the Bank of Korea's international department also told Dow Jones Newswires that the won is expected to stabilize against the U.S. dollar since the U.S. Federal Reserve was unlikely to cut interest rates next month.   

Exports On Slowing Trend   

Although exports showed a big recovery in October, the government noted the trend of overseas sales was a touch slower than earlier in the year.   

"Exports averaged 11.3% growth on year to $32.09 billion in September and October put together while imports averaged a 11.9% rise to $29.81 billion, which is slower than the performance shown in the earlier part of this year," the ministry said.   

Exports increased in October because of a rise in demand for general machinery, wireless communications devices, automobile, petrochemical products and liquid display devices, the ministry said.   

On the other hand, semiconductors, steels and ships and vessels, other mainstay export items, contracted on year.   

"We should keep a close watch on the drop in semiconductor and steel exports, which was due to continued falls in chip prices and the rise in domestic steel demand," the ministry said.   

Oh said steel producers may be turning to the local market because the won's appreciation cuts into the profits from selling overseas.   

Imports rose due to a surge in international crude oil prices and a recovery in domestic consumption, according to the data.   

The National Statistical Office attributed the on-year rise in consumer prices to costly oil and higher vegetable prices. Analysts had forecast October consumer prices to rise 2.8% on year.   

Trade Surplus Shrinks A Touch   

The trade surplus was $2.20 billion in October, narrowing slightly from September's $2.35 billion and $2.39 billion a year earlier, the preliminary data showed.   

Economists had forecast the trade surplus at $1.82 billion on the back of exports rising 21.8% and imports increasing 26.0%. In September, exports fell 0.9% to $29.38 billion and imports dropped 2.2% to $27.03 billion.   

Economic data in September and October tend to differ drastically, depending on the timing of the Chusok holiday. The holiday fell in the last week of September this year and in the first week of October last year.   

"The exports result (in October) is due to a 3.5-day increase in working days because the Chusok holiday was in October last year," the ministry said in a statement.   

By region, exports to the U.S. rose 32.6% on year in the first 20 days of October, a turnaround from a 9.2% fall in the same period last year, because of strong demand for liquid display devices, wireless communications equipment and automobiles.   

Exports to China jumped 33.1% on year and sales to the E.U. rose 23.7%.   

-By Jin-Young Yook, Dow Jones Newswires; 822-732-2165; jin-young.yook@dowjones.com [ 01-11-07 0521GMT ]

title: S.Korea BOK says may step in again in swaps market
text:
SEOUL, Sept 12 (Reuters) - South Korea's central bank may intervene again in the local dollar/won swaps market if it is necessary to stabilise the market, a senior official at the Bank of Korea (BOK) told Reuters on Wednesday.   

Ahn Byung-chan, director of international department, also said the central bank intervened in the market on Tuesday because a prolonged short supply of dollars.   

"I hope the market will return to normal gradually, but we will take action if any such supply-demand imbalance takes place in the future," he said.   

Currency traders estimated the Bank of Korea had injected about $500 million into the market through the intervention on Tuesday, but Ahn declined to disclose the size or nature of its market manoeuvres.   

The Bank of Korea banned last month commercial banks from providing foreign-currency loans whose proceeds are eventually to be converted into the won <KRW=> and are not for settlements on purchases of production equipment.   

Banks have complained the measure, aimed at preventing the won from strengthening against the dollar, has sparked a severe shortage of dollars on the swaps market, in the process pushing up the costs of hedging for export companies.   

Exporters and institutional investors in overseas markets hedge against the risks from future currency changes by selling dollar/won forwards to banks, which in turn borrow dollars or swap the won for the dollar to take up the deals.

title: ANALYSIS-S.Korea's  FX intervention  too costly for the economy
text:
SEOUL, Aug 7 (Reuters) - South Korea's effort to restrain a rising won looks like an exercise in futility: It's expensive, unlikely to work, and not needed to support exports.   

Intervention by the authorities, buying dollars and flooding the market with won, also contradicts efforts to control inflation caused by a rise in the money supply, analysts say.   

Politicians want to appease manufacturers who worry a strong currency hurts export competitiveness, but the reality is that South Korea's exports are booming and the won will rise to where the market thinks it should be.   

"The won overvalued? Yes, if we had the KOSPI at 1,500 and if the world economy was so bad that the Fed cut interest rates twice," said Oh Suk-tae, an economist at  Citigroup.

The Seoul stock market's benchmark index <.KS11> has recently roared past 2,000, before retreating 8 percent, and the world economy is faring better than many expected earlier in the year.   

Recent central bank intervention and a global sell-off in riskier assets combined to push the won <KRW=> sharply below an almost 10-year high and away from what officials say is an overvalued level. That's unlikely to last.   

The country's rise in exports -- up 20 percent last month -- rising interest rates, firm economic growth and a bright stock market all point to a higher won, analysts say.   

"They (Finance Ministry officials) may feel happy now with the won's recent drop, but everyone knows it's a temporary turbulence and the won will rise again. Exports are really strong and ship makers continue to win orders," Oh said.   

On July 25, it was trading just 0.2 won away from a decade high against the dollar of 912.5, when the authorities stepped in with heavy dollar purchases, sending it into a 1 percent reverse.   

On Tuesday, it traded around 923 won to the dollar.   

CONTRADICTORY POLICY   

South Korea's foreign exchange reserves, the world's fifth-largest, expanded by $4.1 billion in July to $254.8 billion. Dealers estimate the Bank of Korea sold more than $2 billion worth of won during the last few days of the month.   

In its desperation to keep a lid on the currency, the central bank on Friday reinstated a curb on foreign-currency lending to domestic customers, abolished six years ago, even though the move runs counter to a pledge to liberalise capital flows.   

The central bank says its fears are not just the impact on exports -- which generate about a quarter of GDP -- but that if the won rises too high, the inevitable tumble back down could wreak havoc on its financial markets and push up inflation.   

Rhee Gwang-ju, who led the Bank of Korea's foreign exchange policy until his promotion as a deputy head of the central bank early this year, has repeatedly warned of the risk.   

In an interview with Reuters in May, he said of the won's continued rise: "It is on the path of overshooting and as time goes on, a correction will take place. We are concerned about a sharp depreciation of the won in a short period of time later this year."   

The won lost half its value at the height of the 1997 Asian financial crisis and is still almost 9 percent below its level at the end of 1996.   

IRONY   

Exports have been growing six years in a row and in the four years to 2006 doubled in value, despite the won's appreciation.   

"This is testament to the fact that Korean industries have rapidly moved up the value-added chain, reminiscent of what Japan went through in the 1980s spurred by a strengthening ... (yen),"  Goldman Sachs economist, Mark Tan, wrote in a research report.   

Analysts also point to the paradox of a central bank pumping money into the markets by intervening in the currency market just as it pledges its determination to curb growth in money supply.   

"The main economic risk from continued intervention is the need to absorb excess liquidity. Already, the authorities have to issue large amounts of Monetary Stabilisation Bonds (MSB) to siphon off liquidity," said Frederic Neumann, an economist at  HSBC Markets based in Hong Kong.   

He was referring to bonds that the central bank sells to drain surplus money from the financial system. The outstanding amount of MSBs on issue had jumped 35 percent in 2004 and 9 percent in 2005 before slowing in growth since then.   

The Bank of Korea raised interest rates by a total of 1.5 percentage points between October 2005 and July this year to cool sizzling money growth, which policy makers are worried will push up asset prices and eventually stoke inflation.   

"Money supply growth continues to be strong in Korea, which prompted the authorities recently to raise interest rates even though inflationary pressures remain low. In a sense, therefore, the costs of exchange rate intervention is borne by the overall economy via higher interest rates," he added.

title: South Korea bonds gain on auctions, weaker stocks
text:
(Updates to close)   

SEOUL, July 18 (Reuters) - South Korean government bonds snapped a three-day losing streak to edge up on Wednesday, as a drop in the local stock market buoyed demand for bonds and after a government bond auction produced strong results.   

But gains were limited due to uncertainties over the U.S. Treasury debt market's direction and worries the South Korean authorities may sell the won for the dollar to cap the local currency's rally, analysts said.   

The yield on the benchmark five-year treasury bonds <KR5YT=KSDA> fell two basis points to end at 5.48 percent, and the three-year treasury bond yield <KR3YT=KSDA> also lost two basis points to 5.40 percent.

The Seoul stock market's benchmark KOSPI <.KS11> slipped 0.96 percent.   

The Finance Ministry sold only 102 billion won ($111.3 million) out of the planned 200 billion won in inflation-linked 10-year treasury bonds at an auction on Wednesday.   

But investors welcomed the outcome because the auction was oversubscribed and they believed the ministry scaled down the sales amount to keep the issuing yield from rising too much.   

The won <KRW=> ended local trade up 0.2 percent against the dollar, racing closer to a near-decade high and sparking fears the authorities may intervene.   

South Korea's Finance Ministry and central bank have pledged to keep the won from rising excessively to protect local exporters from a sharp erosion in their price competitiveness in overseas markets and in their profit margins.   

When the central bank buys dollars to cap the won's strength, it usually sells bonds to absorb the increased won liquidity afterwards, pressuring the overall trading sentiment in the fixed-income market.

title: UPDATE 1-S.Korea producer inflation boosts rate rise bets
text:
(Adds analyst, background)   

SEOUL, July 9 (Reuters) - South Korea's producer inflation in June hit a nine-month high, data showed on Monday, giving fresh ammunition to a central bank that is already seen poised to raise interest rates for the first time in almost a year.   

The central bank said the producer price index in June rose 2.7 percent from a year earlier, the fastest since a 3.1 percent gain in September last year, led by accelerating growth in service prices such as utility fees.   

The data comes just a day after figures showing the country's money supply growth picked up in May and the government's upgrade of its 2007 export forecast provided more incentive for the Bank of Korea to lift interest rates at its July 12 policy meeting. [ID:nSEO44783] [ID:nSEO359896]   

"Annual producer prices have risen, giving support to increasing expectations that the central bank will raise interest rates in July amid faster growth in the domestic economy," said Lee Sang-jae, an economist at  Hyundai Securities.

Echoing such expectations, a majority of bond dealers said in an industry survey on Monday that the Bank of Korea would raise the overnight call rate target on Thursday, after having held it steady at 4.50 percent for 10 months. [ID:nSEO20591]   

Investors have already priced in an interest rate increase after Bank of Korea Governor Lee Seong-tae warned in early June high liquidity could stoke inflation and later said that interest rates were not so high as to hurt economic growth.   

Figures released last week also underscored that Asia's fourth-largest economy was gathering steam, with the June trade surplus hitting an all-time high on brisk exports and that month's consumer inflation picking up. [ID:nSEO355036]   

ROOM FOR WON'S RISE   

Analysts expect higher local interest rates and resilient export demand for South Korean products to create room for the won <KRW=> to gain further after having risen 25 percent against the U.S. dollar over the past three years.   

"There is a strong possiblity that the local currency may rise after the Bank of Korea tightens its monetary policy, but the central bank has other means to keep the won down, by intervening in the forex market," Lee said.   

The government-run  Korea Development Bank forecast on Monday the won would rise to an average of 915 per dollar for the second half of this year from 933.6 for the first half. The won was quoted at 920.1 by 0421 GMT, down 0.11 percent.   

South Korean policy makers have expressed concern that the won's appreciation against major currencies was hurting export companies by making their products more expensive in dollar terms and eroding exporters' profits in won terms.   

But analysts say South Korea would not intervene in the currency market as actively as they did in 2003-2004, due to increased pressure over billions of dollars in losses incurred from the prior intervention.   

They said strong exports despite the won's rise also left the Finance Ministry and the central bank with little excuse to dump the local currency and that intervention could risk pushing up already-buoyant local liquidity growth.

title: Emerging  FX -S.Korean won rallies, others lose momentum
text:
SINGAPORE, July 3 (Reuters) - Asian currencies dithered on Tuesday after a four-session rally driven by the dollar's weakness, amid verbal intervention in South Korea and fears elsewhere that the gains were overdone.   

 Still, Korea's won <KRW=> managed to rise 0.4 percent and hit a 7-week high of 916.8 per dollar at one point. The Thai baht <THB=> rose 0.45 percent and the Singapore dollar <SGD=> hit a one-week high near 1.5220 per U.S. dollar.   

 China's yuan <CNY=CFXS> also rose to its highest level against the dollar since the July 2005 revaluation, hitting 7.5951 per dollar, giving traders another reason to be bullish on Asia.   

 The Singapore dollar has gained more than a percent in the past four sessions.   

 The U.S. dollar's weakness was broad-based. It matched a 26-year low versus sterling and stayed near a record low against the euro <EUR=>, undermined by the view that the Federal Reserve is unlikely to lift rates anytime soon given a recent run of soft inflation data and concerns over the mortgage market.   

 But some of the Asians seemed to have lost steam. Heading into the U.S. Independence Day holiday on July 4, traders expected other currencies also to take a breather.   

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> retreated from a 2-week high of 45.73 to end the day nearly steady. The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> barely budged from near 9,000 per dollar.   

 "U.S. equities are rallying on the lower rate hike risk and that seems to be the story Asia is running with: no Fed hike so the party is on!," said Sean Callow, Westpac Bank's strategist.   

 "Personally, I don't think it's sustainable," he said, adding that oil prices near $71 a barrel would start to hurt Asian sentiment at some point.   

 Meanwhile, Korean authorities were clearly worried about the won's rise above 920-per dollar this week.   

 The foreign exchange authorities, which include the central bank and finance ministry, said the currency was overshooting its fundamental values and they were watching the market. They expressed concern the won was gaining even as foreigners have turned net sellers of Korean equities.   

 The charts, however, seemed to suggest further upside for the won. The next target for the falling dollar/won pair is the 913-per-dollar level, which was its December 2006 trough, said Winston Tang, an analyst at 4CAST. Tang said the dollar/won downtrend was firmly established after the pair broke through the May 2007 lows near 922.

title: UPDATE 1-S.Korea  FX  reserves fall in June on swap deals
text:
(Recasts with details, background)   

SEOUL, July 3 (Reuters) - South Korean foreign exchange reserves fell in June for the first time in a year as the central bank expanded currency swaps as a way to cheaply soak up liquidity, the Bank of Korea said on Tuesday.   

The central bank, under mounting pressure to cut the costs of draining surplus liquidity through bonds, said it swapped about $660 million in foreign currencies for the won with the state-run pension agency and local banks in June.   

The amount was more than the usual $500 million swapped in the past, an official at the central bank said.   

It was also greater than the capital gains from investments of the reserves funds, resulting in a decline in the foreign exchange reserves by $40 million from a month before, to $250.70 billion at end-June, the central bank said.   

It was the first time that the country's foreign reserves, which the central bank manages, recorded a monthly decline since dropping by $332 million in June 2006.   

The central bank has been struggling to contain the costs of skimming off growing won liquidity, which it undertakes to keep inflationary pressures in check.   

It posted a net loss of 1.76 trillion won ($1.91 billion) in 2006 after losing 1.88 trillion won in 2005, mainly because it paid more than 6 trillion won in each year in interest on monetary stabilisation bonds (MSBs), central bank data shows.   

The Bank of Korea has pledged on several occasions to seek alternative ways to absorb liquidity and had actually sharply cut net new issuances of MSBs offered in 2006, according to central bank data posted on its Web site (  http://www.bok.or.kr  ("http://www.bok.or.kr")).   

The outstanding amount of MSBs issued grew only 2 percent by the end of 2006 from a year before after rises of 9 percent in 2005 and 35 percent in 2004.   

Swapping some of the reserves held in foreign currencies for the won held by the National Pension Service, which manages more than $200 billion, helps the Bank of Korea absorb the extra won in the financial system without selling bonds.   

South Korea has been enjoying a net capital inflow for years due to trade surpluses and foreign investment, and the central bank has bought much of the surplus dollars on the market to keep the won <KRW=> from appreciating quickly.   

South Korea's government has said such intervention was inevitable to protect exporters, important contributors to the growth of Asia's fourth-largest economy, from the won's rises. A strong local currency can hurt exporters' profitability and competitiveness.   

But despite several years of dollar-buying intervention, the won has continued to gain against the major currencies and was not far from its strongest mark in nearly a decade against the dollar on Tuesday afternoon.
