title: OECD Recommends Korea Steady Policy Rate, Flexible  FX  Policy
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--South Korea should focus on achieving its mid-term inflation target while maintaining a flexible exchange rate policy, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development said Wednesday.   

"Monetary conditions are now judged to be tighter than at any time since the 1997 financial crisis, while the pace of economic activity (has) slowed and inflation remained low and stable," the OECD sad in its economic survey on South Korea.   

"Additional monetary tightening appears unnecessary in such an environment."   

It said further hikes in the short-term interest rate could hurt households and small to medium enterprises, two sectors of the economy where debt has been increasing.   

The OECD recommended that the Bank of Korea focus its monetary policies on achieving the 2.5%-3.5% medium-term inflation target and avoid using key interest rates as a tool to stabilize real estate prices. The OECD is estimating a 2.5% rise in the consumer price index for 2007 and a 3.0% gain in 2008, which are well within the BOK's target band.   

The international organization blamed the BOK's interest rate hikes for the won's appreciation.   

"The upward pressure on the won has occurred in the context of a significant hike in interest rates by the Bank of Korea, even though inflation has been below the target zone," it said.   

The central bank raised its policy interest rate by 125 basis points to 4.50% in five rate moves between October 2005 and August 2006.   

The Korean won appreciated 2.3% against the U.S. dollar in 2005 and by 8.8% in 2006. However, during the BOK's monetary easing in 2004 to stimulate growth, the won appreciated 15.2% against the dollar.   

The OECD discouraged the BOK from using monetary policy to affect the property market, which was one of the reasons the central bank raised interest rates in August 2006.   

"Monetary policy is a blunt instrument for influencing real estate prices, particularly as the largest house price increases are limited to specific areas of the capital region," the OECD said.   

It said Korea's increase in the average nationwide house price since 2000 is well below the average of other OECD countries and remained moderate in 2005-2006.   

As for the government's housing policies to curb property prices, the OECD said the policies should focus more on developing an efficient market than on controlling prices.   

"Despite the merits of the objective of stabilizing housing prices, some of these policies have the potential to create substantial harm if allowed to persist in the long term as they tend to reduce the supply of housing," the OECD said.   

Regarding foreign exchange, the OECD said South Korea should pursue a flexible policy by limiting intervention in forex market.   

"The liberalization of controls on capital outflows should aim at improving long-run efficiency rather than moderating upward pressure on the won in the short run," the OECD said.   

The OECD said there was no need for continued accumulation of foreign exchange reserves, which totaled $250.74 billion at the end of May, because the reserves are nearly double short-term overseas debt. Data from the Bank of Korea showed short-term overseas debt totaled $129.75 billion at the end of March.   

The OECD said Korean exports have grown less sensitive to the appreciating currency because of the steady improvement in product quality and a shift toward knowledge-based products that tend to be less price-sensitive.   

The OECD is forecasting South Korea's gross domestic product growth at 4.3% in 2007 and 4.8% the following year. It estimates Korea's potential growth rate to be around 4.5%, a view shared by the International Monetary Fund.   

The 2007 forecast is barely below estimates made by the Bank of Korea and the International Monetary Fund, both of which predict 4.4% growth this year.

The Korean won appreciated 2.3% against the U.S. dollar in 2005 and by 8.8% in 2006. However, during the BOK's monetary easing in 2004 to stimulate growth, the won appreciated 15.2% against the dollar.   

The OECD discouraged the BOK from using monetary policy to affect the property market, which was one of the reasons the central bank raised interest rates in August 2006.   

'Monetary policy is a blunt instrument for influencing real estate prices, particularly as the largest house price increases are limited to specific areas of the capital region,' the OECD said.   

It said Korea's increase in the average nationwide house price since 2000 is well below the average of other OECD countries and remained moderate in 2005-2006.   

As for the government's housing policies to curb property prices, the OECD said the policies should focus more on developing an efficient market than on controlling prices.   

'Despite the merits of the objective of stabilizing housing prices, some of these policies have the potential to create substantial harm if allowed to persist in the long term as they tend to reduce the supply of housing,' the OECD said.   

Regarding foreign exchange, the OECD said South Korea should pursue a flexible policy by limiting intervention in forex market.   

'The liberalization of controls on capital outflows should aim at improving long-run efficiency rather than moderating upward pressure on the won in the short run,' the OECD said.   

The OECD said there was no need for continued accumulation of foreign exchange reserves, which totaled $250.74 billion at the end of May, because the reserves are nearly double short-term overseas debt. Data from the Bank of Korea showed short-term overseas debt totaled $129.75 billion at the end of March.   

The OECD said Korean exports have grown less sensitive to the appreciating currency because of the steady improvement in product quality and a shift toward knowledge-based products that tend to be less price-sensitive.   

The OECD is forecasting South Korea's gross domestic product growth at 4.3% in 2007 and 4.8% the following year. It estimates Korea's potential growth rate to be around 4.5%, a view shared by the International Monetary Fund.   

The 2007 forecast is barely below estimates made by the Bank of Korea and the International Monetary Fund, both of which predict 4.4% growth this year. -By Jin-Young Yook, Dow Jones Newswires; 822-732-2165; jin-young.yook@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 1- South Korea  renews  currency intervention  pledge
text:
(Recasts throughout with officials, OECD)   

SEOUL, June 20 (Reuters) - South Korea renewed its pledge on Wednesday to stem the won's rise, dismissing suggestions that criticism over losses from past intervention was blocking the government from stepping in now to tame the currency.   

The authorities have both the ability and the will to intervene in the currency market when necessary to cap the won's <KRW=> appreciation against the U.S. dollar, Deputy Finance Minister Kim Sung-jin told a private seminar.   

His comments, which came hours after similar warnings by Finance Minister Kwon O-kyu, were in contrast to an Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) call for more tolerance of the won's appreciation.   

"Some say the hands of the government and the Bank of Korea remain tied because of losses incurred from past intervention, but it's completely wrong," said Kim, the highest official after the minister and vice minister to decide on intervention.   

The Paris-based OECD pressed South Korea, Asia's fourth-largest economy, to be flexible over the currency.   

"Maintaining a flexible exchange rate policy will help boost domestic demand, while export growth appears increasingly resilient to currency changes," the agency said in a report.   

South Korean policy makers are worried about the won's steep appreciation over the past few years, not only against the dollar but also compared to the currencies of chief export rivals Japan and China.   

The won has gained only 0.2 percent against the dollar this year but has jumped about 4 percent against the yen <JPYKRW=R>, hitting a 9-1/2-year high on Wednesday.   

NO INFLATION WORRY   

Both South Korea's central bank and the OECD sounded upbeat on the economic growth and inflation outlook for 2007-2008.   

"The economy is expected to gradually reverse the slowdown experienced during (the latter part of) 2006, with growth of around 4-¼ percent in 2007, despite the tightening of monetary conditions," the OECD said.   

South Korea's economy grew by 5.0 percent in 2006 after 4.2 percent in 2005.   

The OECD forecast gross domestic product growth would rise further to 4-¾ percent in 2008.   

The economy looks relatively free of any immediate risk from inflation, both the central bank and the OECD said.   

"We don't much worry about this year's price growth," Lee Ju-yeol, a deputy governor at the central bank, told the same seminar for financial market experts.   

"It's true to some extent that inflation pressure is growing along with rising inflation in China, but, overall, that will not likely pose a serious threat through next year," he said.   

The OECD also noted the tame inflation in South Korea, advising the central bank to focus its monetary policy on the stable inflation trend rather than use it as a tool to cool the booming housing market.   

The Bank of Korea has held interest rates steady for 10 successive months after lifting them by a combined 1.25 percentage points on five occasions until August 2006.

title: S.Korea May  FX  reserves soar as  intervention  spotted
text:
SEOUL, June 4 (Reuters) - South Korea's foreign exchange reserves rose the most in five months in May, central bank data showed on Monday, as currency dealers and analysts suspected that the country bought dollars to check the won's <KRW=> strength.   


 The country's foreign exchange reserves -- the world's
fifth-largest in April -- rose to $250.7 billion as of the end of
   

May from $247.3 billion a month ago, the Bank of Korea said in a statement.   

 The gain of $3.48 billion , or 1.4 percent, was the largest since a $4.7 billion rise posted in December 2006.   

Currency market players have said huge changes in foreign reserves usually reflect the country's intervention in the foreign exchange market.   

 The Bank of Korea attributed the rise in May to investment gains.   

 But dealers and analysts in Seoul said the country's foreign exchange authorities had been suspected of buying about a combined $2.5 billion during the month.   

 Officials at the finance ministry and the central bank declined to comment.   

 South Korean foreign reserves have risen by 4.9 percent, or $11.78 billion, so far this year, Bank of Korea data shows. Its reserves rank behind those of China, Japan, Russia and Taiwan.   

 The central bank said 88.2 percent of April's total reserves were invested in securities, compared with 11.6 percent deposited at financial institutions.

title: UPDATE 3-S.Korea suspected of  FX intervention  for 2nd day
text:
(Adds central bank official's comment in paras 8-9)   

SEOUL, May 18 (Reuters) - South Korea authorities were suspected of intervening heavily on Friday to sell the won for the dollar, pushing it to a six-week low and underlining their determination to prevent the local currency from rising further.   

Currency dealers said they believed authorities had bought $1 billion for the second day in a row. On Thursday, the won hit its highest level in almost a decade against the yen and it was gaining against the dollar.   

"Investors will not dare to build up dollar-short positions for the rest of this year after the government took extremely strong action," said a foreign bank dealer.   

Dollar spot trading volume hit a record high of $12.49 billion on Friday, the Seoul Money Brokerage Services Ltd. and  Korea Money Broker Corp. said.   

That was almost twice the daily average volume in 2007 of $6.9 billion.   

The intervention has helped knock the won down more than 1.2 percent over two days against the dollar and by 0.8 percent against the yen <JPYKRW=R>.   

The won fell to an intraday low of 935.1 per dollar on Friday, its lowest value since 936.2 on April 5.   

An official at the central bank told Reuters after the end of the local trading that exporters had sold more than $5 billion over the two days, much higher than normal volume of less than $1 billion on a typical day.   

The official, who declined to be named, did not elaborate.   

The suspected intervention followed warnings by a deputy central bank governor on Tuesday that the won was overvalued.   

The Bank of Korea and the finance ministry issued a rare joint statement on Thursday saying they were closely watching the won's movements and will take action if necessary.   

The won has risen about 30 percent against the dollar in 2004-2006, but is one of the poorest performers in Asia so far this year.   

However, South Korean policy makers have complained the past gains were already excessive when compared to rival currencies.   

They say they are concerned with the won's strength not just against the U.S. dollar but against Asian currencies as well.   

A rise in the currency can make South Korean exports more expensive compared with those of regional competitors and can undermine exporters' profitability when they repatriate overseas earnings. (Additional reporting by Kim Yeon-hee and Lee Soo-jung)

SEOUL (Dow Jones)--The South Korean won closed Friday at its lowest level against the U.S. unit in six weeks, as foreign banks covered shorts actively on suspected hefty dollar buying by the Bank of Korea, market participants said.   

"The BOK may have intervened and pushed the local pair above KRW934.0, in order to help the yen/won cross rate climb back to its psychologically important KRW7.70 level," said a foreign bank trader.   

According to a second foreign bank trader, "the central bank may have bought more than yesterday's purchase of around $1 billion," bringing the suspected dollar purchases by the BOK to more than $2 billion over two sessions.   

The BOK's suspected buying pushed the daily trading volume to $12.48 billion Friday, the biggest ever daily foreign exchange trading volume in the market, traders said.   

The dollar/won is likely to extend its gains Monday, as many players are expected to favor the dollar-buying stance because "the BOK has clearly proven its intention to support both the dollar/won as well as the yen/won cross rate," said the second foreign bank trader.   

Traders said local importers, mainly oil refiners, are likely to assist the pair's upside trend Monday, given their active dollar demand recently.   

The dollar is likely to trade between KRW932 and KRW937 Monday.   

Government bonds closed lower on active selling after positive U.S. jobs and manufacturing data overnight indicated a stronger U.S. economy, which could provide an added boost to trade-dependent South Korea's economy.   

In addition, the BOK's recent intervention has left the foreign exchange market flush with won, which the central bank is expected to absorb through heavy issues of stabilization bonds in the near term.   

On the domestic front, there are no fresh cues nor economic data to reflect on, thus "players are slowly beginning to react to offshore data," said a local securities firm trader.   

Looking ahead, bond yields are likely to rise further Monday as "players expect the government to sell large sums of stabilization bonds due to massive won outflows recently in the foreign exchange market," said  SK Securities' analyst Kong Dong-Rak.   

Middle- and longer-term yields will continue to receive upside pressure as the certificate of deposit rate is rising due to banks' ongoing short-term liquidity shortage.   

The three-year yield is tipped to move in a 5.12%-5.19% band, and the benchmark five-year yield in a 5.16%-5.23% band Monday.

title: UPDATE 2- South Korea  suspected of $1 bln  FX intervention
text:
(Adds amount of suspected intervention, economist comment)   

 SEOUL, May 17 (Reuters) - South Korean authorities were cited as having intervened strongly to cap a surging won on Thursday and they sent markets a stark warning that they would do whatever was needed to curb the currency's strength.   

 Dealers suspected authorities bought up to $1 billion in the foreign exchange market after the won <KRW=> hit its highest level against the yen in almost a decade and as it gained on the dollar.   

 The currency ended the day down 0.5 percent against the dollar -- its biggest daily percentage drop in 10 weeks -- and it also backed off the highs against the yen <JPYKRW=R>.   

 "We saw sudden dollar bid inflows, which were suspected to be from the government's intervention, so it is becoming more difficult to buy the won from this level," said a foreign bank dealer.   

 In a rare joint warning, the Bank of Korea and the finance ministry said they were closely watching the won's movements and will take action if necessary.   

 "The won's recent gains do not reflect economic fundamentals and supply/demand conditions," said Kim Yun-chul, head of the Bank of Korea's foreign exchange market team.   

 Moon Hongsung, director of the finance ministry's foreign exchange market division, made similar comments.   

 But officials from the Bank of Korea declined to comment on whether authorities had intervened in the currency market.   

 Dealers said they expected the won to stay under pressure from wariness of further dollar-buying intervention. But it's downside may also be limited in the absence of further action by authorities.   

 "The government will have to push down the won to 935 with additional strong intervention tomorrow; otherwise, exporters and offshore players will chase the won on dips," said another foreign bank dealer, who asked not to be identified.   

 Offshore players, who heavily influence the local currency market, bought much of the won during the session, he said.   

 South Korean policy makers say they are concerned with the won's rise not just against the U.S. dollar but against Asian currencies as well.   

 A rise in the currency can make South Korean exports more expensive compared with those of regional competitors and can undermine exporters' profitability when they repatriate overseas earnings.   

 The chief economist at the Samsung Economic Research Institute said the won was overvalued.   

 "We have done calculations recently based on 1993, when the country's current account was in balance, and it shows the won is 15 percent overvalued now," said Hong Sun-young, director of the economic research department at the institute.   

 Earlier in the week, a senior Bank of Korea official told Reuters the central bank was concerned that the won was overvalued and ran the risk of a sharp correction this year. [ID:nSP54563]  (Additional reporting by Yoo Choonsik and Lee Kyoung-ho)

title: Emerging  FX -Firm tone in Asia, rupiah at 2-1/2-mth high
text:
SINGAPORE, May 3 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah hit its highest level in 2-½ months against the dollar on Thursday as investors snapped up local assets, while rising regional stock markets boosted other Asian currencies.   

The high-yielding rupiah <IDR=> rose as high as 9,038 per dollar, up about 0.4 percent from late Asia trade on Wednesday and its highest level since mid-February, as foreign investors bid to buy into the country's stock markets.   

"The rise is mostly driven by offshore buying of local assets, such as stocks," said a dealer in Jakarta.   

The South Korean won <KRW=> rose to 926.4 per dollar, its highest in a week, as exporters sold dollars. The currency had weakened in early trade amid caution over central bank intervention.   

South Korea's foreign exchange reserves swelled by about $3.3 billion in April, the fastest in four months, central bank data showed on Thursday, which dealers said reflected increased central bank intervention to curb the won's strength.   

Most Asian currencies were firm against the dollar, shrugging of yen <JPY=> weakness, but trade was slow with markets in China and Japan closed for holidays.   

The interest in the rupiah was largely sparked by expectations that the Indonesian central bank was nearing the end of a series of rate cuts, while others said the currency had underperformed the market.   

The Philippine peso <PHP=>, another high-yielder, gained nearly a quarter of a percent to about 47.60 per dollar.   

Asian stocks rose on Thursday as MSCI's measure of Asia Pacific stocks excluding Japan <.MSCIAPJ> climbed 0.94 percent.   

Analysts in general remain bullish about the underlying strength of Asian currencies, given the region's solid economic fundamentals buoyed by a hefty trade surplus and capital inflows.   

"Regional currency strength should still be the name of the game and given that we think the opposite for the U.S. dollar what we're seeing is pretty logical," said Magnus Prim, chief Asia currency strategist at SEB.   

SINGAPORE DOLLAR   

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose to 1.5217 per U.S. dollar, a day after it slipped to 1.5283, its weakest level since mid-March, as overseas banks moved to cover short positions in the U.S. currency.   

"They were buying (the U.S. dollar) in the last few days, so they are just taking some profits," said a dealer in Singapore.   

Soma analysts said the near-term upside for the Singapore dollar may be limited by low local interest rates, central bank intervention and the U.S. dollar's gains versus the Japanese yen.   

Singapore's central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), manages the currency within an undisclosed, trade-weighted band. In its semi-annual policy review last month, it stuck with a policy of letting the currency appreciate gradually within the band.   

Claudio Piron and Yen Ping Ho at  JPMorgan estimated that the Singapore dollar's nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) had slipped into the bottom half of the band for the first time since December 2005.   

"The local rates decline was likely the dominant driver. The more cautious read to the MAS statement last month could have contributed in part to this post-statement decline," they said in a research note.   

But analysts also saw opportunities to buy into the currency.   

"As the central bank's stance is still to go for the Singapore dollar's appreciation to curb rising inflation, further weakening of SGD would present a good entry point to enter a Singapore dollar-basket trade," Shiang Hue Lye, currency strategist at ABN AMRO, said in a research note. title: UPDATE 1-S.Korea's  FX  reserves up as  intervention  cited
text:
(Recasts with intervention talk, adds background)   

SEOUL, May 3 (Reuters) - South Korea's foreign exchange reserves rose the most in four months in April, central bank data showed on Thursday, as foreign exchange dealers and analysts said the country conducted intervention to curb strength in the won.   


 The country's foreign exchange reserves -- the world's
fifth-largest in March -- rose to $247.3 billion as of the end of
   

April from $243.9 billion a month earlier, the Bank of Korea said in a statement.   

The gain of $3.3 billion , or 1.4 percent, was the largest since a $4.7 billion rise posted in December. Currency market players have said big changes in foreign reserves usually reflect the country's intervention in the foreign exchange market.   

The Bank of Korea attributed the rise in April to strength in non-dollar currencies and investment gains.   

But dealers and analysts in Seoul said the country's foreign exchange authorities had been suspected of buying about a combined $1 billion during the month.   

Officials at the finance ministry and the central bank declined to comment.   

South Korean foreign reserves have risen by 3.5 percent, or $8.3 billion, so far this year, Bank of Korea data shows. Its reserves rank behind those of China, Japan, Russia and Taiwan.   

The central bank said 85.5 percent of April's total reserves were invested in securities, compared with 14.3 percent deposited at financial institutions.

title: Emerging  FX -Rupee at 9-yr high, won slips on current account
text:
SINGAPORE, April 26 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee hit a 9-year high on Thursday as investors doubted the central bank would intervene, but South Korea's won slipped after data showed the country's current account swung into deficit.   

Most Asian currencies were range-bound as the dollar remained within sight of its record low against the euro <EUR=> after mixed U.S. data that did little to allay market fears of a slowdown in the world's largest economy.   

"I guess the dollar continues to be in the doldrums with sentiment towards Asian currencies still positive," said Emmanuel Ng, a currency strategist at  OCBC Bank.

Suspected dollar-buying by the Bank of Korea also weighed on the won <KRW=>, dealers said, after data showed South Korea's current account swung to a seasonally adjusted deficit of $446 million in March from a surplus in February.   

"They don't want the won to go up further as the appreciation may affect the economic picture, but investors, especially foreign investors, still think it's still too cheap," said a dealer at a major Korean bank in Seoul.   

The won weakened as low as 930 to the dollar, down almost 0.4 percent from late Asian trade on Wednesday.   

UBS analysts said in a research note that they expected the pace of the won's appreciation against the dollar to slow, but they maintained a three-month forecast of 920 per dollar.   

The analysts estimated that the Bank of Korea's average monthly dollar-buying intervention had eased to $1.5 billion in the first quarter of this year from $2.0 billion in 2006.   

RUPEE SHINES   

The Indian rupee <INR=IN> rose as high as 40.71 per dollar as investors shrugged off worries of official steps to limit further gains in Asia's best-performing currency this year.   

It rallied past 41 on Wednesday for the first time in nine years.   

The rupee has risen 8.4 percent against the dollar this year, including an increase of about 3 percent in the past week, which some analysts said could help India check inflationary pressures.   

But Reserve Bank of India Governor Yaga Venugopal Reddy said on Wednesday that might not be the case and in fact could fuel demand.   

The Philippine peso <PHP=> rose moderately to 47.435 per dollar as concerns over the surprise resignation of the national treasurer eased.   

The peso came under brief selling pressure on Wednesday after Omar Cruz quit.   

"It's in a tight range but the market seems to have absorbed concerns about Cruz's resignation," a Manila-based trader said.   

"They are looking at the possibility that the fiscal position improvements stay intact."

title: Emerging  FX -Rupee powers to 9-year high, won at 16-week peak
text:
SINGAPORE, April 23 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee extended gains to a nine-year high versus the dollar on Monday, outpacing most other Asian currencies on strong capital inflows.   

 Foreign buying in South Korea's equity market helped push the won <KRW=> to a 16-week high, while the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> tested last week's nine-year peaks before suspected dollar-buying intervention by the central bank pushed the currency down.   

 Asia's other currencies nudged lower, with a rally in the yen encouraging investors to unwind yen carry trades for now. Most regional units have benefited from such trades that involve selling the low-yielding yen to fund investments in assets that offer a higher yield.   

 The rupee <INR=IN> briefly rose to 41.56 per dollar, its highest level since May 1998, helped by a rally in the stock market <.BSESN> and news on Friday that India's annual inflation rate unexpectedly jumped back above 6 percent in early April.   

 It has gained more than 6 percent this year, putting it clearly ahead as Asia's best performing currency against the dollar. This month alone the rupee has jumped 4 percent.   

 "Everybody's looking at the rupee and there has been a sudden surge of interest in the Indian currency," said BNP Paribas currency strategist Thio Chin Loo.   

 "People are searching for value in Asia and the fact that the Indian rupee hadn't moved that much, so traders are looking at the opportunities there."   

INTERVENTION CAUTION   

 Dealers said wariness about central bank intervention to curb rupee strength forced the currency to give up some of its gains.   

 And elsewhere in the region, dealers remained watchful of possible dollar-buying intervention by central banks.   

 A trader in Kuala Lumpur said Malaysia's central bank was suspected of intervening in the market after the ringgit strengthened to 3.42 per dollar -- matching a nine-year high set at the end of last week.   

 "I think they (the central bank) were in the market at 3.42," said the trader. "Given the strong sentiment towards Malaysia, we will break 3.42 soon."   

 The won rose to 925.10 per dollar, its highest level since Jan. 3, amid strong foreign buying of Korean shares.   

 The benchmark KOSPI <.KS11> share index hit a record high on Monday and foreign investors were net buyers for a seventh consecutive session, bringing their total during that period to a net 1.2 trillion won ($1.30 billion) worth.   

 Still, the upbeat won sentiment was tempered slightly by wariness about intervention.   

 On Friday, South Korea warned speculators against piling borrowed foreign funds into the won, and the central bank said monitoring of the currency market had shown excessive speculative trading of foreign currencies by some companies.   

 "We suspect this reflects genuine worries about the possibility of a new surge in exporter selling taking dollar/won still lower," ABN AMRO currency strategist Shahab Jalinoos said in a note to clients.   

 "Exporters such as shipbuilders have been less active in the market than in 2006, but in recent days their presence has been noted."   

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> touched a fresh six-year high at 47.43 per dollar before declining to a session low at 47.67 as investors booked profits on recent peso gains.   

 A trader in Manila said he did not think the central bank had stepped into the market to curb the peso, although it has been suspected of intervention in the last few weeks.   

 "We hit 47.43 and then there was some profit-taking and some short-covering," he said. "It looks like some people were looking to reverse the market."

title: Emerging  FX -Sing dlr pushed off highs, peso hits six-year peak
text:
SINGAPORE, April 10 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar was knocked back from 9-1/2-year highs on Tuesday by suspected central bank intervention, but the Philippine peso climbed to a six-year peak thanks to inflows that had piled up over Easter.   

 Wariness about official intervention to curb currency gains kept other Asian units in a tight range, although sentiment remained positive due to the firm tone in equity markets.   

 Stronger-than-expected economic growth and the central bank's decision to stick to a policy of modest currency appreciation lifted the Singapore dollar to 1.5110 per U.S. dollar <SGD=>.   

 But the gains proved fleeting and it fell as low as 1.5188 on suspected U.S. dollar-buying intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).   

 Still, dealers said the central bank's monetary policy stance and optimism about the economy meant that bullish sentiment towards the local dollar would hold sway.   

 "We definitely had first-quarter GDP on the strong side of expectations, so that would seem to indicate that Singapore is handling the downturn in the electronics cycle quite well," said Magnus Prim, chief strategist for Asia at SEB.   

 "The MAS still has a modest tightening bias and that basically translates into a stronger currency, even though at this point in time we are at the stronger end of the band and that is why we probably saw them intervening."   

 Singapore's economy grew an annualised 7.2 percent in the first quarter, well above forecasts, although a little slower than in the previous quarter.   

 The central bank maintained its policy of a "gradual and modest appreciation" in the Singapore dollar. It uses the exchange rate rather than interest rates to conduct monetary policy and guides the currency in a secret trade-weighted band.   

 "I think the Sing dollar will continue to appreciate against the U.S. dollar but in a slow creeping movement," said Alvin Cheng, a trader at  Fortis Bank Hong Kong Branch.   

 PESO IN DEMAND   

 The peso <PHP=> rose as far as 47.94 per dollar, compared with about 48.05 late on Wednesday, April 4, when Philippine markets were last open before an extended Easter break.   

 "The market is expecting inflows from over the long weekend -- a combination of remittances and equity flows," said a trader in Manila, explaining the peso's rally.   

 "A strong break of the 48 level would lead us to test the 47.50 area."   

 Some traders thought the Philippine central bank had stepped into the market to stall a rapid appreciation of the peso.   

 There was also caution about possible intervention in South Korea and Malaysia.   

 The won <KRW=> held a narrow range between 932 and about 934 per dollar. The ringgit <MYR=> was steady at 3.4455 per dollar, having touched a nine-year high at about 3.4420.   

 Elsewhere, the Thai baht <THB=TH> was little moved at about 34.95 to the dollar in the onshore market.   

 Traders expected the currency to come under pressure after army-appointed Prime Minister Surayud Chulanont was admitted to hospital on Monday for a four-day medical check-up amid rumours he would resign.

title: Bank Of Korea Gov: Korea GDP To Grow Mid-4% In 2007
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--Bank of Korea Governor Lee Seongtae said Thursday that the country's gross domestic product will grow around the mid-4% range this year, slower than last year's 5% growth.  

"The economy is moderating with private consumption slowing, but given a continued recovery in exports, the economy will show mid-4% growth this year," Lee told the National Assembly's finance and economy committee. [ 22-02-07 0551GMT ]  

Lee also said exports will remain strong, although he admitted that domestic demand is slowing.  

Future monetary policy will be aimed at taming inflation, which is likely to stay stable throughout this year, and at improving the economy, he said.  

The Bank of Korea said in a statement that it would monitor the country's asset market even more closely this year. Spurred by higher housing costs, asset prices have been rising in South Korea, threatening inflation.  

The governor said efforts by the government and the central bank to curb property costs appear to be working because the real estate market is showing signs of stabilization.  

"Since the rise (in housing prices) is slowing, it seems like the policies are showing effects... but it still needs to be watched continuously," Lee said.  

Lee said the record-high foreign exchange reserve level isn't the result of the central bank's aggressive dollar-buying intervention in the currency market.  

At the end of January, South Korea's foreign exchange reserves rose to $240.23 billion, up $1.27 billion from a month earlier, largely because of capital gains from investments of U.S. dollar holdings.  

South Korea's foreign exchange reserves are the fifth-largest in the world.

title: Emerging  FX -Philippine peso at new high, others range-bound
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 16 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso extended this week's gains to hit a six-year peak against the U.S. dollar on Friday, while the Singapore dollar drew support from tax changes in the budget.  

The yen rallied more than half a percent against the dollar <JPY=>, holding near a one-month high hit the previous day after strong Japanese economic growth data.  

This lent some support to Asian currencies. But wariness about central bank intervention limited gains, while trade was also subdued before next week's Chinese New Year holiday in parts of the region.  

Markets in China, Hong Kong, Malaysia, Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan are closed on Monday.  

The peso <PHP=> strengthened as far as 48.09 to the dollar, its highest level in almost six years. It is Asia's strongest currency so far this year with a gain of 1.8 percent, spurred by strong inflows of remittances from overseas workers and a rally in the local stock market.  

"Upbeat regional sentiment is making the peso stronger," said a Manila trader. "There is always the possibility of the central bank coming in, but I don't think they have been in yet."  

Another peso trader said the central bank was suspected of capping peso gains at around 48.23/25 per dollar on Thursday.  

Dealers in Singapore and South Korea were also on guard over central bank intervention to curb local currency strength.  

South Korea is watching the won's <KRW=> recent sharp rise against the yen <JPYKRW=R> but is not targeting a specific rate, senior finance ministry official Hur Kyung-wook said on Friday.  

The won dipped as much as a quarter of a percent to almost 937 per dollar.  

UPBEAT SINGAPORE DOLLAR  

In Singapore traders remained wary of the Monetary Authority of Singapore after it was suspected of buying U.S. dollars aggressively in the market earlier this week.  

But they said sentiment towards the Singapore dollar <SGD=> remained bullish, helped by Thursday's budget.  

The Singapore government said it would raise the goods and services tax (GST) to 7 percent from 5 percent from July 1 and cut corporate tax by 2 percentage points to 18 percent from next year. This helped send Singapore's Strait Times Index <.STI> to a record high in early trade on Friday before easing.  

"The outlook remains very positive -- stocks are doing well, the budget was reasonably good and the corporate tax cut adds to the feel-good factor," said one Singapore dollar trader.  

"The MAS is likely to be in the market around the 1.5320 area to buy U.S. dollars, but the overwhelming feeling is to sell the U.S. dollar on rallies."  

The Singapore dollar was trading about 1.5330 per U.S. dollar, up about 0.7 percent from a one-month low hit on Tuesday.  

Sean Callow, a senior currency strategist at Westpac Bank, said U.S. capital flows data on Thursday suggested U.S. investors' appetite for foreign assets was growing and this boded well for Asian currencies.  

The United States reported a net overall capital outflow of $11 billion for December, the first outflow in nearly two years.  

"U.S. investors are increasing their demand for equities and Asia is clearly getting a chunk of that," Callow said.  

Elsewhere, the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> briefly strengthened to about 9,030 per dollar -- its strongest in just over a month.  

There was some focus on comments by Aslim Tadjuddin, a deputy governor at Bank Indonesia, who said the central bank sees room for a cut next month in its reference interest rate.  

Bank Indonesia has cut its key rate nine times in less than a year, reducing it from 12.75 percent in April last year to 9.25 percent this month, as price pressures eased significantly from the inflation shock in late 2005.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia gets a supportive hand from the yen
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 25 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were largely steady on Thursday, underpinned by a strong recovery in the yen on reports that European officials may complain about yen weakness at a Group of Seven (G7) meeting in February.  

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> was in focus before an interest rate decision, with comments earlier this week from the central bank governor dampening expectations for a rate reduction.  

 Gains in some regional currencies, such as the Singapore dollar <SGD=>, South Korean won <KRW=> and Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> were limited by wariness that authorities would or had stepped into the market to cap currency gains.  

 Westpac Bank analysts said the market was wary of central bank intervention on the Singapore dollar around the 1.5350 per U.S. dollar area.  

 In Seoul, the won ended the day around 936 per dollar after what dealers called "smoothing operations" by the authorities.  

 South Korean Finance Minister Kwon O-kyu warned on Thursday against excessive dollar/won forward sales by local exporters, which the government has blamed for the won's sharp rise versus the dollar and yen.  

 "It is interesting to see how central banks in Asia are managing liquidity and encouraging outflows," said Mirza Baig, a currency strategist at Deutsche Bank.  

 "That does take pressure off central banks to intervene."  

South Korea said last week it planned to encourage local companies to invest abroad by giving them tax breaks, the latest in a series of efforts to take pressure off the won.  The fortunes of the yen <JPY=>, meanwhile, remained in focus.  

 Yen carry trades, where investors have sold the low-yielding yen to invest in higher yielding currencies, helped push the yen to a four-year low versus the dollar earlier this week.  

 But on Wednesday a short-covering rally that continued after reports about next month's G7 meeting won the yen a reprieve. It traded around 120.40 per dollar, up 0.4 percent from late Wednesday levels.  

 A PHILIPPINE RATE CUT?  

 The peso was little moved at about 48.90 per dollar, with attention fixed on this session's central bank rate decision.  

 Expectations that interest rates would be lowered this week were dampened on Monday when Governor Amando Tetangco suggested that a rate cut was not a done deal.  

 His deputy said on Wednesday that rates could be held steady and a tiering system for overnight rates maintained, but that the central bank's board would make the final decision.  

 "Markets are largely expecting no change but will look at the rhetoric from the monetary policy board," a Manila trader said.  

 Elsewhere, the Thai baht <THB=> edged higher and was quoted at about 35.75 per dollar in the onshore market, compared with about 35.95 on Wednesday.  

 A trader in Bangkok said dollar selling by exporters had pushed the baht up in thin volumes.  

 "There's also a rumour that maybe the Bank of Thailand will take action soon on the exchange rate -- there is a lot of pressure on it to ease the capital control regulations."  

 Since the central bank unveiled capital controls in December, there has essentially been a two-tier market in the baht, with an offshore and an onshore aspect.  

 Analysts said reports this week that Thailand could take measures to improve trading liquidity in the offshore market and investor-friendly comments from officials have helped sentiment.  

 "In the last few days the government and central bank have sounded more investor friendly," said OCBC currency strategist Emmanuel Ng. "As long as the capital controls remain, a two-tier market will persist."  Change on the day at 0748 GMT

title: UPDATE 2-S.Korea plans tax breaks on investment to curb won
text:
(Adds market reaction, economist, details)  

 SEOUL, Jan 15 (Reuters) - South Korea said on Monday it planned to encourage local companies to invest abroad by giving them tax breaks, the latest in a series of efforts to take pressure off a strong won currency.  

 Finance Minister Kwon O-kyu told a media briefing that he anticipated a sizeable outflow of funds this year as a result of the move.  

 "The following measures are expected to see results of an outflow of around $10 billion-$15 billion, which is an outstanding effect to the market," Kwon O-kyu said.  

 Kwon added it was a conservative estimate, giving room for a possibly larger effect after the proposals are implemented.  

 The government is to exempt taxes on further marginal profits generated from overseas investment by South Korean investment firms and securities companies, starting from the first quarter of this year for the next three years.  

 Until recently, the government had deducted tax from income at source at the rate of 14 percent  

 "The measures are to maintain a balance of the supply and demand in the foreign currency market by promoting an outflow of foreign currencies and adjusting the inflow to an optimum level," the finance ministry said in a statement.  

 Local financial market showed littled reaction to the news. The won <KRW=> rose slightly to 938.3/8.7 against the dollar from Friday's close of 939.70, treasury bond futures were quoted four ticks lower at 108.15, and the stock market's KOSPI <.KS11> edged up 0.19 percent.  

 "The announcement didn't have any vast changes in it which could affect the market in the short term. Although, three years of tax-free investment is certainly an attractive proposal and will probably heat up overseas investments eventually," said Ryu Seung-sun, economist at Mirae Asset Securities.  

 Meanwhile, South Korea's Export-Import Bank is to issue $0.1 billion worth of foreign currency bonds while increasing bonds in won-terms to a total of 1.7 trillion won ($1.81 billion) this year from 0.7 trillion won issued in 2006.  

 ONE-SIDED POLICY  

 Financial authorities are looking to follow up on existing measures to stimulate overseas investment and pump more dollars out of the South Korean economy.  

 "Financial institutions still remain too reluctant in investing abroad. They should be encouraged to invest more abroad," said Rhee Yeung-kyun, a deputy governor of the Bank of Korea, said over lunch with foreign journalists on Monday.  

 "As you know, we need to pump out (capital)."  

 However, analysts said that government measures to cool the won could backfire.  

 "This may be the same as pouring oil into the fire. The government is only thinking about one side of the problem. What if the won suddenly turns lower?" an economist at a local securities firm said.  

 The central bank forecast in December that South Korea would post a current surplus of about $2 billion in 2007, marking a record of 10 consecutive years of surplus.  

 Meanwhile, foreign exchange reserves from Asia's third-largest economy jumped $4.7 billion in December for the sixth straight month, data showed, amid dealer reports of heavy government dollar-buying intervention aimed at capping the won's rise.  

South Korea has already eased rules on overseas investment in securities and real estate to take some air out of the won, which gained 28 percent in the past three years against the dollar.  ($1=939.7 Won)  (Additional reporting by Yoo Choonsik and Lee Shin-hyung)

title: Emerging  FX -Asia inches down, shrugging off yen gains
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 5 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies edged lower on Friday, undermined by a sell-off in commodity currencies that overshadowed strong gains in the Japanese yen.  

Against the trend, the Philippine peso <PHP=> held near a six-year peak of 48.80 per dollar, supported by upbeat inflation data.  

In contrast, the South Korean won <KRW=> fell to a six-week low at about 935 per dollar, the Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> eased 0.3 percent to 32.66 to the U.S. dollar and the Singapore dollar <SGD=> dipped to a session low of 1.5374 per U.S. dollar, within sight of Thursday's one-week trough.  

"People are a bit edgy that a pull-back in commodities could mean an adjusting of positions in Asian currencies as well," said Sean Callow, a currency strategist at Westpac Bank.  

"We're also coming up to the payrolls report and, if it surprises on the strong side, it could cause a reassessment of the Fed outlook -- so perhaps it's not the best day to be long on risky assets like Asian equities and currencies."  

U.S. non-farm payroll figures are due at 1330 GMT. The median forecast in a Reuters poll was for the payrolls to show a gain of 100,000 jobs in December after a 132,000 rise in November.  

The Australian and New Zealand dollars <AUD=><NZD=> fell sharply against the U.S. currency, weighed down by softer industrial metals and gains in the yen.  

The yen traded at about 118.30 per dollar <JPY=>, up almost 0.9 percent from late Asian trade on Thursday.  

The peso was helped by news that Philippine consumer prices in December rose 4.3 percent from a year earlier, at the lower end of the central bank's forecast range, bolstering the prospects of an interest rate cut early this year.  

PROBLEMS FOR BAHT, WON  

The Thai baht hovered near 36 per dollar <THB=> and was in focus following talk in the market of another coup after the military takeover in September.  

Sentiment towards the baht has been hurt in recent weeks, first by the imposition of capital controls and then by bomb attacks that killed three people in Bangkok on New Year's Eve.  

"At the moment the talk of a counter-coup in Thailand is being treated as a rumour," said a trader in Hong Kong.  

"But the baht is unlikely to follow gains in other currencies. It is a spillover from the New Year bombing and people are afraid of further bad news."  

Jitters about Thailand's political situation continued to weigh on the stock market <.SETI>, which was down more than 2 percent.  

Sentiment towards the Korean won was undermined by concern about possible government measures to curb the currency's strength.  

South Korea's finance minister said late on Thursday the country would not take measures to restrict dollar inflows, a day after the president said he would prevent the won from damaging the economy.  

Analysts at UBS said South Korea was more likely to step up intervention in the currency market to rein in the won than introduce the sort of direct capital controls brought in by the Bank of Thailand in December.  

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> weakened about a quarter of a percent to 9,020 per dollar.  

"The market is just trying to square up positions," said a dealer in Jakarta. "Liquidity is not too high, so small deals can have a bigger impact." CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0743 GMT

text:
(Update to close)  

SEOUL, Jan 3 (Reuters) - The South Korean won was virtually unchanged on Wednesday in dull trade, lacking fresh direction with Tokyo financial markets closed for holidays.  

Investors remained wary of possible dollar buying intervention by South Korean authorities, while offshore players bought the U.S. currency, but exporters also sold dollars for the won.

Investors almost ignored South Korea's forecasts for this year's export growth.  

Asia's third-largest economy expects export to grow 10.4 percent in 2007, decelerating from a 14.6 percent gain in 2006 hit by a slowdown in the U.S. economy. Imports will probably rise a faster 10.9 percent, resulting in a surplus of $17 billion vs $16.7 billion in 2006. [ID:nSEO143087]  

But the won is expected to be supported, given the forecast of a trade surplus, in the longer term although growth in exports is seen slowing, analysts said.  

The Japanese yen <JPY=> was quoted at 118.81/83 per dollar, compared with 118.85 late in New York, with a holiday in Tokyo keeping trading thin.

title: S.Korea  FX  reserves jump amid  intervention  talk
text:
SEOUL, Jan 3 (Reuters) - South Korea's foreign exchange reserves jumped $4.7 billion in December, data showed on Wednesday, amid dealer reports of heavy government dollar-buying intervention aimed at capping the won's rise. The central bank said the country's foreign exchange reserves, the world's fifth-largest, rose for the sixth consecutive month to $239.0 billion by the end of December from $234.3 billion a month earlier.  

The Bank of Korea attributed the rise to investment gains, receipt of proceeds from the country's sales of about $1 billion in overseas bonds and deposits of required cash reserves from financial institutions.  

But the data comes after local currency dealers have suspected the government and the central bank purchased billions of dollars on the local market in intervention aimed at capping the won's <KRW=> strength against the dollar and yen.  

Traders and analysts are closely looking at the data as any unusual change in the foreign reserves, a majority believed to be invested in dollar assets, could reflect the central bank's intervention in the currency market.  

Compared with the end of 2005, the country's foreign reserves rose by $28.57 billion, or 13.6 percent, the data showed.  

The Bank of Korea said in the statement the country held 84.5 percent of the total reserves in securities including sovereign bonds and mortgage-backed securities, compared with 15.2 percent held in deposits at financial institutions.

 SEOUL, Dec 19 (Reuters) - The South Korean won <KRW=> dropped against the dollar for a third session on Tuesday after Thailand's central bank announced steps to rein in sharp gains in the baht and amid caution over possible dollar-buying intervention by South Korea.  

 Some investors kept covering dollar-short positions, putting pressure on the won, although the local currency cut losses due to exporters' dollar supplies.

text:
(Recasts, adds background)  

 SEOUL, Dec 4 (Reuters) - South Korea's foreign exchange reserves rose the most in seven months in November, central bank data showed on Monday, a month in which dealers said the country carried out heavy intervention to contain a rallying won.  


 The country's foreign exchange reserves -- the world's
fifth-largest in October -- rose for the fifth consecutive month
  

to $234.26 billion by the end of November from $229.46 billion a
month earlier, the Bank of Korea said.  

 The rise of $4.80 billion, or 2.1 percent, was the largest
since a $5.55 billion gain posted in April. Currency dealers and
analysts have said big changes in foreign reserves usually
reflect the country's intervention in the market.  

 The Bank of Korea in a statement attributed the rise in
  


November to strength in non-dollar currencies -- which boosts
dollar value of holdings in other units -- and investment gains.
  

 Dealers in Seoul had earlier said South Korean authorities
purchased about a combined $2 billion in two days of heavy
intervention during November, and an additional unspecified
amount for several other days during the month.  

 South Korean foreign reserves have risen by 11 percent, or
$23.87 billion, so far this year and have doubled in four years,
Bank of Korea data shows. Its reserves rank behind those of
China, Japan, Russia and Taiwan.  

 Senior officials at South Korea's finance ministry and
central bank have repeatedly voiced concerns that the won <KRW=>
has overshot its fair value and that its sharp rise would hurt
exports or export profitability at local companies.  

 But recent trade figures appeared to belie their concerns as
data on Friday showed that shipments abroad by Asia's
third-largest economy jumped by a fifth in November from a year
earlier, even at a time of a slowing U.S. economy.  

 The commerce ministry said last Wednesday that exports for
all of 2006 would grow 14.6 percent from last year, far outpacing
its earlier projection of 11.8 percent growth.  

 The Korea International Trade Association said on Sunday
exports in 2007 would grow another 10.1 percent.

title: UPDATE: Japan, S Korea Agree To Expand Bilateral Swap Agreement To $70 Billion
text:
-- Japan, South Korea expand bilateral swap to total of $70 billion from $13 billion

-- BOJ, BOK boost yen-won swap agreement tenfold

-- BOK, Japan's MOF agree on new currency swap agreement

(Adds background of deal, statements from two countries, further background in 2nd-3rd, 5th-7th paragraphs)


 
   By Tatsuo Ito and Se Young Lee 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

TOKYO (Dow Jones)--Japan and South Korea said Wednesday they agreed to raise the size of their bilateral currency swap agreement to a total of $70 billion from the current $13 billion to help reassure foreign exchange and financial markets amid growing uncertainty stemming from the European debt crisis.

The issue was on the agenda of Wednesday's summit between South Korean President Lee Myung-bak and visiting Japanese Prime Minister Yoshihiko Noda.

The two countries sought to increase the swap arrangement to a "sufficient" level so that it would act as a mutually beneficial, pre-emptive stability measure, South Korea's Ministry of Strategy and Finance said in a statement. The ministry said the arrangement will help strengthen local banks and corporations' competitive environment, as the deal will ease worries about foreign currency liquidity and lower funding costs. It also said the agreement will help Korea in maintaining a stable sovereign credit rating. Korea currently has an A1 sovereign debt rating from Moody's and an A rating from Standard & Poor's, both with a stable outlook.

Of the total, the central banks of both countries agreed to expand a yen-won swap contract to $30 billion from the current $3 billion. The contract will last until the end of October 2012.

"This action will mitigate adverse influences of heightened uncertainty in the global market on the two sound and well-managed economies and contribute to enhancing stability in regional financial markets," the Bank of Japan said in a statement.

To supplement the measure, Japan's finance ministry and the Bank of Korea sealed a new bilateral currency swap agreement worth $30 billion. Under the agreement, using its external reserves worth $1.2 trillion, Japan's finance ministry can provide South Korea with dollars in exchange for the won if needed. Japan can also obtain dollars from South Korea in exchange for the yen. The pact will be in place for one year.

The announcement was seen by the foreign exchange market as helping South Korea deal with the weakening won, which has been falling against the yen. Following the news, the yen fell to as low as KRW14.716 on EBS from around KRW14.900 earlier in the day. On Oct. 4, the yen had been as high as KRW15.759.

A Japan Ministry of Finance official said that in theory, South Korea could use raised dollars through the swap agreement with Japan for currency intervention. South Korea's external reserves are around $300 billion.

In addition, both countries maintained the existing Chiang Mai Initiative deal--a multilateral currency swap agreement aimed at dealing with short-term liquidity problems--at $10 billion.

The crisis-prevention measures, created after the Asian financial crisis in 1997-1998, have never been used.

-By Tatsuo Ito, Dow Jones Newswires; +813-6269-2780; tatsuo.ito@dowjones.com

--Megumi Fujikawa contributed to this article [ 19-10-11 0543GMT ]

title: ECONOMIC SIGNALS-South Korea adds new weapons to arsenal as clouds gather
text:
SEOUL, Oct 11 (Reuters) - South Korea's surprisingly small currency interventions in September were probably based on lessons learnt from past crises, and underscored a policy dilemma in tackling the opposing risks facing one of Asia's most vulnerable economies.

As global investors dumped riskier assets in recent weeks, the Bank of Korea sold only $3-4 billion to slow the won's

sharp fall, out of the more than $300 billion of reserves it manages, central bank data showed last week.

Many analysts said they were surprised at the central bank's relative restraint, especially as government officials were calling for calm and reviving weekly crisis meetings to try to stem capital flight.

Analysts noted the overall intervention was less than what regional rival Taiwan spent defending its currency . The won ended up losing over 9 percent to the dollar in September, far more than the Taiwan unit's 5 percent fall.

The following figures and graphics explain the complicated risks facing South Korea's policymakers and Asia's fourth-largest economy, which relies heavily on exports for growth as domestic demand remains depressed:

WHY DIDN'T IT SPEND MORE ON INTERVENTION?

The country's foreign reserves stood at a record $312 billion, twice the size of its short-term overseas debt and sufficient to cover some seven months of imports, but defending the highly symbolic $300 billion mark was important politically.

Despite fears of massive outflows, the actual amount of foreign funds leaving the country was relatively modest as countries such as China, Thailand and Kazakhstan kept on buying South Korean won bonds to diversify their reserves away from the dollar or euro, offsetting sales of Korean assets by panicky Western investors.

Some analysts also said the Bank of Korea had room to short dollar/won positions in derivatives markets to stem the won's decline, limiting the use of reserves money which is disclosed to the public every month.

LESSONS FROM CRISES, NEW CAPITAL CONTROLS

South Korea saw its foreign reserves plunge by one-fifth or nearly $50 billion in four months in late 2008 as the global financial crisis raged. Policymakers spent most of the funds fighting to prop up the free-falling won, only to witness the currency lose over 30 percent of its value against the dollar.

That lesson, combined with current-day worries over how long Europe's festering debt crisis will last and how much damage it will inflict on the global economy, likely persuaded South Korea to save as much ammunition as possible in case things get worse.

South Korea's heavy short-term overseas debt and easy flows of capital leave it especially vulnerable during times of crisis, undermining the won. But policymakers have implemented a string of more sophisticated measures since 2008/09 aimed at reducing the economy's exposure to external shocks.

The country has cut the ratio of short-term debt to foreign reserves to less than 50 percent from nearly 80 percent a few years ago.

Since last year, it also has introduced three sets of capital controls, including outright limitations on the amount of currency derivatives trade, and can now adjust these measures if needed to try to control capital flows.

INFLATION PAST PEAK, EXPORTS LOSING STEAM

To be sure, a weaker won will also help South Korean exporters cope better with shrinking global demand, adding to the argument against massive forex intervention to pin the currency to stronger levels. In 2008-2009, exporters boosted global market share on the back of a 40 percent fall in the won's value over several months.

South Korea's exports have held up well when measured in dollar value terms, offsetting sluggish domestic demand, but manufacturing production has been weakening while inventories of finished goods are piling up as global consumption ebbs.

The won had risen more than 8 percent against the dollar by mid-summer, helping curb imported inflation and thus giving authorities more leeway in deciding the pace of interest rate increases. The currency gave back all those gains in the late summer market rout, and is now down 2.7 percent in the year to date.

Consumer inflation is believed to have peaked in August and eased in September, and a collapse in farm product prices from unusually high levels in 2010 should offset the rise in import prices due to the won's weakening. That would give the central bank more room to focus on the risks from an economic slowdown and further market turmoil.

Both the finance minister and central bank chief admitted in a surprisingly swift manner that this year's inflation target would not be reachable, indicating foreign exchange policy will not be fully skewed toward curbing inflation.

(Editing by Jonathan Hopfner & Kim Coghill)

title: WRAPUP 4-South Korea's gloomy economic data spooks markets
text:
* S.Korean manufacturing activity shrinks most in 11 mths-survey

 * Falling demand from China, others worrying - economists

 * Stocks plunge as markets play catch-up after Monday's holiday

 * Won slumps, govt warns of stronger dollar-selling intervention

(Adds government warning of intervention)

 By Yoo Choonsik

 SEOUL, Oct 4 (Reuters) - South Korea's manufacturing sector activity shrank the most in 11 months in September as new export orders fell sharply, reinforcing fears of a slide back into global recession that are battering financial markets in one of Asia's most vulnerable economies.  

 Economists said findings from the survey of South Korean purchasing managers at manufacturing firms were worrying as they indicated shrinking demand from China and other emerging economies as well as from the advanced economies.

 "The fall in the PMI export orders component comes at what should be the strongest quarter for Korea's exports," said Tim Condon, head of Asia research at ING in Singapore.

 "The failure of export shipments to claw back more of the August contraction in September was a worrying signal that global growth might be slowing," he added, referring to a sharp decline in export shipments in August from July.

 The benchmark stock index fell as much as 6 percent before cutting losses to finish down 3.6 percent, partly catching up with markets elsewhere in the region after a public holiday on Monday. The sharp falls prompted the bourse operator to suspend programme sales for five minutes. 

 The won fell to a 14-month low, prompting authorities in Seoul to intervene again in foreign exchange markets to support the retreating currency.

 Vice Finance Minister Shin Je-yoon later issued a rare warning of intensified intervention at a briefing arranged after local trading finished. 

 Government data released last week showed South Korea's goods shipments for export markets fell by a seasonally adjusted 0.2 percent in August over the month before, in addition to a 1.7 percent fall in July.

 South Korea is home to some of the world's leading suppliers of electronics and cars, while its exports include half-assembled kits that are completed elsewhere and re-exported to developed countries.

 POSSIBLE DOWNGRADES

 The latest economic data pointed to the central bank, which has been slow to raise rates, keeping borrowing costs on hold.

 Some economists have already said they expected South Korea's quarterly economic growth to nearly halve in the third quarter from the 0.9 percent rise in April-June and that they may have to review such projections for a possible downgrade.

 The HSBC/Markit Economics survey showed the country's manufacturing-sector activity probably shrank for a second consecutive month and by the most in 11 months during September as export orders tumbled. 

 The survey findings were in line with results of similar surveys on other manufacturing powerhouses, including China, but were released later due to a public holiday on Monday.

 The won pared some of the losses on buying by exporters and talk of government intervention, but still ended down 1.3 percent against the dollar. It has lost 5 percent so far this year, largely in the last few months as investors globally dumped riskier assets for the relative safety of the dollar.

 In addition, the won also received some relief after industry sources told Reuters foreign central banks and funds have been purchasing South Korean won bonds. 

 As the global turmoil makes it hard for smaller trading firms to secure dollar financing, the top financial regulatory agency called a meeting on Thursday with policy banks to discuss lending to the firms in foreign currencies. 

 STUBBORN INFLATION

 Separate government data, released before markets opened, showed consumer price inflation eased by a full percentage point in September but stayed above the central bank's target range for a ninth consecutive month. 

 Core inflation remained stubbornly high at 3.9 percent year-on-year, down from 4.0 percent in August, and, while a weaker won will feed through to higher inflation, lower oil prices will help tame rising prices, economists said.

 Persistently high inflation, even as the country's heavily export-dependent economy cools, puts the central bank in the most difficult position since the 2008 global financial crisis in managing its interest rate policy.

 Bank of Korea governor, Kim Choong-soo, said in August it  would not raise rates as long as uncertainty persisted in  global markets.

 It had raised the policy interest rate by a total of 125 basis points between July last year and June this year, unwinding part of reductions of 325 basis points delivered during the height of the 2008-2009 global crisis.

 The central bank has held the 7-day repurchase agreement rate for the past three months in a row and meets again on Oct. 13. 

(Additional reporting by Joonhee Yu and Lim Seung-gyu; Editing by Kim Coghill, Alex Richardson and Ramya Venugopal)

title: EM ASIA  FX -Fund redemptions hit baht, Philippine peso
text:
* Equity market outflows hurt baht, peso

* Won gives up Friday's gains on lack of intervention

* Intervention from Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia spotted

(Updates text, prices)

By Jongwoo Cheon

SINGAPORE, Sept 26 (Reuters) - The Thai baht and Philippine peso fell on Monday, with talk of equity fund redemptions driving investors to sell off what had been two outperforming Asian currencies earlier in the year.

Authorities in Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia were battling the market on Monday, selling U.S. dollars from their reserve stockpiles to protect their currencies, though South Korea notably did not intervene.

The outlook on emerging markets globally is dark as most dealers are looking for chances to sell those units on rebounds on persistent worries about the euro zone's sovereign crisis. A sharp decline in emerging market currencies has preceded broader weakness in risky assets.

"I will keep buying dollar/Asia on dips as we have not seen signs of an end in the crisis yet," said a senior currency dealer at a European bank in Singapore.

"Asian authorities are expected to keep intervening, but their intervention would be a just temporary tool, which will not be able to stop the trend."

Emerging Asian currencies have been pressured by dollar-demand in non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) from leveraged and institutional investors, who have over the past few weeks rushed to hedge against more local currency weakness. Some funds were building up dollar-long positions against the regional units.

Last week, the Singapore dollar, once the safe-haven in Asia, posted the largest weekly percentage fall by losing 4.6 percent against the U.S. dollar, according to Reuters' calculation based on the central bank data. The Indian rupee

also saw the worst week in more than 15 years.

The losses came as other emerging currencies and growth-linked units broadly fell. The Brazil's real lost 7.5 percent last week, although the central bank's sale of $2.75 billion of currency swaps limited its falls.

On Monday, the Australian dollar also fell to a 10-month low against the U.S. dollar.

WON

The won slid to a one-year low versus the greenback, wiping out Friday's intervention-driven gains, without signs of dollar-selling by the authorities.

The South Korean currency ended local trade at 1,195.8, slightly stronger than Friday's 1,196.0, the softest since early Sept last year.

Earlier, the won had found some relief from bond inflows, but investors dumped the unit again with no sign of authorities.

"There is a consensus that the authorities will defend 1,200 after last week's intervention. But people are using strategies to buy it (dollar/won) until levels where the BOK is seen and sell it there, given no sellers except the BOK," said a trading head of a foreign bank in Seoul.

After domestic market closed, Deputy Finance Minister Choi Jong-ku said the country will closely monitor any speculative trade behind the recent won's falls.

SINGAPORE DOLLAR

Macro funds, leveraged accounts and U.S. investment banks pushed the Singapore dollar down to near the 50 percent retracement level of its appreciation between June 2010 and July this year.

The city-state's currency also suffered from stops in U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar above 1.3050, while macro funds bought the pair from 1.2915, dealers said.

BAHT, PHILIPPINE PESO

The Thai baht and the Philippine peso

suffered from fund redemption, which hit local stocks, and the currencies are expected to weaken more.

Thai stocks and Philippine shares tumbled a near 9 percent and more 4 percent, respectively.

The baht weakened to as soft as 31.26 per dollar, the softest since late January, breaching the support of 31.00, the level which was where a rejection of dollar/baht's rally was seen just ahead of the Thai election earlier this year.

If the Thai currency stays weaker than that 31.00, it is seen weakening to 31.21-31.29. The 31.29 is the low of Jan 31 and 31.21 is a 100-week moving average.

The Thai central bank was spotted selling dollars from 31.05 level, dealers said, while real money funds kept selling it.

A deputy governor said the central bank is ready to act on excessive move in the baht.

The Philippine peso shed as much as 0.7 percent, weakening past the 61.8 percent retracement of its appreciation between January and August.

The peso may head to 44.02, the session's low of 44.02 per dollar on March 17, while it also has the 76.4 percent retracement around the level.

RINGGIT

The ringgit lost 0.7 percent against the dollar as interbank speculators continued to build up dollar-long positions.

"We stay long as the euro is below 1.3460," said a Kuala Lumpur-based dealer.

But the Malaysian central bank was spotted selling dollars to limit falls in its currency, dealers said.

The central bank was seen at 3.1820 per dollar earlier and it moved dollar offers to 3.1880 and 3.1900 later, they added.

title: DJ CORRECT(9/9): INTERVIEW: Japan Trade Official Slams S Korea Efforts To Weaken Won
text:
("INTERVIEW: Japan Trade Official Slams S Korea Efforts To Weaken Won," on Sept. 9, misquoted Hideichi Okada as referring specifically to intervention by South Korea in the 1st and 7th paragraphs. The correct version follows:)

-- Japan's top trade official expressed concern over South Korea's efforts to weaken won

-- Says cheap won versus yen poses "serious challenge" to Japanese industries

-- Says nations must resolutely fight signs of trade, currency wars

-- Says Japan should deal with any sudden yen rises but also consider positive aspects of a strong currency

-- Expects Japan to make progress on free trade negotiations with EU, China, Korea

By Mitsuru Obe and Arran Scott

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

TOKYO (Dow Jones)--Japan's top trade negotiator Friday expressed concern over South Korea's efforts to depress the value of the won, saying that the currency's relative weakness against the yen posed a "serious challenge" to Japanese industries and indicating that it was inappropriate for Seoul - or indeed any country -- to intervene in the currency market except in extraordinary circumstances.

But Hideichi Okada, vice minister for international affairs at the Ministry Of Economy, Trade and Industry, also praised progress by South Korea in crafting free trade agreements and stressed the need for Japan to strike similar deals with its major trading partners.

Okada emphasized the need for countries to continue to open up global trade, and played down the risk of a rise in protectionism that some analysts have warned may emerge if the global economy takes a turn for the worse.

"Countries still remember that protectionist measures taken after the Great Depression spiraled the global economy into a worldwide depression, so the risk of a similar trade war repeating itself is very small," Okada told Dow Jones Newswires in an interview. "But this does not mean we can drop our guard. We have to fight against any signs of trade and currency wars with strong resolve."

At the same time, the senior official expressed frustration with moves by the Bank of Korea to curb a rise in the won. The BOK has intervened frequently in the foreign exchange market to fight rises in the won, which like other Asian currencies, has faced strong upward pressure as a result of dollar weakness brought on by the U.S. Federal Reserve's easy monetary policy.

Korea has had much more success in tempering the strength in its currency than Japan has had in curbing the rise in the yen, which has set post-World War II highs against the dollar despite interventions by the Japanese authorities. The won's relative weakness against the yen has given Korean exporters an edge over their Japanese rivals in export markets like the U.S. and Europe, where Japanese and Korean automakers and electronics companies compete fiercely.

"The Korean won has gotten very cheap in relation to the Japanese yen. This has posed a serious challenge to Japanese industries competing against their Korean rivals," Okada said. "It is undesirable for any nation to continue interventions in the absence of any unavoidable emergency situation."

"A country should not intentionally depreciate its currency. The value of a currency should be decided in the market," he added.

Okada pointed out, however, that a relatively weak won did have some drawbacks for Korea, noting that some Korean companies depend on Japan for key components in the production of automobiles and electronics products.

With respect to Japan's currency policy, which is set by the Ministry of Finance, Okada said "a sudden appreciation of the yen needs to be dealt with."

He said the yen is on the strong side, noting that the dollar, which traded at Y77.78 late Friday, was below the Y80 level that the bulk of Japanese companies have been counting on. But he said Japan also needs to take into account the positive aspects of the currency's strength, and said he didn't think the yen would return to much lower levels any time soon.

"It is necessary to think of the strong yen as a plus for the country," Okada said. For instance, he said, the strong yen could allow Japan to acquire key resources, such as coal and natural gas, helping the nation prepare for an expected decline in the supply of nuclear-generated power in the future, following the disaster at the Fukushima nuclear plant in March.

He said he expects Prime Minister Yoshihiko Noda to reiterate Japan's intent to pursue free trade agreements with its major trading partners when he makes a policy speech in an extraordinary parliamentary session expected to begin next week. The remark suggests Noda may renew a commitment to join negotiations for a trans-Pacific free trade area involving the U.S. in the near future.

This autumn, the leaders of Japan and the European Union are expected to launch formal negotiations for free trade, he said. Also, Japan is proceeding at pace with the aim of launching talks with Korea and China next year aimed at creating a trilateral FTA, he said.
