title: WSJA(11/8) South Korea Report: The Wild Won
text:
(From THE WALL STREET JOURNAL ASIA) 
   By Min-Jeong Lee 

What's the won worth? In South Korea, you just have to look up to find out. The value is visible nearly everywhere, even flashed on electronic signs as people wait for buses and subway trains.

The reason for the obsession is simple: The won changes value frequently and sometimes wildly. In part, that's because it's one of the few currencies in Asia to float freely. And in part, it's because South Korea's $1 trillion economy depends heavily on international trade, so the currency can't help but be buffeted by global trade and financial flows.

For South Korea, such a free-market approach to its currency is a point of pride: As a developed country, it wants to avoid imposing the kind of strict regulations on the movement of capital that so many less-developed countries practice.

At the same time, though, the won's volatility can be a big problem for a country where more than 40% of economic output comes from the value of the goods it exports, 70% of food is imported and hundreds of thousands of students study overseas. It forces companies of all sizes to routinely engage in currency hedging -- and parents to simply guess when to time transfers for overseas tuition payments. And for foreigners operating businesses in the country, the won's volatility can have a big impact on their plans for sending money into the country to open offices, build factories or make payroll.

Curt Olson, a former chief executive of the South Korean branch of a major financial company, says accountants at headquarters assigned an exchange rate for the won on which internal incentives were based.

"Our actual transactions would reflect the exchange rate, but as a business we were graded on a fixed rate," Mr. Olson says. "That was very internal, a fake number to make sure we didn't do crazy things running the business because of the exchange rate."

Some economists and government officials argue the country could fix the problem by putting some -- though not strict -- restrictions on currency trading, while others say it would be better to go the opposite way and loosen the existing rules on the won. What's more, South Korean officials are seeking agreement at this week's G-20 summit on a "safety net" that would guarantee assistance to countries that are subject to volatile fund flows and currency swings. They want to find a way to tame volatility in the won without having to opt for aggressive currency-market intervention.

South Korea also supports plans by the International Monetary Fund to create new credit lines that would go beyond the regional currency-swap agreements that are now the chief means of stability.

"The country is in dire need of the government's efforts to reduce that volatility," says Kim Seung-hyun, an economist with Taurus Investment & Securities.

The path of the won in recent years is a testament to the dilemma the country faces. Before the Asian financial crisis in 1997, the won was allowed to appreciate against the dollar only within a certain range designated by the government. Today, many other Asian currencies remain at least partially pegged to the dollar.

In order to receive financial assistance from the IMF and global banks in 1997, South Korea had to open its currency market so that the won could float against the dollar and other currencies. That's when the won became driven by capital flows. The local currency floats against the dollar, but the spot market is open for only six hours, which limits trading activity when the local financial markets are shut. Overnight, the won can only be traded via the forward market.

South Korea's big companies have adjusted, hiring accountants and advisers who engage in currency hedging to seek some protection from the volatility. Indeed, shipbuilders are the biggest users of currency hedges. They use them to protect the value of orders because it routinely takes three to four years to deliver a finished ship.

But South Korea's smaller companies have a tougher time, even after trying to hedge against currency swings themselves. Saracom, a midsize maker of marine navigation and communication gear, was delisted from the Kosdaq Stock Market, the smaller of Korea's stock exchanges, early last year after the won's rapid plunge in 2008 left the firm with significant losses from foreign-exchange options contracts. Saracom declined an interview request.

The won's volatility, however, has created the biggest problems for the central bank and government.

In late 2008, with foreign capital flowing out and the won losing value, the central bank sold dollars to try to slow the decline of the won. The result: The bank's foreign reserves fell sharply, low enough to stir worries about the country's ability to cover its short-term borrowings at a time when investors around the world had become extremely averse to any institution or country with a debt problem.

South Korea's central bank has since rebuilt its foreign-exchange reserves and the ratio of short-term foreign-denominated debt to reserves is now 55%, down from 80% during the crisis.

But a debate still rages in the country over how to fix the interwoven problems of capital flows and currency values.

Some economists argue South Korea should take steps toward making the won develop into a more widely exchanged currency on international markets by letting it be traded around the clock on the spot market, instead of just six hours a day. Such a move, they say, would allow the local currency market to grow large enough to become more immune to temporary capital flows. The argument goes that if South Korea allowed the won to be exchanged via the spot market all the time, then more people would use the won and capital flows in and out of the country would have less influence on its value.

In June, though, the government went in a different direction by placing restrictions on currency hedging at companies and forex derivative trading at banks, a move that critics likened to capital controls. The government was trying to prevent companies from over-hedging, which can be as dangerous as not hedging at all. One of the new rules include a limit on companies (mostly importers and exporters) that prevent them from hedging more than 100% worth of the revenue they're hedging. Before the new rules the ceiling was 125%.

Meanwhile, as the won continued its climb against the U.S. dollar, the central bank routinely stepped into the market, selling won, to smooth out its rise. Traders say they've come to expect such moves, but not everyone is pleased.

"The foreign-exchange rate bodes well when it's predictable, but artificial intervention doesn't make the exchange rate stay at a certain level," says Hong Gidon, who until recently was chief financial officer of EMLSI, a semiconductor maker in Jeju. "Rather, it increases market uncertainty, which really doesn't help much."

title: DJ AT A GLANCE: Exchange Rates Dominate G-20 Finance Officials' Meeting
text:
THE EVENT: Finance ministers and central bank governors from the Group of 20 leading industrialized and emerging nations are gathering in Gyeongju, southeastern Korea, for meetings Friday and Saturday. Dow Jones Newswires' coverage of the event can be found by searching the code N/G20.

THE SITUATION: While the meeting is for the ministers and governors to prepare for the G-20 summit in Seoul next month, the issue of exchange rates will likely dominate discussions amid the U.S. dollar's continued weakness, the Chinese yuan's relative strength and interventions by emerging economies to damp their currencies' rise.

An early draft communique being circulated shows the group aims to work toward a "more market-determined exchange-rate system" and promises to "refrain from competitive undervaluation" of their currencies.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner said Thursday he plans to use the meetings to advance efforts to "rebalance" the world economy so it is less reliant on U.S. consumers, to move toward establishing "norms" on exchange-rate policy, and to persuade others the U.S. doesn't aim to devalue its way to prosperity.

IN THE BACKGROUND: The U.S. has been pressuring China to speed up the appreciation of the yuan, saying it is being kept artificially low to support its exporters, resulting in the U.S. posting a massive trade deficit with the Asian giant. China has maintained, however, that the problem lies with U.S. and its easy money policies, which have weighed on the dollar.

In the meantime, other emerging nations, notably G-20 members Brazil and South Korea have had to repeatedly intervene in markets to slow the rise in their currencies and the tide of capital inflows as money from low-yielding developed markets seek higher returns in the less developed world.

There is concern that the currency tensions could escalate into an all-out "currency war" that leaves no winners.

Australian Treasury Secretary Ken Henry Thursday called on major world economies not to retreat to protectionist policies, warning that current weak conditions globally are a likely breeding ground for bad economic policy making.

MARKET ACTION: Foreign exchange majors are trading in a tight range as investors adopt a cautious approach. The dollar, which rose against its major rivals on Thursday, is steady as traders appear reluctant to push the greenback much higher before the G-20 outcome is known.

At around 0100 GMT, the euro was fetching $1.3906 against the dollar, from at $1.3922 late Thursday in New York, and at Y112.96 against the yen, from Y113.22. The dollar was buying Y81.23, compared with Y81.35.

title: Q+A-Will Japan  intervene  again?
text:
TOKYO, Oct 22 (Reuters) - The dollar has fallen within spitting distance of its post-war record low against the yen and market players say Japanese authorities might intervene again if it falls sharply, after they intervened in September.

But there is a growing impression among some traders that, with a debate globally about competitive currency devaluation and Japan's recent criticism of South Korea for intervention, Tokyo may not intervene again, even though its policy makers say they might.

The dollar has lost 3.5 percent on the yen since the end of August and 13 percent so far this year, despite 2.1 trillion yen or $25 billion worth of intervention last month, with the U.S. currency sold across the board after the Federal Reserve signalled it was ready to ease policy again.

The dollar dipped to its lowest in 15 years this week, to 80.84 yen <JPY=>. It has recovered above 81.00 yen but the market is jittery about the possibility that Japan will intervene as the U.S. currency grinds down towards its 1995 post-war low of 79.75 yen.

<^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^


 Q+A on Japan's intervention capacity        [ID:nTOE68S07S]
 Q+A on unsterilised intervention            [ID:nTOE68G02P]
 Graphic on trade weighted fx:   http://r.reuters.com/qun86pCurrency tensions map:          http://r.reuters.com/jec96p
 PDF report on currencies:       http://r.reuters.com/gez77p("http://r.reuters.com/gez77p")

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

WHAT MIGHT PROMPT JAPAN TO INTERVENE AGAIN?

The Bank of Japan acts on behalf of the Ministry of Finance in FX intervention, and those who think it might step back in say it could do so if there were a rapid rise in the yen specifically, rather than a general drop in the dollar, possibly through 80 yen per dollar, and accompanied by a sharp drop in the Nikkei <.N225> share average.

If yen crosses such as the euro/yen and Australian dollar/yen rates remain reasonably stable, intervention is seen as less likely. But general yen strength could change the equation, especially if it is being driven by a build up of speculative positions.

Some traders say a sharp fall in Japanese share prices could alarm the authorities and prompt intervention. If the Nikkei falls below a 16-month low near 8,800 hit in early September, the Japanese government may feel more pressed to act.

WON'T THE CURRENCY WARS DEBATE STOP THEM?

The debate makes intervention more difficult, when China is under pressure to allow more rapid appreciation of the yuan, and this is one reason why some in the market think the likelihood is diminishing.

Japan escaped overt criticism from its G7 counterparts for its Sept. 15 intervention, the only confirmed bout so far. But behind the scenes it got heavy criticism from the Europeans, which has now made it very difficult for Tokyo to justify intervening again, a G7 source told Reuters.

Indeed the tone of Japanese policy makers' comments changed after the October IMF and G7 meetings in Washington. Finance Minister Yoshihiko Noda was at pains to stress that intervention was aimed at stopping excessive moves from hurting the economy, rather than the start of a big, long campaign aimed at targeting a specific foreign exchange level.

Noda then criticised South Korea for intervening to keep down its currency, saying Seoul's leadership of the G20 would come under question due to its regular intervention, a barb some analysts took to mean: "If we can't do it, then neither can you."

By criticising South Korea, Noda also did not sound to some like a finance minister considering immediate intervention.

SO WHAT'S THE AUTHORITIES' STRATEGY?

The strategy is hard to fathom at this stage because of the politics involved and because the only confirmed intervention in the past six years is the Sept. 15 action, so the market does not have a lot to go on.

Levels the market thought might be lines in the sand have been and gone, with the next potential one at 80 yen.

While at first some thought Sept. 15 marked the start of a longer campaign, now it may be that the authorities keep the action down to a few opportunistic occasions to counter rapid yen moves and remind the market of the two-way risk.

In the meantime, policy makers keep up a steady stream of verbal reminders that they will act decisively when needed.

HOW FAR IS THE YEN LIKELY TO RISE?

If no intervention occurs and the yen strengthens through 80 per dollar and then 79.75, some see it moving up to 78-76 per dollar to start with. Daisuke Uno, chief strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp, told Reuters in September that his personal forecast was for the yen to reach 50 next year.

A Reuters poll in early October showed a median forecast of 88 yen per dollar in six months' time and 92 yen in a year. <FXJPY>

A dollar drop below 80 yen would likely turn that level into resistance which the greenback could struggle to break at first.

In the options market, implied volatilities are subdued, suggesting that option market players expect the yen's rise will be slow, with one-month volatility at 11.5 percent

But a trader at a Japanese bank also noted there has been buying in longer-dated dollar puts/yen calls, such as six months and nine months, with strike prices far below the record low of 79.75 yen, suggesting expectations of a deeper fall in the dollar. (Reporting by Masayuki Kitano, Hideyuki Sano, Leika Kihara and Charlotte Cooper; Editing by Edmund Klamann)

title: G20 host S.Korea: protectionism is top concern
text:
SEOUL, Oct 15 (Reuters) - South Korean President Lee Myung-bak, who will chair next month's G20 summit, expressed concern on Friday over the possibility of trade protectionism emerging due to conflicts of national interest.

Lee also said there was an urgent need for the Group of 20 major economies to compromise on the issue of foreign exchange.

"What's worrying me the most is that conflicts of interest between countries could develop into trade protectionism," Lee was quoted as saying in a statement from the presidential office.

title: WSJA(10/15) Japan, Korea Tussle Over  Currencies
text:
(From THE WALL STREET JOURNAL ASIA) 
   By Evan Ramstad 

SEOUL -- Japan's decision to criticize South Korea for its currency interventions threw a spotlight on a little-noticed reason for South Korea's economic success this year -- the Korean won's weakness compared with the Japanese yen.

Like the yen, the won has been rising against the U.S. dollar in recent months. But the lingering difference between the yen and the won helps South Korean companies maintain an edge in pricing and profit margins in the industries in which they compete with Japanese rivals, including automobiles, shipbuilding, steel and electronics.

The tussle between South Korea and Japan is part of the broader currency turmoil shaking up governments and businesses across the world. Also Thursday, the Singaporean dollar soared after the city-state tightened monetary policy. U.S. dollar weakness also sent the Australian dollar to a new 28-year high, while the Swiss franc rose to a record against the U.S. currency and the euro climbed above $1.41.

The U.S. dollar has fallen 12.8% so far this year against the yen but is down only 4.8% against the won. The two traded nearly evenly against the U.S. dollar in 2007 but their performance diverged sharply in 2008 as investors worried about the global economy dove into currencies considered safe, like the yen, while moving out of currencies considered more speculative, like the won. The gap reached its widest point in January 2009, but is now almost as wide.

That makes Japanese products more expensive than Korean products when translated into other currencies. Because most companies choose to adjust prices to compete, the impact is usually seen on the bottom line.

Speaking at an event in Tokyo last month, Sharp Corp. President Mikio Katayama said the yen's strength and Japan's corporate-tax rate put the company at a disadvantage to Korean competitors. "It's unfair competition, like carrying dumbbells tied to your arms and legs," he said.

On Wednesday, Prime Minister Naoto Kan and Finance Minister Yoshihiko Noda for the first time blamed South Korea along with China for creating artificially low currency rates, citing the Bank of Korea's near-routine interventions in currency markets.

"I want South Korea and China to take responsible actions within common rules," Mr. Kan said, though he cited Japan's own recent market intervention to bring down the yen.

In Seoul on Thursday, the Bank of Korea and key government economic agencies criticized Japanese leaders for making inappropriate remarks but declined to talk about their substance. In the past, Korean officials have said the central bank's currency interventions are intended to smooth the direction of the won's value, not change it.

Currency analysts expect both the won and yen to continue gaining strength against the U.S. dollar in the months ahead, though the gap in relative values may tighten and reduce some of the advantage Korean exporters hold.

The exchange-rate issue spilled into Thursday's decision by the BOK's monetary policy committee to leave interest rates unchanged. Many analysts speculated the bank's policy makers worried that higher interest rates would attract capital flows that would further drive up the won's value. BOK Gov. Kim Choong-soo said the won's value was one of many factors influencing the decision to hold the interest rate steady.

In recent months, Korean businesses and government officials have worried about the won's gains against the U.S. dollar, which have brought the currency nearly back to where it was in early September 2008 just before the collapse of Lehman Brothers triggered a global credit crunch and currency devaluation in many countries.

At the same time, the won's relative advantage against the yen has actually gotten better -- helping Korean exporters along the way. That has meant, for instance, that South Korea's Hyundai Motor Corp. vehicles have a pricing advantage of 10% to 15% on Japanese manufacturers.

For Sung Min Electronics Co., which makes switches and lights for electronics products, the won's advantage against the yen has paid off in Germany, where sales are up 20% compared with last year, says Lim Hyuk , a sales manager. "I think our products have better price competitiveness than Japanese ones," he said.

Having a pricing edge against a main competitor is especially important to South Korea because exports account for 43% of its economy, the most of any developed nation, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. And its export strength is the main reason South Korea's overall economic growth is expected to be around 6% this year, well ahead of Japan's expected 2%.

"Japanese firms are struggling with the strong yen against the dollar, but what they have been telling us is the strong yen against the Korean won is much worse," said Minori Uchida, a currency analyst at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi UFJ. "There are so many cases that Japanese firms lose in infrastructure project auctions overseas, such as India, against Korean rivals and the firms say the exchange rate is one of the big factors."

Mitsubishi Motors Corp. President Osamu Masuko, speaking at news conference on electric cars Thursday, faced questions about the won's advantage over the yen. "It is not just an issue of won," he said. "Governments have a common idea now to get their economies back on the recovery trend by weakening their countries' currencies to boost exports, but it seems like Japan is lagging behind."

Today's competitive situation between South Korea and Japan is a sharp contrast to 2007, when the won was occasionally stronger than the yen against the U.S. dollar. Executives from South Korean manufacturers complained for much of that year about being at a price and profit disadvantage to Japanese rivals.

---

Juro Osawa, Takashi Mochizuki and Yoshio Takahashi in Tokyo and Jaeyeon Woo in Seoul contributed to this article.

title: GLOBAL ECONOMY- Currency  tensions persist as markets await Fed
text:
* China slams U.S., Japan over currency stance

 * All eyes on Bernanke, U.S. currency report

 * Verbal jousting mars run-up to key G20 meetings

 * ECB policymakers demand more emerging mkt flexibility

 By Aileen Wang and Tetsushi Kajimoto

 BEIJING/TOKYO, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Recriminations over currencies reverberated worldwide on Friday ahead of a speech by Federal Reserve chief Ben Bernanke, whose loose policies are blamed by China and others for destabilising capital flows.

 Beijing kept up the heat on the United States, saying Washington should not make China a scapegoat for its own problems by constantly pressing for a swifter rise in the yuan.

 Speaking hours before the U.S. Treasury Department is due to deliver its semi-annual assessment of whether China manipulates its currency, Commerce Ministry spokesman Yao Jian said it was not fair to criticise Beijing's exchange rate policy simply by pointing to China's trade surplus.

 "Other countries have no right to comment on what is a reasonable level for a country's trade surplus," Yao told a monthly news conference.

 Sniping over what exchange rates are appropriate to put the world economy back on course is intensifying ahead of a pair meetings of the Group of 20 leading economies in South Korea.

 European Central Bank policymaker Juergen Stark was reported as saying countries must avoid a 'fatal' race to devalue and instead coordinate better to smooth out currency swings.

 Both he and his colleague, Jose Manuel Gonzalez-Paramo, said China, which is resisting pressure from the United States and other developed nations to allow its yuan to revalue faster, needed to be more flexible.

 G20 Finance ministers meet next week in Gyeongju to prepare for a summit of their leaders in Seoul on Nov. 11-12.

 U.S. data on Thursday showed America's trade deficit with China swelled to a record high of $28 billion in August -- grist to the mill of U.S. politicians who say that China keeps the yuan artificially cheap to help its exporters.

 Spot yuan ended at its highest closing level against the dollar since its landmark revaluation in July 2005  but U.S. critics say it is still 20 percent or more undervalued.

 LOGGERHEADS

 Japanese Finance Minister Yoshihiko Noda stressed that countries must work together to strengthen the global currency order. Governments would find it tough to cope with the current environment on their own, he told reporters.

 Noda struck a more conciliatory tone than on Wednesday, when he criticised South Korea for intervening repeatedly to curb the won, and China, for dragging its heels in letting the yuan rise.

 "Before saying this or that about other countries' currency policies, we must do what we should do," Noda said.

 Yao, the Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesman, was in no mood to forgive or forget. Japan has "no reason, no grounds and is not qualified" to criticise China's currency policy, he said.

 Some South Korean newspapers weighed in too, saying Japan risked sacrificing friendly diplomatic relations with its neighbours to placate its export companies, which are suffering due to the yen's rise to a 15-year high against the dollar.

 The dollar hovered near a 10-month low versus a currency basket as the conviction hardened that the Fed will further ease monetary policy next month to try to kick-start the lethargic U.S. economy.

 WAITING FOR BERNANKE

 Financial markets, which expect the U.S. central bank to begin soon a second round of buying of U.S. Treasury bonds with new money -- to the tune of $500 billion or more -- will hang on Bernanke's words for clues about the likely scope.

 Bernanke is due to speak at 1215 GMT.

 The Fed's policy remit is domestic, but the side-effects of minting new dollars to pay for the asset purchases are a weaker dollar and investors' rush into emerging markets, where growth prospects are brighter and yields are higher.

 In response, several governments have stepped into forex markets or tried to curb capital inflows, raising fears of a currency "race to the bottom" that may trigger protectionism and hit global growth.

 "With the recovery slow in the advanced countries, each country relies more on exports for growth and tension surrounding foreign exchange rates is intensifying," South Korean Finance Minister Yoon Jeung-hyun said. "There are signs that this could develop into trade protectionism."

 Lawrence Summers, a top economic adviser to U.S. President Barack Obama, also flagged protectionism as a rising threat to the global economy that destroys value.

 Singapore decided on Thursday not stand in the way of market forces and said it would let its dollar rise more quickly.

 But India intervened to temper a rising rupee, while South Korea tried to deter unwanted inflows by keeping interest rates steady even at the risk of allowing inflation to build.

 Thailand this week imposed a withholding tax on foreign purchases of government bonds. But the new chief of the central bank said Bangkok would be wary about further steps.

 "Stringent measures will have side effects, so what to use and when, we have to look at the real situation," Bank of Thailand Governor Prasarn Trairatvorakul said.  (Writing by Alan Wheatley and Mike Peacock; Editing by Toby Chopra)

title: Japan PM Suggests Further  Intervention  As Yen Touches Highs-Kyodo
text:
DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

Prime Minister Naoto Kan said Thursday that Japan could take action to address excessive volatility in foreign exchange rates and prevent a further sharp rise of the yen, which has reached levels against the U.S. dollar unseen in over 15 years, Kyodo News reported.

Kan suggested Japan would again step into the currency market following its intervention on Sept. 15, the country's first in over six years. But it is widely seen as increasingly difficult for Tokyo to take such a step as some emerging economies have come under pressure to stop any moves to manipulate exchange rates.

"We still believe that rapidly changing exchange rates are not desirable," Kan told reporters after the U.S. dollar briefly traded in the Y80 range for the first time since April 1995. The Japanese currency's all-time high of Y79.75 against the dollar was marked on April 19, 1995.

"Amid a big shift like this, we need various options, and I have said that when necessary, we will take decisive action," he said.

The yen's strength adversely affects the earnings of Japanese exporters and is believed to be slowing the nation's economic recovery.

Kan's comments came a day after he called on China and South Korea to "take responsible actions under common rules" in reference to their currency policies. He told a Diet committee that efforts made by individual countries to depress their currencies never fall within the principles of cooperation among the Group of 20 leading economies.

The G-20, which groups both major developed and developing economies, is to hold a summit in Seoul next month with possible cooperation on currency policy high on the agenda.

China has come under growing pressure from the U.S. and other advanced economies to stop maintaining the yuan at a weak level to protect exports.

The Group of Seven industrialized economies agreed last week that emerging economies with huge current account surpluses should implement reforms for a more flexible currency system.

The Bank of Korea, South Korea's central bank, is widely seen as actively intervening to curb the won's appreciation.

South Korea, which will host the Nov. 11-12 G-20 summit, rejected Kan's comments, lodging a protest with Japan, and Tokyo pledged not to make further "improper" comments regarding Seoul's foreign exchange policies, Yonhap News Agency reported Thursday, citing South Korean finance ministry officials.

Kan has admitted it is difficult for him to comment on other countries' currency policies given Japan's own intervention. Meanwhile, Finance Minister Yoshihiko Noda has said Japan's action was intended to ease the yen's excessive volatility rather than to lead the currency to a certain level.

The G-7 finance ministers and central bank governors, who met Oct. 8 in Washington, reconfirmed that disorderly movements in exchange rates have adverse implications for economic and financial stability, Noda said.

title: GLOBAL ECONOMY-Japan questions S.Korea G20 leadership over  FX
text:
* Japan wants South Korea, China to play by same FX rules

* Tokyo says its own intervention is different

* Geithner sees "no risk" of currency war

* China says G20 should not focus on specific currency

* Fed says easing may be needed before long (Adds U.S. lawmaker on China currency legislation)

By Stanley White and Linda Sieg

TOKYO, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Japan called into question South Korea's leadership of the Group of 20 nations forum on Wednesday because of Seoul's interventions to stem the won's rise, at the same time insisting its own currency action was qualitatively different.

The remarks by Japan's finance minister underscored deep divisions over currency policies, an issue that will dominate G20 meetings in South Korea this month and next after a weekend International Monetary Fund meeting failed to produce any agreement.

"As chair of the G20, South Korea's role will be seriously questioned," Yoshihiko Noda told a parliamentary panel when asked about South Korea's currency interventions.

Record low interest rates in rich countries have pushed global investors into emerging markets in search of higher yields, driving up their currencies.

In response, several governments have stepped into foreign exchange markets or tried to curb capital inflows, raising fears of a currency "race to the bottom" that may trigger protectionism and hobble global growth.

Japan intervened in the currency market last month for the first time in more than six years to try to stem a rise in the yen that threatens its fragile economic recovery.

Noda drew a distinction between that action and more frequent intervention by South Korea and China.

"In South Korea, intervention happens regularly, and in China, the pace of yuan reform has been slow," Noda said. "Our message is that we have confirmed at the Group of Seven that emerging market countries with current account surpluses should allow their currencies to be more flexible."

South Korea did not immediately comment on the remarks.

NO CONSENSUS

Pressure on China to allow its currency to rise more quickly is likely to intensify. But hopes for a G20 consensus look slim.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner said he saw no risk of a global currency war. But asked about the need for a stronger yuan, he said: "We just want to make sure it's happening at a gradual but still significant rate." For more, see: [ID:nN12218440]

The U.S. Senate plans to follow the House of Representatives in passing legislation aimed at pressuring China to let the yuan rise more quickly, Senate Finance Committee Chairman Max Baucus said in the text of a speech given in Beijing. [ID:nN13269803]

Ewald Nowotny, a European Central Bank governing council member, said the G20 was the best forum to discuss the uneven global growth that is leading to the currency disputes. [ID:nN13250117]

But he said his fear is retaliatory action by the U.S. Congress against China if it fails to let its currency strengthen more rapidly.

"What clearly would make us very nervous ... is if some, let's say, unilateral steps would be taken which could spark, let's say, a political crisis. That is something that would be damaging for the world economy in general," he said.

China's insistence that the yuan's rise must be gradual is a huge obstacle to the appreciation in Asian exchange rates policymakers say is needed to reduce global imbalances.

China and other countries counter that the prospect of the Federal Reserve printing money again will flood the world economy with more liquidity, weaken the dollar and push emerging currencies yet higher.

"It'll be impossible for the G20 to reach a consensus on currencies. Many emerging economies feel that they are being forced to intervene because of a weak dollar," said Etsuko Yamashita, chief economist at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp.

"China will not succumb to outside pressure."

Minutes of the Fed's last policy meeting showed its policymakers thought easier policy may be needed "before long" to bolster a struggling recovery. [ID:nN12188145]

China's chief G20 currency negotiator, Cui Tiankai, said Beijing was trying to avoid a currency stand-off but that no specific currency should be on the G20 agenda.

"We are doing our best to avoid that," Cui, a foreign vice-minister, said on the sidelines of a conference in Seoul. "But it requires efforts of all the G20 members, not China alone."

The major world currency not being talked down is the euro, which rose again on Wednesday, as the ECB ponders a reversal of ultra-loose policy while the Fed is poised to ease further and Japan has already cut rates to zero.

"In the G4 space, the ECB is the only central bank that is talking of an exit policy and that is helping the euro," said Ankita Dudani, G10 currency strategist at RBS.

Analysts said Tokyo's criticism of Seoul stemmed from its worries about competitiveness. The yen is up about 13 percent against the dollar this year, the won only about 4 percent.

"Japan feels it has been under pressure not to intervene because of G7 rules but people outside (of G7) seem to be playing by different rules," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Morgan Stanley MUFG Securities in Tokyo.

Japanese Prime Minister Naoto Kan urged Seoul and Beijing to act responsibly but acknowledged Tokyo's delicate position.

"I want South Korea and China to take responsible actions within common rules, though how to say this is difficult because Japan has also intervened," he told lawmakers.

Japan sold 2.1 trillion yen ($26 billion) last month to curb the yen's strength versus the dollar. South Korea has intervened to the tune of about $13 billion since late September, but analysts said it has acted more aggressively in relative terms. title: LIVE: News And Notes From IMF, World Bank Annual Meetings In Washington
text:
The International Monetary Fund and World Bank are holding annual meetings in Washington where world financial leaders are grappling with how to fuel a more balanced global economic recovery and avoid a possible global currencies war. The meetings, a stepping stone toward a major gathering of Group of 20 political leaders in Seoul in mid-November, are expected to offer glimpses on how a number of global economic issues might be addressed or not addressed by world leaders.

(12:50 EDT) The so-called "currency war" may see several emerging markets ramp up efforts to curb currency advances, say analysts, as pressure to keep exports competitive overrides official warnings that such interventions could frustrate a flagging global recovery. The chatter about currency war has grown louder in recent weeks and is a hot topic during the IMF and World Bank annual meetings. "We are seeing so much intervention because countries do not want to lose competitiveness," said Ousmene Mandeng, a former IMF economist who heads public-sector investment advisory services at Ashmore Investment Management in London. Central banks that have already intervened to slow currency gains include those in Colombia, South Korea, Peru and Taiwan. (Carla Mozee)

(12:25 EDT) French Finance Minister Christine Lagarde tried to bring a touch of grace to fractious talks on currencies at this weekend's IMF meetings by saying she is not in a "mood for war on currencies." Attempting to cash in on the popularity she acquired with fellow ministers during the financial crisis, she appears to be trying to convince them that being in a mood for peace is more likely to bring success than U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner's strong tone to achieve agreement on rebalancing of the global economy and getting China to allow more flexibility on the yuan. The French are wary that petulant talk on currencies could get in the way of their own agenda for the upcoming G-20 presidency in November, when President Nicolas Sarkozy hopes to set the basis of a more efficient international monetary system. Rather than confront currency levels head-on, the French are hoping to tackle the issue in a more oblique way, through financial safety nets and capital flow controls. It remains to be seen whether the exclusive Pierre Herme macarons, an almond-based confection, Lagarde brought her Group of Seven colleagues for dinner Friday night have succeeded in relaxing the atmosphere. (Nathalie Boschat)

(11:40 EDT) Even oil cartel OPEC gets a say at the annual IMF meeting. In a statement to the fund's advisory body, the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries said demand for its crude oil was only forecast to grow next year by 200,000 barrels a day as the global financial crisis continues to take a toll on the economy. Total demand is seen increasing by one million b/d next year, with the bulk of new consumption coming from emerging countries such as China and India and in Latin America. Non-OPEC supply, including oil and natural gas liquids, is expected to grow by 900,000 b/d this year but only by 400,000 b/d in 2011. (Ian Talley)

(11:30 EDT) Apropos of building forex strains, the IMF's policy and strategy advisory board, the International Monetary and Financial Committee, Saturday was consumed with the issue. Aside from putting currencies officially on the agenda--one topic item is titled, "Perspectives from selected currency areas"--top financial leaders also highlighted the issue in their statements to the panel. Geithner urged the IMF to exercise greater oversight and candor on exchange rate and market-distorting reserve accumulations. And in a rare explicit linking of the currency problems with China, European Commissioner for Economic and Monetary Affairs Olli Rehn called for China to make exchange-rate regime more flexible so that the global financial system is not subject to volatility and instability. (Ian Talley)

(11:15 EDT) Provocative language is certainly one way to turn heads your way and Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega has no problem saying that was precisely his goal when he invoked a worldwide "currency war" and "trade war." The issue is that there is an "undeclared currency war" in which "each day every country is taking their own exchange-rate measures leading to exchange-rate imbalance," he said Friday night, adding that he plans to put this on the agenda for the G-20 leaders summit in Seoul set for November. The source of these imbalances is that developed economies like Germany and the U.S. shorted their fiscal stimulus measures and are instead trying to rely on ultra-loose monetary policies, which only go so far, he said. It's no surprise he wanted to flag the issue since Brazil has been on the receiving end of the "excessive dollar liquidity." The solution: "developed economies must rethink, reposition fiscal policies." (Kejal Vyas)

(10:29 EDT) Hungary's central bank governor, Andras Simor, was very circumspect on Saturday morning about when his country might join the euro zone and adopt the single currency. Pressed a couple of times on the matter on a panel discussion with several European Central Bank members, Simor said it was a matter for the government--even while he said Hungary needed to "speed up" its integration within the euro zone. But there was one thing Simor was certain of. Asked by the British panel moderator whether Hungary would join the euro before infamously euro-skeptic Britain ever decided to, he said, "Yes. Absolutely." (Laurence Norman)

(9:18 EDT) G-7 finance leaders dined privately Friday night during the annual IMF and World Bank meetings and though the dinner was an informal gathering among the items discussed was Japan's recent intervention aimed at restraining the strength of the yen. "Excessive fluctuations in exchange rates have a negative impact on Japan's economy and thus can't be overlooked," Japanese Finance Minister Yoshihiko Noda told the Japanese press at a midnight briefing that followed the dinner. Noda said he gave a speech at the G-7 dinner explaining Japan's actions but "can't say assertively" what his peers thought because his remarks "didn't lead to broader debates." (Takashi Nakamichi)

title: UPDATE: US To Press  Currency  Issues At IMF--Treasury Official
text:
(Adds additional official comment, details and background, in the third through ninth, 12th and 13th paragraphs.)


 
   By Ian Talley and Michael R. Crittenden 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--U.S. officials plan to press their foreign counterparts to avoid interfering in global currency markets at this weekend's International Monetary Fund meetings, warning of the potential effect on the global rebalancing efforts.

A senior Treasury Department official, speaking to reporters at a briefing, said U.S. officials will stress the need for countries to allow for "market-oriented exchange rates" as part of a broader rebalancing of the world economy.

Besides China's undervalued yuan, intervention by South Korea, Brazil and Tokyo in their currencies have raised foreign-exchange tensions, propelling the sensitive issue to the forefront of international talks.

The chorus of complaints internationally has grown louder for China to appreciate its undervalued yuan, particularly as Beijing's policy is exacerbating the global imbalance of trade and investment. Turbulence in the foreign-exchange markets was taken to a new level after Brazil warned of a currency war.

Earlier Tuesday, European Economic and Monetary Affairs Commissioner Olli Rehn warned that the euro area's economic recovery may suffer if the euro appreciates against the yuan and other world currencies. Officials in Brussels met with Chinese Prime Minister Wen Jiabao.

Asked about Japan's recent intervention on behalf of the yen, the Treasury official implicitly criticized Tokyo for the action as contrary to its commitments to the Group of 20 nations.

The official said Japan and others in the G-20 are focused on cultivating a more robust recovery, and that countries with trade surpluses, including Japan and China, have committed to encouraging domestic demand as a bigger engine of growth and so becoming less reliant on exports over time.

"Explicitly in those agreements are structural policies as well as ensuring that exchange rates represent market forces," the senior official said.

The official said those commitments would be "central to our conversations" at the upcoming IMF meetings.

The U.S. believes the IMF should play a more aggressive role in ensuring countries live up to their commitments on exchange-rate policy, the official said, stressing the fund's "very important surveillance mandate."

"The IMF has to have an ability to speak forcefully," the official said.

While the IMF has labeled the yuan as "substantially undervalued," the IMF has yet to call the currency "manipulated," which would ostensibly ratchet up pressure on Beijing to act.

Fueling tensions, the U.S. House of Representatives last month approved legislation targeting the yuan that would slap punitive tariffs on imports from countries such as China that have undervalued currencies.

The official said the Obama administration shared the underlying concerns addressed by the bill, but was reluctant to say whether the Treasury supported the legislation. Previously, officials have raised concerns about World Trade Organization obligations and the potential political and trade backlash such legislation may engender.

The issue of currencies is one of a range of topics finance ministers and central-bank officials are expected to discuss at a series of multi- and bilateral discussions in Washington over the weekend.

title: Dow Jones Asia-Pacific Top Stories Sked For September 29

MACRO/FOREX/FIXED INCOME:


 
=2ND UPDATE: JAPAN TANKAN SHOWS SEPTEMBER IMPROVEMENT, BUT OUTLOOK DARKENS 

Sentiment among Japan's big manufacturers picked up for the sixth straight quarter at a faster pace than expected, the Bank of Japan's September tankan survey showed Wednesday, but companies are turning more cautious in their outlook for the coming quarter due to the surging yen and increased uncertainty over the global economy. (published 0212 GMT)


 
=UPDATE: HSBC CHINA SEPTEMBER PMI RISES TO FIVE-MONTH HIGH 

The HSBC China Manufacturing Purchasing Managers Index, a gauge of nationwide manufacturing activity, rose to a five-month high in September, likely reassuring markets China isn't facing a rapid slowdown, but sharp increases in the input and output price subindexes may renew concerns about a buildup of inflationary pressures. (published 0337 GMT)


 
=UPDATE: RESERVE BANK OF AUSTRALIA'S BROADBENT EXPECTS HIGHER AUSTRALIA GROWTH IN 2011 

Australia's economy will see stronger growth in 2011 spurred on by China, said Reserve Bank of Australia board member Jillian Broadbent Wednesday ahead of a closely watched rate decision next week when the bank is expected to tighten policy in an effort to manage the country's surging economy. (published 0513 GMT)


 
S KOREA: SHOULD BALANCE INFLATION, EXTERNAL RISKS WHEN OPERATING MACRO POLICIES 

South Korea authorities should weigh the risk of faster inflation and a softer recovery in the global economy when implementing macroeconomic policies, the Ministry of Strategy and Finance said Wednesday. (published 0500 GMT)


 
=2ND UPDATE: S KOREA AUGUST CURRENT ACCOUNT SURPLUS FALLS; TO BEAT 2010 TARGET 

South Korea ran its smallest current-account surplus in four months in August as trade gains shrank due to summer holidays, but the country is expected to chalk up a surplus for the full year that will easily surpass the central bank's $21 billion estimate. (published 0207 GMT)


 
=2ND UPDATE: NZ EXPORTS WEAKEN, REDUCING SUPPORT FOR RECOVERY 

New Zealand's goods trade balance recorded a deficit in August after exports came in weaker than expected, stoking concerns over the strength of the country's economic recovery. (published 0235 GMT)


 
=UPDATE: SINGAPORE GIC SEES BETTER OPPORTUNITIES IN REAL ESTATE, PRIVATE EQUITY 

Government of Singapore Investment Corp., or GIC, said Wednesday it sees more rewarding opportunities in real estate and private equity, and that it will continue investing in publicly listed equities as part of its emerging market strategy. (published 0548 GMT)


 
=UPDATE:AUSTRALIA'S REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT MINISTER SUPPORTS CHINESE INVESTMENT 

Australia's Regional Development Minister Simon Crean Wednesday said he is a strong believer in foreign investment to help develop the country, given the historical lack of large domestic savings to fund investments and infrastructure development. (published 0557 GMT)


 
CARLOS SLIM SAYS AUSTRALIA, ASIA PACIFIC ARE VERY IMPORTANT RIGHT NOW

=UPDATE: BAHT RISE STILL IN LINE WITH REGIONALS - THAI CENTRAL BANK

=UPDATE: THAI FINANCE MINISTRY EXPECTS GREATER FUND INFLOWS 

Thailand's Ministry of Finance said Wednesday it expects more funds to enter the country's financial markets, adding that the Bank of Thailand's recent comments suggesting the country's policy rate will rise have intensified inflows. (published 0654 GMT)

title: Asian Central Banks Keep Up  Intervention  As Dollar Weakens
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The central banks of South Korea, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia were suspected of intervening in forex exchange markets Wednesday to contain gains in their currencies, but analysts say the continued weakness of the U.S. dollar means Asian units should extend their rallies.

The wave of intervention, which has continued across the region for most of this year, hasn't been strong enough to reverse the strengthening trend in Asian currencies, as many policymakers are allowing their currencies to rise slowly to limit imported inflation.

That stance was reinforced after China, the top trading partner for key Asian countries, said in June it would let the yuan strengthen against the dollar -- meaning that other Asian countries can maintain their export competitiveness against China even if their currencies rise a bit.

On Wednesday the Thai baht and the Malaysian ringgit hit their highest levels since the 1997 Asian currency crisis, while the Singapore dollar rose to an all-time high.

In a note to investors, Standard Chartered analysts said global dollar weakness, closely tied to market expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve may launch another round of quantitative easing by boosting purchases of U.S. securities, is likely to keep Asian and other emerging market currencies in strong demand. In recent days, the central banks of countries ranging from Russia to Colombia have been suspected of intervening in forex markets because of dollar weakness.

"The prospect of another round of quantitative easing by the Fed in the fourth quarter of 2010 should be seen as broadly negative for the dollar," StanChart said.

Intervention Wednesday was particularly significant in Indonesia, which has attracted a surge of inflows thanks to its solid economic performance and high interest rates.

Jakarta-based traders said the central bank was suspected of buying around $50 million at IDR8,950 in early trade, and then an unspecified amount at IDR8,945. Neither move managed to send the rupiah lower, however, and the dollar last traded at IDR8,935.

"The dollar is still under pressure against the rupiah, as investors' appetite for riskier assets is improving," one dealer in Singapore said.

Intervention by Bank Indonesia has continued for the past two years, but is now likely at its highest volume ever. Bank Indonesia's forex reserves rose 9% in the first three weeks of September, a huge amount even by East Asian standards, mostly due to dollar-buying in forex markets.

The Bank of Thailand and Monetary Authority of Singapore also were suspected of early intervention moves Wednesday. In Bangkok, traders said the BOT was spotted intervening at THB30.50 against the dollar, but the baht rose further and last traded at THB30.46.

In Singapore, the MAS managed to weaken the local dollar slightly after it soared to an all-time high at S$1.3152 against the greenback. The Singapore dollar last traded at S$1.3170.

Seoul traders said intervention by the Bank of Korea was relatively mild, as the Korean won is still some distance away from two-year highs hit earlier this year. The dollar last traded at KRW1,141, having fallen as low as KRW1,139 earlier in the day.

title: MONEY TALKS: Fed's Mending Ways May Put Asia In A Bind
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--As Ben Bernanke maneuvers the Federal Reserve closer to further quantitative easing, Asian policy makers may find themselves bearing some of the pain of keeping the U.S. economy afloat.

The Fed made it amply clear this week it is concerned about low inflation--and indeed the risk of deflation--in the U.S. and stands ready to act to fulfil its mandate of promoting maximum employment and price stability.

It's likely that Bernanke & Co. will be compelled--unless they are blessed with a sudden and apparently-sustainable improvement in data prints--to embark on another round of monetary loosening. An announcement on QE looks a distinct possibility at the next policy meeting in November.

Flooding the market with more U.S. dollars to lower the cost of credit and inflate the economy may be the way to go; in Asia, however, we may see some fallout from the Fed's actions.

Further easing from the Fed could send the U.S. dollar down and already-strong Asian currencies up, endangering the region's export-dependent economies.

Asian central banks could be forced to continue intervening in the foreign exchange market to support the dollar and temper the impact on exporters. Japan last week was forced to intervene massively for the first time in six years, as a surging yen threatened an already-sluggish economic recovery. Other countries in the region, such as South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan, have intervened to prop up the greenback.

Asia will also have to contend with the potential surge in hot money flows to sectors such as housing, heightening the risk of asset price bubbles. With Treasury yields likely to ease on any fresh QE, more investors will turn to Asia for yield.

Central banks in the region may lay low for some months on rates, but if they start hiking to curb inflation that will only accentuate rate differentials.

Such a scenario will pose a policy dilemma for Asia's central banks. Thailand is already moving to introduce rules to boost capital outflows, while the Philippine central bank said Thursday it's mulling changes to foreign exchange regulations to address a surge in portfolio investments that has buoyed the peso.

With Asia already battling rising currencies, the last thing it needs is for the Fed to further frustrate the situation.

Still, the way the cards are stacked up, policy makers in the region will probably be the first to acknowledge that the Fed cannot sit on its hands and risk deflation in the U.S.

* Won up 0.3 pct on exporters, intervention spotted

By Cheon Jong-woo

SEOUL, Sept 17 (Reuters) - Asian currencies, including the Malaysian ringgit and the South Korean won, rose on Friday helped by a rally in stocks globally and broad weakness in the dollar.

The Philippine peso found support from strong portfolio inflow data and demand from speculative funds, although some dealers suspected its rally was capped by central bank intervention.

Authorities in South Korea were spotted buying dollars to cap the won's <KRW=> strength, feeding into market speculation that Asian policymakers are increasingly concerned about export competitiveness.

"Given strong Asian economic fundamentals and growing appetite for assets in the region, Asian currencies are expected to rise more. But I don't think FX authorities in the region will just let them rise, considering their exports," said Jeon Seung-ji, a currency analyst at Samsung Futures Inc.

WON RISES

The won <KRW=> rose against the dollar on exporter demand before holidays next week and bids linked to foreign stock buying.

Dealers said foreign exchange authorities bought dollars to prevent the won rising beyond 1,160 per dollar. The currency closed up 0.34 percent at 1,160.5 from Thursday's domestic close of 1,164.5 <KRW=KFTC>.

It rose as high as 1,159.2 during the day.

"The won is regaining a bullish trend, although the authorities will be a variable," said a foreign bank dealer.

The upside was also limited because dealers were wary of exposure to long won positions ahead of Korean holidays next week on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.

Foreign investors bought a net 263.0 billion won in stocks, helping the benchmark KOSPI <.KS11> rise 0.86 percent.

PESO

The peso rose to 44.25 per dollar, up 0.3 percent, after data showed net portfolio inflows in August hit a 15-month high. [ID:nSGE68G00P]

But gains were checked by speculation that the central bank (BSP) had intervened to tap the rally on the head. The central bank will maintain its presence to prevent the currency rising too rapidly, a dealer said.

"There was talk of the BSP buying spot below 44.25 providing some support," said the dealer in Singapore. "Bids are expected to come at 44.15-20 again with the BSP supporting spot ahead of 44.00."

The Philippine currency is expected to rise further on a brighter outlook for the economy.

"Given strong growth expectation, we are pretty bullish on the peso. We think it will go to 44.00 per dollar at the end of this year," a currency strategist in Singapore, asking not to be identified.

BAHT

The Thai baht <THB=> rebounded in mid-afternoon trade to around 30.74 per dollar from 30.82 in the morning and 30.77 late on Thursday.

"It is broadly in line with euro and Asian gains as the local concern over any capital controls by the central bank fades. Finance Minister Korn's comments on encouraging offshore investment are an old story that should have very little to do with the baht's rebound this afternoon," a Bangkok-based trader said. [ID:nSGE68G06G]

The baht has risen 8.5 percent against the dollar this year.

YUAN

The yuan <CNY=CFXS> fell slightly against the dollar, breaking a straight six-session run of gains that pushed the currency around 1 percent higher.

The rise marked the currency's biggest six-day rally since January 2008 but dealers had become increasingly concerned about a pullback.

Still, traders said the yuan's uptrend would remain intact, arguing it could rise 2 percent or more in the coming three months. [ID:nTOE68E04U]

Traders said the latest yuan rally, engineered by the PBOC's setting of daily mid-points for trading, was a political move as U.S. pressure increases once more for Beijing to allow the currency to rise more quickly, dealers said.

title: FX  ASIA: Asia Reserves Creep Up, Countries Look To Diversify
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asia's foreign exchange reserves rose 1% in June from the previous month, bouncing back after a steep drop in May, as Asian central banks bought more U.S. dollars to cap gains in local currencies.

The rise, an indication that the fast-growing region keeps attracting capital inflows despite concerns of a global economic slowdown, highlights the dilemma faced by Asian authorities as they look for ways to reduce their exposure to U.S. Treasurys--as China appears to be doing on a small scale, by stepping up its purchases of Japanese bonds.

Reserves held by 11 key Asian central banks, excluding China's, amounted to US$2.803 trillion at the end of June, up from US$2.776 trillion at the end of May, but remained just below an all-time hit in April, according to calculations by Dow Jones Newswires.

Reserve accumulation in June came as the euro remained essentially steady against the dollar--following a 7.5% drop in May--and minor reserve currencies like the yen and the British pound posted significant gains, boosting the dollar value of securities denominated in those currencies.

The yen and the pound together are estimated to account for around 8% of central bank reserves in developing countries, on average, compared with almost 30% for the euro. However, speculation over increased central bank interest in these currencies increased this week after news that China poured twice as much money into Japanese government bonds in the first four months of 2010 than its record full-year purchases in 2005.

This move underscores a willingness of some Asian countries to diversify their reserves into currencies other than the greenback and the battered euro, at a time when countries from Thailand to South Korea intervene to keep their currencies down and protect the competitive edge of their exporters. In recent years, this diversification has been done predominantly by purchasing euro-denominated securities.

Analysts say the dollar's role as paramount reserve currency remains safe, as the yen and the pound present drawbacks that should stop them from becoming major challengers, including uncertain valuation prospects since Japan is looking for a weaker currency and the U.K. faces a dire fiscal picture.

Still, a small, slow increase in yen allocations going forward is possible, said Tim Condon, chief Asian economist at ING Bank, noting that yields on U.S. Treasurys and top euro bonds have fallen towards the low levels of Japanese government bonds, removing a key obstacle that has made yen holdings unattractive for years.

"If G-3 rates remain in this sort of low level convergence, then Japanese bonds will be relatively more attractive, and holdings of Japanese bonds should rise," Condon added.

International Monetary Fund data show the yen has never accounted for more than 9% of global official reserves -- well below the 87% peak hit by the dollar in 1976, and its 61.5% share in the first quarter this year -- while the pound has been below the 5% mark since 1974.

title: =DJ  FX  ASIA: Asian  Currencies  To Gain Gradually As Yuan Peg Ends
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian currencies surged Monday as China's decision to drop the yuan's peg to the dollar revived expectations of a regional rally.

Central banks in South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand intervened to curb gains in their currencies, but strategists said Asia's authorities will likely tolerate a gradual appreciation after Beijing said Saturday it will let the yuan move more freely.

Gains in Asian currencies, as central banks tighten monetary policy, will likely be slow and in some cases fitful. Concerns about Europe's sovereign debt-crisis may continue to sap risk appetite, complicating the Asia rally.

The People's Bank of China drove home the message that it will allow only gradual moves in its currency, setting the yuan's central parity rate at 6.8275 to the dollar, the same as Friday's fixing--and a weaker yuan level than the dollar's over-the-counter close Friday at CNY6.8262.

This was the central bank's first operational evidence of its policy of allowing more flexibility in the yuan exchange rate. Beijing had essentially pegged the dollar around CNY6.8300 since July 2008 as an emergency measure to combat the global financial crisis.

"It seems they're trying to avoid being seen as very aggressive," said Frances Cheung, a currency strategist at Credit Agricole Corporate and Investment Bank. She forecasts the yuan will rise 1.5% against the dollar by the end of the year.

Investors, after the surprise fixing Monday morning knocked Asian currencies back from early highs, nonetheless resumed buying yuan and other regional currencies. The dollar dropped to CNY6.8015, its lowest under China's modern exchange-rate system, before rebounding somewhat. At 0650 GMT it was quoted at CNY6.8090.

"At the beginning the market was trying out around the level of Friday's close, but it has since turned to focus on the prospect of yuan appreciation in the near term," said a Shanghai trader at a foreign bank. "Everyone is selling dollars now."

Other Asian authorities are looking to China for cues. As the region's biggest export market with a rapidly growing economy, China is hugely important for other countries in Asia, and each government will likely try to ensure its currency doesn't deviate too much from those of its rival exporters.

Spencer Lin, the head of the foreign-exchange department at Taiwan's central bank, said Taipei will pay attention to movements in Asian currencies after China's currency shift.

Bank Indonesia Deputy Gov. Hartadi Sarwono said, "The rupiah will adjust, as China's new policy will help trigger global economic recovery." Yet, the central bank later intervened to temper the rise in the rupiah, which had jumped to its highest level since May 10. The dollar was at IDR9,065 at 0705 GMT, off its early low of IDR9,030.

The Bank of Korea, warning against "one-sided" currency moves, bought an estimated $1 billion for won, boosting the greenback to KRW1,172 from KRW1,169, Seoul traders said. The dollar remained well below late Friday's KRW1,202.6.

The Bank of Thailand was suspected to have bought a few hundred million dollars to slow the rise in the baht, which is up 3.1% against the dollar year-to-date.

Asian currencies may remain under gentle upward pressure. Barclays Capital expects a roughly 5% yuan rise by the middle of 2011, forecasting the dollar will fall to around CNY6.5000.

Standard Chartered says one way to play a yuan rise is through the New Taiwan dollar, which should benefit from the yuan de-pegging, given cross-strait trade links. The bank recommends selling the U.S. currency via three-month nondeliverable forwards at an outright entry of TWD31.550, targeting a decline to TWD31.000.

"In our view, the Taiwan dollar is likely to catch up with other Asia ex-Japan currencies as the Taiwan central bank is likely to become more tolerant of gradual currency appreciation," the bank said.

ING Bank is most bullish on the won, Taiwan dollar, Singapore dollar and Malaysian ringgit, "based on cheapness on real effective exchange-rate grounds and our assessment of central banks' tolerance for currency appreciation," said economist Tim Condon.

SEOUL (Dow Jones)--The South Korean won was lower late Monday largely due to suspected central bank intervention in support of the dollar in late trade.

The Bank of Korea likely intervened to prevent the local currency from rebounding on active export settlements, several traders said.

The local foreign-exchange authorities are suspected of having intervened frequently in recent months to curb any sharp gains in the won amid concerns that undue strength in the local currency may sap an export-led recovery. But the latest move comes as a bit of a surprise as the local currency has fallen 7.8% in May--in the wake of the euro-zone debt crisis--its biggest monthly loss since February 2009.

Two traders estimated the central bank to have purchased between $300 million and $500 million, possibly via two foreign banks. "They (the authorities) may be wanting the dollar to flirt a while longer with levels above KRW1,200," before the won resumes its uptrend on a solid local economic recovery, said a foreign bank trader.

The dollar opened the domestic session sharply higher at KRW1,224 following news late last week that Fitch downgraded its credit ratings on Spain. But it quickly trimmed those gains to a low of KRW1,195 on active month-end export settlements before bouncing back up to KRW1,202.5 on the suspected intervention.

Domestic treasury bonds and bond futures were moderately higher on weaker-than-expected industrial output data.

June bond futures gained nine ticks.

Official data released before the market open showed output in April rising 0.2% on a seasonally adjusted basis from the previous month, falling short of economists' expectation for a gain of 0.5%. Output was up a revised 1.7% in March.

The output data "will give more credence to the view that the local economic recovery momentum is slowing, leading treasury yields to continue heading to fresh lows for the year," said Daishin Securities fixed income analyst Jeong Im-bo.

The benchmark five-year yield had ended at a 2010 low of 4.26% on April 29.

Inflation data due Tuesday morning local time will come under intense scrutiny. The consumer price index likely rose 0.1% from a month earlier in May, according to the median forecast of 11 economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires. That would be a slowdown from April's 0.5% increase.

title: =DJ UPDATE: Korea Vows More Active  FX Intervention  If Needed
text:
(Recasts, adds market moves, intervention details.) 


 
   By Kanga Kong 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SEOUL (Dow Jones)--South Korea said Wednesday it is ready to intervene more actively in the currency markets if needed, a day after making a massive defense of the won, which had been battered by tensions over North Korea.

"We will, in close cooperation with the Bank of Korea, act more aggressively to stabilize the forex market if it is biased to one side on excessive sentimental unrest," the finance ministry said in a statement after an emergency meeting with the Bank of Korea, the financial-market regulator and the Ministry of Knowledge Economy.

The central bank bought won for the first time in more than a year Tuesday after the currency fell to a nearly one-year low. The BOK sold $2 billion to $2.5 billion for won, traders estimated, in a bid to brake this month's 13% plunge by the local currency.

Korea's tumbling markets helped unnerve global investors as North Korea's saber-rattling compounded concerns over Europe's debt crisis. Tensions have risen since Seoul last week accused Pyongyang of torpedoing the South Korean warship Cheonan near a disputed maritime border March 26, killing 46.

A group of defectors from the North said Tuesday that Pyongyang, which denies involvement in the sinking, last week ordered its citizens and troops to be ready for combat. The North further ratcheted up tensions late Tuesday by announcing it would "totally freeze" relations with the South and pull out of a bilateral nonaggression pact.

Tuesday's huge won-buying intervention--which accounted for as much as 20% of the day's heavy trading volume--pushed the dollar down sharply from KRW1,277.0, its highest since July 2009. The won weakened a bit Wednesday, with the dollar edging back up to KRW1,253.30 late in the day from KRW1,250.00 late Tuesday.

Seoul's main stock index rose 1.4% Wednesday, despite continued selling by foreign investors, recouping some of Tuesday's 2.7% loss.

"Overall, we can't say that the market has stabilized yet," said a currency trader at a local bank. "It'll probably take some time for that."

In its bid to reassure the markets, the government said Wednesday it is ready to take additional measures, such as providing efficient foreign-currency liquidity if deemed necessary for market stability.

It attributed Tuesday's won plunge partly to a market overreaction, saying the Korean economy is strong enough to weather news from the North with its sound finances, sizable foreign exchange reserves and a current-account surplus.

title: FX  ASIA: As Asian Reserves Rise, Euro May Fall Into Disfavor
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asia's foreign exchange reserves rose 1.5% in April from March as continued intervention in foreign exchange markets offset a drop in the value of central banks' euro-denominated holdings.

That trend that may emerge as an additional negative for the euro if it forces some of the world's top reserve holders to review the preference they've shown for the European currency in recent years.

According to calculations by Dow Jones Newswires, reserves held by 11 key Asian central banks, not including China's, stood at US$2.810 trillion at the end of April, up from US$2.777 trillion at the end of March. That compares with a 0.3% increase posted in March from February.

China, which releases its data on a quarterly basis, reported US$2.447 trillion in reserves at the end of March.

Combined, Asian central bank holdings account for around two-thirds of the world's overall amount, and analysts believe some 20%-25% of that amount is in euros. That's likely below the international average of 27.4% as of last December, according to International Monetary Fund data, but Asia's percentage has grown steadily in recent years.

Worries about a possible reduction of central bank euro holdings hit the market earlier this year and are gaining pace as the euro loses ground against the dollar, eroding its status as the top alternative to the greenback. That's important because the latest data show that while market speculators (including hedge funds) are active euro sellers, observers believe most "real-money" managers like central banks and pension funds haven't yet joined the euro-bashing party.

In a recent report, Credit Suisse analysts said the euro-zone's structural problems and handling of the Greek debt crisis have "severely damaged" the notion--particularly among managers of central bank reserve funds--that euros can be held as a "safe alternative" to the dollar.

So far this year, the euro has lost 11% against the dollar; that includes a 1.6% drop in April and a 4.9% drop so far in May. But that may be just the beginning if Asian central banks start to unload euros.

In 2002, when the euro replaced individual euro-zone currencies, it accounted for only 23.8% of global reserves. It's up 50% against the dollar since, supported by the continued decrease in the dollar as a percentage of global reserves as central banks have diversified in favor of the euro.

Meanwhile, strong purchases of dollars in forex markets continued in many Asian countries in April. That matches the recent trend as central banks remain wary of allowing their local currencies to rise on the strength of sustained flows into fast-growing Asian markets.

Seven Asian central banks reported reserves at all-time highs, including Indonesia's, where reserves grew a whopping 9.5% on-month in April on the back of continued intervention. Bank Indonesia has been trying to contain the appreciation of the rupiah, one of Asia's best performers this year with a 3.9% gain against the dollar since January on top of a 12% rise in 2009.

Strong reserve increases in Singapore and South Korea also were likely driven by continued intervention in forex markets.

title: =DJ  FX  ASIA: Will  South Korea  Take Bolder Steps On  Intervention ?
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--The recent appointment of several key economic officials has players expecting a more forceful government presence in South Korea's foreign exchange market--but a closer look at the country's fundamentals suggests their concerns may be misplaced.

With the appointment of former Vice Finance Minister Choi Joong-kyung as President Lee Myung-bak's economic adviser, market players expect the authorities to meddle in the currency market more frequently, particularly with data suggesting the won will strengthen for the rest of the year.

Many traders recall aggressive intervention to curb won strength and maintain the country's export competitiveness when Choi was a mastermind of the Finance Ministry's foreign-exchange policy in 2004 and 2008.

But the preference for a weaker won, shared by Choi and former Finance Minister Kang Man-soo, contributed to a spike in imported inflation in 2008, and the pair eventually stepped down. Kang returned last year as chief of a presidential council promoting the nation's economic competitiveness.

Choi and Kang "support policies that let domestic products have more price competitiveness abroad via high foreign-exchange rates," one senior trader at a foreign bank in Seoul said. Because Choi "is such a supporter of a high exchange rate, interventions are likely to take a step toward being stronger."

Choi wasn't available for comment. Kang declined to comment on the foreign-exchange rate.

Currency players expect to see stepped-up intervention as the dollar approaches the psychologically important KRW1,100 level: If that's breached, they say, the won could sprint higher. In the past week or so, market players say they've spotted intervention on three different days around KRW1,107-KRW1,108.

Neither Choi nor Kang is now directly responsible for intervention--that's up to the Finance Ministry and central bank--but the market expects the two policymakers to push for a weaker won to help exporters.

They may face an uphill battle: Several market participants said won strength is due to fundamentals that authorities can hardly fight. For example, the expected appreciation of the Chinese yuan against the dollar could drag other regional currencies higher.

"The dollar-selling interest is explosive amid robust sentiment for Asian currencies in general," one local bank trader said. "I don't think (the authorities) can do much to stop this."

Fund inflows to the local stock and bond markets also should keep won demand solid, especially after Moody's Investors Service upgraded Korea's sovereign debt ratings earlier this month.

Moreover, as one central bank official said, Choi may return to office a chastened man.

"Choi had an experience that he aggressively pushed for a weaker won and faced strong headwinds in the market," the BOK official said. "He may have changed now. I don't think he'll go against the market."

Given the current global context--with U.S. authorities leading a push to make China appreciate its currency--more aggressive intervention is likely to face criticism.

"Ask yourself, will (the BOK) solely bid up the dollar even more aggressively, while others are talking about China letting the yuan appreciate?" another foreign bank trader said. "You've got to be global."

(Seoul-based correspondent Min-Jeong Lee has covered South Korea's foreign exchange market since 2008. She can be reached at 82 2 3700 1908 or min-jeong.lee@dowjones.com.)
