SEOUL (Dow Jones)--The South Korean won was nearly unchanged late Friday as strong demand for the local unit helped offset the renewed concerns over debt-ridden Greece.

Given the country's relatively solid economic fundamentals, the trend for next few weeks will be of a further appreciation in the won, except when the central bank intervenes to cap the gains, traders said.

South Korea's growth likely accelerated in the first quarter from the previous three months as consumption improved, economists said. GDP likely grew a seasonally adjusted 1.5% in the first quarter. In the fourth quarter of 2009, GDP grew 0.2% on-quarter.

"Exporters and offshore hedge funds are still waiting for any rallies in the dollar to dump their dollar holdings," said a foreign bank trader.

"After about, let's say, a month, exporters and other players are bound to realize how the current dollar levels had been attractive to sell their dollars," said a local bank trader. "I expect the dollar to be at least off by some 20 won from here."

The negative impact on the won of news that Moody's Investors Service downgraded Greece's ratings was minimal, even though the euro fell to an 11-month low against the dollar following the announcement.

"This Greece issue has been such a prolonged one that its (negative) impact on the Seoul foreign-exchange market has somewhat worn off," said Byeon Ji-young, an analyst at Woori Futures.

Domestic treasury bonds and bond futures rose marginally as trade remained quiet ahead of the nation's first-quarter gross domestic output data. June bond futures gained seven ticks.

Bond prices have neared their previous highs again, so those anticipating a range bound market should consider taking profits around current levels, said Kim Sang-hoon, a fixed income analyst at Hana Daetoo Securities.

"So long as foreign investors--betting on stronger won-denominated assets in general--don't turn away from local bonds and bond futures, excessive selling doesn't seem appropriate," Kim said.

title: S.Korea March  FX  reserves second largest ever
text:
SEOUL, April 2 (Reuters) - South Korea's foreign exchange reserves in March rose to their second largest ever, central bank data showed on Friday, as foreign exchange authorities were spotted buying dollars to curb the won's <KRW=> strength.

Foreign exchange reserves held by Asia's fourth-largest economy gained $1.67 billion during the month to $272.33 billion by the end of March, the Bank of Korea said in a statement.

The central bank attributed the rise to investment gains, with officials declining to comment on earlier market talk about dollar-buying intervention to check the won's rise.

South Korea had the world's sixth-largest foreign reserves at the end of February after China, Japan, Russia, Taiwan and India. title: S.Korean won hits 2-wk high,  intervention  spotted
text:
* Won gains 0.5 pct to 2-week high

 * Foreign investors buy local stocks for 13th session in row

 * Dealers report dollar-buying intervention  (Updates to close)

 SEOUL, March 30 (Reuters) - The won rose half a percent to a near 2-week high against the dollar on Tuesday as the euro's rebound eased concerns about Europe's debt problems and as foreign stock funds kept rushing into South Korea.

 Dealers reported South Korean authorities buying dollars in intervention aimed at stemming the won's <KRW=> <KRW=KFTC> fast appreciation, which policymakers in the country are worried would hurt the competitiveness of its exporters.

 Dealers said the won was supported by growing risk preference, but demand for dollars remained solid from importers and foreign shareholders in local companies, who recently received dividend payouts for the last year.

 "Offshore players have been leading bids for the won since yesterday but I think the won's upside will be limited at around 1,128 (per dollar)," said a foreign bank dealer.

 The won ended the session at 1,130.1 per dollar after rising to as high as 1,129.6, its strongest since March 18, compared with Monday's domestic close of 1,135.5.

 Foreign investors extended their net buying spree on Seoul's main stock exchange to a 13th consecutive session, setting the longest successive buying streak since September last year.

 The exchange's benchmark KOSPI <.KS11> ended up 0.5 percent at 1,700.19 points, its strongest finish since Jan. 21, as foreign investors bought a net 258 billion won ($228 million) worth of local shares.

Goldman Sachs added to the bullish mood by upgrading its 3-month view on the won to 1,100 from 1,150 previously, citing prospects for an improving international balance of payments and an interest rate increase later this year.

Central bank data also showed on Tuesday that South Korean manufacturing firms, relying heavily on exports, were the most optimistic in at least seven years about their business conditions in the coming month. [ID:nSUL000014]

SEOUL (Dow Jones)--The South Korean won rose sharply late Wednesday, likely prompting a second straight day of intervention by the Bank of Korea to prop the dollar.

The Bank of Korea may have intervened several times in the local currency market during the session to slow the won's rise by purchasing small batches of dollars, three Seoul-based traders said.

They may have intervened largely through one foreign bank and one local bank, buying dollars around the KRW1,141-KRW1,143 levels, they added. One of those traders estimated the purchases to total between $500 million and $600 million.

The suspected intervention came after the central bank was seen supporting the dollar near KRW1,150 Tuesday.

"It's not about keeping the dollar at a certain level since they can't reverse the direction of the dollar's move," said a foreign bank trader. He forecast the dollar to trade in a KRW1,130-KRW1,150 range Thursday.

The won gained 0.8% on a broad return of risk appetite, tracking overnight gains in the euro and robust regional stocks during the Asian hours.

Most domestic treasury bonds ended flat after a listless session. March bond futures ended three ticks higher at 110.40 after moving in a tight 110.29-110.40 range.

"Bonds are just taking a breather. There wasn't a lot of trading and there weren't any big moves in futures either," said a local securities firm trader. "It might take a while, but the three-year yield is likely to fall to as low as 4.00% eventually, given weak prospects for a domestic rate hike."

He expects the yield curve to move aimlessly, with buying interest likely shifting back and forth between shorter and longer-end bonds.

The Bombay Stock Exchange's 30-share index could rally to 16,530, according to charts.

But the short-term bullish view would be negated if the index falls below Friday's intra-day low of 15,980.

A move past this immediate resistance would be a sign of strength and could trigger a rally to 4,970.

The short-term bullish outlook would be invalidated on a close below 4,825. A fall below this would suggest that the index is headed to major support at 4,540.


 
 
US STOCKS 

U.S. stocks rose broadly Monday as better-than-expected quarterly earnings from Exxon Mobil and a rebound in crude oil prices lifted the energy sector, while materials stocks including Alcoa and DuPont were boosted by a rise in metals futures.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 1.17%, marking its first rise in three sessions and its biggest one-day gain since Jan. 4. The measure is still off 2.33% for the year to date, thanks to a rough losing spell in the latter part of January.

Alcoa and DuPont were the Dow's best performers, with Exxon Mobil not far behind. Alcoa jumped 5%, while DuPont rose 3.2%, as metals futures climbed, with gold futures snapping a three-session losing streak and silver and copper ending four-session losing streaks.

Exxon Mobil climbed 2.7% after its fourth-quarter earnings beat expectations, though they were still down 23% as lower margins on refining and fuels and lower natural gas prices were partly offset by higher crude prices.

Monday's stock gains came as manufacturing data from the Institute for Supply Management came in above expectations, showing the U.S. factory sector booked its best performance in more than five years in January.

The excitement over the ISM report largely outweighed investors' concerns about President Barack Obama's budget plan, which would shrink the current deficit to $727 billion, or 4.2% of the gross domestic product, by 2013, but add $8.5 trillion to the federal debt through 2020, pushing the debt as a percentage of GDP to 77%, up from 53%.


 
 
ASIAN STOCKS 

Asian stock markets were higher Tuesday as gains in Wall Street buoyed sentiment, with auto makers in Japan rising after Toyota Motor took steps to fix recalled vehicles.

Japan's Nikkei 225, Australia's S&P/ASX 200, South Korea's Kospi Composite and New Zealand's NZX-50 were all higher. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were up 4 points in screen trade.

"I think we're in for a good day's trade, but you still have to consider the downside risks because it's a fickle market," said IG Markets Institutional Dealer Chris Weston in Sydney. "I think people want to see Wall Street prove itself."

In Japan, auto makers were rising on short-covering. Toyota's shares were heavily sold recently after it recalled vehicles in the U.S. and Europe because some gas pedals were sticking.

Toyota was up 4.3%. Honda Motor, which also announced a worldwide recall of 646,000 compact cars to examine defective window switches, advanced 2.2%, and Nissan Motor rose 2.8%. Shipping and oil plays were higher, with Nippon Yusen up 2.0%, Mitsui O.S.K. Lines up 2.5% and Inpex 2.0%.

South Korean shares were led higher by gains in steelmakers and technology names, mostly tracking their U.S. peers. "The U.S. markets' rebound overnight following recent falls improved sentiment, leading foreign investors to resume stock buying," said Lee Sun-yup at Shinhan Investment Corporation.

Samsung Electronics added 0.6% and LG Display rose 1.4%; among steelmakers, Posco was up 2.3%. However, Hyundai Motor gave up 2.6% and Kia Motors fell 1.7% on profit-taking, despite data Monday showing strong January car sales.

FOREX

The dollar slipped from six-month highs Monday as evidence of a global economic recovery drove investors to higher-yielding currencies. SEOUL (Dow Jones)--The South Korean won was higher late Wednesday on active dollar-selling by local exporters, but its gains were again capped by suspected central bank intervention.

The Bank of Korea may have intervened in the local currency market toward the end of the session to cap a rise in the won, four Seoul-based traders said.

The central bank likely bought the dollar around KRW1,163, largely via a state-run bank, they said. One of those traders at a local bank estimated the central bank to have bought between $300 million and $500 million.

Market participants observed that the central bank has been stepping into the market frequently in recent months to curb the local currency's rise, which has gained around 35% since its low in March. Domestic authorities are concerned that the won's persistent strength may sap an export-led recovery in Asia's fourth largest economy.

A foreign bank trader said that the greenback is poised for more falls next year.

"With the continued current account surpluses, (the dollar's) supply still outweighs demand. And we will see more selling from heavy industry firms next year," said the trader. "The appropriate direction for the dollar/won is for it to go downwards," which will likely prompt further intervention by the domestic authorities.

After a listless session in the morning, the dollar hit an intraday low of KRW1,162.60 in the afternoon as exporters started selling aggressively due to their year-end settlements while offshore investors also sold greenbacks.

The won was up 0.6% for the day, 8.2% for this year.

Wednesday was the last trading day for the local spot market for the year. Trading will resume Monday, when the market will open at 0100 GMT, an hour later than its usual opening time.

Domestic treasury bonds ended mixed after a listless session. March bond futures lost six ticks as foreigners were net sellers of bond futures for a sixth straight session.

Bonds largely brushed off government data issued earlier in day that showed South Korea's industrial production increased 17.8% in November from a year earlier, accelerating from 0.2% growth in October.

"The numbers are good, but the data aren't much of a surprise," as the market had expected some 17% growth, said a bond manager at a local asset management firm.

Bargain hunting may provide support for bonds next week after some steep falls since early December. But any strong rebound from current levels seems unlikely as investors aren't anticipating the central bank's governor to make dovish comments at the upcoming Bank of Korea's meeting in January, he added.

On Thursday, the regular local bond market will be closed while the over-the-counter bond market will open as usual. Both markets will be closed Friday and resume trading Monday.

The benchmark five-year yield has gained 115 basis points so far this year.

SEOUL (Dow Jones)--The South Korea won was a touch higher late Tuesday, paring gains on corporate demand for the greenback and concerns the central bank could intervene should the currency climb too fast.

The won had opened stronger against the dollar, reflecting rising risk appetite following gains in U.S. stocks overnight, but companies buying the greenback on dips helped to cushion the dollar.

Among those fuelling demand was state-run Korea Electric Power Corp. (015760.SE), which entered the Seoul foreign-exchange market for the second straight day, a person familiar with the matter told Dow Jones Newswires.

The person said the purchases were made so the company could repay its foreign-currency-denominated debt, but declined to comment on the amount that Kepco bought on either day.

Kepco, which has a total of $1.25 billion of euro- and yen-denominated offshore debt falling due next week, plans to buy more than $1.2 billion in Seoul's foreign-exchange market this week, the person said.

"Dollar demand (from Kepco) seems have been quite significant today," said a local bank trader.

After rebounding from an intraday low of KRW1,149.70 hit after the market just opened, the dollar ended the session at its weakest since Sept. 23, 2008, when it sank to KRW1,149.00.

"The dollar remains bearish. But for the dollar-won to make a convincing break below the 1,150 level, the euro would have to continue trading comfortably above the key $1.5000 resistance," said a foreign bank trader.

The euro--a general barometer of risk appetite--was trading lower at $1.4955 in late Asian trade, compared with $1.5005 in New York Monday.

Domestic treasury bonds and bond futures rose sharply after monetary authorities both in the U.S. and domestically further bolstered perceptions that interest rates will stay extremely low for an extended period of time, with December bond futures gaining 24 ticks.

Bank of Korea Senior Deputy Governor Kim Jae-chun said in a statement prepared for a global financial conference in Seoul: "If we raise the policy rate hastily, it'll hurt the recovery of the Korean economy," though Kim added that "keeping the rate low for too long will also impair the long-term growth potential."

Overnight, U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke sounded a cautious note on the U.S. economy, prompting investors to stock up on U.S. Treasurys.

"The buying interest spread to the longer tenor bonds today," which had been underperforming the shorter ones recently, said a bond manager at an asset management firm.

"Bonds might correct some gains on the way, but the overall bullish sentiment will likely persist" until the release of economic data at the end of the month, he added.

title: HIGHLIGHTS-South Korean  central bank  chief's comments
text:
(For full coverage, double-click [ID:nSP479672])

SEOUL, Oct 9 (Reuters) - The Bank of Korea's chief prompted investors on Friday to scale back their bets on a rate rise this year, noting signs of cooling in the property market and predicting economic growth would taper off this quarter.

The central bank held its key interest rate steady at a record low of 2.0 percent on Friday for the eighth month in a row as expected, saying uncertainty over the global demand remained and the domestic inflation was stable.

Following are a selection of Bank of Korea Governor Lee Seong-tae's remarks at a news conference, translated by Reuters:

ON PROPERTY MARKET

"The real estate market shows signs of moderating since mid-September. Stabilising property market should reduce the burden on monetary authorities...But it's too soon to say the property market has fully stabilised. We need to watch more whether property prices will stabilise further or revive after a break."

"The government has taken several regulatory steps, which seem to be working in bringing down the pace of mortgage lending growth...And the recent rise in borrowing rates appears to have had some effect, as well, I believe."

ON INTEREST RATES, EXIT STRATEGY

"Current policy rate represents a considerable monetary easing, when taking into account our economic growth pace, inflation and market rates. The rate is also low when taking into account the mid- to long-term economic prospects."

"We don't decide rates only based on the property market situation. It's true that the property issue has been a major concern for us since the second quarter. (But) the most important determinants are consumer prices and economy."

"In September I wanted to send signals that rate hikes were not far away and could come earlier than expected, and it seems that some people took the comments as indicating an imminent rate change."

"Australia raised its rate to 3.25 percent from 3.0 percent but that cannot be viewed as an exit strategy."

"Market rates have risen but they are not yet so high as to give big troubles to households or companies."

"I understand the global coordination in exit policy as a call for countries to consider its influence, positive or negative, on the global economy as well as on the other nations when setting a policy."

ON ECONOMY, INFLATION

"Global economic conditions, which are a major factor for our economy, are improving gradually since the start of the second half but I'm not confident of a strong recovery yet. There remain many uncertainties over the global economic growth."

"Our economy continues its recovery. The third-quarter GDP growth is likely to be better than expected. But the fourth-quarter growth is not seen as strong as in the second and third quarters."

"Inflation will likely stabilise in 2009 and 2010 from high levels seen in 2007 and 2008. The domestic inflation is expected to hover around our target of 3 percent level."

ON CURRENCY, CURRENT ACCOUNT

"As a small open economy, South Korea needs to carry out some intervention if needed in the foreign exchange market."

"The won's tumbling to 1,500 to the dollar in the wake of the global financial crisis was an over-reaction, given our economic strength. The recent rise is understood as a correction to that."

"It's hard to say what is the proper level for the foreign exchange rates. But a sharp fluctuation is a concern."

"The current account surplus for this year can be far bigger than initially expected. The surplus will decline next year but not to a worrisome extent." (Reporting by Seo Eun-kyung; Editing by Yoo Choonsik)

title: UPDATE: IMF Urges BOK To Keep Rates Low Amid Asset Inflation
text:
(Adds economist's comment, background)

SEOUL (Dow Jones)--The International Monetary Fund said the Bank of Korea should keep its monetary policy loose, but that the Seoul authorities haven't ruled out rate hikes if general asset prices rise.

The IMF, in an annual assessment report on South Korea issued Thursday, said that after the BOK slashed rates by 325 basis points from October to February, "Monetary-policy accommodation should be maintained for now, while concerns about asset-price appreciation are best addressed through prudential regulation."

The Korean authorities, in a meeting that ended July 7, "agreed with the need for an accommodative monetary stance but remained concerned about its effect on asset prices," the IMF said. "The authorities did not rule out interest-rate hikes should more generalized asset-price rises become a concern."

Bank of Korea Governor Lee Seongtae said earlier this month that the central bank's next move, when it comes, is "clearly up," causing a massive sell-off in the bond market on fears that a rate increase could come earlier than expected.

Both the government and the BOK have said they would step up monitoring of the property market following a rise in mortgage lending and higher housing prices in recent months.

But many economists expect the central bank to switch to tightening some time in the first quarter of next year given as-yet tame inflation and uncertain economic growth prospects.

"Most indicators, including inflation, don't point to a rate increase any time soon. Asset price hikes in some areas alone won't be an excuse for any rate move," said Chun Chong-woo, head of macroeconomics and asset allocation department at Samsung Securities.

In its latest report, the IMF also said: "While there are signs of excess liquidity, stock market valuations and house prices remain well in line with global peers and don't warrant an immediate monetary policy response."

Earlier this month the BOK left its benchmark interest rate steady at an all-time low of 2.00% for a sixth consecutive month.

Korea should also keep its fiscal stance expansionary in 2010 as the economic recovery is likely to be "drawn out," but the authorities also need to demonstrate a plan for fiscal consolidation in the medium term, the IMF said.

It said the Korean won is "considerably below most estimates of its long-term equilibrium level" as a result of capital outflows, but that this should be temporary.

South Korea has "abstained completely" this year from intervening in currency markets, the IMF said, but if the authorities should step in, any "intervention in the spot market should remain confined to smoothing operations."

At 0530 GMT Friday, the dollar fetched KRW1,253.3, up from its close Thursday of 1,246.9.

SEOUL, May 11 (Reuters) - The South Korean won hit its strongest in more than six months on Monday as foreign investors kept buying Seoul stocks after better-than-expected U.S. job data that bolstered appetite for riskier assets.

The won <KRW=>, however, gave up some of its early gains as investors became more cautious over possible dollar-buying intervention by South Korea's foreign exchange authorities to prevent the country's exporters from losing overseas price competitiveness.

Analysts said the local currency was expected to rise further as more investors sought assets amid hopes for economic recovery, although the pace of the currency's rise was expected to slow on possible intervention by the authorities.

"Considering firmer stocks and recovery hopes, there are no bearish factors for the won. But I wonder how fast it will rise from this level," said Jeong My-young, a currency analyst at Samsung Futures Inc.

"We also need to keep an eye on the authorities, as their actions would just slow the speed of its rise," she added.

The South Korean unit was quoted at 1,237.7/8.0 per dollar as of 0600 GMT, compared with Friday's domestic close <KRW=KFTC> of 1,247.0.

It strengthened to as much as 1,230.8, the strongest since Oct. 31, 2008.

Foreign investors bought a net 273.8 billion won worth of stocks on the country's main exchange, helping Seoul shares <.KS11> end up 0.21 percent, recovering earlier losses.

Foreigners purchased a combined net 2.12 trillion won in shares during the previous six consecutive sessions.

Their continuous purchases were expected to support the won, but the further the local currency rose the more wary of potential intervention investors would grow, analysts said.

That, along with demand from exporters, was likely to lock the won in a range, they added.

"The won may see some consolidative action within the 1,230-1,246 band for now. Sentiment is turning cautious. There was talk of suspected smoothing operations by South Korean authorities as well. There were signs of speculative short covering and good importer demand near 1,230," said Daniel Soh, a strategist at FORECAST Pte Ltd.

Investors will be keeping an eye on the central bank's monetary policy meeting on Tuesday. The Bank of Korea is expected to hold interest rates at a record low of 2.00 percent for the thir month in a row. [ID:nSEO274360]

title: Emerging  FX -Asia rises on stock gains, China stimulus hopes
text:
SINGAPORE, March 4 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rose on Wednesday as investors snapped up stocks in the hope that China will step up efforts to spur its economy, with suspected intervention boosting South Korea's won and the Singapore dollar.

The Philippine peso <PHP=> rose a third of a percent to 48.65 per dollar as a senior central bank official said falling inflation had created room for the central bank to cut interest rates, a day before the interest rate review.

Deputy central bank governor Diwa Guinigundo also said the central bank would avoid intervention given the peso's relative stability. [ID:nSP405920]

The peso is down 2.4 percent against the dollar so far this year -- the second best performing currency after the Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> in those that are tracked daily by Reuters.

Meanwhile, the Thai baht <THB=TH> gained almost 0.4 percent to 36 per dollar.

The volatile South Korean won <KRW=> rose as much as 1 percent to 1,535.2 per dollar as dealers suspected the authorities were selling dollars to support the ailing unit.

The won, the worst performing Asian currency, is still down 19 percent against the dollar this year.

A senior Chinese planning official said on Wednesday the government will increase spending in areas such as infrastructure and manufacturing on top of the 4 trillion yuan ($585 billion) stimulus package unveiled in November. [ID:nL4384]

The comment, along with signs of a recovery in China's economy highlighted by a big improvement in the purchasing managers' index, helped boost Asian stocks.

The MSCI index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> rising 1.5 percent as of 0747 GMT.

"The bounce in equities probably is the most obvious cue while the broad dollar index has stabilised somewhat, with the additional boost coming from in China of course," said Emmanuel Ng, currency strategist at OCBC Bank.

But he cautioned that the near-term outlook for most Asian currencies remained grim due to the worsening global downturn.

The Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> hovered near 6.84 per dollar, but one-year dollar/yuan non-deliverable forwards <CNYNDFOR=> eased to 6.9553, which implied a fall of 1.6 percent from the spot.

Elsewhere, the Singapore dollar <SGD=> edged up to 1.5510 to the U.S. dollar as traders cited official intervention to limit the currency's losses.

"There was a lot of U.S. dollar buying this morning by U.S. houses and funds," said a Singapore-based trader, adding the unit is supported by U.S. dollar sales by the central bank.

title: WRAPUP 2-S.Korean won hits 11-yr low as global woe lingers
text:
* Won falls to weakest since March 1998

* Worries about local dollar-funding shortages weigh

* Risk aversion seen barring quick turnaround (Adds more details, stocks)

By Yoo Choonsik and Cheon Jong-woo

SEOUL, Feb 27 (Reuters) - The won fell to an 11-year low on Friday on investor concern about a shortage of U.S. dollars in South Korea and analysts said risk aversion fueled by the fragile global financial system would bar any quick turnaround.

Analysts conceded that some of the steps taken by the government of President Lee Myung-bak could help improve dollar funding in the long term but said that there was little the government could do to put an immediate halt to the selloff.

South Korea's massive dollar-selling intervention late last year had helped the won <KRW=> recover some momentum, but troubles in eastern European economies this year have again sapped investors' confidence in emerging markets.

Investors are worried that the heightened risk aversion would make it extremely difficult for South Korea to tap into the global market to secure sufficient dollar funding to pay back maturing foreign debt.

"(The won is) just friendless at the moment, it's unwanted. But I think most of the bad news is already in the price. I don't think investors are taking sufficient encouragement and notice of the better numbers, such as on external debt," said Patrick Bennett, a strategist at Societe Generale in Hong Kong.

"In an environment where risk appetite is low, you're not seeing the flow that would help lead a recovery in the won."

The won <KRW=> fell to as low as 1,542.9 per dollar, its weakest since March 1998, before recovering slightly to 1,534.8 by 0740 GMT on market talk of dollar-selling intervention by foreign exchange authorities in the afternoon.

Seoul shares <.KS11>, which gained as much 2.09 percent earlier in the session, fell back as the won fell, closing up 0.78 percent.

South Korea said on Thursday it would exempt foreign investors from income and capital gains taxes on investment in local treasury bonds and monetary stabilisation bonds to lure more foreign capital into the country.

HEAVY FOREIGN DEBT

The won's drop came even after data showed on Friday that South Korea's balance of payments surplus hit a near 2-year high in January as domestic investors sold off their foreign portfolio holdings and foreigners bought local shares. [ID:nSEO194004]

Banks in South Korea, including those run by foreigners, had $126.6 billion of foreign debt due this year as of the end of January, out of the total $182.3 billion worth, the government said Friday. [ID:nSEO212505]

South Korea has said its foreign currency reserves of more than $200 billion and currency swap arrangements sealed with the United States, Japan and China totalling some $90 billion were more than sufficient to cover any emergency situation.

It has also said it was not obliged to repay all the debts because some were owed by foreign banks and some others were linked to currency hedging contracts of their corporate clients.

The won came under more pressure in recent months as evidence mounts that the heavily export-dependent economy will be hit especially hard by the financial and economic crisis.

South Korea's government expects the economy to shrink by about 2 percent this year but analysts forecast a contraction of as much as 7 percent, which would be the sharpest fall in the country's nearly 40 years of industrialisation.

The government has offered about $100 billion worth of fiscal spending and tax cut plans and the central bank slashed interest rates by 3.25 percentage points in less than five months to lift domestic demand and make up for collapsing exports.

title: UPDATE 1-S.Korea warns against  FX  speculators-Yonhap
text:
(Recasts with finance minister)

SEOUL, Feb 22 (Reuters) - South Korea on Sunday issued a warning against speculative traders as its won currency has tumbled on worries about its ability to secure dollars to pay back maturing foreign debt, Yonhap news agency reported.

"The government will not sit idle when the foreign exchange rate is excessively tilted toward one direction or when there are speculative forces," Yonhap quoted Finance Minister Yoon Jeung-hyun as saying in Phuket, Thailand.

Yoon was visiting the Thai resort island to co-chair a meeting of finance ministers from 13 east Asian countries -- 10 southeast Asian countries and China, Japan and South Korea.

Finance ministry officials in Seoul could not immediately be reached for comment on the strongest indication of a possible dollar-selling intervention aimed at defending its ailing currency since Yoon took office early this month.

There has been no report of intervention by South Korean authorities as the won fell for nine consecutive sessions to trade near an 11-year low against the dollar set in November last year.

The central bank issued a statement on Thursday, in which the Bank of Korea dismissed worries about the country's foreign debt burden as overblown, saying the maturing debt was small compared with the country's massive foreign currency reserves.

Analysts said $24.5 billion worth of foreign debt South Korean banks have to pay back or roll over this year was small in value, but warned unstable global markets could make it difficult for South Korean banks to raise sufficient dollars.

Yoon's reported comment came hours after Yonhap quoted unnamed central bank and finance ministry officials as saying they may use some of the foreign reserves to shore up the tumbling won even if the reserves fall below $200 billion.

"Whether the foreign reserves fall below $200 billion is not the subject of consideration at all in deciding whether to intervene in the foreign exchange market," Yonhap quoted an unnamed Bank of Korea official as saying.

There has been a perception among traders and analysts that South Korea was holding off from dollar-selling intervention in recent weeks because it did not want foreign reserves to fall below $200 billion.

South Korean foreign reserves fell to a near four-year low of $200.5 billion at the end of last November as a result of dollar-selling intervention for months, before edging up to $201.7 billion by the end of January.

Yonhap said another unnamed official at the Ministry of Strategy and Finance also dismissed market talk that South Korea was not intervening in the foreign exchange market to keep foreign reserves above $200 billion.

"All of the foreign reserves can be used when it's deemed necessary," the finance ministry official was quoted as saying.

The Bank of Korea usually carries out intervention in the currency market but the finance ministry has the final say.

The won has lost 17 percent so far this year to a three-month closing low of 1,506 per dollar on Friday, making it the worst performer among major Asian currencies this year, raising concerns about the country's financial stability as a whole. (Editing by Erica Billingham)

SEOUL, Feb 12 (Reuters) - The South Korean won fell against the dollar to hit a two-month closing low on Thursday despite a central bank rate cut as worries about a slowing economy and disappointment over a U.S. bank rescue plan hit Seoul shares.

The won <KRW=>, however, found some relief from persistent caution over possible dollar-selling intervention by South Korea's foreign exchange authorities.

The local currency is expected to weaken further as investors look for safer assets on fears that global stimulus packages will not prove enough to revive the economy, analysts said.

"Technically, the won is more likely to fall more as it broke through the long-time support line of 1,400 (per dollar)," said Jeong My-young, a currency strategist at Samsung Futures Inc.

"Risk aversion will strengthen on higher external risks and as South Korean authorities have admitted how serious the state of the economy is," Jeong said.

The South Korean currency was quoted at 1,403.9/4.6 versus the U.S. unit as of 0600 GMT, compared with Wedensday's domestic close of 1,393.5. Thursday's closing was the weakest since Dec. 9, 2008.

After the rate cut, the central bank chief said it was uncertain when the economy would bottom out and noted concerns over credit risk persisted in financial markets.

Seoul shares <.KS11> ended down 0.87 percent as foreign investors sold a net 202.4 billion won worth of stocks in the country's main exchange.

Foreigners unloaded a combined net 319.2 billion won during the previous two consecutive sessions.

title: S.Korea won falls briefly on suspected  intervention .
text:
SEOUL, Nov 22 (Reuters) - South Korea's won currency dropped suddenly from 7-year highs in Monday afternoon trade on suspected intervention just hours after the finance minister held a rare meeting to discuss its rise with the central bank chief.   


The won             fell to 1,068.8 per dollar in local trade soon
after 0500 GMT, having earlier reached 1,060.0, its strongest against
the dollar since November 1997. It stayed only briefly at its low,
which was just weaker than Friday's close of 1,068.7, before recovering
towards 1,065.
  

"The dollar rose suddenly because of intervention by authorities, but there are still lots of dollars in the market," said a dealer at a local bank.  

The strength of the won, which has gained 6 percent this month against the dollar and 12 percent so far this year, also sent the local stock market tumbling almost 2 percent.  

Earlier on Monday, Finance Minister Lee Hun-jai asked central bank chief Park Seung for a stronger stance in capping the won's rise, according to a government source.  

"He asked Governor Park that the central bank take bolder and more aggressive counter measures," the source said by telephone, adding that this could include the central bank using its right to print money.  

However, dealers say any impact of such moves would only be limited unless they are followed by actual intervention.  

"This is driven by a dollar oversupply and looks inevitable," said Park Yong-il, a senior foreign exchange trader at DBS Bank's branch in Seoul. "Many appear doubtful that the central bank can keep printing money without limit to absorb all the supply."  

The rare meeting between Lee and the governor of the Bank of Korea came as the won's rally raised concerns about the export-dependent economy being damaged as slowing exports combine with a persistent slump in local demand.  

The Bank of Korea has taken the leading role in controlling the won's rise since the finance ministry was criticised last month in parliament for keeping the won undervalued.  

The amount of money the ministry can mobilise to fund intervention has also been limited by parliament.  

The rising won has added to concerns about Chinese demand for exports after Beijing raised interest rates for the first time in nine years to step up a drive to cool its economy.  

China is the largest market for South Korean exports, soaking up a fifth of its total shipments abroad.  

Last week the finance minister all but abandoned a long-standing target of 5 percent economic growth this year, saying the chance of meeting the forecast was extremely slim.   


The firmer won also hit export-reliant manufacturers on the Seoul stock
market. Chipmaker Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd.  fell 3.1 percent and
automaker Hyundai Motor Co.             lost 2.4 percent. (Additional
reporting by Lee Shin-hyung and Cheon Jong-woo).

title: Seoul shares to open lower, oil price dip to support.
text:
SEOUL, Nov 17 (Reuters) - Seoul stocks look set to open lower on Wednesday, pausing from a recent rally spurred by an unexpected cut in interest rates, but falling oil prices may boost export and utilities stocks.   

Central bank comments that the won's recent gains had been too rapid may also help exporters such as Hyundai Motor Co. .   

"The domestic markets are likely to continue a correction after recent gains, following a similar movement among U.S. shares," said Kim Hak-kyun, an analyst at Goodmorning Shinhan Securities. "But there is still potential for further gains after the rate cut and as oil prices continue falling."   

The benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) fell 0.65 percent on Tuesday to 876.61 points.   

Seoul stock trading is to start at 0100 GMT, an hour later than usual, because of the country-wide college entrance examinations. The market will close an hour later than usual.   

U.S. shares fell on Tuesday, marking a pause for breath after the market's strong post-election rally.   

U.S. crude oil futures tumbled, easing concerns about the impact of higher energy costs on corporate profits. Oil traded at $46.16 a barrel on Wednesday.   

South Korea is the world's fourth-largest importer.    


A senior South Korean central bank official said the won         was
rising too fast.
   

The warning followed data showing a jump in South Korea's forex reserves amid suspected heavy intervention to control a rise in the won.

title: Bk of Korea: Worried  FX  Sentiment 'Excessively' Lopsided
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--In the first verbal intervention from local authorities in many months, the Bank of Korea Wednesday said the U.S. dollar's fall against the won has been of a greater magnitude compared with the trend in other currencies, and warned it is "fully prepared to take necessary action."  

"We're worried that the sentiment in the currency market is excessively tilted to one direction," Rhee Gwang-Ju, director-general of the bank's international department, said in a statement.  

In an apparent warning to exporters who lately have been blamed for the sharp dollar retreat, the Bank of Korea said it is "closely watching" the currency activities of companies as well as individual onshore and offshore players.  

The unusually strong-worded statement on intervention comes after the dollar Tuesday dipped to levels not seen since 1997, at the height of the Asian financial crisis. [ 10-11-04 0025GMT ]  

The statement Wednesday also marks the first time the Bank of Korea has stepped past the Ministry of Finance and Economy to helm foreign exchange policies since the second half of 2003. The central bank had been deferring to the ministry, which has publicly favored a weak won policy to support the export-reliant domestic economy.  

The finance ministry has kept a conspicuously low profile on currency issues recently, after being grounded by politicians for its earlier, all-out won-weakening efforts. Imported inflationary pressure due to strong global oil prices and stubbornly sluggish domestic consumption have also weakened the ministry's opposition to a stronger currency.  

Tuesday, the dollar finished at KRW1,103.6, down from KRW1,105.3 Monday. Tuesday's level was the lowest close since KRW1,085 on Nov. 24, 1997.  

The dollar has been declining against currencies around the globe due to mounting concerns about the U.S. deficit, but its fall against the won stands out.  

The won has gained 7.5% against the dollar this year, compared with a 1.7% rise in the Japanese yen and a 3.2% advance in the New Taiwan dollar. This means products from these competing exporters are likely to be priced more attractively than South Korean goods to consumers in key markets like the U.S.  

Many economists have warned the won is gaining too fast, considering the deteriorating fundamentals of South Korea's economy.  

Wednesday's verbal intervention so far has had sufficient effect in tempering the won-bullish sentiment, sending the dollar as high as KRW1,111 since market opening.  

At 0100 GMT, the dollar was at 1,107.6.

title: UPDATE 2-S.Korea  FX  reserves up,  intervention  seen slowing.
text:
SEOUL, Nov 2 (Reuters) - South Korea's foreign exchange reserves rose $3.7 billion in two weeks to a record high at the end of October, central bank data showed on Tuesday, signalling continued government intervention in the currency market.  

But dealers said the authorities were not as active in the market as late last year when heavy verbal intervention and direct dollar buying helped keep the won down against the U.S. currency.  

Bank of Korea data showed South Korea's foreign exchange reserves, already the world's fourth largest, rose $3.71 billion or 2.1 percent in the second half of October to a record $178.39 billion.  

"The data shows the authorities are still buying dollars to cushion some of the pressure (on the won to rise), but their intervention does not appear as strong as in the past when they tried to turn the direction around," said Lee Jin-woo, research head at NACF Futures Co.  

Dealers estimated the authorities had bought nearly $3 billion in the market in the latter half of October.  

Intervention is rarely commented on by South Korean authorities, although the finance ministry and the central bank say they undertake smoothing operations if the market moves too rapidly.  

South Korea's foreign reserves jumped nearly a quarter between July last year and February this year, when the country enjoyed rapid export growth.  

Over the period, the won underperformed the yen by as much as 13 percent. The Japanese currency is closely watched by dealers and policy makers in Seoul, whose exporters are in fierce competition with Japanese counterparts.  

DOMESTIC CRITICISM  

But strong global oil and raw material prices have since pushed inflation up to three-year highs and the finance ministry has come under pressure to allow some appreciation of the won to cushion import prices.  

Opposition lawmakers have criticised Finance Minister Lee Hun-jai for intervening too heavily. They argue a cheaper won has helped import inflation and hindered an early turnaround in a two-year slump in local spending by consumers and companies.  

Exports have been the main driver of growth in South Korea, Asia's third-largest economy, since it escaped a brief recession early last year, but a persistent slump in local demand is threatening the recovery as exports begin to soften.  

The Bank of Korea, which many economists believe wants the finance ministry to allow some appreciation in the won to help cap inflation, also said on Tuesday in a statement a stronger won could help boost corporate investment.  

"Empirical analysis on the influence of interest rate cuts on corporate investment shows it is influenced more by GDP growth or foreign exchange rates than by interest rates," it said.  

While the central bank appears to be more worried about inflation, finance ministry officials have said they support further cuts in interest rates to support the economy. (Additional reporting by Kim Kyoung-wha).

title: S Korea Govt: Monitoring USD/KRW,No Official Comment Yet
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--South Korea's government is "closely" monitoring the won's movement against the U.S. dollar to determine whether it needs to take action after the local currency hit a four-year high Monday, a senior official said.  

At 0030 GMT, the dollar plunged to 1,136.3 won, down from the KRW1,140.7 close Friday. It marked the U.S. unit's lowest level since Nov. 15, 2000, when it ended at KRW1,135.8. It is also the first time the U.S. currency has slid below KRW1,140 in four years.  

The won's gains came after the U.S. dollar slid below 107 yen.  

"We're watching the market and whether various factors require our actions," Kim Ik-Joo, director of the Ministry of Finance and Economy's foreign exchange policy bureau, said.  

The government hasn't decided to issue an official oral intervention yet, he said. The won, he told Dow Jones Newswires, was reacting "too sensitively" to the Japanese currency's movement. [ 25-10-04 0052GMT ]  

Kim said the government is studying whether the won's rise reflects differences in economic fundamentals between South Korea and Japan. While Korea's economy is yet to recover from a slowdown, the local government believes the Japanese economy is performing better than expected.  

The Japanese government has kept a low profile on foreign exchange matters in recent months. South Korea, too, has intervened less in the currency markets to support the U.S. dollar amid rising global oil prices that have raised concerns over imported inflation. The country is the world's fourth-largest crude importer.  

Since September last year, Korean authorities have publicly favored a weaker won to sustain an export-reliant economic recovery amid sluggish domestic demand. The government spent heavily until the first half of this year to curb the won's gains.  

Still, as of Monday, the won had risen 4.7% since the beginning of the year.  

The government has issued KRW1 trillion in treasurys so far this month to fund its currency operations. It issued KRW2 trillion in treasurys each month from July to September.  

"We can still issue additional treasurys for currency stabilization this month to send a signal to the market," Kim said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Singapore dlr, won surge as dlr falls.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Oct 20 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar and the
South Korean won rose to their strongest levels in six months
on Wednesday as an uncertain outlook for the U.S. economy and
interest rates knocked the dollar lower against major
currencies.
    The dollar weakened to a seven-and-half month low against
the euro and hit a three-month low against the yen. The yen's
one percent gain on Wednesday helped support Asian currencies,
eventhough oil was trading above $53 a barrel.
    The Bank of Thailand raised its key 14-day repo rate by 25
basis points to 1.75 percent, citing inflationary pressures.
The baht was already stronger on the day and showed little
reaction to the move, which had been expected by most analysts.
    While the baht reached one-week highs, the Singapore
dollar, seen as a proxy for some of Asia's biggest exporting
countries with pegged currencies such as China and Malaysia,
and the won headed towards their 2004 peaks.
  


    The Singapore dollar and the won have been rising in the
past two weeks after a string of weaker-than-expected U.S. data
and on a growing U.S. trade deficit, mainly with Asia.
 
    "We may see more and more of these days in the future,"
said G.K. Goh economist Song Seng Wun.
    "We're seeing a growing school of literature arguing for a
  

weaker dollar. When more and more people begin doubting the  

sustainability of the U.S. current account balances, that's  

where it's going to go."  

Asian currencies got a further boost from a Nikkei  

newspaper report that said Japan may be nearing the end of its  

deflationary years and that the Bank of Japan would likely  

forecast a rise in consumer prices next fiscal year in a report  

due on Oct 29.  

A return of inflation in Japan, which some analysts expect  

sometime next year, would mean higher interest rates and a  

return of foreign investment in Japanese property and bonds.  

"Performance of inflation-linked Japanese government bonds  

will improve significantly from mid-2005," Goldman Sachs said  

in a report from Tokyo.  

Still, further gains in Asian currencies may be capped by  

reluctance of the region's authorities to let their currencies

strengthen against neighbours who compete in the same export  

markets.  

Currency regulators in South Korea and Taiwan have  

intervened occasionally to buy dollars to stem gains in their  

currencies, analysts said.  

The trade-weighted Singapore dollar could already be close  

to the upper end of an undisclosed band set by the Monetary  

Authority of Singapore, said Song.  

Further gains in Asian currencies could also be restricted  

by the surging price of crude oil which may derail an economic  

recovery in Japan and other Asian countries and restrict trade  

demand from outside the region.  

"While there are substantial signs of recovery in Japan and  

the rest of Asia, every central bank in the region is looking  

over his shoulder about what oil's doing to the region's  

economies," said Song.  

U.S. oil futures have traded above $50 a barrel for most of  

this month, after jumping from below $40 in June. Earlier this  

week Morgan Stanley and J.P. Morgan downgraded their global  

economic forecasts for 2005 because of high oil prices.  

Officials at the Bank of Japan and other Asian countries  

have also voiced concerns about the impact of the oil prices on  

economic growth.

title: UPDATE 1-S.Korea sees consumer sentiment improving further.
text:
SEOUL, Oct 15 (Reuters) - South Korea expects consumer sentiment to see a further improvement in October after a recent survey showed sentiment brightening for the first time in five months in September, Finance Minister Lee Hun-jai said on Friday.  

Lee also said during a weekly media briefing the economy, the third largest in Asia, should achieve 5 percent growth in 2005 helped by government steps to boost construction spending.  

"The government expects further improvement in consumer sentiment in October," Lee said. The key consumer expectation index rose slightly in September, although still showed a majority of consumers remained pessimistic about the economy.  

"Plans to expand fiscal spending and boost construction demand will enable the country to achieve optimal growth potential," Lee said. The government has said South Korea's economy has the potential to grow by 5 percent or more annually.  

The ruling party and the government recently announced a string of measures to boost the economy, including income tax cuts and increased budget spending on projects to create more jobs and boost investment. The steps are pending parliamentary approval.  

The government is concerned economic growth next year will fall below its current target of 5 percent mainly because net exports - income from exports minus expenditure on imports - will stagnate after a sharp rise in 2004.  

Instead, the government is pining its hopes on the private consumption and the construction industry, together accounting for about 60 percent of the country's annual gross domestic product, leading economic growth in 2005.  

Central bank data shows net exports were responsible for nearly three-quarters of the 5.5 percent growth in gross domestic product in the year through the second quarter.  

Despite inflation worries, a delayed recovery in domestic demand has forced the Bank of Korea into cutting its overnight call rate target by a combined 75 basis points to a record 3.5 percent since early last year.  

But record high oil prices helped prevent the bank from delivering a fourth cut last week, defying market expectations that rates would be cut to 3.25 percent.   


Meanwhile, Lee repeated the government's official stance that it was
not targetting won/dollar             at a specific level. But he also
said the government needed to have the capacity to deter any
speculative forces aiming to send the won up or down sharply.
  

South Korea has heavily intervened, notably in late 2003, in the currency market to keep dollar inflows from exports and share buying by foreign investors from pushing the won higher, saying an appreciation in the currency would hurt its exports when domestic demand remained in a slump.

title: UPDATE 1-S.Korea fin min says won not too cheap.
text:
SEOUL, Oct 11 (Reuters) - South Korea's finance minister dismissed
criticism on Monday that the government's heavy intervention to cap the
won's         rise versus the dollar had done the economy more harm
than good.
   

Minister Lee Hun-jai told a parliamentary committee audit on economic policy that the won had actually strengthened more than the currencies of smaller regional rivals Taiwan, Thailand and Singapore since 2002. He did not comment on a more recent timeframe.   

"The country has not been keeping the exchange rate high on purpose," Lee said.   

The central bank also said in a separate report to parliament that the won's value against the U.S. dollar was not far from an appropriate level when taking into account the country's economic health, but it did not mention a specific rate.   

"The won has appreciated 14.4 percent on average since 2002, compared with a 3.5 percent gain in Taiwan's currency, 6.8 percent in Thailand's and 9.8 percent in Singapore's," Lee said, referring to the value of each currency against the U.S. unit.   

South Korea's parliament, in which the ruling Uri Party holds a slim majority, is undergoing an annual audit of state affairs.   

Earlier on Monday, lawmaker Lee Hye-hoon of the opposition Grand National Party said government intervention to cap the won's rise has contributed to discouraging investment and private consumption.   

She also slammed in a statement the cost of the policy and said the government had to pay nearly 5 trillion won ($4.35 billion) in interest on bonds issued to fund its dollar purchases in the first eight months of 2004.   

"Since the 1990s, the (won/dollar) exchange rate has had a negative relation with growth in domestic demand and with growth in capital investment," she said, adding that a cheaper won had made imported materials more expensive and kept inflation high.   

South Korea has heavily intervened to prevent the won from rising due to dollar inflows from strong exports and foreign stock investments since late last year, leaving the won 0.5 percent weaker than a year before at the end of 2003.    


This was in stark contrast to more than 10 percent gains in the
Japanese yen  and the euro        respectively against the U.S. dollar
over the same period.
   

The country's foreign exchange reserves rose about a quarter to $174.45 billion, the world's fourth-largest, in the year through the end of September. Dealers say much of that growth represented direct dollar purchases from the market.   

The central bank, however, repeated the government's stance that the current exchange rate was not a poor reflection of the country's economic fundamentals.   

The criticism came a few weeks after one of the seven policy board members of the central bank, the Bank of Korea, told reporters intervention did little to help boost the economy and harmed consumption and consumer price stability.   

Finance ministry officials have said South Korea could not allow the won to appreciate significantly at a time when the economy, the third-largest in Asia, is relying heavily on exports for its recovery since hitting a brief recession in 2003.   

The government expects gross domestic product in 2004 to be at least 5 percent higher than a year ago, but major research institutions have recently downgraded their forecasts to far less than that, citing stubbornly weak local demand. ($1=1150.0 Won) (Additional reporting by Lim Moon-kyung).

title: S.Korean official-Little won impact seen with yuan float.
text:
WASHINGTON, Oct 2 (Reuters) - The South Korean won is not expected to strengthen sharply against the dollar should the Chinese government decide to remove the yuan currency's peg against the greenback, a top Korean finance official told Reuters on Saturday.   

The Chinese yuan, which is effectively pegged at 8.28 to the dollar, has been one of the major topics all weekend at the meeting of the Group of Seven rich economies and the semi-annual gathering of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.   

China on Friday quashed expectations it would move to a more flexible exchange rate regime anytime soon.   

But if China decides to remove the peg, that could have a widespread impact on other Asian currencies because they all compete in the global marketplace.   

Not so for South Korea, said Joong-Kyung Choi, Director-General of the Korean Ministry of Finance and Economy's international finance bureau.   

"The yuan float will have limited impact on the won because our currency has appreciated," considerably over the past year, Choi said. The won has closely tracked the yen because of the similarities in the Japanese and South Korean economies.   

The won has been one of the strongest Asian currencies against the dollar, Choi said, speaking on the sidelines of the semi-annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.   

Since August this year, the won has risen around 1.5 percent against the dollar thanks to a still sizable trade surplus, estimated at $1.8 billion in August.   

Analysts say South Korea, just like Japan, would have liked a much weaker currency because it makes that country's exports cheaper overseas. For this reason, South Korea has sometimes relied on intervention, or buying dollars and selling the won, to keep the currency weak and preserve that competitive price advantage, analysts noted.   

But more than the prospect of a strong currency, analysts fretted about South Korea's economic prospects.   

The combination of relatively high unemployment - a three-year high of 3.6 percent in August - and the slow pace of job creation will continue to weigh on consumer confidence and salaries into 2005. That could threaten to limit the scope for an upturn in consumer spending in the months ahead.   

Analysts at Scotia Capital in Toronto, however, said in a research note that a gradual recovery in domestic spending in 2005 will reinvigorate investor confidence in Korean assets.   

"This, coupled with the appreciation of the yen against the dollar will induce the Korean authorities to accept some companion strengthening of the won against the dollar," said Scotia Capital.

title: S Korea Govt Official: Will Leave USD/KRW To Mkt Forces
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--The South Korean government will let the local currency's direction be decided by market forces and doesn't plan to intervene to slow the won's gains against the dollar, even as the won strengthens to a two-month high, a finance ministry official said Wednesday.  

"We don't have a specific target for the dollar/won and we plan to leave the pair completely up to the market," Kim Ik-Joo, director of the Ministry of Finance and Economy's foreign exchange market division, told Dow Jones Newswires.  

The dollar slipped to 1,148.2 won soon after opening Wednesday, a level not seen since July 12. It had closed at KRW1,150.8 Tuesday. [ 08-09-04 0026GMT ]  

Many players had expected dollar-buying intervention from the government to defend the psychologically important KRW1,150 level, and the dollar/won lost ground early Wednesday due to the absence of such government action, participants said.  

Kim added that the government can step in to "smooth" operations if sentiment in the currency market excessively favors one direction, or on volatility in the currency.  

However, he declined to comment on whether he sees such a need at the moment.  

The government has intervened in the local currency market throughout the year, mopping up dollars in support of South Korea's trade-reliant economy amid extremely sluggish domestic demand.  

But recent government comments and actions suggest eased opposition to a stronger won on growing inflationary pressure due to high global oil prices.  

The government decided to issue KRW1 trillion in treasurys this month to fund its currency operation, instead of an expected KRW2 trillion, even after it gained parliamentary approval to issue an extra KRW11 trillion worth of treasurys for intervention funds this year.  

South Korea's headline inflation surged to a three-year high in August, gaining 4.8% over the year.

title: S.Korea counts cost of  FX  policy, c.bank loss eyed.
text:
SEOUL, Sept 8 (Reuters) - South Korea's heavy intervention in the currency market may tip the central bank into its first loss in 10 years in 2004, government sources say, rekindling a debate over the value of a policy aimed at boosting exports.   

The Bank of Korea, the central bank, faced heavy interest payments on monetary stabilisation bonds it issued to fund its policy of buying dollars to cap the won's strength, the sources said.   

"The bank has probably suffered a loss in the first half and the trend could last through the rest of the year," said a government source close to the bank's balance sheet. The Bank of Korea does not release half-year balance sheet figures.   

The finance ministry argues the policy helps keep exports competitive, a rare bright spot in the economy, Asia's third largest.   

But many economists say it incurs not only huge direct costs but fails to cushion the economy from imported inflation stemming from high global oil and raw material prices.   

"In addition to the direct cost involved in the policy, its impact on the domestic inflation trend is a major problem," said Lim Ji-won, an economist at JP Morgan Chase.   

Consumer inflation hit its highest rate in over three years in the year through August.   

The finance ministry expects to pay 1.8 trillion won ($1.56 billion) in interest on this year's monetary stabilisation bonds, up a fifth from last year, an official at the ministry's international finance department said.   

The ministry plans to sell up to 18.8 trillion in bonds to fund currency market operations this year, up 47 percent from last year.   

Separately, the central bank paid 2.76 trillion won during the first six months of this year in interest on bonds issued to absorb increased won liquidity, a bank official said.   

The huge sums outweigh an estimated 2.6 trillion won economic stimulus package that the ruling party put forward last week.   

"The money paid as interest of course went to people who bought the bonds but a problem is that these are rich people, and the government should have spent the money on those who really want help," said Oh Suk-tae, an economist at Citigroup.   

South Korea's foreign exchange reserves rose by a quarter to $170.49 billion by the end of August from a year ago, making them the fourth-biggest in the world. Currency dealers and economists say much of the increase came from intervention.   

The won fell 0.5 percent against the dollar in 2003, in stark contrast to a more than 10 percent gain in the Japanese yen and a nearly 20 percent rise in the euro against the dollar during the same period.   

The won has gained about 4 percent so far this year against the dollar, while the yen and euro weakened by about 2 percent and 4 percent respectively. Dealers said the won's rise was technical after last year's weakness rather than a change in policy.   

The finance ministry appeared unmoved by arguments that some of the rise in inflation stemming from high raw material prices could have been choked off by allowing the won to rise.   

"We will not intentionally use forex policy to solve the inflation problem," Choi Joong-kyung, head of the ministry's international finance bureau, told Reuters last week. ($1=1152.7 Won).

title: S.Korea bonds end flat, await next week's rate meet.
text:
SEOUL, Sept 3 (Reuters) - South Korean government bond prices
ended flat on Friday as doubts deepened over whether interest
rates would be cut in September. Expectations of a cut have been
driving a rally in a market flush with ample liquidity.
    Bonds managed to recoup early falls after a correction over
the last 2 days, as cash-rich investors continued to bet the Bank
of Korea could still lower rates in coming months.
    Strong inflation data and government measures to boost weak
domestic demand had dampened appetite for bonds in recent
sessions, dealers said, but some buying interest remained because
economic fundamentals had yet to show signs of improvement.
    "Now the market seemed to see the chance of a rate cut to be
about 50 percent from the previous 80 percent, with investors
taking a cautious stance ahead of next week's monetary policy
meeting," said a fixed income analyst at a local securities firm.
   


    The yield on three-year treasury bonds
finished unchanged at 3.62 percent. The five-year treasury bond
yield  was down 1 basis points.
    Expectations for further monetary easing had pushed the
benchmark 3-year treasury yield down by almost 50 basis points
since the central bank unexpectedly cut 25 basis points off rates
to a record low of 3.5 percent in August.
 
    The Bank of Korea will hold a monetary policy meeting on
Sept. 9.

title: S.Korean  forex  reserves up at $170.5 bln by end-Aug.
text:
SEOUL, Sept 2 (Reuters) - South Korea's foreign exchange reserves rose 1.5 percent in August as a weakening dollar increased the conversion value of assets in other currencies, the central bank said on Thursday.  

Interest income from U.S. Treasury holdings also helped lift the reserves, ranked the world's fourth-largest, to $170.5 billion at the end of August from $168 billion the previous month, the Bank of Korea said in a statement.  

The figure was slightly lower than a record $170.7 billion reported in mid-August.  

The reserves were up 9.7 percent, or $15.1 billion, from the end of 2003.  

Dealers suspect monetary authorities have intervened heavily to buy dollars and safeguard the won's export competitiveness, leading to a steady rise in South Korea's forex reserves.  

The central bank denies intervening and provides few details of its reserves.

title: South Korea's  forex  reserves up to record in July.
text:
SEOUL, Aug 3 (Reuters) - South Korea's foreign exchange
reserves rose slightly to a record $168 billion at the end of
July, mainly due to investment gains, the central bank said on
Tuesday.
    The reserves, the fourth-highest in the world, rose by $977
million from $167 billion at the end of June, the Bank of Korea
said in a statement.
 
    The reserves were up 8 percent, or $12.65 billion, from the
end of 2003.
    Dealers suspect monetary authorities have intervened

heavily to buy dollars and safeguard the won's export  

competitiveness, leading to a steady rise in South Korea's  

forex reserves.  

The central bank denies intervening and provides few  

details of its reserves. It said 82.8 percent of reserves were  

held in securities such as U.S. Treasuries, but it did not  

elaborate.

title: S.Korea bonds flat ahead of Greenspan testimony.
text:
SEOUL, July 20 (Reuters) - South Korean government bond prices were barely changed early on Tuesday, with investors reluctant to trade ahead of testimony by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan that could set the tone for future U.S. interest rate rises.    


By 0022 GMT, the yield on three-year treasury bonds             was
flat at 4.19 percent. The five-year treasury bond yield            was
bid up 1 basis point at 4.49 percent, dealers said.
   

"Bond market players are sticking to the sidelines ahead of Greenspan's testimony," said a bond trader.   

Greenspan will deliver his semi-annual testimony on monetary policy before the U.S. Senate late on Tuesday and again to the House of Representatives on Wednesday.   

Analysts predict the central bank chairman will reiterate the Fed intends to raise rates at a measured pace to help keep inflationary pressure in check.   

Local bond dealers said market sentiment was still uncertain after the National Assembly decided last week to approve a government plan to issue up to an additional 11 trillion won ($9.51 billion) in treasury bonds this year to fund its intervention in the currency market.   

On the economic front, South Korea's seasonally adjusted jobless rate was 3.5 percent in June, unchanged from May, the National Statistical Office said.   

On the Korea Futures Exchange, the key September contract for three-year treasuries rose 1 tick to 110.16.   

On the local stock market, the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index fell 1.32 percent. ($1=1157.2 Won).

title: S Korea Govt Official:Strong  FX Intervention  Possible 2H
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--Buoyed by expected parliamentary approval of a sharp increase in this year's treasury issues for foreign exchange operation, South Korea's Ministry of Finance and Economy toned up its interventionist voice Thursday, with a senior official warning that its market actions to weaken the local currency will come in the form of a "downpour" from now on.  

"From now on, we will show the art of concentration. When we take part in the currency market, it will be a downpour and not a drizzle to make our intentions clear," Choi Joong-Kyung, director-general of the ministry's international bureau, told Dow Jones Newswires and Yonhap Infomax.  

His comment comes as the Parliament is expected to give a go-ahead Thursday afternoon to the ministry's proposal to hike this year's ceiling to issue treasurys to fund its campaign to keep the won stable against the dollar by another 11 trillion won ($=KRW1,156) on top of an initial KRW7.8 trillion. [ 15-07-04 0152GMT ]  

Choi explained that his ministry concluded that it would be appropriate to have KRW11 trillion more in coffers for its second-half currency policy based on domestic currency market size, dollar/yen movement and intervention funds of competing Asian countries.  

The dollar/won jumped immediately after Choi's "downpour" comment, with the dollar trading at KRW1,157.7 - more than a three-week high - at 0210 GMT versus its opening at KRW1,152.5 and Wednesday's close of KRW1,153.  

"Everyone's turning frantically dollar-long from both offshore and onshore now that the fear of intervention looks more like a reality," said a local bank dealer.  

The dollar/won, that has kept to a narrow range since late May, slipped briefly below KRW1,150 earlier this week on expectations of an easing in Seoul's efforts to weaken the won to support exports amid growing price pressure from higher energy costs.  

-By Hye-Seung Seo, Dow Jones Newswires; 822-732-2165; hyeseung.seo@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 1-S.Korea to more than double bonds to cap won.
text:
SEOUL, July 2 (Reuters) - South Korea will more than double its planned offering of bonds to fund its foreign exchange market operations, a finance ministry official said on Friday, in what is seen as showing its strong intention to keep the won cheap.   

The official said the government would seek parliament approval to raise this year's ceiling on treasury bond offerings to fund foreign exchange market operations to 18.8 trillion won ($16.29 billion) from the previous 7.8 trillion.   

The move came as data showed a slump in domestic spending was poised to last for an extended period. That makes exports more important to keep the recovery in Asia's fourth-largest economy on track.   

"We have decided to increase the ceiling on treasuries for the foreign exchange market by 11 trillion won and all of them will be denominated in Korean won," the official told Reuters.   

The government has never confirmed its direct intervention in the currency market, but dealers suspect monetary authorities have intervened heavily to buy dollars and rein in the won to ensure South Korean exports are competitive.   

The won was almost unchanged at the end of 2003 from a year earlier against the U.S. dollar whereas the Japanese yen and euro gained sharply over the period - making the won cheaper in comparison to these major currencies.   

The central bank said earlier on Friday the country's foreign exchange reserves, ranked fourth in the world, rose slightly by $487 million to $167.03 billion by the end of June from the previous month.   

The Bank of Korea attributed the rise to investment gains, but dealers believe some of the rise represented interventions.   

South Korea has issued six trillion won of bonds so far out of the original 7.8 trillion won planned.   

On Thursday, a central bank survey showed South Korea's business sentiment dipped at an 11-month low as companies grew more pessimistic about a swift turnaround in the sluggish consumption, that began sagging at the end of 2002. ($1=1154.0 Won).

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Modest gains amid stumbling blocks.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, April 19 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were
firmer on Monday, with the Korean won leading the pack, after
unexpectedly weak U.S. economic data soothed fears of a
near-term monetary tightening there and caused the yen and euro
to rally.
    Still, the pace of gains in the yen       , Singapore
dollar  and other Asian currencies was unhurried and
reflected investor caution ahead of a Group of Seven meeting on
the weekend and U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's
testimony on the economy on Wednesday.
    Some analysts said an appreciation in Asian currencies
could be derailed in the longer run by any steep rise in U.S.
rates and the threat of slower growth in China.
    "Away from the short-term position squaring that has
occurred on bullish Asian currency views, there are two real
risks," Lehman Brothers said in a note.
  


    "The first is whether Fed tightening derails the Asian
equity rally and the constant inflow of equity capital that has
supported it."
    "The second risk to Asian currencies is the building signs
of a slowdown in China, the region's engine of growth for the
past few years," Lehman's report said, adding that it was
however too early to be worried about China.
 
    The yen hovered around 108 per dollar, the dollar still up
three yen from last week's lows.
    The Singapore dollar        remained around 1.6770/80 per
dollar, up about a cent from last week's lows, while the Taiwan
dollar  settled on the firmer side of 33 per dollar.
    The Thai baht        was in a range of 39.30 to 39.40 per
dollar, up a percent from last week's trough.
    Last week's consumer sentiment and industrial production
  

data in the United States was weaker than markets expected, and  

there was an easing of optimism over the economy, which had  

driven up the expectations of the Fed hiking rates sooner.  

After comments by Fed Governor Ben Bernanke and Richmond  

Federal Reserve Bank President Alfred Broaddus, analysts said  

markets were preparing for Greenspan too to be cautious in his  

statements and to play down the chances of rate hikes.  

"We've already had a flag on what Greenspan is going to be  

talking about," David Simmonds, markets strategist with Royal  

Bank of Scotland, said.  

Simmonds said the Fed might shift its view on inflation to  

suggest that the risks between inflation and disinflation were  

balanced if not tilted toward inflation, but it would still  

convey patience on monetary policy.  

Analysts said the G7 meeting would probably be a non-event  

for currency markets, given the perception that most Asian  

countries were allowing their currencies to rise to ward off  

external inflationary pressures.   


 
    "There will be a less obsessive focus on currencies,
although China will be discussed," Simmonds said.
    WON POLICY
    The Korean won                   was traded around 1,153
  

per dollar, a gain of almost 10 won since Friday. It has risen  

2.5 percent in two months, prompting speculation that the  

authorities have moderated their won-selling intervention.  

South Korea's foreign exchange reserves fell in the first  

half of April by $600 million to $162.96 billion on April 15,  

but the central bank said that was due to a decline in the euro  

and yen against the dollar during that period.   


 
    "There is little doubt that intervention was reined back
quite considerably over that period," Simmonds said.
    And, despite reports that the Bank of Korea had been
  

intervening again in recent days, the scale of intervention

would be far lower than in the past months, he said.
