title: S.Korea poll to cut risks, no big policy shift seen.
text:
SEOUL, April 15 (Reuters) - The expected victory by the pro-government Uri Party in South Korea's parliamentary election on Thursday should cut political risks hindering the economy, but is not seen having a big impact on economic policy or markets.  

The political turbulence created by the impeachment of President Roh Moo-hyun last month by the opposition-controlled parliament created a new headache for Asia's fourth-largest economy already struggling to cope with weak local consumption.  

"If the political uncertainty eases soon, that would be good for business confidence and for foreign investment," Rob Subbaraman, senior Asia economist at Lehman Brothers in Tokyo.  

But he added: "The Korean economy is run by the ministries, technocrats, and so I do not expect it (the election) to have a major impact on the economy."  

Foreign investors and the opposition Grand National Party have said they were concerned the centre-left Uri Party, which expects to have won 151 or 152 seats in the 299-seat National Assembly, could use a majority to indulge militant labour.  

But Chung Sye-kyun, Uri's top policymaker, said his party would be asking foreign businesses what they needed to invest more in South Korea.  

"We will be showing that we are committed to letting the market work and that there will be continuity in policy without dramatic changes," he told Reuters soon after exit polls.  

International ratings agency Fitch Ratings was broadly positive on the election.  

"Perhaps, the Uri-dominated parliament will press ahead with corporate governance and reform. We also expect a more effective legislative body than we've had in nine to 12 months," said Brian Coulton, senior director for Asian sovereign ratings.  

President Roh came to power in February, 2003, pledging to curb the power of the sprawling family-run conglomerates, known as "chaebol", smooth labour relations and make the country into a regional business hub.  

But tangible progress has been limited with Roh facing an opposition-dominated parliament and distractions ranging from a crisis over North Korea's nuclear aims to a bursting local consumer debt bubble and, most recently, the impeachment crisis.  

STOCKS SEEN UP ON VOTE  

Major South Korean stocks trading overseas were trading mixed after early results of the vote. Market analysts said the local stock market was expected to get an initial boost on Friday on hopes for political stability, but as in the case of currency and bonds U.S. trends were likely to set the pace thereafter.  

"The Uri Party's win is not likely to influence the foreign exchange market. The dollar/yen rate and dollar supply/demand here are more important factors", said a dealer at KorAm bank.   

Currency dealers say South Korea may ease heavy intervention to keep
the won             from strengthening against the U.S. dollar after
the election.
  

But they say a change in a policy, which has been aimed at maintaining the competitiveness of South Korean exports, would be due to worries a weak won could fan mounting inflationary pressure rather than a change in parliamentary leadership.  

Brisk sales abroad of computer chips, cars and mobile handsets pushed South Korea's exports up 39 percent in the first quarter from a year before, and that prompted the central bank to upgrade last week its economic growth forecast.  

Analysts have called for more foreign direct investment and stronger domestic consumption to provide a buffer for when cyclical export markets falter.  

But they concede there do not appear to be many options for the government to give an immediate boost to consumption without creating negative side-effects on inflation and other fronts. (Additional reporting by Jean Yoon).

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Recover, seen benefiting from US outlook.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, April 15 (Reuters) - Asian currencies partially
recovered in Thursday afternoon deals after two sessions of
weakness forced by a rallying U.S. dollar and stronger U.S.
economic data.
    Traders said the regionals had bottomed and firmer Asian
currencies could co-exist with a stronger dollar as the
region's export-driven economies would benefit from a U.S.
recovery.
 
    The Japanese yen        was also steadier after its two
percent fall on Wednesday to near the 109 a dollar.
    However it remained vulnerable after reports that two more
  

Japanese civilians had been taken hostage in Iraq, not to  

mention the recent data showing an unexpectedly sharp rise in  

U.S. consumer prices and a narrowing of the huge U.S. trade  

deficit.   


 
    "We are likely to see some amount of dollar strength from
now on," said M.R. Madhavan, a strategist with Bank of America.
    "But Asia is still a leveraged bet on the United States and
if the U.S. does better than Asia will do even better," he
said.
    The Singapore dollar        was down over two cents or over
  

a percent from Tuesday's four-year peak. It fell as far as  

1.6868, a two-week low, paring all the gains it made on the  

back of a surprise monetary tightening by the central bank on  

Monday.  

The Taiwan dollar weakened to 33.16 per dollar,  

down more than a percent from Tuesday's three-year highs, and  

then rallied back to 33.   


 
    The Philippine peso        was marginally weaker and the
Indonesian rupiah  fell to 8,630/8,635 per dollar.
    Markets in Thailand were closed for the New Year holiday
and Korean markets were shut for parliamentary elections.
    The Indian rupee          extended losses to a two-week low
of 43.95 per dollar.
    On the crosses, the regionals outperformed the yen, with
the Singapore dollar  around 64.6 yen, the highest
the cross rate has been in a month.
    Traders said there would be more bids for Asian currencies
once markets sensed the dollar's upward momentum was easing.
    "I think the appreciation pressure on the yen will continue
  

because the intervention has been diluted," said Bhanu Baweja,  

currency strategist with UBS, citing Japan's deepening economic  

recovery as the reason why the Japanese were comfortable with a  

stronger yen.  

The story in the rest of Asia was similar. Economic growth  

was broadening in most countries, except South Korea, and the  

currency-weakening intervention by authorities was moderating,  

he said.

title: UPDATE 1-S.Korea  central bank  says no policy change on won.
text:
SEOUL, April 8 (Reuters) - South Korea had not changed its current policy on the won despite a growing current account surplus, a senior central bank official said on Thursday, indicating it would continue to favour keeping the won low.   

 Bank of Korea Assistant Governor Park Jae-hwan told reporters the bank's views on the local currency had not changed because of booming exports, which prompted it to upgrade this year's current account surplus to $15 billion from the previous $6 billion.   

 "Our views are the same because the U.S. economy is growing much faster than had been expected and there are also other accounts to look after other than the current account balance," Park told reporters.   

 A weaker won helps keep South Korean exports more price competitive in international markets.   

 But there has been growing speculation that South Korea has been loosening its grip on the currency given that exports have been booming and on the view that a firmer won could help contain inflationary pressures coming from higher global raw material prices.   

 The won has risen 4.6 percent against the dollar so far this year.   

 The latest comments came hours after the finance ministry announced a plan to offer one trillion won ($877.9 million) in five-year treasuries next week to fund the government's foreign exchange market operations.   

 As in the case of most other countries, South Korea rarely confirms intervention in the local currency market, but has admitted to conducting what it terms are "smoothing operations" to stabilise the market in the face of speculative trading.   

 Economists and currency dealers say South Korea, mindful of the still fragile base of its economic recovery, has spent billions of dollars in the currency market containing the won's rise.   

 Earlier on Thursday, the Bank of Korea raised its forecast for this year's economic growth by more than a half percentage point to as high as six percent from a previous forecast for about 5.2 percent rise.   

 But Bank of Korea Governor Park Seung said domestic consumption remained stubbornly weak and the recovery was largely driven by booming exports, supported by strong demand from China.

title: S Korea Shifting  FX  Policy To Spur Consumption -StanChart
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Authorities in South Korea are gradually scaling back interventionist sales of the local currency, the won, mirroring policy shifts underway in other parts of Asia including Japan and India, said Standard Chartered regional economist Mike Moran.  

The won has risen sharply in recent weeks against the dollar, helped by foreign capital flows into Korea and a slightly less interventionist approach by the local Ministry of Finance and Economy. Korean markets are shut Monday for a holiday, but the spot dollar ended Friday at KRW1,141.7, near its lowest level since November 2000, and down from around KRW1,200 at the start of the year.  

"Official resistance to a stronger won is...gradually receding," Moran said in a research report released Monday. "Rising external balances and higher commodity prices have prompted a reevaluation of recent forex policy."  

In a research report, Moran said a stronger currency will help neutralize import price pressures, allowing the central bank to keep interest rates low to support the domestic economy.  

But the keyword for policy-makers, he said, remains "gradual," adding that intervention will continue if volatility remains high.  

A policy of less aggressive yen sales was reflected in data issued Friday by the Bank of Korea. It said South Korea's foreign exchange reserves reached $163.56 billion at the end of March, up from $163 billion at the end of February. Selling won for dollars builds foreign exchange reserves, which explains the sharp increase in Korea's reserves since September.  

Moran said the gradual shift in forex policy reflects the two-speed nature of the Korean economy, with exports strong but domestic demand still relatively anemic.  

"Diverging trends in external and domestic growth remain well-entrenched," he said. "The strength of Korea's export sectors are having little discernible impact on the domestic economy (due) to the increasingly capital-intensive structure of local industry and smaller proportion of total jobs being accounted for by this sector."  

Indeed, while Korea's chaebols, the local name given to conglomerates, continue to report strong earnings, domestic small and medium-sized enterprises are still struggling. "Their greater dependence on the domestic economic cycle is keeping upside risks for this sector limited," Moran said.  

One obstacle to a recovery in domestic demand is public discontent about political developments - such as the impeachment proceedings against President Roh Moo-hyun - ahead of parliamentary elections later this months.  

"Public discontent could weaken confidence in the short run, delaying our initial timetable for a consumption recovery. Following our recent country visit, the 'feel good factor' is still clearly lacking and a significant rebound in spending may not emerge until year-end," said Moran.  

He said the political tug-of-war over impeachment is being won by the pro-government Uri Party. Public support for the impeachment has remained damagingly low for the opposition, said the economist, allowing the Uri Party to boost its support by tapping public discontent.  

Roh has vowed to step down if the Uri Party fares poorly in the ballot. Major newspaper polls published earlier this week predicted the party would win a majority in the National Assembly.  

"For the opposition parties, the decision to push for Roh's impeachment could turn out to be their biggest political miscalculation, costing them their parliamentary majority come April 15," said Moran.

text:
SEOUL, April 2 (Reuters) - South Korea's foreign exchange reserves hit a new record in March, but the monthly rise was only about a tenth of the gain in February, providing more evidence of a switch in policy away from intervening to weaken the won.  

Reserves rose by $550 million to $163.6 billion at the end of March from a month earlier, the Bank of Korea said in a statement on Friday.  

March's net increase in reserves was dwarfed by the $5.56 billion gain in February, an indication that authorities were winding down intervention to cap the won, dealers said.  

"The smaller rise in forex reserves in March is attributed to the government's weakened intervention and the easing in the dollar against major currencies," a foreign bank trader said.  

"Authorities hardly stepped into the forex market after the won broke through the 1,150 mark late last month", the dealer added.

signs of economic recovery and the yen's strengthening against the
dollar.

The bank operates most of its foreign currency reserves in bonds and other securities that represent 77.4 percent of the total balance, with dollar deposits of financial institutions making up 22.1 percent.

title: UPDATE 1-S.Korea says sharp  FX  volatility should be curbed.
text:
SEOUL, March 16 (Reuters) - Excess volatility in South Korea's exchange rate should be curbed, a senior finance ministry official said on Tuesday, suggesting authorities were again focusing their attention on keeping the won competitive. Allowing a market-determined exchange rate was only possible in major markets like the United States, said Choi Joong-kyung, chief of the Finance Ministry's international finance bureau, suggesting the smaller Korean foreign exchange market was more susceptible to wild speculative swings.   

"Sharp volatility (of dollar/won) in the foreign exchange rate should be prevented," Choi told a seminar.   

He said the authorities would monitor the market for the time being, unless movements in the exchange rate hurt the stability of the economy.   

His comments appeared to contrast with the central bank chief's statement last week that the market should dictate the exchange rate.   

Like other export-dependent Asian countries, South Korea has intervened heavily and bought dollars to stop its currency rising for fear of hurting a still fragile economic recovery.    


This policy kept the won  nearly flat against the dollar last year
while the Japanese yen        gained over 10 percent versus the U.S.
currency. South Korea and Japan compete in major export markets.
The won             rose for a second session on Tuesday against the
dollar, ending local trade at 1,170.7, compared with Monday's close of
1,175.3. It has gained 1.8 percent against the dollar so far this
year.

title: UPDATE 1-Won level now no problem for Korean economy-source.
text:
BASEL, Switzerland, March 7 (Reuters) - The current exchange-rate level of the Korean won poses no problem for Korea's economy, which will achieve growth of 5 percent or more this year, a Korean monetary source said on Sunday.    

 Speaking to Reuters on the sidelines of a bimonthly meeting of central bank governors from the G-10 industrialized nations and major emerging markets, the source said: "Because the yen has depreciated so much, we have some room to allow market forces to determine (the level of won). I think there is no problem with current level of the won for the Korean economy."    

 "We expect that our economy will get momentum and go into a (full) recovery. I'm sure we can meet five percent or more growth this year," he added.    

 Korea's Central Bank has forecast 2004 gross domestic product of 5.2 percent after an estimated 2.9 percent in 2003. South Korea's new Finance Minister Lee Hun-jai has estimated 2004 economic growth of 5 percent to 6 percent.    

 Like other Asian countries, South Korea has spent billions of dollars intervening in the foreign exchange market in an effort to curb export-damaging appreciation of its currency.    

 Thanks to such intervention, the won remained nearly flat against the dollar during 2003. Meanwhile, the yen and the euro gained over 10 percent and about 20 percent against the greenback, respectively.    

 Upward pressure on Asian currencies, including the won, has eased in the past few weeks partly as expectations of heavy intervention by the Japanese authorities pushed the yen down.    


The yen hit a four-month low against the dollar beyond 110.40  last
week while the won        stood at 1,173.00 per dollar.

title: WRAPUP 1-S.Korea signals softer  foreign exchange  line.
text:
SEOUL, March 3 (Reuters) - Remarks by South Korea's new finance minister appeared on Wednesday to provide the latest sign authorities will allow a gradual appreciation of the won.  

Lee Hun-jai seemed to diverge subtly from his predecessor when answering a question on foreign exchange policy put to him at a lunch meeting of foreign reporters.  

"The exchange rate will be decided by supply and demand and economic fundamentals", said Lee, who was appointed in early February.  

Former finance minister Kim Jin-pyo had said the won's rate "should" be decided by the market and economic fundamentals.  

Lee's remark indicated market forces would be given more emphasis in determining won levels against the U.S. dollar, foreign exchange dealers said.  

Like other Asian countries, South Korea has spent billions of dollars intervening in the foreign exchange market in an effort to stop its currency rising. A rising currency makes exports less competitive on world markets.  

South Korea, the fourth-largest economy in Asia, has intervened as foreign investment in local stocks and mounting current account surpluses sucked in dollars.  

Thanks to intervention, the won remained almost flat against the dollar between the start and end of 2003. The yen and the euro gained more than 10 percent and nearly 20 percent, respectively.  

The won ended at 1,177 per dollar on Wednesday, up 1.26 percent from the end of 2003.  

Lee's remark came shortly after central bank data suggested government intervention to cap the won had weakened.  

"The comment was made as dealers are already sensing some changes in the government's attitude," said a senior currency dealer at a local bank. "Dealers say the government has become more flexible even when intervening."  

Market speculation over a shift in intervention policy began to grow when the finance ministry abruptly rescinded some restrictions on currency forward trading by local financial institutions. The ministry announced the move a week after Lee took office and a month after the controls had been imposed.  

In a further sign the government's attitude could be changing, data on Wednesday showed a marked slowdown in South Korea's foreign reserves growth.  

The central bank's figures showed reserves rose only $420 million in the second half of February, after rising $5.14 billion in the first 15 days.  

MISLEADING?  

Some dealers said, however, it was too soon to say South Korea was ditching a policy of keeping the won cheap against major currencies, noting authorities may have felt they could not fight the tide of a strengthening dollar in the past month.  

Rising international prices for oil and other key raw materials have also forced South Korea to adopt a lower profile in currency markets as a further weakening in the won would inflate import bills, they said.  

"The government is in a situation where it can not actively push the dollar higher against the won mainly because of the heavy pressure on prices from strong raw materials prices," a dealer at a foreign bank said.  

Lee said he would stick to policies promoting economic growth because the recovery was still fragile. The country has kept interest rates at record lows since July to try to boost the economy, which fell briefly into recession in mid-2003.  

He predicted 2004 economic growth of five to six percent. The central bank has forecast 2004 gross domestic product of 5.2 percent after an estimated 2.9 percent in 2003.

title: WRAPUP 1-S.Korea recovery signs grow, c/a surplus surges.
text:
SEOUL, Feb 26 (Reuters) - South Korea's finance minister said on Thursday recovery was gathering pace in Asia's fourth-largest economy, a view seemingly endorsed by the International Monetary Fund, which raised its forecast for South Korea economic growth.  

Finance Minister Lee Hun-jai told a weekly news conference there were increasing signs the economy had moved past its worst point.  

"The sectors are increasing where signs show the situation is improving," said Lee. "Be it a consumer sentiment index or a business survey index, indices continue to show positive signs."  

The comment comes ahead of industrial production figures due on Friday that are expected to show growth of about eight percent in January from a year earlier, marking an eighth consecutive month of gains over the year before.  

Ten economists polled by Reuters on Wednesday estimated the month's industrial output to have grown 8.0 percent on the year, although the month-on-month growth was seen slowing to 0.5 percent in January from a 2.7 percent rise in December.  

They said the anticipated slowdown in monthly growth was not seen as serious enough to hurt the generally upbeat trend in the economy as domestic consumption stages a modest recovery.  

On Wednesday, the IMF upgraded its forecast for South Korea's 2004 economic growth to 5.5 percent from 4.75 percent, reflecting views the recovery in the economy, which briefly fell into recession last year, was gathering pace.  

The revised forecast was in line with the South Korean government's expectation of between 5.0 and 5.9 percent growth and the central bank's forecast for a 5.2 percent gain.  

The central bank said on Thursday the current account surplus more than doubled in 2003 to a four-year high due mainly to record exports, and expected the balance to stay in the black for the seventh consecutive year in 2004.  

The $12.3 billion surplus, and another $13.1 billion surplus in the capital account, reflected the pressure over South Korea's won to appreciate - and the scope of intervention South Korea had to mobilise to keep the currency cheap against major currencies.  

"The central bank's expectation of another surplus in 2004 means that the upward pressure for the won will continue to pile up," said Lee Sang-jae, an economist at Hyundai Securities.  

Many Asian countries, whose economies rely heavily on exports that again are sensitive to the currency value, have been faced with international pressure to let their currencies move up according to the rush of capital inflows.  

The South Korean government has stepped up its foreign exchange purchases, contributing to a $34 billion increase in reserves to $155 billion in 2003, limiting the won's rise against a weaker dollar and keeping the average nominal effective exchange rate for the year essentially unchanged.  

The IMF also said in its annual review report South Korean authorities should allow market forces to determine the won currency's exchange rate by scaling back on foreign exchange purchases, which should be limited to smoothing excessive volatility.

title: UPDATE 1-S.Korea reserves surge, heavy  intervention  cited.
text:
SEOUL, Feb 17 (Reuters) - South Korea released data on Tuesday showing foreign exchange reserves surged by more than $5 billion in just two weeks, providing what dealers said was clear evidence of the extent of intervention in the currency market.   

 The Bank of Korea said on Tuesday foreign reserves, valued in U.S. dollars, rose to a record $162.6 billion by mid-February from $157.5 billion at the end of January. It listed a stronger euro against the U.S. dollar as the key factor.   

 But local currency dealers said the increase reflected South Korea's heavy intervention in the currency market to keep the won from strengthening too much versus the dollar at a time when exports are the driving force for economic recovery.   

 "We believe some 70 to 80 percent of the increase came from the central bank's dollar buying in the market," said a dealer at a local bank. "We even think authorities had bought close to $1 billion every day at least during the first week."   

 Once faced with a sovereign debt default in late 1997 after massive outflows of foreign capitals had left it with less than $4 billion in reserves, South Korea now boasts the world's fourth-largest reserves behind Japan, China and Taiwan.   

 Senior officials at various government authorities would not comment on the market talk, maintaining that a stronger euro was the main factor. The euro gained two percent against the U.S. dollar in the first weeks of February.   

 But even if South Korea held half of its reserves in euros, the rise in the euro would have pushed up the dollar value of the country's reserves by about $1.6 billion. South Korea has never said how much of its reserves are held in euro assets.   

 Assuming South Korea holds 20 percent of its reserves in euros - the IMF said euros made up 14.6 percent of global reserve holdings at the end of 2002 - the stronger euro would have seen the value of euro holdings rise by about $600 million.   

Central bank officials said gains on its investment in unspecified assets had also pushed up the reserves. But even a six percent gain per annum - which is a tough task - would have generated only about $390 million at the most.   

 Some dealers believe virtually all of the increase in reserves came from intervention.   

South Korea has intervened heavily in the market, effectively keeping the won flat against the dollar between the end of 2002 and the end of 2003, while the yen gained about 11 percent and the euro about 20 percent against the dollar, respectively.   

 During the same 12-month period, the country's foreign reserves rose $34 billion. (Additional reporting by Jeon Chong-woo and Kim Yeon-hee).

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Taiwan dlr hits high,  intervention  eyed.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Central banks eyed, T$ at 19-mth high.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Feb 17 (Reuters) - The Taiwan dollar        rose
to its highest in about 19 months on Tuesday but most Asian
currencies edged back from recent highs on fears of central
bank intervention to curb exchange rate gains.
    The Taiwan dollar          hit 33.075 per U.S. dollar, its
strongest since July 2002, before the central bank stepped in
to cap the rise, dealers said.
    Dealers in Singapore said settlement of stock purchases by
foreign investors was pushing the currency higher. They said
while foreign investors were net sellers on Monday, they had
bought over $700 million of Taiwan stocks last week.
    Central bank intervention was also suspected in South Korea
where the won             touched a high of 1,157.0 per
dollar in local trade, just shy of Friday's four-month high of
1,156.0 hit in offshore trade.
    The Singapore dollar        fell to 1.6775 per U.S. dollar,
moving further away from its four-year peak of 1.6675 hit last
week.
  


 Dealers said the move was inspired by a sharp fall in the
Thai baht .
    The baht fell to a one-week low of 39.04 per dollar amid
talk that a foreign bank was buying U.S. dollars on behalf of
the central bank to curb currency gains, dealers said.
    However, they said rising exports and capital inflows into
Asian equities meant the appreciation pressure on regional
currencies would continue despite central bank intervention.
    MANAGING APPRECIATION
    James Malcolm, strategist at JP Morgan Chase in Singapore,
said gains in Asian regionals so far this year suggested that
central banks were only smoothing rises.
    "It is going exactly as was expected," he said.
    "No one said that central banks would completely get out of

The Taiwan dollar has gained about 2.7 percent, against 2.24

versus a depreciation of about one percent last year.

title: Most Asian  Currencies  Up Late; Central Banks Battle G7
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian currencies rose against the dollar Wednesday as investors tested whether the region's central banks could withstand a push from the Group of Seven powers for them to stop restraining their currencies.  

Several Asian central banks bought dollars to fight the rising tide of their own currencies, but they couldn't overcome waves of selling as the G7's weekend call for more Asian currency "flexibility" sank in, analysts said.  

For a second day, the Singapore dollar notched a four-year high and the Korean won also gained, leading the region's advance on a wave of what traders called speculative dollar-selling. Analysts said Asian currencies will likely keep grinding higher in coming days.  

The G7's message "is clearly supportive of Asian" currencies, said Patrick Bennett, foreign-exchange strategist at Commerzbank. But the region's monetary authorities "will continue their own policies to pursue competitive FX rates to ensure external demand."  

Finance Ministers and central bankers from the G7 - the U.S., Japan, Germany, France, the U.K., Italy and Canada - reiterated Saturday that they want freer exchange rates, specifying they want more flexibility where it is currently lacking. They also said that "excess volatility and disorderly movements in exchange rates are undesirable for economic growth." Traders take the statement to mean the G7 wants Asian central banks to let their currencies rise to take some of the pressure of the dollar's global fall off the soaring euro.  

The central banks of Singapore, Taiwan and South Korea were apparently buying dollars in the market Wednesday, traders said.  

Sameer Goel, regional strategist at Bank of America, said Asian central banks are unlikely to concede to strengthening in their currencies in the short term, though the central banks may allow gradual and grudging appreciation this year.  

U.S. Trade Representative Robert Zoellick Wednesday renewed Washington's call for China - which the U.S. views as the chief currency manipulator - to loosen the yuan's peg to the dollar.  

"One of the issues we're going to have to deal with over time is the currency," Zoellick told reporters during a Tokyo visit. China "must give a fair shake to others including U.S. producers."  

On Monday Beijing strongly denied a weekend report that it would widen the yuan's trading band, allowing the currency to rise within the next couple of months.  

In South Korea, another persistent intervener, a senior central bank official defended Seoul's aggressive attempts to support the dollar to prevent the won - and thus Korean exports - from becoming too expensive.  

Seoul prefers a weak won to help support exports because domestic consumption isn't picking up quickly enough despite a recovery in the global economy, said Yeung-Kyun Rhee, director general of the Bank of Korea's international department.  

Rhee, in a recent interview with Dow Jones Newswires, sought to put the ball in Tokyo's court, saying G7 member Japan's own yen-selling interventions are helping Seoul subdue the won. "If the Japanese government continues to block the yen's rise, then there is a limit to how much the won can rise," he said.  

Japanese officials have stressed since the weekend G7 meeting in Boca Raton, Fla., that the call for more currency flexibility doesn't apply to them and that they, too, will keep propping up the dollar.  

While Asian central banks are likely to continue their heavy dollar-buying interventions, they could face difficulties in keeping their exchange rates competitive in the overseas markets down the road, analysts said.  

Bank of America expects faster economic growth in Asia, a change in the yuan peg and other factors to increase the impetus for appreciation in Asian currencies this year.  

Around 0808 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at KRW1,160.6, down from Tuesday's KRW1,162.1 close. Against the Singapore unit, it was at S$1.6747, down from S$1.6758 late in Asia Tuesday, and versus the rupiah it was at 8,399 rupiah, lower from its close Tuesday at IDR8,400.  

Against the Thai baht, the dollar was quoted at THB38.97, up from THB38.94 Tuesday. It fell against the New Taiwan dollar, to NT$33.147 from NT$33.195, but was marginally higher against the Philippine peso, at PHP55.905, up from PHP55.845.

title: Bk Of Korea Aide:Japan  FX  Policy Affects Won's Direction
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--Japan's aggressive intervention in the foreign exchange market to sustain its economic recovery may have the knock-on effect of helping South Korea in its efforts to hold down the value of the won and support its own export-led recovery, a Bank of Korea official said.  

"If the Japanese government continues to block the yen's rise, then there is a limit to how much the won can rise," Yeung-Kyun Rhee, director general of the Bank of Korea's international department, told Dow Jones Newswires in a recent interview.  

He also predicted that the dollar's weakness against Asian currencies, including the won, won't continue for long given the aggressiveness of Japanese efforts to defend the U.S. currency.  

Rhee said Seoul prefers a weak won to help support exports because domestic consumption isn't picking up quickly enough despite a recovery in the global economy.  

"The Korean economy isn't recovering as fast as other economies. In that aspect, the local won cannot strengthen at the same pace as other currencies," he said.  

Rhee said South Korea's foreign exchange policy remains unchanged despite a call by the Group of Seven leading industrialized nations for Asian countries to allow their currencies to strengthen. G7 finance ministers met in Boca Raton, Florida over the weekend.  

"We are relieved by the G7 statement. It remains surprisingly unchanged from September. Japan, the euro zone and the U.S. have all incorporated their views in the statement," he said.  

Rhee indicated that South Korean authorities weren't greatly worried about the won's gains following the G7 meeting, saying they weren't as significant as those seen after the previous G7 meeting that initially called for more flexibility in Asian currencies.  

"We have kept an eye on foreign exchange fluctuations and there haven't been any rapid rises or falls since the G7 meeting," he said. "Sure, the dollar fell but it's not like plunges of 10-plus won like after the previous G7."  

At 0612 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1,160.6 won, down 0.6% from a close of KRW1,168.1 Friday before the G7 released its communique over the weekend.  

The U.S. unit had lost 1.5% in the three trading days following the last G7 meeting Sept. 22.  


 
      Tighter NDF Rules Aimed At Speculation, Volatility 
   

On new restrictions recently imposed in the non-deliverable forward market, Rhee said the regulations were aimed at protecting the market from speculative forces and excessive volatility, but that the authorities need more time to determine whether the move will prove effective.  

Last month, the South Korean government tightened regulations on trading in the NDF market. The multi-pronged move was said by many currency traders to be an attempt by the government to slow the won's rise against the dollar in order to keep exports competitive.  

Rhee said the central bank will continue to focus on the foreign exchange rate rather than inflation for the time being.  

"Aside from the forthcoming elections, there are concerns about inflation due to rises in crude oil and global raw material prices, but it's premature to be worried about inflation," he said.  

On whether South Korea may be more open like Japan about its interventions in the foreign exchange market, Rhee said there is no rule that prevents South Korea from doing so but that it is unlikely to happen.  

"Japan publicly announces the size of its interventions in the foreign exchange market. There's no rule that says Korea can't do that, but the dollar-won market is very small and we can't behave like developed countries," he said.  

Rhee declined to comment on what defines excessive volatility for the South Korean government.  

"There's no fixed criterion for determining what a rapid rise or fall in the foreign exchange rate is. It depends on the situation. For example, the dollar fell to Y112 from Y115 after the previous G7 meeting. In such a situation, there's no way that we can prevent the dollar from falling against the won," he said.  

"There would have been no way to reverse the trend even if we had poured in all the money available," he added.  

Rhee also rejected criticism of the government's intervention in the foreign exchange market.  

"Smoothing operations is different from controlling the foreign exchange rate. Japan poured in $70 billion so far this year, but no one says Japan manipulates the market."  

He stressed that the central bank has sufficient resources to step into the market if necessary and downplayed speculation among currency dealers that South Korean authorities have started to run out of funds to intervene.  

"There's an unlimited amount of money piled up in the vault," Rhee said. "Unlike the government which has to issue bonds to raise funds to stabilize the foreign exchange market, the central bank can do it unnoticed because it can desterilize money supply through issuance of monetary stabilization bonds."

title: Dollar Weakness Resumes As Market Unfazed By G7 Warning
text:
LONDON (Dow Jones)--Investors are continuing to sell the dollar Monday after a weekend meeting of policymakers from the world's richest nations produced no expressions of discomfort over the U.S. currency's weak level.  

While top economic officials from the Group of Seven leading industrialized nations warned in a joint statement Saturday that "excess volatility and disorderly movements in exchange rates are undesirable for economic growth," they made no reference to currency valuation.  

They added the G7 "would continue to monitor exchange markets closely and cooperate as appropriate" and reiterated a call for "flexibility" in exchange rates.  

It was yet another vaguely worded statement that made no direct threat to intervene to stop the dollar from falling further. Unlike the 1985 Plaza Accord, which launched a concerted effort to weaken a strong dollar, the communique from the meeting in Boca Raton, Fla., wasn't specific enough to have a real impact on currency trading.  

Market players have interpreted the communique to mean that G7 officials would, in fact, be untroubled if the dollar, already down 30% since 2002 versus its main rivals, declines even further - as long as it's not too fast.  

"G7 still wants the dollar to fall. All that has changed is that it does not want the dollar to fall in a volatile way," wrote analysts with Bear Stearns in a Monday report.  

As global trading got underway Monday in Asia, the G7 outcome initially sent the dollar as high as Y105.87, from Y105.45 Friday afternoon in New York, as some investors were impressed by the warning against excess volatility. The euro dropped to a low of $1.2575 from $1.2697.  

But it didn't take long for markets to realize the G7 statement brought no real news, and investors resumed selling the greenback. By around 1130 GMT, the dollar had slipped to Y105.64 while the euro had bounced to $1.2746.  


 
           Consensus Has Dollar Falling Further 
   

The consensus market view remains that the dollar is set to drop further against the euro and the yen in the coming months, or at least until the Federal Reserve raises interest rates. A rate cut by the European Central Bank, for its part, would put a drag on the euro, but ECB President Jean-Claude Trichet suggested Saturday such a move is not in the cards.  

In Japan, authorities are expected to continue intervening in the market to smooth the appreciation of the yen. Even though the G7 communique called for flexibility in currency regimes, analysts think the statement is mostly targeted at China and South Korea, since Japanese intervention has not been enough to stop the yen from gradually rising.  

The introduction of the warning against excess currency volatility in the G7 communique follows European demands for a coordinated verbal effort to stem the dollar's sharp decline against the euro, which has risen 20% in the past year alone and is slowing Europe's economic recovery.  

Spearheaded by Trichet, European policymakers had embarked on a campaign to talk the euro down a few weeks before the G7 meeting in Boca Raton.  

Many economists saw the volatility warning as a European victory, because it meant that they had managed to persuade U.S. officials to risk slowing a dollar depreciation that has boosted U.S. corporate earnings and helped job creation in an election year.  

Yet large currency risks may be looming in the euro zone.  

Shahab Jalinoos, a senior currency strategist with ABN Amro in London, thinks European policymakers have made a mistake by preempting the G7 statement with verbal intervention before the meeting. He argues the G7 would have had a greater impact on the market had Trichet and his colleagues stayed quiet and let the communique first bring up official concern against abrupt moves in currencies.  

This is not yet the consensus view, but it makes sense: The risk is that investors who pared positions ahead of the G7 meeting because of Trichet's warnings may now feel encouraged to challenge Europe's resolve in curbing the euro's rise, now that Europe seems to have played its full hand.  

"Europe overplayed," said Jalinoos. "They have shown the market their limits, and now the market will feel encouraged to take them on," he said.  

-By Adriana Arai, Dow Jones Newswires, 44 207 842 9483 adriana.arai@dowjones.com

title: S Korea Govt Official: Expect Stronger Dlr On G7 Mtg
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--The South Korean government expects the pressure on the won to strengthen against the U.S. dollar to ease due to the statement by the Group of Seven industrial powers over the weekend, an official at the Ministry of Finance and Economy said Monday.  

"We think the meeting results could reverse the dollar's weakening trend," Yoon Yeo-Kwon, director of the ministry's foreign exchange market division, told Dow Jones Newswires.  

Yoon interpreted the new language on exchange rates in the statement following the G7 meeting in Florida as specifically referring to the U.S dollar.  

After the two-day meeting, G7 finance ministers and central bankers warned in a statement that "excess volatility and disorderly movements in exchange rates are undesirable for economic growth."  

In a separate phone interview, Lee Jae-Ouk, assistant governor at the Bank of Korea, said post-G7 comment by Japan's finance minister would likely affect foreign exchange policies of other Asian countries.  

"We don't expect significant changes in the foreign exchange market due to the G7...but Japan's (post-G7) moves will likely influence other Asian countries, including us," said Lee.  

Japanese finance minister Sadakuza Tanigaki said after the G7 meeting, "The newly inserted words in the statement, such as 'excessive volatility' and 'disorderly moves,' are what I myself and Europe have been suggesting to be included."  

Monday morning, before the official market opening, the Bank of Japan is suspected to have intervened in the market by selling yen.  

Like Japan, South Korea has justified dollar-buying market interventions as "smoothing operations" to ease the volatility of the local currency.  

Yoon of the Ministry of Finance and Economy predicted the G7's renewed call for "more flexibility in exchange rates" won't likely disrupt the won as it did after the meeting in Dubai in September.  

From the last G7 meeting to last Friday, the won has gained 2.9% versus the dollar to KRW1,168.1. At 0130 GMT, the dollar had fallen further to KRW1,167.5, reflecting the belief of many players that the G7 statement won't change the dollar's direction in the long term.  

Yoon maintained the Seoul government will continue with its foreign exchange policy to help sustain strong exports until there is a change in "economic fundamentals."

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Peso wins reprieve, rest cautious.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Feb 5 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso rose more
than half a percent on Thursday after the central bank raised
the amount of currency reserves banks are required to hold with
it.
    The peso        jumped to 55.85 per dollar, from near
record lows of 56.22 in early trade, as the central bank raised
the liquidity reserve requirement to 10 percent from eight
percent.
    It was the bank's first policy change since last August and
is expected to drain 30 billion pesos from the financial system
-- effectively a monetary tightening.
    Dealers in Manila said there had been some rumours about
the move early in the day, but most players were caught off
guard.
    Analysts said given the bleak outlook for the peso amid
worries over presidential elections in May, a mix of
intervention and policy measures by authorities to support the
currency should be expected.
  


    "As we approach the elections and the market begins to
price in the inherent risks, the central bank will come in to
implement some sort of change in the trading regime in order to
stem the tide," said Simon Flint, strategist at Bank of America
in Singapore.
    Dealers in Manila said the move would provide temporary
support to the peso as banks cut back on dollar purchases and
square long dollar positions to meet the new reserve
requirement.
 
    Analysts fear the upcoming elections could compound the
country's fiscal and balance of payments problems.
    Moody's Investors Service last week lowered its long-term
ratings for the Philippines, saying unstable election year
politics threatened to worsen the country's budget woes.
    G7 FOCUS
    Elsewhere, most Asian regional currencies posted cautious
gains ahead of a Group of Seven industrial nations' two-day
meeting starting on Friday.
    Dealers said bullish sentiment on regional currencies would
remain intact for the medium term given the improved economic
outlook for the year.
    But few were now looking for strong near-term gains as the
market has scaled back hopes of a tough stand by the G7 against
Asia's policy of resisting appreciation versus the U.S. dollar.
    Analysts saw the meeting of G7 finance ministers and

    "The medium-term outlook remains unchanged. Strategy-wise
you would want to maintain short dollar/Asia," said James
Malcolm, strategist at JP Morgan Chase in Singapore.
    "Perception around the G7 has been scaled back but nobody
is sure. There could be an upset on comments on the sidelines."
    Taiwan and South Korea's suspected intervention on
  

Wednesday to curb gains in their currencies underlined market  

fears that Asian central banks would stick to their policy  

stance.  

The Taiwan dollar was steady but stayed off  

Wednesday's 18-month high of 33.23 per U.S. dollar. The South

title: UPDATE 1-S.Korea  FX  reserves at record high on  intervention .
text:
SEOUL, Feb 3 (Reuters) - South Korea's foreign exchange reserves reached another record in January, the central bank said on Tuesday, in large part a reflection of continued dollar-buying by authorities trying to prevent the won currency from climbing.  

With no sign the government is weakening in its resolve to keep the won down to protect price competitiveness of exporters, forex reserves are expected to continue rising this year.  

"Foreign exchange reserves cannot help rising for some time, given the government effort to contain the won's strength spurred by a trade surplus and foreign buying of local stocks," Ahn Byung-chan, a deputy director general of the Bank of Korea, told Reuters by telephone.  

Reserves grew $2.1 billion from a month earlier to a record $157.45 billion at the end of January, lifted by investment gains and a rise in dollar deposits of banks at the central bank, the central bank said in a statement.  

The country's foreign exchange reserves, the fourth-largest in the world, rose almost $34 billion in 2003 after the government stepped repeatedly to keep the won virtually unchanged against the dollar. That sent the won plunging against the Japanese yen and the euro.  

As the economy is emerging from a brief recession last year, the central bank also has left interest rates at historic lows, despite concerns over inflationary pressure on rising import prices.   


But heavy dollar supply from strong exports and a global trend of a
weak dollar has put upward pressure on the won        , driving it to
the highest level in three and a half months by noon on Tuesday.
  

South Korea had less than $4 billion in foreign exchange reserves at the height of the Asian financial crisis in late 1997 when the International Monetary Fund arranged a $58 billion bail-out for the country.  

It repaid the last tranche of the loan in August 2001, three years ahead of schedule.

title: S Korea Govt: Concerned About Recent  FX  Volatility
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--In its second verbal intervention this month, South Korea's Ministry of Finance and Economy warned Wednesday that it will take "necessary" action to stabilize the foreign exchange market.  

"The government is concerned about recent excessive volatility in the foreign exchange market. It will closely watch the market situation to take appropriate action," said the ministry in a statement issued minutes before the local foreign exchange market opened for trading.  

The dollar slipped to 1,176.2 won Tuesday from its previous close of KRW1,180.5, and well off a Dec. 26 close of KRW1,200 despite measures by the authorities to slow the won's rise.  


 
   The last time the dollar traded at such levels was two weeks ago when the government then issued a verbal warning, quickly followed by a new regulation to cap offshore investors' dollar sales via the nondeliverable forward market.   

But the curbs on the NDF market had only a short-term impact and the won marched up, pressured by a surge in foreign fund inflows to the local stock market.  

Wednesday's verbal warning didn't stop the dollar falling further at the open. At 0055 GMT, the dollar was down at KRW1,174.3, a level last seen in mid-November, as exporters offloaded the U.S. unit for month-end purposes.  

"The market just doesn't think the government has much more to do to change the big picture - the won's eventual appreciation," said one dealer.  

So far this year, the government has issued KRW2 trillion in treasury bonds to raise funds to slow the won's rise.  

The government has parliament approval to issue up to KRW7.8 trillion in treasurys in 2004 to stabilize the foreign exchange market.  

-By Hye-Seung Seo, Dow Jones Newswires; 822-732-2165; hyeseung.seo@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 1-Economic recovery to pinch S.Korean trade surplus.
text:
SEOUL, Jan 1 (Reuters) - South Korea's trade surplus, which expanded 50 percent in 2003 to more than $15 billion, is set to shrink in 2004 as an accelerating economic recovery sucks in more imports, the commerce ministry said on Thursday.  

"Along with a recovery in the global economy, a revival in domestic consumption will keep imports growth at the level of 2003, whereas exports growth will slow to around 10 percent," the ministry said in a statement.  

Exports on a customs-clearance basis jumped 19.6 percent in 2003 from a year earlier, powered by chips, automobiles and wireless telecommunications equipment.  

Imports increased 17.5 percent, led by crude oil and electronic parts, allowing the country's trade surplus to expand by 50 percent over 2002 to a provisional $15.54 billion.  

Earlier in December, Deputy Trade Minister Kim Chil-doo said the trade surplus would narrow 42 percent in 2004 to around $9 billion compared with 2003.  

But the continued surplus would put upward pressure on the won, making South Korean exports more expensive.  

"A possible appreciation of the Chinese yuan and any move by other countries to step up import restrictions will have a negative impact on our exports," the commerce ministry statement said.  

South Korea heavily intervened in the currency market in 2003 to keep the won virtually unchanged against the dollar but sending it plunging against the Japanese yen and the euro, which gained 11 percent and 20 percent respectively over the dollar.  

In December alone, South Korea posted a trade surplus of $2.3 billion, with exports up 32.5 percent over a year earlier and imports up 22.1 percent. It marked the ninth straight monthly trade surplus.  

Soaring exports of cars, chips and mobile phones, especially in late 2003, pulled South Korea's economy out of recession in the third quarter but imports have grown much more slowly because domestic consumption remained in the doldrums.  

The central bank has forecast South Korea's gross domestic product in 2003 would be 2.9 percent greater than in 2002, when the economy grew 6.3 percent.  

An expected 1.1 percent drop in private consumption was attributed for the forecast 2003 economic slowdown, it said.  

The central bank forecast the South Korean economy would grow more than five percent in 2004.

title: ANALYSIS-South Korea looks west to win its won battles.
text:
SEOUL, Nov 28 (Reuters) - For years South Korea has looked east, across the waves to Japan, to help it set currency policy.   

Now the country is looking west, across the Yellow Sea, with an anxious eye on maintaining competitiveness in fast-growing China - its biggest export market and a key competitor.    


To keep the South Korean export machine running, Seoul has spent up to
$26 billion, by market estimates, buying foreign currencies to keep the
won's value             closely tied to the Chinese yuan, which in turn
is pegged to the retreating U.S. dollar.
   

China is the key driver of export growth throughout Asia and by anchoring its currency to the yuan, South Korea has an advantage over rivals such as Japan whose currencies are rising.   

But while the won policy may help reflate the South Korean economy, analysts say it could cause fresh problems - including upward pressure on the won when Seoul comes to sell its dollar hoard.   

"I think that the current heavy intervention would end up with an abrupt fall in the dollar/won rates," said Oh Suk-tae, an economist at Citibank.   

As the Bank of Korea (BOK) has dumped won on the market, it has been issuing bonds to soak up the money. It's a process known as sterilisation, and it prevents money supply from ballooning and ultimately leading to inflation.   

But it also means there's an awful lot of local currency debt hitting the market through Monetary Stabilisation Bonds (MSBs) and other bonds, which puts upward pressure on interest rates.   

BUNDLES OF BONDS   

"As international reserves increase, the BOK sterilises that increase by issuing MSBs. However, there are limits to how much the BOK can issue in MSBs without crowding out other borrowers," said John Chambers, the deputy head of sovereign ratings group at Standard & Poor's.   

"Unsterilised increases in international reserves provoke an increase in monetary aggregates, which in turn can lead financial agents to anticipate higher prices for assets and eventually for consumer goods," he said.   

South Korea does not admit to currency intervention but analysts say most of a $26 billion rise in government foreign currency reserves is due to won sales.   

The central bank sent the won sliding last week when it said it would manage its currency policy to support exports.   

EXPORT ENGINE   

As South Korean mobile phones, computer chips and a host of other goods have been snapped up by Chinese customers, Seoul's trade surplus has surged to its highest in five years.   

China this year became South Korea's number one export market. It took 17.9 percent of exports in the 10 months through October, versus 17.6 percent for previous number one, the United States.   

"There has been nothing short of an explosion in Korea's exports to China, especially since mid-2003," Goldman Sachs analyst Sun-Bae Kim said in a client note issued on November 17.   

Investment bank Morgan Stanley has estimated that China alone is responsible for 40 percent of South Korean export growth.   

Despite rising demand from South Korean exporters, the heavily managed won has risen less than five percent against the dollar in the past eight months. During the same period, the yen's rise against the dollar was twice that.   

The won selling not only protects Seoul's competitiveness in China and the United States. Many other customers also pay in U.S. dollars.   

WON STALLED   

Previously the yen and the won had moved in lockstep. Last year dollar/yen fell 11 percent. Dollar/won fell 10 percent.   

This year the yen has found favour due to a recovery in Japan. Were the won to move in line with the Japanese currency, South Korea could risk choking off exports just as its economy climbs out of recession.   

"The Korean government wants to keep the won moving in a very narrow range when the yuan is pegged to the dollar and when the yen is appreciating on the back of the Japanese economy's recovery," Oh said.   

Both Japan and South Korea have intervened massively but Seoul - operating in a smaller market with daily inter-bank currency trading of around $3 billion - has been more effective.   

Policymakers in Seoul, who say they only conduct smoothing operations aimed at protecting the market from speculation, argue it's only normal that the won fails to keep pace with the yen.   

"It is a natural phenomenon that the won has depreciated against the yen recently, reflecting different economic fundamentals in South Korea and Japan," said Deputy Finance Minister Kwon Tae-shin, South Korea's top foreign exchange policy maker.   

Economists say there's more to it than that.   

"Export-led growth requires keeping the exchange rate undervalued to repress consumption and promote saving and a high investment rate, which is the source of rapid GDP growth," said Tim Condon, chief regional economist at ING Financial Markets in Hong Kong. ($1=1,202.8 Won).

title: S.Korea won ends lower on  intervention , yen.
text:

"After foreign investors switched into net stock sellers, concerns over reduced supply of dollars redoubled the impact of the intervention," said a foreign bank dealer. "After the dollar rebounded as authorities expected, it looked like they made all-out efforts to push the level up further towards the close."  

Compounding the impact of government action, the central bank said in a statement on Tuesday that it needed to consider taking countermeasures against any sharp appreciation of the won, hinting at more intervention by authorities in the future.  

South Korea's benchmark stock index fell 1.10 percent, with foreign investors offloading a net 51 billion won of shares.  

The won/yen cross rate , a calculated rate based on each currency's value against the dollar, stood at 10.8176/35 against 10.7381/40 late on Monday, indicating the won's firmness.  

The yen was quoted at 108.80/86 to the dollar on caution over intervention, after the Japanese unit climbed to a three-year high of 107.82 in overnight U.S. trade.

title: UPDATE 3-S.Korea must prepare for sudden North fail-S&P.
text:
SEOUL, Nov 3 (Reuters) - The collapse of North Korea's economy is just a matter of time and South Korea should prepare for an emergency that may cost three times its annual economic output, ratings agency Standard & Poor's said on Monday.   

 John Chambers, the managing director for sovereign ratings at S&P, said South Korea's sovereign rating was unlikely to change even if North Korea pulled out of talks on Pyongyang's nuclear weapons ambitions.   

 "In our view, it's only a question of time when North Korea collapses because its current economic model is not sustainable," Chambers told reporters.   

 He said estimates of the cost of North Korea's economic collapse - and the resultant collapse of the country itself - to the capitalist South ranged from 40 percent to 300 percent of South Korea's annual GDP, a range of $190 billion to $1.4 trillion based on current GDP of about $480 billion.   

 Some have estimated the cost of South Korea digesting the collapse of the North would exceed an estimated $750 billion bill from the reunification of Germany.   

 The credit rating agency, like its rivals, sees the North Korean nuclear crisis as a key issue constraining South Korea's credit ratings. S&P has an A-minus long-term foreign currency credit rating on South Korea.   

 But Chambers said South Korea's domestic politics could also affect credit ratings because they can influence the government's commitment to pushing ahead with further reforms.   

 President Roh Moo-hyun shocked the country when he proposed an unprecedented referendum next month on his rule, after a close aide was arrested for taking bribes. The date for the referendum, and even whether it will take place, remain uncertain.   

 The rating by S&P, whose views are important as they influence the interest rate the country pays on its loans, puts South Korea in the same group as Malaysia, Hungary and Israel.   

 Although unification has long been a stated goal of South Korea, Seoul has been taken aback by the damage far wealthier West Germany sustained in absorbing East Germany, which was more prosperous than North Korea.   

 South Korean economists have estimated unification will cost Seoul anything from $200 billion over ten years to six times that sum in a shorter period, depending on the pace of events.   

 The immediate diplomatic focus is on whether North Korea would join another round of six-country nuclear talks with China, the United States, South Korea, Japan and Russia. Pyongyang agreed in principle last week to resume negotiations.   

 But Chambers said the matter of greatest importance for South Korea's credit ratings was not the talks themselves. He said the "red line" in the year-old saga was now the North proliferating its nuclear weapons.   

 On economic reforms, S&P referred to the need for South Korean conglomerates to concentrate on key competencies, for improved corporate governance, lowering the state's participation in banking and making the government's budget more transparent.   

 It also said building large foreign exchange reserves - South Korea has $141.5 billion at the end of September - had a downside because the central bank had to issue securities to mop up its intervention.   

 "South Korea would be better served in improving efficiencies in its own economy to obtain competitiveness with foreign trading partners than in building a high level of international reserves to counter won appreciation," S&P said in a statement.   

 South Korea's reserves are enough to cover nearly nine months of the country's imports, although currency dealers in Seoul have said South Korea often bought dollars when the U.S. currency fell against the won.

title: S Korea Denies  FX Intervention ; Says Just Smoothing Ops
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--South Korea's financial authorities Wednesday denied that they recently intervened in the foreign exchange market to put a lid on the won's appreciation against the dollar and the yen.  

Kwon Tae-Shin, a deputy minister of the Ministry of Finance and Economy, denied that Kim Jin-Pyo, who heads the ministry, told the Financial Times that the government would continue to "intervene" to keep the won down if it rises further against the dollar and the yen.  

Kim merely said the government would conduct "smoothing operations" to protect the local currency against market volatility and speculative forces, Kwon explained.  

"The word 'intervention' never came up," Kwon told Dow Jones Newswires in a telephone interview.  

The Bank of Korea, which is responsible for foreign exchange operations, also said its recent efforts to bring down the won against the dollar were a form of "indirect smoothing" to alleviate outside shock, said Rhee Young-Kyun, director-general for the central bank's international department.  

He denied market speculation that the central bank has spent more than $10 billion to buy dollars via state-run banks to lift the U.S. unit from KRW1,150-levels to the current level of around KRW1,180. "That's outrageous", Rhee said when asked about the rumor during a separate telephone interview.  

The U.S. dollar gained 2.6% from KRW1,151.3 on Sept. 22, shortly after the G-7 Dubai meeting called for more flexible Asian currencies, to KRW1,181.8 Tuesday. During the same period, the dollar slipped 2.5% to Y109.43 from Y112.18.  

The finance ministry and central bank said their smoothing operations were in accordance to international convention, and haven't prompted complaints from the U.S. or the International Monetary Fund, which monitors foreign exchange policies and operations of its member countries.  

But Rhee conceded the finance minister's comment on "intervention" could be "misleading" and could lead to complaint from the U.S. government.  

"From looking at the (FT) report, the U.S. could think we are manipulating foreign exchange," he said.  

The two officials also said South Korea doesn't have target levels for the won against the yen or dollar, and therefore declined comment on whether they were happy with where the won is currently trading at.  

"It's not that the government wants the won to depreciate against the yen. The decoupling of the two currencies has happened because of market forces," said the ministry of finance's Kwon.  

"The fundamentals of the two countries are different. It is natural for the two currencies to go separate ways," Kwon said.  

South Korea has said it would resort to "smoothing operations" if the won strengthens to a level that could undermine exports without clarifying what that level is.  

The government hopes the recent double-digit growth in exports will continue to spur economic recovery as local consumption remains sluggish.

title: GLOBAL MARKETS-Wall St rally sends dollar, Asian stocks up.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Japanese and South Korean stocks soared on Tuesday after strong results from Motorola Inc spurred Wall Street to 2003 highs, but most Asian stocks erased early gains and the dollar rose against the euro and the yen.  

The U.S. unit jumped to a one-week high versus the euro and rose against major currencies, helped by Wall Street's rally and extending gains after the European Central Bank chief said a Group of Seven (G7) call last month for exchange rate flexibility was not aimed at the European currency.  

Japan's Nikkei average surged over two percent to break the 11,000 barrier, driven by big banks such as Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group.  

But MSCI's broadest index of Asia Pacific shares ex-Japan lost some steam to shed 0.78 percent, after earlier chalking up a three-year high for the 11th day running.  

Motorola, the world's second-largest mobile phone maker, posted on Monday a quarterly profit twice the estimates of analysts and forecast stronger-than-expected sales in its current fourth quarter, sending U.S. stocks soaring.  

The Dow rose 0.93 percent at 9,764.38 and the Standard & Poor's 500 Index gained 0.7 percent at 1,045.35 - their highest closes since June 2002. The Nasdaq ended at its highest close since January last year at 1,933.53.  

ECB President Wim Duisenberg's attempt on Monday to clarify why the dollar has fallen so far against the euro seemed to make thin currency markets dispel dollar-bearish sentiment, for now.  

The G7 call for flexibility was viewed as a demand that Japan and China stop market intervention to weaken their currencies to boost their export markets, an issue that could be raised by President George W. Bush during his Asia trip this week. Intervention by South Korea and Taiwan has also drawn criticism.  

Some analysts said Duisenberg's remarks opened an opportunity to adjust positions after the euro rose last week to within a cent of its record high of $1.1932 earlier this year. Others said the recent dollar-selling sentiment had not changed.  

"I don't think what Duisenberg said was anything new. The market's position was tilted towards the euro and so I think the fall was an adjustment," said Junya Tanase, foreign exchange strategist at JP Morgan Chase.  

On Tuesday morning the euro fell more than one U.S. cent to a one-week low of $1.1606 versus 1.1712/16 in late U.S. trade, when it also fell almost one percent. As of 0623 GMT, the euro was trading at $1.1604/09. It dipped to around 126.83 yen compared with 127.45.  

The dollar rose to 109.36 yen, about a quarter of a percent above 108.90/00 in late U.S. trade, and more than one yen above a three-year low of 108.28 yen on Friday.  

HOPES FOR ECONOMY  

Japan's benchmark index shed some gains to close up 1.67 percent at a one-month high of 10,966.43, while the broad TOPIX index ended up 1.25 percent at 1,087.31, its highest close since June last year.  

Traders said the market was beginning to erect resistance to the yen's recent strength, seeing it as a sign of an improving economy and foreign inflows into Japan.  

"Barring a surge in the yen to around 105 or higher, the market seems willing to ignore yen strength for now," said Masayoshi Okamoto, head of dealing at Jujiya Securities. "Banks continue to rally, which reflects strong hopes for the economy."  

The Bank of Japan also upgraded its assessment of the economy for the second straight month in a report on Tuesday, supporting recent signs of a nascent recovery.  

Analysts also said Japanese technology issues, mostly exposed to the yen's moves, have underperformed since September and could rise.  

Samsung Electronics Co Ltd and exporters such as Hyundai Motor Co drove South Korea's benchmark index up 1.25 to end at a one-month high of 766.52.  

But Hong Kong's benchmark index slipped in afternoon trade after failing to hold above the key 12,000-point mark on investor concerns the market had overheated after surging 40 percent in nearly six months.  

Motorola's results earlier pushed up Singapore technology, but the benchmark index pulled back from 18-month highs to dip 0.8 percent.  

Taiwan stocks also erased gains to end 0.57 percent lower at 5,938.42, down from a 17-month high, as tech shares such as United Microelectronics Corp fell as investors cautiously awaited third-quarter results at home and in the U.S.  

Focus would be on Intel Corp's third-quarter earnings later on Tuesday, with analysts hoping that the world's largest chip maker would post revenue growth as the semiconductor sector rebounded from its worst slump.  

Japanese government bond prices fell sharply, under pressure from the Nikkei's brief rise above 11,000 and gained little from a monetary easing by the Bank of Japan late last week.  

Oil prices dipped to intraday lows with NYMEX November futures down 15 cents to $31.80 a barrel, but traders said OPEC output cuts and tightening heating fuel supplies gave support.  

Gold opened slightly lower in Europe at $373.20 on the dollar recovery.

title: UPDATE 2-S.Korea puts brave face on rapid rise in won.
text:
SEOUL, Oct 10 (Reuters) - South Korea's central bank put on a brave face on Friday over a sustained rise in the won, but analysts cast doubt on whether authorities could control a currency appreciation that may threaten an export-led recovery.    

 In the latest comments aimed at trying to sap the strength of the won, Lee Sung-tae, deputy governor of the Bank of Korea, told Reuters by telephone that a flagging economy should knock some of the wind out of the Korean won .    

 The local currency market - faced with mounting dollar supplies from offshore selling, exporter deals and persistent inflows of foreign capital - has seen the won climb more than nine percent against the dollar since a March low.    

 "It's true that the won is coming under pressure from a current account surplus and foreign buying of domestic stocks," Lee said.    

 "But there won't be any rapid appreciation in the currency over the short run given that the economy is not reviving yet," he added.    

 The won stood at 1,148.0 at 0700 GMT after opening at 1,149.0. It closed on Thursday at 1,148.6, the strongest finish since November 20, 2000 when it ended at 1,143.7.    

 Authorities have kept up their rhetoric against the won's advance as it erodes the competitiveness of South Korean products in overseas markets. Exports are a rare bright spot for South Korea's recession-hit economy.    

 Dealers estimated the government has soaked up more than $3 billion in the currency markets this week alone through quasi-government agencies such as state-run banks.    

 WASHINGTON'S HIT LIST    

 But it will not be an easy battle for a government facing growing doubts over the effectiveness of its intervention and outside pressure to let market forces dictate movements.    

 "We'll see how long the government can hold out," said Oh Suk-tae, an economist and currency strategist at Citibank. "If intervention is to be justified as a support for future growth, it is worth asking how much incremental growth can Korea expect."    

 Oh, who expects the won to hit 1,100 per dollar by year-end based on his forecast of 110 yen per dollar, said that the costly intervention had led to an accumulation of foreign exchange reserves, which now stand at an all-time high of $141.53 billion.    

 Compounding the government's worries, a growing number of domestic exporters are opting to settle their export deals at an earlier date on a belief that the won has further to rise.    

 LG Electronics Inc , South Korea's top home-appliance maker, has converted sizable dollar deposits into the won as part of its hedging strategy.    

 "We are trying to minimize our dollar exposure," said an official at LG's financing division. "We don't rely on the government's pledge or warnings any longer and have an internal strategy to reshuffle our forex structure."    

 Fuelling more concerns over the sustainability of government policy, there has been growing pressure from the United States on Asian countries to allow greater currency flexibility.    

 Some analysts said heavy intervention put South Korea in a danger of being tagged as part of a U.S. black list.    

 "With the Federal Reserve watching more closely and trying to build its case, Seoul may now have to act more cautiously," said Strategic Forecasting Inc, a private Texas-based intelligence firm.    

 "This could prompt the won to appreciate more quickly, especially if South Korea joins China and Japan atop Washington's currency hit list," it said in a research note.
