title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Higher Late, Tracking Yen Up
text:
MANILA (Dow Jones)--Asian currencies were mostly up late Monday, riding on the yen which gained ahead of the corporate half-year closing, but central bank buying of dollars left the New Taiwan dollar and the South Korean won flat.  

Market participants said they expected more losses in the dollar-yen, with the Bank of Japan failing to make an appearance Monday, and with its quarterly "tankan" corporate sentiment survey expected to show an improvement Wednesday.  

David Simmonds, senior emerging markets strategist for Asia at The Royal Bank of Scotland, said the recent Group of Seven industrialized countries' statement for more flexible exchange rates merely "helped to cement the break of the ranges" in dollar-yen and dollar-Asians. The dollar, he said, was declining and the G7 statement only accelerated the fall.  

Speculation on an early appreciation in the Hong Kong dollar have eased somewhat, but the expectation the currency will be revalued at some point persisted.  

The U.S. dollar was quoted at HK$7.7485, compared with HK$7.7605 Friday, while the Hong Kong dollar forwards discount deepened, in line with the decline in the spot rate. The one-year forward was quoted at a discount of 62 to 54 to the spot rate, compared with a discount of 41 to 20 Friday.  

The China yuan also ended up against the dollar, with exporters selling the dollar ahead of a weeklong holiday and to meet month-end foreign exchange requirements. In the spot market, the U.S. dollar closed at CNY8.2770, down from CNY8.2771 Sunday. But the bid-and-offer quote for the one-year dollar-yuan NDF stood at a discount of 3500/3350 points to the spot rate, wider than 3300/3000 late Friday afternoon. The NDFs don't have a direct influence on the spot dollar-yuan rate, but they reflect market psychology about exchange rates.  

Among the gainers Monday was the Singapore dollar, which was trading around S$1.7306 to the dollar around 1010 GMT, compared with late Friday's S$1.7315. The dollar traded a range of S$1.7268 to S$1.7293 during the Asian session.  


 
   Wary Of MAS At S$1.7240/45 
   

A dealer at a foreign bank said the Monetary Authority of Singapore didn't appear to be in the market although the market remains wary as the U.S. dollar nears S$1.7240/45.  

Singapore's United Overseas Bank, in a report Monday, said with pressure building up on the yuan and the Hong Kong dollar, the ringgit risks being "the next rotational play. However, given the absence of an NDF market, USD/SGD is likely to be employed as proxy trade."  

However, the central bank could effectively weaken the Singapore dollar again by tweaking the midpoint of its trade-weighted policy band, it said. "As such, USD/SGD looks trapped around 1.7250-1.7350 for the time being."  

Meanwhile, suspected government intervention in South Korea offset exporters' dollar sales, helping the dollar to finish unchanged from Friday's close at 1,150.5 won.  

"The Korea Development Bank and commercial banks snapped up about $500 million on behalf of the government," a dealer at a foreign bank estimated.  

"It's going to be hard (for the dollar) to slip below KRW1,150 with the government guarding" that level, said a dealer at a local bank.  

Taiwan's central bank was also believed to have bought dollars aggressively in late trading. The U.S. dollar closed at NT$33.790, little changed from NT$33.791 Friday.  

In the Philippines, the peso closed higher as some banks trimmed overbought dollar positions amid thin corporate demand early in the day and strong regional currencies.  

The dollar closed at PHP54.90 on the Philippine Dealing System, down from Friday's close of PHP55.02. Volume was higher at $136.5 million from $115 million due to late buying, which traders interpret as a sign of persistent weak investor sentiment for the Philippine peso.  

"The risk premium on the political side is being factored in, so you have a limited upside for the peso," said a trader with local bank.  

The Thai baht, meanwhile, was stronger. The dollar closed at 40.09 baht, down from THB40.145 late Friday as offshore players focused on strong Thai economic fundamentals.  

The Indonesian rupiah closed slightly higher in quiet trading on speculation of further capital inflows into the local market. The dollar closed at 8,420 rupiah, down from its close Friday at IDR8,440.  

Dealers said some market participants sold dollars on expectations of a rise in supply from overseas investment in Indonesian Satellite Corp.'s IDR1.75 trillion bond offering. Indosat, the country's second-largest phone company, will close book building for the bond Friday.

title: Asia Econ Growth On Track Even With Stronger  Currencies
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asia is expected to remain the world's fastest growing region even if the area's currencies edge up in value after major industrial powers called over the weekend for freer currency movements.  

But a sharp drop by the dollar in the wake of the Group of Seven meeting could seriously dent the prospects for a region just emerging from the economic damage of SARS and the Iraq war, economists say.  

G7 finance ministers and central bankers, meeting in Dubai over the weekend, called for "more flexibility in exchange rates" to promote "smooth and widespread adjustments in the international financial system."  

This amounts to a challenge to Asian export powerhouses, especially G7 member Japan and China, not to sell their own currencies to foster export-led growth.  

The G7's call "is a reflection of confidence that the global (economic) growth is on track," says David Cohen, a regional economist at MMS International in Singapore.  

But if Asian governments were to let the markets set their currency levels, it would mark quite a change in dearly held policies.  

Japan has bought an estimated $100 billion for yen so this year - well above the previous full-year record - while China also regularly must buy dollars to keep the yuan pegged around CNY8.28 to a dollar. Malaysia and Hong Kong also have currency pegs, while South Korea and Taiwan intervene to keep theirs in check.  

The result in Asia has been a massive swelling of already huge foreign-exchange reserves as national authorities sell their own currencies for dollars. In the U.S., manufacturers and some lawmakers charge that artificially undervalued Asian exchange rates are flooding the world with cheap Asian goods, ramping up the U.S. trade deficit and costing American jobs.  

Although Japan agreed to the G7 call for freer currencies and a G7 finance minister said China didn't object, Tokyo, Beijing, and Seoul made clear Monday they haven't changed their plans to keep their currencies stable to prevent exports from derailing.  

But the International Monetary Fund's director for Asia-Pacific, David Burton predicted little economic damage from the dollar's decline.  

"Most of these economies are growing robustly, and many of their exchange rates in real effective terms have depreciated somewhat in recent times, so I don't think modest appreciations would have a major effect on them," Burton told Dow Jones Newswires in an interview in Dubai.  

In its semiannual World Economic Outlook last week, the IMF forecast Asia excluding Japan would grow 5.9% this year, nearly twice the global average and trimmed hardly changed from the April forecast of 6.0% despite the ravages of SARS. The IMF more than doubled its 2003 growth forecast for Japan to 2% from 0.8%.  


 
           Bank Of Japan In The Spotlight 
   

A key issue for Asian economies in the wake of the G7 statement will be whether Tokyo can let the yen rise without roiling the markets or damaging its damaging the economy.  

After a decade of stagnation, Japan's economy grew an 3.9% annualized in the second quarter - the best in the G7.  

There is room for the yen to strengthen to Y110-Y115, says Cohen at MMS International. Morgan Stanley equity strategist Naoki Kamiyama says a Y108-Y112 range is still endurable for Japan.  

The dollar, which had already sagged Y3.5 last week, plunged in early Asian trade Monday to as low as Y111.37 - its lowest level since December 2000 - from Y114.27 late Friday in New York. Around 1000 GMT the dollar was at Y112.34.  

Some traders said they thought the Bank of Japan was selling yen covertly Monday, but Tokyo appeared to have lowered its dollar target. The Finance Ministry all year has ordered the Bank of Japan to sell yen heavily to defend the dollar at Y115 - a level that finally broke Friday as G7 ministers were arriving in Dubai.  

The dollar is now below the Y115 average rate that some exporters, such as Toyota Motor Corp., are counting on for the six-month period to next March. Shares of Japanese exporters tumbled Monday, helping drive the recently rallying Nikkei 225 Stock Average down 4.2%.  

While growing, the world's second-largest economy is still not out of the woods. Its banking system is choked full of bad debts, while consumers remain reluctant to spend.  


 
          China Pressured To Break The Peg 
   

Although the G7 didn't name names, it was clearly joining U.S. Treasury Secretary John Snow in pushing China to loosen up on the yuan.  

The yuan is convertible only on the current account, and Beijing has kept it around its current level for five years.  

Speculation regime-change has dogged the dollar for weeks in the market for forward delivery against the yuan, which can be used in place of the spot market to make bets on the yuan's long-term direction. The dollar's one-year discount steepened to a record 2400 points at one stage Monday, implying expectations of the dollar falling nearly 3% to 8.0374 yuan over the next 12 months.  

But the Chinese central bank and currency regulator insisted again Monday they;re in no change to give up currency stability, saying it's an internal matter.  

Many analysts agree China likely won't budge soon.  

"The yuan won't see much movement," says Dong Tao, an economist at Credit Suisse First Boston in Hong Kong.  

The head of research at a U.S. brokerage said China's exchange rate will remain a "political issue" ahead of the U.S. presidential elections next year, and the question is whether Beijing will be able to withstand the pressure.  

An Asian central banker, who declined to be named, said China needs to "do something," but just how and when it does will remain a mystery.  

What's not a mystery is the Chinese position.  

"A stable yuan is not only good for us, it's good for our immediate neighbors and for the whole world," deputy governor of the Bank of China, Li Ruogu, said recently.  

Li acknowledged China has a big trade surplus with the U.S., but said cheap labor costs - not exchange rates - are the main reason.  

"We're committed to liberalization, but I can't give you a very clear timetable of how long it will take," Li said.  


    -By Hasan Jafri, Dow Jones Newswires; 65-6415-4151; hasan.jafri@dowjones.com   

(Benjamin Pedley in Dubai and Arran Scott in Tokyo contributed to this item.)

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Falls in equities and yen weigh.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Sept 11 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were
pressured on Thursday morning by weakness in regional equity
markets and the drop in the yen  driven by the fear of
dollar-buying Japanese intervention.
    Trade was thinned by holidays in South Korea and Taiwan.
    The Thai baht        was forced off Wednesday's 14-month
highs and the Indonesian rupiah  failed to profit from
news of another sale of bank shares by the Indonesian Bank
Restructuring Agency (IBRA).
    "The overriding near term factor might be the equity
markets, where we had a sharp pullback," said Claudio Piron,
currency strategist with Standard Chartered Bank.
  


    "Asian central banks have been willing to allow their
currencies to appreciate, given that the asset valuations were
re-inflating and helping all the balance sheets."
    "But the equity pullback and the fact that the BOJ (Bank of
Japan) has been in the market as well means we have a pause in
the appreciation in some of the regional currencies," Piron
said.
    Japan's Nikkei average         followed the downtrend in
U.S. technology stocks, the latter weighed down by the second
anniversary of the September 11 attacks and the release of what
was said to be a new tape of al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden.
    Regional stock markets also paused after strong rallies.
    Singapore's stocks were down for a third day, dragged down
by technology stocks and Tuesday's news that a 27-year old
medical researcher in the city-state had Severe Acute
Respiratory Syndrome (SARS), the world's first case since the
global outbreak was declared over in July.
 
    But the Singapore dollar        was not as worried, holding
near Wednesday's two-week highs around 1.7480.
    PESO SUPPORTED, BAHT LOWER
    The Philippine peso        was supported on the firmer side
  

of the sensitive 55 per dollar level by a central bank order,  

issued on Tuesday, banning residents from buying dollars to  

purchase dollar-denominated bonds.  

Manila-based traders said the measure would not make much  

of a difference to speculators who have conventionally used the  

black market to bet on peso weakness.  

Meanwhile, despite the baht's light pullback, analysts said  

the Thai authorities seemed comfortable with the rapid gains  

the currency has made in recent months.  

James Malcolm, currency strategist at JP Morgan, said the  

baht's real effective exchange rate was just modestly above  

levels immediately after the 1997/98 Asian financial crisis and  

that valuations did not appear stretched.  

Peter Redward, strategist at Deutsche Bank, said there  

already were heavy short dollar-baht positions in the market,  

and fresh positions betting on a higher baht would be  

attractive only after the baht rose past 40.20.  

"The central bank's main concern is the pace of the move,  

particularly after the baht has strengthened considerably  

relative to Thailand's regional currency index," Redward said.

title: S.Korea won firmer by midday,  intervention  concern.
text:
0300 GMT - South Korea's won firmer versus the dollar but trades in tight range, closely tracking the Japanese yen's movement in Asia trade.  

- Won briefly rises to two-week highs at one point as foreign investors keep buying local shares but retreats on concern over possible intervention.  

- The currency finishes morning session at 1,170.4 against the dollar, compared with Monday's close of 1,171.5. It opened at a session low of 1,171.3 and touched a high at 1,169.8.  

- "The won has little room to move as fears about intervention continue to provide a floor for the dollar while the market sees steady dollar supply from equity investors," said a local bank dealer.  

- Traders largely ignored the central bank's decision to keep interest rates unchanged as the move conformed with market expectations.  

- In Tokyo, the yen is at 116.63/67 to the dollar, versus 116.83 late in New York trade on Monday.  

- Boosting the won is foreign stock buying, which has continued for 16 days in a row, raising expectations of rising dollar supply in the coming sessions.  

- The benchmark stock index up 1.38 percent.  

- Dollar offers from exporters are steady, if not massive, so far this week ahead of the September 10-12 Chusok holidays.  

- Market attention was also focused on any comments from North Korea during events marking the 55th anniversary of the communist country's foundation on Tuesday.  

- The won/yen cross rate , a calculated rate based on each currency's value against the dollar, is at 10.0309/69 versus 10.0162/22 late on Monday, showing the won weakening.

title: S.Korea won ends down, losses pared by export deals.
text:
SEOUL, Sept 8 (Reuters) - The South Korean won         closed lower on
Monday, tracking the yen's early drop and snapping a three-day winning
streak, but losses were pared by exporter dollar sales ahead of a local
holiday, dealers said.
  

The turn of foreign stock investors to a net buying position on the local stock market also helped the won recover most of its early losses, which some dealers attributed to dollar buying by government-run banks early in the morning.  

The won closed trading at 1,171.5 to the dollar, down from Friday's 1,170.6, but well above a session low of 1,174.5. It opened at 1,173.0 and touched a high of 1,171.4.  

"The government seems to be trying to spread sentiment that the won could gain further after the holidays, but there are not many people who expect that to happen unless the yen moves up steadily and strongly," said a local bank dealer.  

South Korean markets will be closed from Wednesday to Friday for a Thanksgiving holiday.  

South Korea has said it is opposed to any direct intervention in the foreign exchange market and that the currency rate should be decided by the market's forces. However, it has pledged to conduct "smoothing operations" if the market shows abrupt moves.  

On Monday, a senior central bank official said in Basel, Switzerland, that the bank was prepared to intervene to smooth out any abrupt moves in the currency market.  

"We let exchange rates be determined by the market itself, but when abrupt change of exchange rates (occurs), we intervene to smooth out (markets)," Bank of Korea Assistant Governor Lee Jae-ouk told reporters in Basel.  

South Korea is keen to stop the won from gaining too much against the dollar, as a firmer won would mean weakening the price edge for its export industries, which severely compete with the Japanese.  

That makes the won's rate versus the yen an important barometer. The cross rate, a calculated rate based on each currency's value against the dollar, stood at 10.0162/22 late on Monday versus 10.0111 late on Friday.  

Dealers said dollar offers from exporters were steady ahead of the September 10-12 Chusok holidays as many companies paid special bonuses to employees ahead of and during the country's major traditional festival.  

In Tokyo, the yen slid against the dollar on Monday amid persistent talk of intervention by the Japanese authorities to halt a recent rise in the currency.  

The yen fell towards 117.75 to the dollar from 116.80 late in New York trade on Friday and 3-1/2-month highs at around 115.75 set last week.  

On the non-deliverable forward market, one-month won was quoted at 1,173.7/4.7 late on Monday versus 1,172.8/3.8 late on Friday and three-month won at 1,179.0/80.0 versus 1,178.0/9.0.  

Seoul's main bourse closed down 0.17 percent but foreign investors, who were net sellers of local shares in early morning, bought a net 143.3 billion won ($122.5 million) worth of shares by the end of the day. ($1=1170.0 Won).

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Support From Stock Markets
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Monday as stronger stock markets generally supported gains, but rises were tempered by suspected government intervention in South Korea and Taiwan. 

 The South Korean won ended weaker and the New Taiwan dollar finished steady. The Philippine peso drifted lower, but the Singapore dollar and Thai baht were modestly stronger. Indonesian financial markets were closed for a public holiday. 

 Overall bids and offers were fairly well matched, which kept trading ranges tight, a trader at a European bank in Singapore said. 

 "It's pretty mixed. There was a sell-off earlier (in the dollar versus regional currencies), but now they (market players) are buying back. It's the same guys (who were buying and selling)," he said. 

 Analysts said regional currencies are underpinned by expectations of better global growth in the current half-year, led by the U.S., which is a major export market for Asia. 

 Hence "people are still looking to expand positions in Asian currencies," said Bhanu Baweja, a currency strategist at UBS AG. 

 Security issues, which were in the spotlight recently, appeared to have largely subsided, except in the Philippines, he said. 

 "I don't think the market is going to trade off that (security concerns) until it (something untoward) happens." 

 After the deadly bombing at a major hotel in Jakarta on Aug. 5, there were fears that Sunday's Independence Day celebrations in Indonesia could be a target for similar terrorist attacks, but the day passed without incident. 

 Meantime, some traders suspected the South Korean government had a hand in reversing the won's gains. Others said an exchange of warning shots between North and South Koreas in the afternoon also helped pushed the dollar higher. 

 South Korea's navy fired warning shots Monday after a North Korean fishing boat entered waters controlled by the South, the military said. 

 The dollar ended at 1,178.2 won, up from KRW1,176.6 at Thursday's close. The market was closed for a holiday Friday. 

 Some dealers said the authorities likely bought the dollar around the intraday trough of KRW1,174. 

 "The dollar suddenly soared when it was just about to go below KRW1,174," said a dealer at Chohung Bank. 

 Taiwan's central bank was also suspected of intervening in the currency market, resulting in the local dollar erasing early gains to close unchanged at 34.358 to the U.S. unit. 

 The New Taiwan dollar's initial rise was related to inflows for equity investments. 

 Trading volume amounted to US$450 million, up from US$433.50 million in the previous session. One dealer said the central bank's trades may have accounted for as much as US$150 million of total volume. 

 "It looked like the central bank was in the market a lot during the afternoon," said a foreign bank dealer in Taipei. 

 Taiwan's central bank prefers to have the local dollar move in tandem with the currencies of export competitors such as South Korea and Japan in order to preserve competitiveness. 

 Both the South Korean and Taiwanese governments don't usually comment on specific interventions. 

 The Singapore dollar rose on the back of fresh investments in the local stock market, and hopes of a brighter economic outlook, dealers said. 

 The U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7472 late in the local session, down from S$1.7480 late Friday. 

 Interbank players unwound long U.S. dollar positions amid hopes the government's plans to lower business costs through cuts in mandatory pension fund contributions would help buoy the economy. 

 Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong late Sunday outlined wage and pension reforms as two key ways of lifting the city state out of its worst ever economic slump. 

 The release of non-oil export data in the afternoon session didn't have much impact on the market, traders said. 

 Non-oil domestic exports, a key gauge of Singapore's economic health, rose 10.8% on year in July, slower than the previous month's 18.7% expansion. 

 The Thai baht moved in a similar pattern to the Singapore dollar. Late in Asia, the U.S. unit was quoted around 41.61 baht, down from THB41.66 late Friday. 

 Elsewhere, lingering security concerns and anticipation of sustained dollar demand from importers pushed the beleaguered Philippine peso to yet another new five-month closing low, dealers said. 

 The dollar ended at the intraday high of 55.090 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP55.060 Friday. This was the dollar's strongest finish since its record closing high of PHP55.099 on March 12. 

 Traders said many banks didn't want to unload their dollar holdings on hopes the U.S. unit would rise to breach PHP55.160, its highest intraday level so far this year. 

 "Many are holding their dollars close to their chest," said a local bank trader. 

 Among the factors fueling bullish sentiment on the dollar are a seasonal rise in imports, and continued worries over the country's security situation after the July 27 mutiny by over 300 soldiers in Manila's financial district.

title: Most Asian  Currencies  Up Late; Yen's Gains Lead The Way
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies strengthened for the fourth straight session Monday, buoyed by the yen's gains against the euro and dollar. 

 The only exception was the Philippine peso, which weakened on dollar demand from corporations and expectations of a decline in foreign direct investment. 

 The yen capitalized on thin market conditions in Tokyo to climb to a three-week high against the euro, which has been retreating against the Japanese currency since failing to break above Y137 resistance last Wednesday. 

 Many traders in Tokyo were away from their desks for the Obon holiday. 

 The yen-euro rally also helped lift the Japanese currency against the dollar, although the U.S. unit fared better than its European counterpart. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the euro was changing hands at Y133.80, down from Y134.46 late Friday in New York. The dollar was quoted at Y118.67, down from Y119.04 in New York. 

 The yen, as it often does, sets the tone for other regional currencies against the dollar. 

 The New Taiwan dollar relinquished some of its gains late in the day, but held on to close stronger. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.389, down from NT$34.415 Friday in Asia. 

 Bargain-hunting by some local and offshore players, as well as foreign banks, helped pull the dollar of its intraday low of NT$34.370, a trader at a foreign bank said. 

 The story was much the same for the South Korean won, which tracked the yen higher in lackluster trading. 

 The dollar closed at 1,179.2 won, down from KRW1,181.1 at Friday's close. 

 Traders said they suspected the government bought the dollar near its intraday low of KRW1,178.7 to keep a floor under the U.S. currency's decline. 

 Authorities in South Korea, and other Asian countries, intervene in foreign exchange markets in an effort to curb strength in their currencies. The belief is that doing so will help keep their country's exports competitive based on cost. 

 U.S. manufacturers have complained that the practice gives their Asian competitors an unfair advantage in global markets. The U.S. General Accounting Office, the investigative arm of Congress, last week confirmed that it will review whether Asian governments are manipulating their currencies to protect exports. 

 Dollar purchases by Philippine importers weighed on the peso, as did weekend comments by Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura regarding the likelihood of a slowdown in foreign direct investment. 

 The dollar closed at 54.87 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP54.71 Friday. 

 Buenaventura said the central bank plans to borrow as much as $500 million in September or October to settle $115 million in debt maturing later this year, and use the balance to boost reserves in the face of the shortfall in FDI. 

 "Comments made by the central bank governor indicate there will be a lack of dollar flows, so why should we unload now?" said a trader with a foreign bank. 

 The absence of any new terrorist attacks in Indonesia provided some support for the rupiah. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the dollar was quoted at 8,540 rupiah, down from IDR8,565 late Friday. 

 Sentiment toward the rupiah continued to improve as the market settled following last week's bombing at the Marriott Hotel in Jakarta that killed 11 people and injured 150 more. 

 The Singapore dollar was little changed in quiet trading. 

 Late in the session the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7553, compared with S$1.7555 late Friday. 

 The U.S. dollar rose in the morning after the government issued a report showing the economy shrank by 4.2% in the second quarter compared with a year earlier, slightly better than the 4.3% contraction estimated last month. 

 The government also lowered its full-year gross domestic product forecast to 1% growth at best, from its previous projection of a 0.5%-2.5% expansion, pushing the Singapore dollar lower in early trading. 

 By midafternoon profit-taking had eroded the U.S. dollar's gains, and the pair traded in a narrow range for the rest of the session. 

 The baht tracked the yen higher, showing little reaction to a central bank official's comments that a sovereign rating upgrade was expected from Standard & Poor's Corp. 

 Late in Asia the dollar was quoted at 41.830 baht, down from THB41.880 late Friday. 

 A S&P team visited Thailand recently to gather information for a regular review of the economy. The major ratings agencies all adopted a positive outlook last year on ratings equivalent to BBB- on the country's long-term foreign-currency sovereign debt.

title: UPDATE 2-China digs in heels over  forex  system - S.Korea.
text:
MANILA, Aug 7 (Reuters) - China has told fellow members of the ASEAN Plus Three grouping that it does not intend to loosen its grip for now on the yuan, South Korean Deputy Finance Minister Tae-Shin Kwon said on Thursday. 

 "They have no plan to change their exchange rate system for the time being," Kwon told reporters at a gathering of finance ministers and their deputies from the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) plus China, South Korea and Japan. 

 "Our Chinese colleague is still very stubborn," he added. 

 China, whose delegation is led by Finance Minister Jin Renqing, explained that Beijing was taking steps to relieve upward pressure on the yuan , or renminbi, by allowing more capital outflows, Kwon said. 

 "But it cannot be a fundamental solution," he commented. 

 Kwon said the representative at the meeting of the People's Bank of China, the central bank, had been particularly firm in his insistence that the policy would remain on hold. 

 Kwon said central bank intervention in the foreign exchange markets should be in line with International Monetary Fund rules, which permit smoothing operations but say governments may not artificially manipulate their currencies. 

 "If a certain country tries to target a certain level of exchange rate through heavy and frequent intervention, that may be against IMF guidelines," Kwon said. 

 Kwon was speaking a day after Japan reported that it spent more than 4.6 trillion yen between April and June, equivalent to $38.36 billion, to hold down the yen. 

 Japan has intervened in record amounts this year to prevent a rise in its currency from hurting the country's exporters. 

 Kwon said that whenever South Korea intervenes, it does so in line with IMF guidelines. 

 The authorities needed to step in occasionally because the South Korean interbank foreign-exchange market had daily turnover of less than $3 billion, resulting at times in either a dearth or an excess of dollars, Kwon said. 

 He noted that whereas the yen's real exchange rate had risen by 5.4 percent since January 2002, the won had appreciated by 12.4 percent. 

 "That is evidence that South Korea is letting the market decide the foreign exchange rate," Kwon said. 

 Asked whether the South Korean won's cross rate of around 9.87 to the yen meant the yen was too weak, Kwon said: "I think so." 

 Japanese and South Korean exporters are keen competitors across a range of industries, and market economists believe Seoul is more comfortable when the cross rate is above, rather than below, 10 won per yen.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Tentative gains as dlr weakens.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Aug 4 (Reuters) - Asian currencies made
tentative gains against a weaker U.S. dollar on Monday, as the
yen's resistance to strength, intervention talk in South Korea
and Taiwan, and political risks in Philippines limited gains.
    A mixed U.S. employment report helped the Japanese yen off
Friday's three-month lows, but it stayed close to 120 on
Monday.
 
    The Singapore dollar        was off Friday's three-month
lows, but did not make much headway past than 1.76.
    Traders speculated the Korean central bank was buying


 dollars, and possibly the yen, to keep the won 

   from firming past 1,180 and to prop the yen-won 

 cross rate. 

 The Taiwan dollar  rallied, but the fear that the 

central bank would persist with last week's intervention to 

 weaken the currency weighed. 

 "Central banks in the region are still actively intervening

 in the market and the dollar-yen is still hovering around 120," 

 said Peter Redward, currency strategist with Deutsche Bank. 

 "Also, investors are generally in a risk-reduction mode 

 after the sell-off we have seen in the fixed income markets and 

 the strength of the dollar, it just means that no one's 

 prepared to push currencies around much at the moment." 

 Data showing a rise of $1.25 billion in Korean foreign 

 exchange reserves in July strengthened the speculation that the 

 Bank of Korea was buying dollars. 

 And that could increase if there is more equity inflow into 

 Korea after North Korea's decision on the weekend to 

 participate in six-way talks over its nuclear crisis, analysts 

 said. 

 The won has come off a 1,177 high last week and the 

 sensitive yen-won cross  rose to 9.85 on Monday from 

 a six-month low of 9.776 last week. The cross fell below 10 two 

 weeks ago. 


 
    Markets believe the Korean authorities are happy to see the
cross above 10 to maintain export competitiveness with Japan.
    Some traders said the BOK probably bought yen for won to
prop the cross rate on Monday. Others said that was unlikely.
    "They may buy dollar-won to move the cross. They won't risk
the ire of the Japanese by selling dollar-yen," a trader said.
    PESO PROPPED
    The besieged Philippine peso        seemed to have overcome



some of the fears of political instability and another mutiny



as it slowly drifted away from Friday's four-month lows and



rose as far as 54.76.



It had been under pressure last week after the failed mutiny



by hundreds of soldiers on July 27 and fell again on Friday



amid talk of unusual troop movements.



Traders said the central bank had sold dollars to ensure



the peso did not fall past 55 towards a 55.16 low struck in



March.



 
    Redward said the Philippines' balance of payments deficit
would keep it weak over the next few months.
    A Philippine monetary official, who asked not to be named,



said at the weekend the central bank was considering a dollar



loan to settle $200 million in debt due in September and to



boost reserves.



The Thai baht  made slow gains. Supported by



improving growth prospects and a rise in exports, it had not



lost much ground late last week when the U.S. dollar was



rallying.



Goldman Sachs said in a report it made sense to buy options



to sell the dollar against Asian currencies, especially those



with low implied volatilities such as the baht and Taiwan



dollar.



"Asian currencies could appreciate if the global activity



outlook improves and central banks stop intervening. Stronger



growth, due to improved external demand, would overshadow the



negative impact on growth of currency appreciation," it said.



"This should support long dollar-put options in Asia."

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Stronger waiting for Fed.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, June 25 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were mostly
stronger late on Wednesday, helped by a steady Japanese yen and
recovering local stock markets, as markets worldwide waited for
the U.S. Federal Reserve to announce its decision on rates.
    And, whether or not the Fed cuts rates later on Wednesday,
analysts said foreign portfolio inflows in search of growth and
return would continue to seek Asian equities, putting upward
pressure on currencies.

firmer side of 1.74, coming off 1-=   month lows even as
markets speculated the Monetary Authority of Singapore would
ease monetary policy next month.
    The Thai baht        was tentative around 41.50, a level
where markets suspect the central bank is intervening. The
Korean won             rose after some initial hesitation
as stocks recovered and foreign investors turned buyers again.



 
    The Philippine peso        and Taiwan dollar          too
were higher.
    "There will be a continuing trend of capital funds coming



into Asia," said Karl Broecker, head of treasury at Landesbank



Baden-Wuerttemberg, adding these would be into share markets in



countries such as Thailand and South Korea.



And, despite the threat of intervention by central banks to



keep their currencies competitive for exports, the currencies


would still gain.



Broecker said the inflows into South Korea have



overshadowed concerns of slowing growth and North Korea's



nuclear threats, and could lead the won higher to 1,180 or even



1,175. Dealers said the central bank intervened heavily before



1,180 last week.



 
    Similarly, the baht would eventually overcome the
resistance at 41.50 and move to 41.40 soon, he said.
    RUPIAH AWAITS FLOWS, SING DOLLAR PRESSURED
    The rupiah        was range-bound on Wednesday but traders



said it would eventually push higher as the timing and extent



of foreign investment inflows for Bank Mandiri's initial public



offering became clear, analysts said.



The IPO for Indonesia's largest bank was subscribed 6.7



times, and would raise $328 million. Of this, two-thirds was



expected to be allotted to foreign investors.



Meanwhile, market expectations of a weakening of the



Singapore dollar, through a shift in the trade-weighted band it



is managed in, remained high. The pressure would build if the



Fed cut rates aggressively, by 50 basis points, and regional



central banks joined the race to ease policy, traders said.



 
    "A moderate easing is very likely in Singapore," Broecker
said.
    "This is one tool to maintain some economic stability and



if you see America putting short term rates below one percent,



then there is the possibility of a very cautious easing and



that means the Singapore dollar could depreciate against the



major currencies," he said.



Yet, authorities would try to ensure the currency was



stable and competitive against currencies of countries



Singapore competes with in export markets, such as China,



Malaysia, Hong Kong and Thailand, he said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Rupiah rallies, others dither.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, May 23 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah
powered to a 21-month high on Friday after the central bank
said the currency was not overvalued, but other Asian
currencies dithered on fears of intervention to thwart any
strength.
    In Korea, the central bank warned against excessive gains
in the won . The Thai baht  and Taiwan
dollar  were also contained by worries over
intervention.
    "There's a new dilemma in Asia, and that dilemma is do you
quasi-peg to the yen or do you quasi-peg to the dollar, because
anybody who appreciates with the yen is appreciating against
China," said Ray Farris, currency and interest rates strategist
with Credit Suisse First Boston.
    "That's why we are seeing so much of dollar buying by
central banks right now because they are beginning to realise
that they are appreciating against the (Chinese yuan) on a
cross of relative stability against the yen."
    The exception seems to be Indonesia.



 Asked on Friday if the
rupiah could reach 8,000 per dollar, last traded in August
2000, senior deputy governor Anwar Nasution said: "Depending on
exports, if oil prices remain high and the IPO of Bank Mandiri
is successful, then it can reach 8,000."
    The remark pushed the rupiah above 8,300 per dollar to a
fresh 21-month high at 8,270-8,280, shrugging off the conflict
between the Indonesian military and separatists in Aceh
province.
 
    Indonesia is scheduled to sell up to a 30 percent stake of
Mandiri, the country's fifth largest bank, later this year.
    In contrast, the won weakened after South Korea's Finance



Ministry said it would intervene if it did not move in line



with fundamentals. The ministry did not nominate an appropriate



level.



The Thai central bank said this week the baht was still



competitive, but was suspected of having intervened. While the



baht was on the strong side of 42 per dollar on Friday, it



stalled before the nine-month highs it hit this week.



The Singapore dollar  held a steady range around



1.7220, stuck like the yen as markets wavered ahead of a long



holiday weekend in America and worried about possible Japanese


intervention and a rise in U.S. jobless claims.



Analysts said the Sing dollar is in the middle of the



undisclosed trade-weighted band authorities manage it in, and



said the central bank might not be averse to some downward



movement.



The Philippine peso  was marginally higher than



Thursday's one-month low at 52.98. Manila-based traders said a



combination of the yen's weakness and import demand had driven



the currency down from eight-month highs struck early this



month.



RUPIAH GETS A BOOST



For several Asian economies, China is among the top three



export markets, though the biggest end buyer is the United



States, and they manage currencies to ensure competitiveness.



As a result, their gains against a weakening U.S. dollar



have lagged those in currencies such as the euro  -



apart from the high-yielding rupiah.



The rupiah is up nearly 40 percent against the U.S. dollar



since May 2001 - and the same amount against the Chinese yuan



 , which is pegged to the dollar.



 
    Over the same time, the baht has gained nearly nine percent
against the dollar and the won 10 percent.
    Lehman Brothers, in a note to clients, the rupiah offered
the best value in the region.
    "Indonesian interest rates remain high, with one-year swap



rates at 10 percent, giving a significant carry advantage over



dollars. The carry for going short dollar/rupiah is 70 basis



points per month," it said.



"Perhaps more significantly, the central bank is also



talking up the currency, implying the same focus on export



competitiveness may not apply in Indonesia, as it does in Korea



or Taiwan," it said.

title: Asian  Currencies  Up Late; Rating Upgrade Boosts Rupiah
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- A one-notch rating upgrade for Indonesia from Standard & Poor's Ratings Services lifted the already buoyant rupiah to a 32-month peak Monday. 

 The dollar closed the local session at 8,430 rupiah, down from IDR8,555 Friday. 

 Other Asian currencies were also driven higher on the back of broad U.S. dollar weakness. 

 The dollar slid against major rivals after U.S. Treasury Secretary John Snow said Sunday that a weaker dollar could help U.S. exports. 

 Snow's remarks "helped set the tone for the beginning of the week," said David Simmonds, senior emerging markets strategist for Asia at Royal Bank of Scotland. "Dollar/Asians feel heavy with the weak international dollar," and could push lower, he added. 

 Earlier in Asia, the dollar sank below the psychologically key Y117 level for the first time since Thursday, while the euro jumped to a fresh 52-month high of $1.1579. At 0930 GMT, the dollar was quoted at Y116.65. 

 Government officials in Japan threatened to intervene to check the dollar's slide. Traders said the Finance Ministry followed through on its yen-selling threat and quietly bought dollars via Japanese banks. 

 Meantime, Indonesia's central bank said it isn't concerned about the dollar's fall below 8,500 rupiah as exporters can still be competitive at that level, Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom said. 

 The rupiah was already trading at a 32-month high earlier in the session as foreign investors sold dollars to finance portfolio investment in the country. 

 The S&P upgrade, which came in the early afternoon, served to give a further fillip to the currency, dealers said. 

 S&P raised Indonesia's long-term foreign currency rating to B-, from CCC+, with a stable outlook. 

 The agency said the move reflects the diminished likelihood that the government will seek additional debt restructuring, a situation made possible by its improving fiscal and external positions. 

 Simmonds said yield-hungry international investors haven't been as keen on the rupiah as other high-yielding currencies because it isn't very liquid. 

 Still, "the offshore market will certainly be short dollars for carry in the appreciating currency," he said. 

 The Singapore dollar briefly spiked to a two-month high, riding on the dollar's weakness and also on hopes that the SARS outbreak in the city state was well under control, dealers said. 

 Near the end of local trading hours, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7320, down from S$1.7420 late Friday, though off an intraday trough of S$1.7310, which was its lowest since early March. 

 Singapore hasn't reported new cases of SARS infection since April 27, and if this continues until May 18, the World Health Organization could declare the island nation as having contained the virus. 

 The Philippine peso closed at an eight-month high on the back of offshore dollar sales and remittance inflows from Filipinos working overseas, traders said. 

 The dollar ended at 52.050 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, its lowest since closing at PHP51.970 on Sep. 12 last year. The dollar finished at PHP52.340 Friday. 

Central bank Deputy Governor Amando Tetangco said the peso was boosted by overseas remittance inflows and investments - particularly portfolio investments. 

 Tetangco said stronger regional currencies also aided the peso. 

 The New Taiwan dollar followed its regional counterparts higher despite underlying concerns about the impact of the recent SARS outbreak. 

 The U.S. unit closed at NT$34.715, down from Friday's NT$34.775. Dealers said the local dollar was pulled up by a stronger Singapore dollar, South Korean won and Japanese yen. Taiwan competes with those economies in key export sectors. 

 Taiwan on Monday reported 23 new SARS cases - its sharpest single-day jump - bringing the total to 207. The death toll stands at 27. 

 In South Korea, fears of government intervention in the foreign exchange market kept a check on the won's strength, market players said. 

 "It was range-bound trading today," said a trader. "Players are expecting a stronger Korean won but possible government intervention is blocking that," he said. 

 The dollar slipped below the psychologically key 1,200 won level to end at KRW1,195.2 won, down from KRW1,200.4 Friday. 

 President Roh Moo Hyun's trip to the U.S. also lent some support to the won as some believe his talks with U.S. President George W. Bush this week may lead to a breakthrough in the North Korean nuclear issue. 

 Elsewhere, the dollar was quoted at 42.37 baht late in Asia, down from THB42.545 Friday. 

 Traders said the dollar was well bid under THB42.40 as local importers and oil companies stepped in to buy the dollar on weakness.

title: S.Korea won turns lower on  intervention  fears.
text:
SEOUL, May 9 (Reuters) - The South Korean won         eased for the
first time in seven trading days on Friday, with the market wary over
possible government intervention and after the central bank warned
growth slip below target this year.



The won ended at 1,200.4 per dollar, versus 1,200.1 at the opening and
Wednesday's close of 1,199.0. It moved between 1,197.5 and 1,201.6. The
market was closed for a public holiday for Buddha's birthday on
Thursday.


 Trading was thin ahead of the weekend and because of fears about possible intervention by authorities at around 1,200 won per dollar, dealers said. 

 "Sentiment was cautious because the market perceived the government would keep the 1,200 threshold for now," said a dealer at a foreign bank. 

 In a similar fashion, the yen fell back to 117.2 yen  per dollar after hitting a 10-month high around 116 on Thursday amid speculation that Japanese authorities may have intervened covertly to curb yen strength. 

 In South Korea, concern about the economy revived after the Bank of Korea said the country's economic growth may fall short of its 4.1 percent target this year. 

 Separately, Finance Minister Kim Jin-pyo said consumer inflation would be stable for the rest of the year, but declined to comment on market speculation that an imminent interest rate cut was in the works. 

 The central bank's monetary policy committee will hold its regular meeting on Tuesday to review monetary policy and decide whether to change the overnight call rate target. 

 Also, helping push the won lower, foreign investors turned net sellers of local shares. 

 However, the main KOSPI stock index  ended up 0.17 percent at 619.11 points. 

 Dollar supply also increased due to an inflow of foreign equity investment earlier this week, limiting the won's drop and sent the currency to as high as 1,197.5 per dollar in the morning session. 

 On the non-deliverable forward market, the one-month won was last quoted at 1,202.7/3.7 versus 1,199.5/1200.5 late Wednesday and the three-month won was at 1,208.1/9.1 versus 1204.7/5.7.

title: S.Korean won opens at 5-mth low on looming Iraq war.
text:
SEOUL, March 20 (Reuters) - The South Korean won  opened at a five-month low on Thursday, as importers chased dollars, wary about uncertainties stemming from a near certain war in Iraq and its fallout on the fragile economy. 

 The won gapped down to 1,264.0 per dollar at the opening, falling for a fourth consecutive session. It closed at 1,256.8 on Wednesday. 

 Dollar buying by importers continued as a U.S.-led military strike against Iraq looks imminent after a U.S. deadline for Iraqi President Saddam Hussein to leave the country or face war passed with no sign of compliance from the Iraqi President. 

 The Japanese yen  also fell to a one-month low of 120.65 in early trade, as investors chased the dollar amid expectations of a swift and decisive war. 

 WARY OVER INTERNVENTION 

 Worried about the sliding won, South Korea's finance ministry issued a fresh warning on Thursday, saying it would take steps to stabilise the market, if needed. 

 "We're worried about excessively weak sentiment on the won (against the dollar)," a high-ranking ministry official told Reuters. 

 After the warning, the won cut some of its losses, trading at 1,261.9 per dollar at 0110 GMT. But dealers expected the won's downward trend would continue throughout the day. 

 They forecast the won would move between 1,257 won and 1,267 won, keeping an eye on whether the won would breach the previous low of 1,267.50 touched in mid-October. 

 "Korean companies are hoarding dollars ahead of the war," a foreign bank dealer said. "The downward trend will continue, but investors need to be cautious, as authorities may intervene." 

South Korea's state-run banks were seen selling dollars on Wednesday, after a series of warnings by government officials of the flagging won. 

 Traders say the central bank has intervened in the market since last week, selling dollars to support the won. They said the Bank of Korea had spent about $1 billion to support the Korean currency. 

 An official at the central bank declined to confirm the reports. But South Korea's foreign exchange reserves fell to $123.54 billion by March 15, compared with $123.99 billion at the end of February, the central bank said. 

 ANOTHER CRISIS NOT LIKELY 

 Sentiment was also hurt after a local newspaper said hedge funds had been attacking the won, Asia's worst performing currency this year, in offshore markets in early March. 

 Traders said some speculative forces were spotted, but could not say which funds were buying what quantity of dollars. 

 "Investors are selling the won, due to the slowing economy and geopolitical risks involving Iraq and North Korea," a local bank dealer said. 

 North Korea is currently locked in a standoff with the United States over its suspected nuclear weapons programme. 

 The International Monetary Fund recently said the country's economic growth could slow to three percent this year under the worst case scenario, around half of last year's estimated growth. 

 "But the situation is not as serious as in late 1997, when the Asian financial crisis broke out," the dealer said. 

 South Korea, Asia's fourth-largest economy, teetered on the brink of national default in late 1997, as the won was severely attacked by foreign speculators.

title: S.Korea c.bank may  intervene  against  FX  speculation.
text:
SEOUL, March 19 (Reuters) - South Korea's central bank said on Wednesday it could intervene in the foreign exchange market if it considers the won  is being depressed by speculative trading. 

 "We can intervene in the market through verbal warning or other means, if the won gets weaker due to speculators," Lee Jae-wook, deputy governor at the Bank of Korea, told economic researchers. 

 He also said authorities would prevent the weaker won from adversely affecting the fragile economy. 

 The Korean won opened lower at 1,250.0 against dollar on Wednesday, after it slid to a fresh five-month closing low on Tuesday, hit by concerns that an imminent U.S.-led military strike against Iraq may damage the economy.

title: Asian  Currencies  Fall;Won At 5-Mo Low,Peso At New Trough
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Korean won ended at a five month trough and the Philippine peso dived to yet another historic closing low as most Asian currencies weakened in tandem with the yen Wednesday. 

 North Korea tensions and accounting scandals at SK Global weighed on the won while domestic security concerns and fears of a war in Iraq again took a toll on the peso. 

 A currency trader in Singapore said most central banks in the region were in the markets, "just to smoothen things out, nothing too major." 

 He suspected that some U.S. investment houses were selling part of their investments in the region because of renewed security concerns in the Philippines, and the North Korea tensions. 

 The won gave up all the previous day's gains and ended at the intraday low of KRW1,245.0 to the dollar, from KRW1,229.9 Tuesday. 

 A last flurry of dollar buying sent the U.S. currency soaring about seven won in the final minutes of the session as market players dared to test higher and higher levels in the absence of intervention. 

 Very vague and unconfirmed rumors that North and South Korea exchanged gunfire Wednesday supported the dollar and underpinned the uneasy and cautious feelings of many market participants. However, there were no reputable media reports of any such incident. 

 "I don't think it (the rumor) is true. If that rumor were real, it would be a big emergency," said a dealer. "Many people are nervous and are making things up." 

 Chong Hui Chin, a currency strategist at J.P. Morgan Chase Bank, said some people believed that beyond Iraq, "North Korea could be a big wildcard in the geopolitical perspective." 

 But she said the bank still believes the issue will be resolved diplomatically though "in the meantime, we don't discount more provocations from North Korea." That should put a floor under the dollar/won, she added. 

 Meantime, foreign selling of stocks in the last two days over the SK Global woes also translated into dollar buying in the foreign exchange market. 

 Prosecutors Tuesday said they uncovered KRW1.55 trillion of accounting irregularities at the trading company. 

 Rising military tension on the Korean peninsula also weighed on the New Taiwan dollar, dealers said. 

 The U.S. unit ended at NT$34.721, up from NT$34.620 Tuesday. The intraday range was between NT$34.639 and NT$34.727. 

 The Philippine peso extended losses to finish at a new all time closing low as companies hedged dollar requirements and banks built up their holdings of the U.S. currency. 

 The peso ended at 55.099 to the dollar on the Philippine Dealing System, wiping out the previous record closing low of PHP54.900 reached on Tuesday. 

 Traders said the market is focused on a March 17 deadline set by the U.S. for Iraq to disarm, or face war. 

 Locally, traders are bracing for more violence as latest reports from southern Philippines said authorities detonated explosive devices in Davao, the site of last week's deadly bombing. 

 The Singapore dollar slipped to a three-week low Wednesday as local banks covered short U.S. dollar positions as the U.S. unit rose against the yen, dealers said. 

 The aggressive buying again fueled speculation that local banks were snapping up U.S. dollars on behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, although most dealers said that was unlikely. 

 "Across the board U.S. dollar short covering has been influential today, but Singapore dollar has also depreciated of its own accord this week," Bank of America said in a research note. 

 Near the end of local trading hours, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7463, up from S$1.7362 late Tuesday, but slightly off the intraday high of S$1.7467, which was its strongest level in three weeks. 

 The intraday range of S$1.7380-S$1.7467 was the widest so far this month. 

 The Thai baht weakened in line with its regional counterparts and was quoted at THB42.68 to the dollar late in Asia, from THB42.46 Tuesday. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was quoted at 8,892 to the dollar, compared with IDR8,885 Tuesday.

title: S Korea Won Ends At New 6-Mo Closing High KRW1,173.2/Dlr
text:
SEOUL -(Dow Jones)- The South Korean won ended at a new six-month high Thursday on expectations of equity-linked dollar inflows and on bets of more downside risk in the U.S currency against the yen, said participants. 

 "It is difficult to have long dollar-won positions because people think the dollar-yen will go down again," said a dealer. 

 The dollar closed at 1,173.2 won, below Wednesday's finish at KRW1,175.4, its worst close since ending at KRW1,170.9 July 25. The dollar kept to a tight band between KRW1,172.2 and KRW1,176.0 during the session. 

 The U.S. currency opened flat, but then offshore players sold dollars, pressuring the dollar down to the KRW1,172-level and prompting long players to sell as well, participants said. 

 Trade was lackluster throughout the session due to concerns over possible government intervention both in South Korea and Japan. The nervousness is helping to keep the dollar supported at KRW1,170. 

 But some say the key support level could be tested Friday due to expectations of continued dollar weakness against the yen, which would pressure the dollar against the won as well. 

 "The yen is getting stronger daily, inch by inch, and will go to 116 in the first quarter," said a dealer. 

 Also, local stock market-related inflows are expected Friday as foreign investors were net buyers of about KRW9 billion in shares Thursday and KRW123.3 billion Wednesday. 

 The dollar is expected to trade between 1,168-1,175 Friday. 

 At 0805 GMT, the dollar was quoted at Y118.01, below Y118.10 in New York and Y118.15 in Tokyo late Wednesday. 

 The yen was at KRW9.94 late Thursday, just below KRW9.96 late Wednesday. 

 South Korean bond yields slid to new closing lows Thursday but came off morning lows after a government official reportedly said the central bank feels the recent decline in bond yields wouldn't last for long, market participants said. 

 The yield on benchmark three-year treasurys fell two basis points to 4.96%, a new 14-month low. The yield on five-year treasurys fell two basis points to 5.14%, a fresh 15-month low. 

 Bond gains came due to the still-favorable supply-demand situation. 

 About an hour into trading, an unnamed government official said, "The latest (yield) fall doesn't seem to reflect the (economic) fundamentals well enough," according to Yonhap Infomax. 

 The official also reportedly said the Bank of Korea would carefully consider the size of its weekly monetary stabilization bond auctions. Traders took that to mean the central bank could overwhelm the market with supply to at least slow the decline of yields. 

 "The comments were very aggressive and intentional," said a trader. "There will be a two-to-three basis points upward correction (of yields). But, there are not much bonds to sell." 

 Indeed, due to the overall lack of supply - the Ministry of Finance and Economy has no plans to offer bonds again until February - market sentiment remains positive, said participants. 

 Partly due to the favorable supply-demand dynamics, JPMorgan said in its monthly report the yield on three-year government bonds may test 4.80% or lower in the near term. A delay in monetary tightening and geopolitical concerns will also support a rise in bond prices, JPMorgan said.

title: S Korea Won Ends Weaker As Yen Falls, Importers Buy Dlrs
text:
SEOUL -(Dow Jones)- The South Korean won weakened Thursday as the yen lost ground and importers bought dollars, with dollar short covering adding to the won's losses, market players said. 

 The U.S. currency finished at 1,192.9 above Tuesday's close at KRW1,186.5. The dollar changed hands between KRW1,188.0 and KRW1,193.4. 

 Financial markets were closed Wednesday for the New Year holiday. 

 Trade was relatively light Thursday since players are still on holiday; the thin trading conditions exaggerated the won's moves. 

 "The market was thin and so the market was volatile. When the dollar hit KRW1,188 there were importers buying," said a dealer. He added that market players aren't very certain of the won's direction since the Japanese financial markets are closed until Monday. 

 Concern that the Bank of Japan could actually intervene in the foreign exchange market there to push up the exchange rate when markets open again also pressured the won, traders said. 

 The won often tracks the yen due to the similar export portfolios of South Korea and Japan. 

 "There are jitters about BOJ intervention," a dealer said. 

 At 0755 GMT, the dollar was at Y119.39, up from Y118.70 in New York late Tuesday and Y118.51 in Asia Tuesday. 

 The yen was at KRW10.0, up from KRW9.99 late Tuesday. 

 The dollar is likely to trade between KRW1,190 and KRW1,200 on Friday, market participants said. 

 South Korean bond yields again tumbled to fresh closing lows Thursday due to geopolitical uncertainties, market participants said. 

 The Ministry of Finance and Economy jumped into the market near the session's close to basically approve of the recent fall in yields, but market participants didn't react much. 

 Rates have been falling for the past three weeks or so on North Korea's nuclear posturing and the growing likelihood of a U.S.-led war in Iraq. 

 "Their (MOFE's) comment is right, but everyone already knew it," said a trader. 

 An unnamed government official said the recent drop in key South Korea bond yields is natural and inevitable given the stock market's losses lately, according to Yonhap Infomax. The official also said the yield on the benchmark three-year treasury could breach 5%, an opinion some market participants held even before the official's remarks. 

 However, Kim Bum-Joong, an analyst at Daewoo Securities, said the benchmark yield isn't likely to drop under 5.00%. He pointed out the yield on one-year monetary stabilization bonds is 4.98% with not much room to drop further since the Bank of Korea must redeem a large amount of monetary stabilization bonds in January. 

 "It (the redemptions) will prevent the short-end rate from going down," he said. 

 The yield on benchmark three-year government bonds slid four basis points to a 14-month closing low of 5.07%. The yield on five-year government bonds fell five basis points to a 15-month closing low of 5.29%. 

 A tighter supply of bonds for the month of January also helped bond prices on Thursday. The government will auction only KRW820 billion worth of three-year treasurys on Jan. 6, with no supply for the rest of the month.

title: Asian  Currencies  Up Late As Yen Gains Ground
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies shrugged off early losses to trade mostly higher late Thursday, taking the cue from the yen's recovery. 

 Several local developments, notably an upgrade of Indonesia's sovereign rating, were ignored by foreign exchange participants who preferred to look to the major currencies for direction amid jitters over possible U.S. military action against Iraq. 

 Traders said that although sentiment on Indonesia was helped by Standard & Poor's upgrade of the country's sovereign rating to CCC+ from selective default, the rupiah scarcely moved. 

 The upgrade was largely expected as S&P had flagged the move for months, but its rating is still one rung below Moody's Investor Service, which has a B3 rating and positive outlook. Furthermore, Indonesia's rating remains well below investment grade, reflecting the country's inability to repay debt it has borrowed from overseas. Earlier this year, S&P downgraded Indonesia's long-term foreign currency rating to selective default from CCC previously. 

 In late Asian hours, the dollar was trading at 8,865 rupiah, unchanged from Wednesday's close, but below the day's high at IDR8,884 reached in the morning. Traders said the rupiah's intraday gains were helped by the central bank which sold dollars near the intraday high. The central bank has a policy of intervening to help the rupiah but doesn't confirm specific actions. 

 However, the dollar's downside was protected at IDR8,550 by local companies with foreign debt, as well as importers. The dollar should trade between IDR8,550 and IDR8,900 Friday, traders said. 


   Philippines' August Inflation Above Expectations



In the Philippines, stronger-than-expected inflation data for August
foreshadowed a rising price trend, but the central bank said monetary
policy is likely to stay neutral for the rest of the year, suggesting
interest rates won't be hiked.



Philippine's consumer price index rose 2.9% on year in August, up from
2.6% in July, and higher than the 2.72% average in a Dow Jones Newswires
poll of private economists. The figure also exceeded the government's
expectations.


Central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said "it should have no
immediate impact (on policy rates) given that inflation is still way
below target."



"But it reinforces our neutral stance taken since the early part of
this year," he added.



Traders said the data weren't worrisome, with markets largely
shrugging off the numbers. The dollar closed at 51.72 pesos on the
Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP51.845 Wednesday.



"What will have more of an impact on the currency market is the
movement in the yen," a bank dealer in Manila said.



Analysts agreed, noting that Asian units will likely to continue
taking the cue from the major currencies.



But heightened risk aversion ahead of the first anniversary of the
Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in the U.S., and prospects of the U.S.
launching a war against Iraq kept market participants jittery.



"Risk appetite globally is not building, which is not bringing
stimulus for a rally (in Asian currencies)," said Chong Hui Chin,
foreign exchange strategist at J.P. Morgan Chase Bank in Singapore.



Concerns about the U.S. economic health are also never far away from
the minds of market participants, with data so far sending mixed
signals, traders said.



To that end, markets will be keeping close watch on more economic
indicators due from the U.S later Thursday and Friday.



The U.S. currency ended at a two-week low against the New Taiwan
dollar as exporters sold the former, especially as key levels were
triggered, dealers said.



The dollar closed at NT$34.122, down from NT$34.236 Wednesday, after
moving between NT$34.105 and NT$34.266 intraday. It was the weakest
close for the dollar since Aug. 22.



Dealers said market participants sold dollars once it broke through
NT$34.20, a stop-loss level. But some short-covering activities helped
offset the dollar's losses.



The central bank was reportedly in the market to curb the local unit's
rise, but it didn't intervene aggressively or too visibly, dealers said.



In South Korea, dollar sales linked to the non-deliverable forwards
market, coupled with the yen's firmer tone, weighed down the U.S.
currency, dealers said.



The dollar ended at 1,191.0 won, down from KRW1,195.3 at the previous
day's close, after trading between KRW1,190.0 and KRW1,198.0 intraday.



"The market is basically watching dollar/yen, but again, lots of
players don't want to escape from the KRW1,190 to KRW1,210 range," said
Oh Suktae, a Citibank economist.



The U.S. currency also slipped against the Singapore dollar and the
Thai baht, both of which tracked the yen higher.

title: Emerging Asia  FX  - Humbled as dollar enjoys correction.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 23 (Reuters) - Asian currencies ebbed to 

 multisession lows late on Tuesday as the dollar staged a 

 broadbased correction after its recent drop. 


    The dollar rammed the euro        below parity for the



first time in a week and shoved the yen to near two-week



lows beyond 117 per dollar.



    Dealers said players in Asian currencies consequently



bailed out of the short dollar positions taken on worries over



the United States' ability to fund a gaping current account



deficit and U.S. corporate accounting scandals that have sent



Wall Street in a tailspin.



    Verbal and suspected physical intervention by regional



authorities further weighed down currencies in South Korea,



Singapore and Thailand.



    Growing wariness over the impact of the U.S. stock slide on



other economies sparked an overdue correction in the massively



oversold dollar.



    Dealers said some U.S. funds also bought spot dollars to



square their positions in the offshore nondeliverable forwards



market or to raise cash to meet redemptions back home.



    "The forex markets are likely to remain volatile in the



short-term, pulled by forces of position liquidation against



the fundamental underpinnings for a weak dollar," said Thio



Chin Loo, senior currency analyst at BNP Paribas in Singapore.



    She, however, said the dollar may not be able to draw



support on this short liquidation rally for long.



    "Trade cautiously, with a view to re-establish short dollar



positions at higher levels," she said.



    The Korean won         -2 ended onshore trade at 1,173.1,



just shy of the 1,174 session low. It closed on Monday at



1,165.60, the highest level in 20 months.



    State banks were spotted buying dollars which exacerbated



dollar demand from offshore players and sent exporters on the



sidelines.



    The Thai baht dropped by about one and a half percent to



touch lows beyond 41 per dollar, for the first time in over a



week, as the central bank governor said he was feeling more



comfortable with the level of the baht after its decline.



"At today's level of 40.70 baht, we are quite comfortable,



as it (baht) is stabilising while the dollar is strengthening,"



Bank of Thailand's chief Pridiyathorn Devakula said.



The Singapore dollar slipped through the 1.7400 per



dollar level to a trough of 1.7480, its lowest point in over a



week, as state names were spotted selling dollars.



    The Taiwan dollar          fell to 33.294 per dollar before



closing onshore trade at 33.289. It closed on Monday at 33.028.



    Fresh economic data also failed to provide any support to



the Taiwan dollar with both export orders and industrial output



for June growing at levels below market expectations.



    The Philippine peso        ended onshore trade at 50.66,



against Monday's 50.38, tracking the regional mood and after



the government said it had overshot its six-month deficit



target by some 53 percent.



    The number is keenly watched by financial markets as a



signal of the government's fiscal efficiency.



    The Department of Finance said the six-month deficit came



in at 119.72 billion pesos, against a target of 78.26 billion



pesos. That raised doubts the Philippines would be able to keep



the deficit within the 130 billion whole year target.



The Indonesian rupiah fell past 9,000 per dollar to



hit a session low of 9,020, more than two percent off against



late Monday's 8,810.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Traders eye Wall Street sell-off.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 22 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies stayed 

 in their recent ranges on Monday as traders focused on the 

 impact that Friday's sell-off on Wall Street will have on the 

 dollar and regional equity markets. 

     Dealers said a sell-off in Asian stocks in sympathy with 

 the U.S. stocks' fall to multiyear lows could potentially 

 reverse some of the recent gains regional currencies had made 

 on the back of equity-related foreign inflows. 

     "Wall Street fears reign. Markets around the region are 

 bracing for more sell-off in the U.S. stock market," said 

 Philip Wee, treasury market strategist at Singapore's DBS Bank. 

     "A defensive mood may also see Asian government's guarded 

 against further currency appreciation," he added. 


    On Friday, the Dow Jones industrial average        lost



4.64 percent, Nasdaq composite fell 2.79 and the



broader S&P 500 index plunged 3.84 percent.



    Dealers said with the yen        back to levels around 116



per dollar, off its Friday's high around 115.50, players would



be wary of testing the tolerance of their central banks.



    The central banks of South Korea, Taiwan and Thailand all


intervened last week in response to their respective currencies


hitting multimonth highs against the dollar.



    Still few players expected to take long dollar positions,



they added.



    WON SHINES



    The Korean won         -2 touched a fresh 20-month high at



1,165.3, about half a percent higher from Friday's onshore



close of 1,170.6.



    Dealers in Singapore said dollar sale by offshore players



and exporters pushed the won higher.



    The sale of 700 billion won worth of foreign exchange


stabilisation bonds later on Monday was expected to cap the



won's rise, they said.



    The Finance Ministry also said it planned to raise the



ceiling, initially to one trillion won, for those bonds to stem



the won's rise.



    The ceiling was previously set at five 5.0 trillion won

has already been issued.



    However, the neighbouring Taiwan dollar dug in its heels at



about 33.18 per dollar, compared with 33.023 where the onshore

    The Singapore dollar        at around 1.7300 per dollar was



off its 19-month high of 1.7275 per dollar hit on Friday as



foreign funds were spotted trimming their short dollar



positions.

The Thai baht rose to 40.35 per dollar, from late

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late;  Intervention  Steadies US Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The struggling U.S. dollar stabilized against Asian currencies Thursday with the help of foreign exchange market intervention by monetary authorities in South Korea and Taiwan. 

 The U.S. dollar finished Asian trading hours little changed against the won, New Taiwan dollar, Singapore dollar and Thai baht, after falling to multimonth lows against all four a day earlier. The Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso weakened. 

 However, any strengthening of the U.S. dollar is likely to be short lived because the underlying sentiment in global markets continues to be biased heavily against the U.S. currency, analysts said. 

 U.S. dollar buying by state-run Korean banks saved the U.S. currency from posting a new low against the won. The state run banks swung into action after the U.S. dollar fell to around 1,172 won early in the session after closing a 19-month low of KRW1,179.4 a day earlier. 

 Traders said they believed state-run banks bought around $500 million on behalf of the government. The move helped the U.S. currency rebound to close at KRW1,179.5. 

 A senior Bank of Korea official later hinted at the government's involvement in the round of U.S. dollar buying, saying it is "natural" for the government to take actions to stabilize exchange rates "when market participants lose their balance." 

 Governments in Korea, Taiwan and Japan have all intervened either directly or indirectly in foreign exchange markets recently to slow the rise of their currencies. 

 Authorities have expressed concern that rapid appreciation of their currencies could undermine the price competitiveness of their exporters in global markets. 

 The Singapore dollar tracked its north Asia counterparts to remain steady against the U.S. dollar. 

 Late in Asia the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7502, compared with S$1.7505 late Tuesday. 

 An announcement by the Monetary Authority of Singapore that it will maintain its neutral policy on the Singapore dollar on a trade-weighted basis for the balance of 2002 had little immediate impact on the currency. 

 However, over the longer term it means there will be room for the currency to continue appreciating against the U.S. dollar, analysts said. 

 JP Morgan is targeting the U.S. dollar to fall to S$1.72 by the end of September and S$1.70 by the end of December. 

 Investors favor countries with positive cash flows like Singapore during times of stock market volatility and heightened risk aversion, said Thio Chin Loo, currency strategist at BNP Paribas. 

 Singapore's large current account surplus, healthy foreign reserves, and balanced budget are all supportive of the local currency because they make Singapore less vulnerable to volatility in global capital flows, she said. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency closed at NT$33.284 compared with NT$33.282 Wednesday. 

 The central bank, which regularly intervenes in the market to smooth out volatility, bought around US$700 million throughout the day, dealers said. 

 The New Taiwan dollar would have substantially eclipsed its 14-month high set Wednesday if not for the central bank's actions to prop up the U.S. dollar, one trader said. 

 Against the rupiah the U.S dollar broke through the key IDR9,000 resistance level for the first time in six sessions. 

 A 1.4% decline in the main index of the Jakarta Stock Exchange and U.S. dollar short covering weighed on the rupiah. 

 At the end of Jakarta trading the U.S. dollar was quoted at a two-month high of IDR9,125, up from IDR8,915 late Wednesday. 

 Bank Indonesia, the central bank, was rumored to have sold the U.S. currency to try to keep the rupiah below 9,000 per U.S. dollar, traders said. 

 The U.S. dollar traded in a narrow range against the baht, finishing the session at THB41.160, compared with a 22-month low of THB41.150 Wednesday. 

 Thailand's Commerce Minister Adisai Bodharamik said the recent strength in the baht against the U.S. dollar hasn't harmed export growth, which is expected to be sustained in June. 

 Adisai told reporters that the country's exports will remain competitive as the baht strengthens along with other currencies in the region against the weak U.S. dollar. 

 He said exports were estimated to rise by between 3.5% and 4.2% in June from a year ago.
