title: Korea won ends touch lower on verbal  intervention .
text:
SEOUL, July 11 (Reuters) - The South Korean won -closed slightly weaker against the dollar on Thursday, weighed down by a barrage of verbal and direct intervention by authorities. 

 The won settled at 1,179.5 per dollar against Wednesday's close of 1,179.4. 

 It opened at 1,178.5 and moved between 1,171.5 and 1,183.5. 

 Dealers said state-run banks and other lenders bought dollars worth $300 million, following repeated verbal intervention by the authorities. 

South Korea's top foreign exchange official at the Finance Ministry said the currency market's instability was excessive and the government would stabilise the market. 

 The won has gained more than 10 percent in the past three months, spurred by South Korea's improving economic fundamentals, weakness in the U.S. dollar and a strengthening Japanese yen. 

 The central bank also expressed concerns about the won's steep rise. 

 "It is natural to take steps when the market loses stability," said an official at the Bank of Korea. 

 But the won's fall was capped by steady dollar selling by exporters such as automakers and electronics makers around 1,180 won per dollar.. 

 Dealers agreed that the timing of the government intervention was apt, but they were mixed over how long the effects of the intervention would last. 

 "The government may be able to adjust the won's strengthening pace, but the upward trend is likely to continue, testing the government will," a foreign bank dealer said. 

 "It would be hard for the authorities to keep pressure on the won when the yen keeps going up," he said. 

 The won tends to shadow the yen due to the overlapping export items of the two countries such as electronics, shipbuilding and automobiles. 

 The greenback continued to fall against the yen on concerns over U.S. accounting practices and Wall Street losses. 

 The dollar was quoted at a 10-month low of 117.35/38 yen . 

 Traders said the market shrugged off the latest cabinet shakeup in which President Kim Dae-jung replaced the prime minister and six other ministerial posts ahead of presidential elections in December. 

 On the non-deliverable forward market, the one-month won was traded at 1,182.0/3.0 per dollar against 1,179.6/80.6 late Wednesday. The three-month won was at 1,187.6/8.6 against 1,185.2/6.2.

title: S Korea Fin Min: Estimates 2Q GDP Growth At 6%-7%
text:
SEOUL -(Dow Jones)- The South Korean economy will likely grow 6%-7% on year in the second quarter, Minister of Finance and Economy Jeon Yun-churl said Friday, citing forecasts from state-run research institutes. 

 Those institutes expect about a 7% on year growth for the entire 2002, Jeon said. 

 The government firmly maintains its official gross domestic product forecast between 5% and 5.9% in 2002. 

 The government is expected to update the forecast around  the end of this month when it reviews the economy's blueprint for the second half. 

 Finance minister Jeon said he doesn't expect major changes in South Korea's "macroeconomic policy framework" in the second half. 

 Government intervention in the foreign exchange market, or any other markets, "isn't a good policy," he said. 

 The government has repeatedly issued verbal comments recently to support the dollar, which has depreciated sharply against the won since mid-April. But it has reiterated that any direct dollar purchases will only be undertaken when, and if the market becomes extremely volatile. 

 A rapid and sharp rise in the won can weigh on the country's export competitiveness. 

 Regarding Seoulbank (Q.SBK), Jeon said 15 unidentified investors are interested in buying a controlling stake in the bank, which is wholly owned by the government. 

 The government hopes to select a buyer for Seoulbank by end-July, he said. 

 The government is trying to sell a controlling stake in Seoulbank or a merger with another bank as part of its privatization efforts. 

 South Korea's medium-sized business group Dongwon Group (Q.DWG) and a consortium led by Dongbu Group have said they will bid for Seoulbank. 

 Chohung Bank (Q.CHB), Korea Exchange Bank (Q.KEB) and Hana Bank (Q.HMB) have also shown an interest in merging with Seoulbank. 

 Jeon said he "personally" think the government needs to raise price of Korea Life Insurance Co., another company owned by the government. 

 The government has been in talks with Hanwha Group (Q.HWG) to sell a controlling stake in the insurer. 

 But the talks have stalled recently because the government wants to raise the pricetag on Korea Life, citing improvement in its business performance. 

 Jeon also said South Korean authorities will need more time to decide on any possible call rate hike. His remarks were in line with what the central bank said Friday morning, that it needs more time to observe economic conditions to determine interest rate policy. 

 While the global demand recovery isn't strong just yet, the won's appreciation against the dollar and stable crude oil prices are helping ease inflation concerns, he said. 

 The effect of increasing exports and capital investment, which will accompany the ongoing economic recovery, on inflation will be "neutral," he said, without elaborating. 

 The current weakness in the local stock market is due to the influence of falling U.S. equities recently, Jeon said. "Again, it's not desirable to intervene deeply in such a trend in the market." 

 With reference to the restructuring of Hynix Semiconductor Inc. (Q.HYY), Jeon said "market principle" will dictate the resolution of the chipmaker's problems. 

 He downplayed nationalistic concerns that selling Hynix to a foreign investor will hurt South Korea's economy, thereby leaving room for further talks with foreign partners. He added that the government wants "a clear resolution," but again he didn't elaborate on this. 

 Meanwhile, Jeon said financial companies that have benefitted from previous public fund injections will mostly have to shoulder the burden of any losses with the government. "The responsibility goes where the profit arises," he said. 

 The South Korean government has spent a total of 156 trillion won ($1=KRW1,221.5) in recapitalizing ailing financial companies since the Asian financial crisis in 1997. It won't be able to recover some of the money spent to pay deposits at failed firms. 

 -By So-Eui Rhee and Shin Jung-won, Dow Jones Newswires; 822-732-2165; djn.seoul@dowjones.com

title: S Korea Won Ends Lower On Govt Verbal  Intervention
text:
SEOUL -(Dow Jones)- The South Korean won finished weaker against the dollar Friday on repeated verbal intervention talk by the government and central bank officials, and dollar buying from state companies, said participants. 

 The dollar ended at 1,227.2 won, higher than Wednesday's close of KRW1,224.3. 

 South Korean markets were closed Thursday for a national holiday. 

 The dollar, which opened at KRW1,226.5, traded in a range of KRW1,225.5 to KRW1,230.9 Friday. 

 The dollar/won swayed throughout the day amid verbal intervention to keep the dollar from falling further after its recent spell of multi-month lows, although dollar selling by exporters capped any substantial rise for the U.S. unit. 

 The government's plan to increase the planned issue of foreign exchange stabilization bonds to KRW700 billion in June from KRW500 billion originally also fueled speculation that the central bank may directly intervene in the market, participants said. 

 On Friday, verbal intervention talk - once in the morning and twice in the afternoon - together with dollar buying from state-run Korea Electric Power Corp. and Korea Development Bank pushed the dollar above KRW1,230. But the dollar then fell to KRW1,220 on heavy selling by exporters, such as electronics and shipbuilding companies, they said. 

 A trader at Hana Bank said state companies bought around $100 million Friday, while local exporters sold $150 million. They sold dollars above the KRW1,228 level. 

 Verbal intervention by the government in support of the dollar, which first began late last month, intensified this week as the U.S. currency fell briefly below the key KRW1,220 level. The dollar reached an 18-month intraday low of KRW1,218.7 Wednesday on three rounds of verbal intervention. 

 Traders speculate that state companies, which have persistently been buying dollars this week, were likely acting on behalf of the government. 

 "The government still seems to be uncomfortable with the dollar/won level," said a trader at Citibank. 

 He said the government hopes the dollar will rise to around KRW1,230, a level that will likely keep the country's exports competitive. 

 Bank of Korea Governor Park Seung said earlier Friday that the central bank may buy dollars in the market if the dollar/won weakens further, as such a scenario would heighten concerns over what impact a stronger local currency might have on the country's economic recovery. 

 The Ministry of Finance and Economy said early in the afternoon that the speed and scale of the strengthening won against the dollar is too excessive compared with gains in the currencies of the country's major competitors. 

 In a statement, the ministry said the government will take whatever steps are necessary to keep the country's economic recovery on track, without actually saying it would act in the foreign exchange market. 

 The central bank then reiterated later that it's closely monitoring the local foreign exchange market and is concerned about the uncertainties prevailing among market players. 

 They expect the dollar to trade in a range of KRW1,220 to KRW1,235 next week on expectations of more government intervention, verbal or actual. 

 Prices of South Korea's key benchmark bonds rose Friday due to a weak local stock market and a rally in U.S. Treasurys overnight, market participants said. 

 South Korean stocks ended lower Friday, tracking a poor performance on U.S. markets, analysts said. 

 The Korea Composite Stock Price Index, or Kospi, fell 14.43 points, or 1.8%, to 795.16 Friday. 

 "Continuing weakness in stock markets brings some concerns over the speed of the economic recovery, which is helping improve bond buying sentiment," says Daewoo Securities analyst Kim Bum-Joon. 

 Also, some imbalance of supply and demand due to limited market liquidity caused yields to fall, analysts said. 

 The Bank of Korea canceled window sales of monetary stabilization bonds Friday due to lack of demand, market participants said. 

 Key Treasury bond yields are approaching the support level of 6% but are likely to move higher next week after the triple-witching-day in the local stock market Wednesday, said Yang Jin-Mo, an analyst at SK Securities Co. 

 Triple witching occurs when the contracts for stock index futures, stock index options and individual stock options all expire on the same day.

title: Asian  Currencies  Up Late; Reach Multi-month Highs Vs Dlr
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies surged against the dollar Friday - some to their highest levels in more than a year - as improving prospects for economic recovery continued to stir investors' interest in the region. 

 The South Korean won and Thai baht strengthened to 15-month highs, while the Philippine peso posted its best performance against the dollar in 14 months. 

 The Indonesian rupiah hit an eight-month high, the Singapore dollar a seven-month high and the New Taiwan dollar a five-month high. 

 "We're starting to see good growth and export numbers from Asia. Current account surpluses are rising and countries are attracting portfolio inflows as well as foreign direct investment," said Thio Chin Loo, senior currency strategist at BNP Paribas in Singapore. 

 Greater tolerance for risk has whetted investor's appetites for emerging market assets, particularly those in Asia, she said. 

 The yen's strength also set a firmer tone for Asian currencies, dealers said. 

 Authorities in South Korea attempted to curb the won's rise with verbal intervention. 

 The Ministry of Finance and Economy issued a statement saying it was concerned about the dollar's sharp fall against the won and would take action if warranted. 

 The dollar rose slightly after the statement, but resumed its slide when the ministry didn't act on its warning. 

 The limited impact from the government's statement was also due in part to seemingly contradictory remarks from Finance Minister Jeon Yun-churl, made at almost the same time. 

 Jeon said that dollar/won exchange rate reflects the health of South Korea's economy, which traders interpreted to mean the government was comfortable with the won's strength. 

 The dollar closed at KRW1,261.6, down from Thursday's close at KRW1,269.8. Friday's close marked the won's strongest finish against the dollar since March 1, 2001. 

 Rising regional currencies and recent upbeat comments from the government regarding Thailand's export prospects underpinned the baht. 

 Near the end of Asian trading, the dollar was quoted at THB42.740, down from THB42.845 late Thursday. It was the baht's best close since Feb. 20, 2001. 

 The peso got swept up in the euphoria driving other regional currencies. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at 49.46 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP49.52 Thursday. It was the peso's strongest finish since March 29, 2001. 

 The peso also was supported by remittance inflows from overseas Filipino workers and thin corporate demand for the U.S. dollar. 

 There was talk in the market that the central bank took advantage of the cheap U.S. currency to buy about US$30 million to boost its reserves, which helped contain the peso's rise. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was buoyed by gains in its regional peers and continued optimism over the government's privatization program. 

 Late in Asia the U.S. dollar was quoted at 9,080 rupiah, down from IDR9,150 late Thursday. It was the rupiah's best showing since Sept. 14, 2001. 

 Still, the rupiah was unable to seriously test key resistance at IDR9,000 to the U.S. dollar as local companies that owe debt overseas picked up the U.S. currency at the lower levels. 

 The Singapore dollar was helped by strong economic data and comments from the Monetary Authority of Singapore that it's comfortable with the currency's current level against the U.S. dollar. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7950, down from S$1.8024 late Thursday. It was the Singapore dollar's strongest performance since Oct. 5, 2001. 

 The government reported that non-oil domestic exports rose a surprising 6.4% on year, the first increase after 13 consecutive months of decline. 

 MAS Assistant Managing Director Khor Hoe Ee told reporters that the trade-weighted Singapore dollar is still within the central bank's undisclosed policy band, "and we are comfortable with it." 

 Foreign funds flowing into Taiwan from the recent sale of US$700 million worth of convertible bonds by Cathay Financial Holding helped lift the local currency. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.458, down from NT$34.538 Thursday. 

 It was its strongest close for the New Taiwan dollar since Dec. 12, 2001.

title: Tsy  FX  Rpt Says Dollar Strength Reflects Strong US Econ
text:
WASHINGTON -(Dow Jones)- The strength of the U.S. dollar last year was largely the result of stronger U.S. economic fundamentals compared with major trading partners, rather than deliberate attempts by trading partners to devalue their own currencies, according to a U.S. Treasury Department report on foreign exchange policy obtained by Dow  Jones Newswires. 

 No major U.S. trading partners were guilty of manipulating their currencies to gain a trade advantage during the second half of 2001, Treasury said in its Report to Congress on International Economic and Exchange Rate Policies. The report, mandated by U.S. trade laws, outlines economic and currency-market developments around the world, and is due to be presented at a hearing before the Senate Banking Committee Wednesday. 

 The release of the report comes at a time when U.S. manufacturers are complaining that the continued strength of  the U.S. dollar is making it impossible for them to compete  abroad.  They blame market intervention, particularly in Asia, and the Treasury's oft-repeated statements extolling the economic benefits of a strong dollar for their troubles. 

 In its report, Treasury noted the euro managed to break $0.90 only during a two-month period between mid-August to mid-October. 

 "The euro's failure to sustain an appreciation against the dollar during 2001 was, at least partially attributable to Europe's vulnerability to the worldwide slowdown," Treasury said. 

 Japan, whose intervention in the foreign exchange markets was confined to the period between Sept. 17-28 following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, sold about $27 billion worth of yen during that time. During the second half of last year, the yen depreciated 5.8% against the dollar, ending the year at Y131.8. 

 While the Bank of Japan has attempted to fight deflation  by allowing the monetary base to grow sharply during the year, the strategy has shown no signs its working. 

 "The weakness in the growth in broad money is a reflection of the weak balance sheets of Japan's financial and corporate sectors," Treasury said.  "Vigorous action is needed to tackle these twin problems." 

 The Canadian dollar also weakened against the dollar last year.  Its long-term decline is in part due to the drop  in inflation-adjusted non-energy commodity prices, Treasury  said, citing the Bank of Canada. 

 Most Asian countries eased monetary policy in line with the Federal Reserve last year. However, reminiscent of Japan, those actions didn't translate into stronger credit growth in most countries, "given that many financial institutions remained capital constrained and many corporations remained overly indebted," Treasury said. Given  weak growth and the threat of deflation,  central banks throughout Asia accumulated reserves to limit the appreciation of their currencies. 


South Korea's increase in official foreign reserves stemmed from
interest earnings and repayment of loans to South Korean banks extended
during the Asian crisis, rather than direct central bank intervention in
the foreign exchange market, Treasury said. South Korea's gross foreign
exchange reserves totaled $102.8 billion at the end of 2001.
   -By Elizabeth Price, Dow Jones Newswires; (202) 862-9295;
elizabeth.price@dowjones.com

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late On Equity Inflows, Yen
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Continuing foreign equity inflows into local stock markets and the yen's gains bolstered most Asian currencies late Wednesday, dealers said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah's new found strength provided additional support to its Southeast Asian peers, although fears of intervention by the central banks in Singapore and Thailand stymied their currencies' rise. 

 The rupiah extended its climb toward IDR9,900 resistance, as interbank participants continued to sell U.S. dollars in anticipation of inflows from the Indonesian government's impending sale of its 51% stake in PT Bank Central Asia, observers said. 

 The rupiah, trading at near five-month highs, hit an intraday high of IDR9,915 before retreating to around IDR9,950 late Wednesday. The rupiah was weaker at IDR9,980 late Tuesday. 

 Improving prospects for the privatization of state-held assets in Indonesia - which would underscore the government's commitment to economic reforms - helped thrust the rupiah through the psychologically important IDR10,000 threshold Tuesday. 

 "With corporate bids for debt repayment still much on the sidelines, the rupiah looks well positioned to test IDR9,800," Bank of America said in a research report. 

 The Thai currency strengthened to an intraday high of 43.490 baht to the dollar, thanks to strong foreign equity inflows and dollar sales by U.S. funds - as they simultaneously unloaded their dollar positions against the yen, dealers said. 

 But the baht subsequently pulled back past the THB43.500 level on market suspicions that the Thai central bank had bought dollars via two of its agent banks based in Singapore to check the baht's advance, market observers said. 

 In an apparent bid to maintain the price competitiveness of Thailand's exports, the Thai central bank had been buying dollars in the last few days when the currency traded at THB43.55-THB43.60, said a dealer at a Thai bank. 

 "It's still in their practice to protect their exporters," he added. 

 At 0915 GMT (4:15 a.m. EST), the dollar was at THB43.515, lower than THB43.665 late Tuesday. 

 Against the Japanese currency, the dollar was quoted at Y131.84, below Y132.13 in New York and Y132.53 in Tokyo late Tuesday. 

 Market speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened to check the strength of the local currency Wednesday provided a floor for the U.S. dollar around S$1.8250, observers said. 

 The U.S. dollar slid to an overnight low of S$1.8222 on long-liquidation, but subsequently bounced back on suspected intervention by the MAS, some dealers said. 

 A large Singapore bank bought a "significant amount" of U.S. dollars around S$1.8260 during the Asian session Wednesday, moderating the upward pressure on the Singapore currency despite the firmer yen and local stock market gains, said a dealer at a European bank. 

 Although some dealers said the Singapore bank was buying U.S. dollars on behalf of its corporate clients, jitters about central bankintervention led some to speculate that the Singapore bank was acting at the behest of the central bank. 

 The South Korean won closed at KRW1,316.3 against the dollar, little changed compared with KRW1,316.4 Tuesday. 

 The won strengthened to an intraday high of KRW1,313.7 earlier, before retreating as foreign investors turned net sellers of South Korean shares and onshore demand for dollars emerged when the U.S. currency traded below KRW1,315 support, said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, a regional currency strategist at UBS Warburg. 

 State-run banks, like Korea Development Bank, or KDB, were snapping up dollars on behalf of corporations and oil importers, said a dealer at a European bank in Singapore. 

 Some market participants also believe that South Korea's central bank had intervened through KDB, he added. 

 Expectations that the yen will remain rangebound - as foreign exchange participants attempt to defend their currency options positions - also limited the won's upside, said Mohi-uddin. 

 Market participants this week established "double no-touch options with barriers at Y131.50 and Y135.50," the strategist said, adding that these players will protect these levels to ensure that the options won't be exercised. 

 "External factors are not that bullish for the won," said Mohi-uddin. 

 The New Taiwan dollar closed stronger on foreign equity inflows, but was off its intraday high as the central bank intervened to curb the local currency's appreciation, dealers said. 

 A Taipei-based dealer estimated that the central bank accounted for about half of Wednesday's turnover. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$35.030, slightly lower than NT$35.069 Tuesday. The New Taiwan dollar hit an intraday high of NT$34.995 Wednesday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Down Late; But Off Lows, Tracking Yen
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies ended the week only slightly lower as the dollar's failure to make a convincing break above Y135 helped them reclaim some ground, observers said. 

 Still, "the yen's decline has probably snapped selected Asian currencies out of their lethargy," said Thio Chin Loo, a regional currency strategist at BNP Paribas. 

 The dollar briefly poked above the Y135 level earlier Friday, pulling the rug under other Asian currencies, which in recent weeks had been buoyed by portfolio inflows. 

 But those currencies regained their footing somewhat along with the yen, which recouped its losses after Japanese financial officials expressed their concern over the speed of the dollar's two-yen rise overnight. 

 At 0900 GMT (4:00 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar was quoted at Y133.98, below Y134.85 in New York late Thursday. 

 The dollar hit a new three-year high of Y135.17 Thursday in New York after U.S. Treasury Secretary Paul O'Neill said he has no sympathy for U.S. manufacturers' complaints about a strong dollar. Good companies don't "live or die" by exchange rate moves, he argued. Players interpreted his commments to mean that Washington isn't overly concerned about the dollar's strength. 

 Although the region's currencies continued to outperform the yen - given Japan's poor economic prospects - they may well play catch-up soon, especially the Singapore dollar, some analysts said. 

 "The currency that is most at risk of tracking the yen and the euro lower is the Singapore dollar, which is expensive on a trade-weighted basis," said Thio at BNP Paribas. 

 She added that, with the Singapore stock market vulnerable to profit-taking, the U.S. dollar will likely continue to be supported above S$1.8300. The local stock index is close to the psychologically important 1,800-point threshold. 

 She expects the U.S. dollar to bounce to S$1.8450 in the near term. 

 Late in the day, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.8368, higher than S$1.8320 late Thursday. The yen's earlier slide to Y135 had temporarily dragged the Singapore dollar past S$1.8400 to an intraday low of S$1.8415 against the U.S. currency. 

 Expectations of an economic rebound and the specter of a sovereign ratings upgrade for South Korea cushioned the blow on the won from the yen's slide to new three-year lows, dealers said. 

 Dollar sales by exporters in South Korea also helped mitigate the pain on the won, dealers added. 

 As a result, the won continued to strengthen against the yen. 

 The dollar closed at 1,317.6 won, slightly higher than KRW1,314.4. The won had earlier floundered to as low as KRW1,326.0. 

 The yen was quoted at KRW9.85, after hitting a low of KRW9.74 earlier in the day. 

 Haruhiko Kuroda, Japan's vice finance minister for international affairs, said Friday that there is little Japan can do to control the yen/won cross rate. 

 Kuroda said he "understands" the concerns expressed by Korean officials about the weak yen, given that some Japanese and South Korean exporters directly compete, but added that he can't take steps to control the level of the currency cross. 

 South Korea - which has in recent months been complaining about the yen's depreciation - appeared resigned to the won's strength against the Japanese currency. 

 Kim Yong-duk, deputy minister for international affairs at South Korea's Ministry of Finance and Economy, said Friday that, although the government is still talking about foreign exchange issues with Japan, South Korea isn't considering direct market intervention - signaling that the government may allow the won to further appreciate against the yen. 

 Exporter U.S. dollar sales helped offset the pressure of the yen on the New Taiwan dollar, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$35.004, slightly higher than NT$34.980 Thursday. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the dollar closed at 51.310 pesos, higher than PHP51.235 Thursday. 

 The Thai currency was at 44.035 baht to the dollar, weaker than THB43.985 late Thursday. 

 The Indonesian currency was marginally weaker at 10,325 rupiah against the dollar, compared with IDR10,320 late Thursday.

 At about the same time, Kim Yong-duk, deputy minister for international affairs at South Korea's Ministry of Finance and Economy, said the government is still talking about foreign exchange issues with the Japanese government. 

 But Kim also said South Korea is not considering direct market intervention, signaling the government may tolerate a stronger won and a weaker yen. 

 "They (South Korean government officials) don't actually seem to want the weak Korean won at this moment," said Citibank economist Oh Suktae. "The yen/won cross rate could continue to fall."

title: Korea Vice Fin Min: Rapid Won Gain Vs Dollar Undesirable
text:
SEOUL -(Dow Jones)- The South Korean government will increase its efforts to stabilize the local bond and foreign exchange markets after the recent sharp gains in the stock market, said Kim Jin-pyo, vice minister of the Finance and Economy Ministry Tuesday. 

 The government will adjust the amount of bonds to be issued and their maturities based on market conditions, Kim said. 

 The won's sharp gain against the dollar is "undesirable" and the "government will take appropriate steps to curb the gain if necessary," Kim said. 

 He declined to elaborate on the measures the government may take, however. 

 Kim's comments echo those of a Bank of Korea official in the foreign exchange analysis department who said earlier Tuesday that the central bank may directly intervene if the latest gains against the dollar continue. 

South Korea's key bond yields have risen sharply on the anticipation that the slowdown in the economy may have hit bottom following the better-than-expected third-quarter gross domestic product data Nov. 22. 

 The won has risen sharply against the dollar recently on the bullish Korean stock market and also on the GDP data. At 0143 GMT (8:43 p.m. EST), the dollar was trading at 1,264 won compared with last Friday's close of KRW1,271.8, but slightly off its high of KRW1,262 hit earlier Tuesday. 

 The finance ministry Monday changed the maturity of its KRW500 billion foreign exchange stabilization bond offering to three years from five years. The cut was initiated to minimize the impact of new bond supply on the market, Kim explained. 

 Key economic ministries and the central bank will form a body to work on future changes to the government's bond issue plans, Kim said. 

 The body will review the way the government auctions bonds and look at improving it, he said. The government wants the changes to better reflect market conditions, he added, without elaborating. 

 Kim expects that even after the government-sponsored bond buyout program ends at the end of the year, the beneficiary companies will be able to refinance their maturing bonds without suffering from further liquidity problems. 

 "The government's goal is to eliminate direct support to the markets (as in the bond buyout program) as much as possible," Kim said. 

 Under the bond program, state-run Korea Development Bank (Q.KDV) will have underwritten KRW2.5 trillion in maturing corporate bonds of select troubled companies. Key beneficiaries of the program include Hynix Semiconductor Inc. (Q.HYY), Hyundai Engineering and Construction Co. (Q.HEC) and Hyundai Merchant Marine Co. (Q.HMM)

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Ctrl Bks Cap Won, TWD Gains

 At 0815 GMT (3:15 a.m. EST), the dollar was quoted at Y120.22, above Y119.99 late Thursday in New York. The dollar was at Y121.00 late Thursday in Tokyo. 

 As foreign funds investing in South Korean shares continued to sell dollars, the won extended its recent ascent to end at a nine-week high, dealers said.

 A state-run bank started to buy dollars when the U.S. currency hit an intraday low of KRW1,280.2; dealers believed the transactions were executed on behalf of the central bank.

 The central bank is widely expected to keep the New Taiwan dollar steady, and manage a gradual appreciation of the currency as the Dec. 1 legislative elections approach, dealers said. 

 But the New Taiwan dollar will likely weaken after the elections to reflect the island state's ailing economic fundamentals, market watchers said. 

 Uninspired by the yen's gains, the Singapore dollar slumped on short-covering of U.S. dollar positions by interbank participants, dealers said. Singapore banks were also believed to be buying U.S. dollars on behalf of corporate clients, dealers said.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late Amid Renewed Pressure On Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Wednesday, as renewed pressure on the dollar helped them sustain their recent gains despite the region's grim economic outlook, dealers said. 

 The Federal Reserve's decision Tuesday to trim short-term interest rates by a quarter percentage point was widely expected, and had little impact on Asian currencies. 

 Instead, the market focused on the Fed's statement accompanying its action, which suggested that the U.S. economy hasn't responded to the central bank's attempts to spur growth. The Fed's latest move marked the seventh cut this year, bringing interest rates to their lowest level in seven years. 

 The Fed also indicated it was more likely to lower than raise rates in the future, saying risks were "weighted mainly toward . . . economic weakness" rather than inflation. 

 "The repeat of the June statement emphasized the fact that business capital spending continues to weaken, suggesting that no upturn is in sight for the high-tech industry that fuels the region's exports," Bank of America said in a report. 

 Repeated verbal warnings by Japanese officials against excessive yen strength did little to offset the pressure on the dollar, which slid overnight following the Fed's announcement. 

 At 0820 GMT (4:20 a.m. EST), the dollar was quoted at Y119.69, slightly higher than Y119.55 late Tuesday in New York. The dollar was at Y120.68 late Tuesday in Tokyo. 

 Despite the yen's resilience, fears of central bank intervention prevented the South Korea won from breaching past KRW1,280 to the dollar, dealers said. 

 In the case of the Singapore dollar, talk of intervention by the local monetary authority overnight kept the U.S. currency supported above S$1.7500, dealers said. 

 In Seoul, the dollar finished at 1,282.70 won, down from KRW1,283.80 Tuesday. 

 After the market closed, the South Korean government said it has reached an agreement to sell large stakes in Hyundai Investment Trust & Securities Co. - and its units, Hyundai Investment Trust Management Co. and Hyundai Securities Co. (Q.HDS) - to a consortium led by American International Group Inc. (AIG). 

 The government's Financial Supervisory Commission will hold a press conference Thursday. 

 The deal is expected to bring $800 million to $1 billion worth of inflows into South Korea, supporting the won, some analysts said. 

 The U.S. dollar's weakness against the yen and the euro failed to inspire the Singapore dollar, dealers said. 

 Speculation by some dealers that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had checked the local dollar's advance when it climbed to as high as S$1.7475 in New York trade Tuesday kept the U.S. currency afloat above S$1.7500 Wednesday, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar briefly received an additional boost late in the day, jumping to around S$1.7540, on the Australian government's approval of Singapore Telecommunication Ltd's (P.SGT) A$14 billion-plus takeover bid for Australia's second-largest telecommunications group, Cable & Wireless Optus Ltd. (A.CWO). 

 But the U.S. currency failed to sustain its gains, and subsequently retreated to S$1.7525, weaker than late Tuesday's level. 

 "There were keen sellers around the S$1.7450 to S$1.7550 level," said a senior dealer at a European bank. 

 The Thai baht was the main beneficiary of the dollar's weakness against the euro and the yen, dealers said. 

 The Thai currency strengthened to 44.52 baht per dollar, compared with THB44.745 late Tuesday. 

 After riding on the coattails of the yen's gains earlier in the day, the New Taiwan dollar lost ground as it yielded to foreign equity fund outflows, which contributed to a 1.7% slide on the local bourse, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.603, higher than NT$34.586 Tuesday. The U.S. dollar had touched an intraday low of NT$34.496. 

 Concerns over Taiwan's sluggish economic fundamentals will likely continue to weigh on the local dollar, observers said. 

 The Ministry of Economic Affairs said Wednesday Taiwan's July export orders sank 16.8% to US$10.8 billion, sharper than the average 14.3% year-on-year drop the market had expected. 

 Taiwan's July industrial output fell 10.4%, compared with a 11.3% decline in June. The data was mostly in line with expectations of a 10.1% drop. 

 Renewed fears of a further increase in local banks' reserve requirements shored up the Philippine peso, dealers said. 

 Somewhat alleviating the market's jitters, Deputy Central Bank Governor Amando Tetangco said later in the day an increase in banks' reserve requirement was only "an option" for draining excess liquidity from the financial system, should it be causing inflationary pressures. 

 The dollar closed at 50.91 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP51.25 Tuesday. 

 The Philippine central bank appeared to have bought dollars as the currency retreated, to replenish its reserves and smooth the peso's volatility, dealers said. 

 Elsewhere, corporate dollar demand weighed on the Indonesian currency, which slipped to 8,650 rupiah to the dollar, compared with IDR8,545 late Tuesday, dealers said.

title: UPDATE 2-Korea finmin sees only rare  forex intervention .
text:
SEOUL, April 12 (Reuters) - South Korea's Finance Minister Jin Nyum said on Thursday the government would not step into the foreign exchange market to support the won unless it saw panic or speculation. 

 "I acknowledge there was lack of communication between the finance ministry and the central Bank of Korea over the foreign exchange policy last week," the minister said. 

 "As for the foreign exchange policy, we will coordinate with the central bank," said the minister. 

 "We may take action and use foreign exchange reserves to stabilise the market. But the authorities' action will be limited to such cases as investors are believed to be in a panic about the rate or any speculative movements are seen," Jin added. 

 As the won continued to weaken against the U.S. dollar following the movement of the Japanese yen, the central bank had said last week it would use foreign exchange reserves, if needed, to support the local currency. 

 The won, which closely tracks the yen, is down about five percent against the dollar this year after falling about 11 percent last year. 

 The won fell to 30-month lows last week, prompting the central Bank of Korea to buy dollars to stem its slide. 

 SEOULBANK SALE 

 Jin, speaking in a news conference, also said the sales of Seoulbank and Hyundai Investment Trust would be completed by the end of June. 

 Seoulbank said last month 18 foreign investors, mostly from the United States, had shown an interest in taking over the nationalised bank and it expected the sale to be completed in the first half. 

 The government, the largest single shareholder of Seoulbank, had pumped 4.8 trillion won ($3.64 billion) in public money into the bank between 1998 and 1999, to help it find a buyer. 

 The government had said it would put Seoulbank under a state-run financial holding company if it was not sold. 

 Hyundai has said for months it was close to concluding a deal to draw nearly $1 billion in investment from a consortium led by American International Group (AIG) and WL Ross. 

 The consortium and the Hyundai companies signed a memorandum of understanding on the planned investment last August. 

 But the sale of ailing Korea Life Insurance is not likely to be completed by June as the government has to select lead managers, Jin said. 

 The government had earlier said it would sell the unlisted life insurer within this year after injecting 1.5 trillion won during the first half of this year to facilitate the sale. 

 State-run Korea Deposit Insurance Corp has injected 2.05 trillion won and owns a 100 percent stake in Korea, which was declared non-viable in September 1999 by the financial regulator.

 The Thai baht, Singapore dollar and Philippine peso all gained on the U.S. dollar, while the Indonesian rupiah weakened.

title: Korea won ends weaker,foreign stock selling weighs.
text:
SEOUL, Dec 4 (Reuters) - The South Korean won -2 closed weaker on Monday, depressed by foreign investors' settlement of local stock sales. 

 Dealers said won sentiment was bleak as investors remained downcast over the crawling pace of government-led restructuring and signs of a slowing economy. 

 The won finished at 1,217.1 per dollar, a fresh closing low for the year and its lowest ebb since September 29, 1999. It had opened at 1,203.0 from Friday's close of 1,209.5. 

 Fears of government-backed dollar sales by state banks kept the market on its toes, but the currency withered lower as oil companies and offshore players continued to buy dollars. 

 "Right now the focus is on how serious the BOK (central Bank of Korea) is about direct intervention and how much foreign investors will sell in the stock market," a dealer at a foreign bank said. 

 Dealers were spooked by state-owned Korea Development Bank's (KDB) aggressive dollar selling on Friday as they saw the move as a government-backed effort to defend the 1,220 level. 

 KDB sold another $50-$100 million on Monday, but volumes were weak and the market took the seemingly passive stance as a green light to break the 1,215 support level. 

 Dealers said direct intervention from the government was unlikely as South Korea was loathe to use up its foreign exchange reserves. Analysts also saw the authorities tolerating a weaker won to boost exports. 

 Finance Minister Jin Nyum said counter-measures would be taken against speculative trade in the non-deliverable forward market and any sharp fluctuation in the dollar/won rate, but did not specify what kind of measures would be implemented. 

 Disappointment about the pace of reforms and slowing economic growth have also plagued the local stock market, which is off 50 percent for the year. The benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) ended down 2.47 percent at 501.73. 

 Investors quickly turned cool on parliament's approval on Saturday of 40 trillion in additional funds to recapitalise financial institutions. 

 Foreign investors were net sellers of 34.2 billion won worth of stocks on Monday after selling a net 400 billion won worth last Thursday and Friday. Though only part of the amount was expected in the market, dealers said settlement of the stock sales would continue to pressure the won. 

 Dealers expected a near-term range of 1,212-22. 

 International Monetary Fund senior representative in Seoul David Coe said South Korea risked seeing another banking crisis if local banks continued to support nonviable companies. 

 Coe also said grouping weak banks under financial holding companies may not help, but saw the probability of a crisis like the one in 1997-98 as very low. 

 On the non-deliverable forward market, the six-month won was last quoted at 1,216.7/17.7 from 1,212.8/13.8 earlier, while the one-year won was last at 1,216.9/17.9 from 1,213.5/14.5.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Won, Taiwan Dlr Extend Falls
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The South Korean won and the New Taiwan dollar extended their falls late Monday on domestic and international pressures, while other Southeast Asian currencies staged a mixed performance. 

 "It's pretty much an established downtrend for the Taiwan dollar and the Korean won," said Chi Lo, a senior economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Hong Kong. 

 The weakness of these Northeast Asian currencies wiped out the Singapore dollar's earlier gains, which were fueled by the Japanese yen's strong performance and the euro's recent boost, dealers said. The Singapore dollar slipped back below S$1.7500 support late in the day. 

 Continued remittance inflows from Filipinos working overseas lifted the Philippine peso, dealers said. 

 Offshore participants showed sparse interest in the Thai baht and the Indonesian rupiah, both of which were steady. 

 Foreign equity fund outflows pressured the currencies of South Korea and Taiwan, although intervention by the Taiwanese central bank earlier in the day cushioned the impact on the latter, dealers said. 

 The dollar was at 1,216.70 won, up from Friday's close of KRW1,209.50. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency rose to a 20-month high of NT$33.071, from the previous close of NT$32.995, after the central bank withdrew its support for the local dollar late in the day, dealers said. 

 Concerns over domestic political bickering in Taiwan and uncertainties over South Korea's progress toward economic reform continued to cloud the currencies of both nations, analysts said. 

 The risk of both economies slipping into a current account deficit next year, as a result of an expected slowdown in exports, could also harm their currencies, said Lo at Standard Chartered Bank. The semiconductor cycle is turning down and personal computer sales are slowing, he added. The authorities should also allow their currencies to weaken to keep their countries' exports competitive, with the Japanese yen expected to lose ground, analysts said. 

 But the pressure on the won will likely be more intense, with the Taiwanese authorities continuing to sell the U.S. currency to control the pace of the local dollar's depreciation, analysts said. 

 "For those investors who don't like the short-term prospects and want to short these currencies, they could use the Korean won as a proxy to the Taiwan dollar," said Lo at Standard Chartered Bank, adding that this could add to the pressure on the won. 

 South Korea's Minister of Finance and Economy Jin Nyum, said Monday the government isn't considering any direct intervention in the local foreign exchange market to stem the won's losses. He reiterated, however, that the government will closely monitor trading in the non-deliverable forward market. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. dollar rebounded to S$1.7525, after pulling back to as low as S$1.7475 earlier in the day. Late Friday, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7521. 

 While the Singapore dollar's early rebound had prompted some dealers to say the U.S. dollar may have found a short-term top at around S$1.7600, UBS Warburg's currency strategist, Mansoor Mohi-uddin, said the Singapore dollar remains vulnerable to potential further weakness in the yen. 

 In the Thai currency market, the dollar edged up slightly to 43.850 baht, from THB43.790 late Friday. The baht was largely steady earlier in the day. 

 The banning of same-day cash sales between onshore and offshore counterparties without any commercial purpose has made the market more cautious of shorting the baht for now, noted UBS Warburg's Mohi-uddin. 

 But he added that the baht's respite will likely be transient amid political uncertainties ahead of Thailand's general elections early next year. 

 "We still have interest from some of our clients to short the baht ahead of elections," Mohi-uddin said, adding that the authorities won't tighten foreign exchange regulations further for now, after clamping down on speculative trading last week. 

 "The market is waiting for the liquidity squeeze to ease, and then they'll start buying dollars," he said. 

 Against the Indonesian currency, the dollar was steady at 9,525 rupiah.

title: FX  dealers in Korea to curb speculative trading.
text:
SEOUL, Aug 25 (Reuters) - Foreign exchange dealers at major banks in South Korea, including foreign banks, plan to hold off on speculative trading to protest against government intervention, a move which would severely curtail liquidity, industry sources said on Friday. 

 Dealers said halting such trade would erase about 80 percent of the currency market's trade volume. 

 "The government's excessive intervention stifles the currency market," said a local bank dealer. "It also severely undermines corporate awareness about the currency risks." 

 Dealers said recent trade has been held to a tight range by what they dubbed "government-instructed" importer and exporter settlements. 

 About 30 dealers met on Thursday and agreed to stop speculative trading, limiting themselves to commercial orders. 

 A central Bank of Korea official said trading volume fell to about $1.2 billion on Thursday, from the current daily average of $2 billion. 

 Officials at the Ministry of Finance and Economy denied intervening in the currency market by directing action by state-run banks or others. 

 "Dealers seem to have taken this action because the current tight range of trade means little opportunity for profits," said Joo Hwan-wook, deputy director of the ministry's foreign exchange policy division. 

 "We are not doing the things the dealers accuse us of," Joo said. 

 On Wednesday, the International Monetary Fund said South Korea should limit foreign exchange intervention to "smoothing operations". 

 The won has appreciated about 1.8 percent since the close of 1999.

title: UPDATE 1- FX  dealers in Korea halt speculative trade.
text:
SEOUL, Aug 25 (Reuters) - Foreign exchange dealers at major banks in South Korea, including foreign banks, have halted speculative trading to protest against government intervention, a move which would severely curtail liquidity, industry sources said on Friday. 

 The government's tight control on the market has frustrated dealers because the subsequent narrow currency range seriously limits their ability to make proprietary trading profits for their banks. 

 Halting speculative trade would erase about 80 percent of the currency market's volume and although the traders admit it would be largely symbolic, it is important for a country to have as liquid a foreign exchange market as possible to facilitate overseas trade and investment flows. 

 A central Bank of Korea official said the impact was seen on Thursday as trade fell to about $1.2 billion from the recent daily average of $2 billion. 

 Trade by late Friday was estimated at a scant $370 million but the won's level was little changed as it hovered at Thursday's closing of 1,114.1 at 0617 GMT. 

 It opened at 1,113.9 and moved between 1,113.9 and 1,114.4. 

 "Our action is a symbolic gesture," said a foreign bank dealer. "We are of an opinion that the government has been behind the current boring, tight range trade." 

 The won has closed between 1,110 and 1,119 every day for the last two months. 

 A dealer at a local bank expressed a similar view: "The government's excessive intervention stifles the currency market. It also severely undermines corporate awareness about the currency risks." 

 Dealers said recent trade had been held to a tight range by what they dubbed "government-instructed" importer and exporter settlements. 

 About 30 dealers met on Thursday and agreed to stop speculative trading, limiting themselves to commercial orders. 

 Dealers said the agreement would hold until at least early next week, while urging the government to allow market principles to prevail. 

 SMOOTHING OPERATIONS

 Monetary authorities deny they are overstepping their mandate, which is basically to ensure that the won, buoyed by the economy's robust rebound this year and last, does not appreciate too fast. 

 On Wednesday, the International Monetary Fund said South Korea should limit foreign exchange intervention to "smoothing operations". 

 Authorities also denied they were influencing the market by directing action by state-run banks or other state agencies. 

 "Dealers seem to have taken this action because the current tight range of trade means little opportunity for profits," said Joo Hwan-wook, deputy director of the Finance Ministry's foreign exchange policy division. "We are not doing the things the dealers accuse us of." 

 WON UNDERVALUED VS DOLLAR 

 Analysts said the won was undervalued given dollar inflows of foreign equity investors and the country's trade surplus. 

 Foreign investors have bought a net $10 billion worth of Korean stocks so far this year and trade surplus by July this year was $5 billion, government figures showed. 

 "The won's fair value should be between 1,050 and 1,110 per dollar," said Namuh Rhee, executive director at Samsung Securities. 

 Kevin Ralph, a regional currency strategist at Sanwa Bank in Singapore, said South Korean monetary authorities had long stopped intervening "directly". 

 "But they are still believed to intervene in the market through state-run and banks and companies," Ralph said. "I believe the won is currently about three to five percent undervalued against the dollar." 

 South Korea has adopted a floating exchange rate system since the Asian currency crisis, when the won plummeted from about 913 to the dollar in October 1997 to a close of 1,806 won three months later. 

 "In textbook theory, South Korea should see much less intervention by the government," said an economist at the state-funded Korea Development Institute. 

 "But our currency market is too small for the economy. So the government still needs to step in to maintain the market's stability," he said. 

 The won has appreciated about 1.8 percent since the close of 1999.

title: Korea's c.bank  intervenes  in  forex  mkt to buy dlrs.

SEOUL, June 5 (Reuters) - South Korea's central Bank of Korea has intervened in the local foreign exchange market to slow the pace of the won's rise against the dollar, a bank official said on Monday. 

 The official, who refused to be identified, said the bank has purchased dollars through state-run banks to help check the local currency from rising too quickly. 

 The intervention came as the won rose to 1,117.6 in mid-afternoon trade, boosted by heavy foreign buying of local stocks. 

 Dealers said the currency market saw about $200 million in dollar demand from state banks. 

 The won dropped to 1,118.8 by 0630 GMT after the intervention. 

 It opened at 1,125.0 compared with Friday's close of 1,125.2.

title: Emerging  FX  - Pressured by dollar bulls.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 4 (Reuters) - Asian regionals currencies

 edged lower in early trade on Thursday, weighed by the dollar's 

 strength which holds despite Wall Street's slip. 

     Dealers said market participants rushed to cover any short 

 dollar positions versus regional currencies due to the dollar's 

 broad-based gains against the major currencies. 


    The sickly euro	    was hovering near its record low of



88.87 cents overnight and dealers said there was little to stop



it extending the slide.



    Dealers said the fact that the euro failed to capitalise on



the recent volatility in the U.S. equity markets had led to



further disenchantment among long-term investors.



    The U.S. unit broke above 109 yen	    in muted trading



due to the Golden Week holidays in Japan.



    KOREAN WON	     -2



    The won edged lower against the dollar in early trade



despite a strong rise in the KOSDAQ.



    Investors were reluctant to push it higher due to fears of



government intervention and the weaker yen, dealers said. South



Korea and Japan compete in similar export markets.



    The Finance Ministry on Wednesday issued a verbal warning



to rein in the won. The move was following by state-run banks



absorbing dollars from the market.



    Dealers in Seoul said they expected the won to trade in a



range of 1,109 to 1,112 won for the rest of the session.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



    The rupiah is expected to move in a narrow range after the



market had discounted the news that the letter of intent to the



IMF might be signed soon.



    The agreement will allow Jakarta to tap a long-delayed loan



worth $400 million.



    Dealers expected the unit to trade in a 7,950-8,000 range



on Thursday. A fall below 8,020 is expected to trigger



stop-loss sales.



    THAI BAHT	



    Dollar bids from offshore players continued to keep the



baht on the defensive, although sporadic profit-taking helped



it gain some ground.



    Dealers see a strong support for the baht at 38.50 where



exporter offers are lined up.



    Swap rates in the offshore market have risen sharply due to



tight baht liquidity as players held on to dollars. One-month



dollar/baht offshore forward rate rose to 5/7 satang from 1/3



satang early on Wednesday.



PHILIPPINE PESO	



The Philippine peso nudged up in early Asian trading, but



wariness over further intervention by the central bank kept it



tightly fixed in a range.



"Everybody is expecting the central bank to step in, so



we're not going to see much activity," one dealer at a major



U.S. bank said.



The central bank sold dollars on Wednesday to curb the



decline of the peso around 41.28 in the face of general



weakness in regional currencies.



Market players expected the peso to trade between 41.20 and



41.28 per dollar on Thursday with 41.40 in sight if it broke



through the bottom of that range.



TAIWAN DOLLAR	



The Taiwan dollar opened Thursday's trade at 30.69,



slightly firmer than Wednesday's close of 30.693.



But dealers said the wider picture was of downward pressure



on the Taiwan dollar in the face of a weakening yen and a



recent poor stock market performance.



    Dealers also said uncertainty surrounding Taiwan and China



added to pressure on the Taiwan dollar.



    Taiwan's Finance Minister Paul Chiu on Thursday called for



confidence in the stock market, saying the island's



fundamentals are strong and pledged to take "necessary"



measures to stabilise the market.



    Turnover through dealers on the main market was heavy at



US$155 million.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The Singapore dollar gained momentum to rise above the key



1.72 level while the market remained cautious of central bank

intervention.



    "The very weak euro, yen and higher U.S. dollar against



other regionals suggest that we are some way from the zone



where authorities might intervene, despite the recent dollar's



upside," Bank of America said in its daily market review.



Dealers said the market was driven mostly by profit-taking



with 1.7250 eyed as the crucial level for the Sing dollar.

title: Korea won ends little changed after tight trade.
text:
SEOUL, March 17 (Reuters) - The South Korean won	    -2 closed marginally lower on Friday after intervention by monetary authorities thwarted dollar-unwinding by long-position holders, dealers said.



The won closed at 1,117.3 per dollar against Thursday's close of 1,117.2. It opened at a low of 1,118.5 and touched a high of 1,117.2.


 "The market is long in dollars due to steady foreign buying of local stocks," said a foreign bank dealer. "But because of the government's dollar-buying intervention, the trading is stuck in a tight range." 

South Korea's Ministry of Finance and Economy said before the market opened it was concerned about the won's appreciation against the dollar though the level of foreign buying of local stocks had recently fallen. 

 The ministry reiterated its pledge to take action whenever necessary to stabilise the foreign exchange rate. 

 Actual dollar buying by state-run banks followed the verbal intervention from the opening bell. The intervention today was estimated at about $150 million, dealers said. 

 Net foreign stock buying was about 176 billion won on Friday, on top of 123.5 billion on Thursday, brokers said. 

 Dealers said the yen's fall against the dollar also helped curb the won's upside. 


The yen	  was at 105.97/98 at 0822 GMT against 105.46/49 late in Tokyo on Thursday.



Dealers forecast the dollar/won rate would range from 1,115 to 1,120 on Monday.



Offshore dollar/won trading was thin as spot trading was stuck in a narrow range, they said.



The six-month non-deliverable forward (NDF) won was quoted at 1,117.8/19.3 against 1,117.5/19.5 late on Thursday.



The one-year won stood at 1,119.5/23.0 against 1,119.0/21.0.

title: Emerging  FX  - Taiwan falls cushioned, won tamed.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 16 (Reuters) - Regional currencies were 

 little changed after a quiet Asian session with markets in 

 Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia shut for a Moslem holiday. 

     The euro was a little easier on both the yen and the dollar 

 as the market failed to find any concrete evidence of the 

 rumoured Bank of Japan intervention on euro/yen. 

     There was much speculation that MOF's forex chief Haruhiko 

 Kuroda, who has just returned from an OECD meeting in France, 

 may have met ECB officials to discuss intervention. 

     The euro was helped by speculation the European Central 

 Bank will raise interest rates later on Thursday. 


    TAIWAN DOLLAR	



    The Taiwan dollar was shielded from the misfortunes of the



stock market, keeping to a tight range despite mainland Chinese



threats to "shed blood" if Taiwan opted for independence.



    While sentiment towards Taiwan has soured in recent weeks



ahead of presidential elections this Saturday, downside in the



local currency has been cushioned by forex intervention by the


central bank.



Mainland Chinese Premier Zhu Rongji said the Chinese were



ready to "shed blood" to stop Taiwan from breaking away and



urged voters to not to act "on impulse".



KOREAN WON	    -2



Verbal and actual intervention by South Korea's Finance



Ministry blunted won gains spurred by persistent stock buying



by foreigners.



    Foreign funds soaked up 40.3 billion won worth of stocks by



0215 GMT after buying 95.4 billion won worth on Wednesday.



    The Finance Ministry reiterated it was ready to take action



if necessary to stabilise the rate.



    Appreciation in the won was not desirable for the country's



economy given the recent trend in the trade account, it said.



    THAI BAHT	



    The baht slipped amid concerns of further delay to



restructuring plans for Thailand's biggest debtor, Thai



Petrochemical Industry (TPI)   .



    Bangkok dealers said a landmark ruling in favour of TPI



creditors the previous day had been well-received but that



there were concerns that existing TPI management had been left



in place.



This gave the impression that the management, sitting on



unpaid debts of $3.4 billion, had won a partial victory, they



said.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



The rupiah was barely changed in thin offshore trade,



caught in a tight 7,415 to 7,480 per dollar band.



A positive outlook for Indonesian growth in 2000 and 2001



fuelled hopes the rupiah would appreciate to around the 6,685



level by year-end, dealers said.



Gross domestic product (GDP) is forecast to rise 3.86



percent in 2000 and 4.95 percent in 2001, according to a



Reuters poll.



PHILIPPINE PESO	



The peso was slightly easier after dollar demand by



corporates to repay external liabilities emerged above the



40.90 level.



    Manila dealers said players had been watching movement in



the baht in the absence of fresh market leads.



    The peso sometimes tracks the baht as the Philippines and



Thailand share similar export markets.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The Singapore dollar remained pressured in holiday-thinned



offshore trade though it was comfortably off an overnight low



of 1.7145 per dollar.



    Strong Sing dollar support was still seen at the $1.7160



level.

title: Emerging  FX  - Yen meddling sours regional mood.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 15 (Reuters) - Heavy yen	


intervention by the Bank of Japan (BOJ) weighed on regional


currencies late on Wednesday despite a brief respite for the 

 baht and peso. 

     The baht and peso edged higher after Thailand's bankrupcy 

 court ruled in favour of creditors in a landmark case involving 

 Thailand's biggest debt defaulter, Thai Petrochemical Industry 

 (TPI)   . 

     In the major currency market, the spotlight trailed on 

 dollar/yen after it jumped more than one percent to a high of 

 105.75 on the BOJ intervention. 

     The central bank last intervened a week ago, selling yen 

 for dollars to weaken the Japanese currency, which has 

 appreciated 6.4 percent against the dollar since February 22 

 amid optimism over Japan's recovery. 


    The euro	    was steady against the dollar and at the



top of its intraday range against the yen following the BOJ



moves.



    THAI BAHT	



    The baht soon surrendered a 0.2 percent gain, sparked by



news of that Thailand's Bankruptcy Court had found TPI



insolvent and ordered it to be restructured.



    The court also ruled that TPI's chief executive officer be



the interim planner for the company while creditors met to pick



their own planner to revamp the company.



    Analysts had expected a ruling in favour of TPI to hurt



Thai markets and investor perception of the government's



commitment to bankruptcy reform.



    The baht's rise was thwarted by confusion over whether


central bank governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul had threatened to



resign due to a bitter dispute with the cabinet.



    A cabinet source told Reuters Chatu had said he would step



down if proposed changes to the Bank of Thailand (BOT) Act were



approved without alterations ensuring the bank's independence.



    But the director of the BOT's legal department later denied



that Chatu had threatened to quit.



    KOREAN WON	     -2



    The won was off intraday highs of 1,115 per dollar after



the yen was swiped off recent peaks, calming fears of won


intervention by the Korean authorities.


South Korea's Ministry of Finance and Economy said it was



ready to take action to cap the won's rise against the dollar



and that it was not desirable for the won to appreciate in line



with the yen.



Dealers said the market had been reluctant to sell dollars



below 1,116/1,117 on Wednesday and that range-trading was



expected on Thursday.



    A Reuters poll showed that South Korean GDP was expected to



grow 6.8 percent in 2000 and 6.0 percent in 2001.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



    The rupiah slipped in line with other regional currencies


after trading in a tight 7,390-7,440 range.



    The rupiah market has come under slight pressure recently



amid worries the International Monetary Fund might again



suspend its loan programme to the country if key players in a



Bank Bali  banking scandal are not brought to justice.



Though the IMF warned lending might be halted the previous



day, Jakarta dealers expressed confidence the matter would be



resolved.



    Indonesian GDP was seen rising 3.86 percent in 2000 and



4.95 percent in 2001, according to a Reuters poll.



    PHILIPPINE PESO	



    The peso was off an intraday high of around 40.7 seen after



the baht steadied on the back of the TPI court ruling.



    But sentiment remained weak due to concerns over likely



U.S. rate hikes, a domestic stock manipulation scandal linked



to gaming and leisure firm BW Resource Corp  and



regional uncertainties like presidential elections in Taiwan.



    Philippine GDP was forecast to grow 3.66 percent in 2000



and 4.05 percent in 2001, according to a Reuters poll.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The Singapore dollar slid back through the 1.71 support as



the yen slid in the wake of the BOJ's dollar buying


intervention.



    With few domestic leads to trade on, analysts said the Sing



dollar was taking its cue from the yen and technical factors.



    The U.S. dollar looked well supported at S$1.7028 for the



time being, SEB Merchant Banking said in a daily report.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR	



    The Taiwan dollar kept its grip despite hefty stock market



losses as pre-election jitters and the U.S. Nasdaq's four



percent overnight drop weighed.



    Fears a pro-independence candidate might win Saturday's



presidential poll continued to discourage investors, but



dealers said the local currency's downside was being cushioned



by the central bank.



Taipei dealers said the bank had intervened actively in the



past two sessions, clearly signalling its desire for exchange



rate stability.

title: Asia Markets-Tokyo leads stocks slide,Taiwan tanks.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 13 (Reuters) - Heavy profit-taking in 

 Tokyo technology stocks prompted a sell-off in regional bourses 

 on Monday. 


    The Nikkei index	     fell three percent as



institutional investors realised gains in high-tech and



Internet stocks ahead of end-March book closings.



    Retail investors were also keeping away from the sector



despite Nasdaq's record close above the 5,000 level on Friday.



     Jakarta	     succumbed to a late bout of selling after



initially fending off the regional malaise as buyers chased



undervalued stocks.



    PRE-POLL FEARS SPOOK TAIPEI SHARES



    The Taipei stock index	     lost a hefty 6.55 percent,



with almost all shares falling by their daily seven-percent



limit as nervous investors dumped shares ahead of Saturday's



presidential election.



The market was hit by fears that already tense ties with



China could worsen if a pro-independence candidate won the



election.



Active buying by state and foreign funds should shore up



the stock market but uncertainty remains after the finance



ministry said a T$500 billion ($16.3 billion) stabilisation



fund would not be used until after the poll because of an



opposition boycott.


Currency traders said the central bank was seen buying at



T$30.77 and this should discourage a sharp drop in the Taiwan



dollar.



PHILIPPINES GETS BOND ROLLING



The Philippines issued a total $1.6 billion of new bonds in



a two-tranche deal on Friday in line with most market



expectations.



The first tranche was $600 million of 9.875 percent bonds



due 2010 at a price of 99.95 to yield 9.883 percent, and the



second tranche of $1.0 billion of 10.625 percent bonds due 2025



at 99.368 to yield 10.698 percent.



Strong demand for the bonds enabled the Philippines to



increase the size of the sale twice from an initial offer of $1



billion.



Robert Voreyer, managing director of high yield debt at



Morgan Stanley Dean Witter in Hong Kong, said most funds chose



stock markets over fixed income markets because they had been



outperformers over the past few years.



"I think opportunistically, investors are willing to look



at a variety of names, anything from a solid double-B to a



triple-C, as in the case of APP China," he told Reuters



Television.



APP China Group Ltd, a subsidiary of Asia Pulp & Paper Co



, sold its 10-year senior notes in a private placement



through Morgan Stanley Dean Witter last week.



"But I think well-structured deals that are broadly



distributed will result in fair pricing for both the issuer and



the investor," Voreyer said.



The APP deal was priced at 86.866 to yield 16.75 percent



and netted the company about $350 million after $403 million in



face value of notes were sold.



WON WANES ON DEFICIT



The won was weaker, sparked by concerns authorities might



step up dollar-buying intervention after a government official



said South Korea ran a trade deficit in early March.



A Ministry of Finance and Economy official said the country



posted a trade deficit of $1.350 billion in the first 10 days



of March.



The figure was slightly larger than the $1.348 billion



deficit in the first 10 days of February and far larger than



the $405 million deficit in the same 10 days last March.



The official said the trade deficit was expected to turn to



a surplus by the end of March as exports tend to rise sharply



toward the end of the month.



South Korea posted a provisional trade surplus of $802



million for February despite a deficit in the early part of the



month. In January, it recorded a trade deficit of $391 million,



its first since October 1997.

title: Korea won ends lower on corporate, bank dlr demand.
text:
SEOUL, Feb 24 (Reuters) - The South Korean won	    -2 ended weaker against the greenback on Thursday on dollar demand from importers and banks settling contracts for foreign investors' recent sales of local stocks, dealers said.



The won closed at 1,140.5 compared with Wednesday's close of 1,135.3.


 It opened at 1,137.0 and dropped to 1,141.4 in late morning trade on the back of the dollar's bullishness versus the yen. 

 "As the dollar/yen was well-bid at around 111 yen, there was little dollar-selling interest spotted in the local currency market," said a city bank dealer. 

 Dealers said the market saw an inflow of more than $70 million from the recent sales of local stocks by foreign investors. 

 Oil refiners and other importers also bought dollars estimated at $50 million. 

 But the dollar/won was pushed back to the 1,137 won level in afternoon trade as players eased positions after the IMF's departing managing director for Asia-Pacific Hubert Neiss said Asian nations should not resist currency appreciation pressures. 

 Neiss told a conference in Hong Kong that large current account surpluses were inevitably putting upward pressure on Asian currencies and it was useless to try to target any specific exchange rate level. 

South Korea's monetary authorities have frequently said they would intervene in the market with "smoothing out" operations if the dollar/won rate became too volatile. 

 The dollar regained ground and went back to the 1,140 won level later in the day as the monetary authorities stepped in, dealers said. 

 The Bank of Korea said on Thursday South Korea's provisional current account surplus for 1999 stood at $25 billion, down from $40.56 billion in 1998. 

 The central bank attributed the falls to increased demand for imports, spurred by the recovering domestic economy. 

 Dealers said the U.S. unit could come under pressure on exporter offers toward the end of the month if the dollar/yen pair remained stable. 

 The won is expected to move between 1,137 and 1,145 on Friday. 

 The six-month non-deliverable forward (NDF) won was quoted at 1,140/41 at 0700 GMT versus 1,136/37 late on Wednesday. 

 The one-year won stood at 1,144/45 against 1,139/41.

title: Korea c.bank  intervenes  to halt won's rise-dealers.
text:
SEOUL, Feb 10 ((Reuters) - South Korea's central bank directly intervened in the currency market to halt the won's steep rise against the dollar, dealers said on Thursday. 

 Dealers said the Bank of Korea began to buy dollars after a senior Finance Ministry official said in the afternoon the won's steep appreciation was not desirable for the country's economy. 

 The ministry official also said monetary authorities are closely watching movements of the dollar/won rate. 

 "The Bank of Korea's direct intervention indicates that the 1,120 level will be defended," said a foreign bank dealer. 

 Dealers said state-run banks, such as Korea Development Bank, have been buying dollars since the 1,129 level earlier this week. 

 The comments by the ministry official followed the won's surge to 1,119 won to the dollar, influenced by expectations of hefty dollar inflows from foreign buying of local stocks and a drop in the dollar/yen rate, dealers said.

title: Korea  central bank intervenes  to buy dlrs-dealers.

SEOUL, Jan 20 (Reuters) - South Korea's central Bank of Korea stepped into the local foreign exchange market in late afternoon trade on Thursday, buying dollars to stem the won's rise as it did earlier in the day, dealers said.

title: Korea 3-yr yields seen falling from mid-2000 - BOK.
text:
SEOUL, Jan 19 (Reuters) - South Korea's central bank governor said on Wednesday he expected the three-year corporate bond yield to begin falling from the middle of the year as the market stabilises. 

 "Generally speaking, although there are some destabilising factors seen for the early part of the year, I expect market interest rates to begin stabilising from the middle of the year," Bank of Korea Governor Chon Chol-hwan said. 

 Speaking at a breakfast session for corporate executives hosted by the Korea Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Chon said the current gap between the overnight call rate and the corporate bond yield was too large. 

 "The current gap represents two to three (percentage points of) risk premiums and inflation expectations," Chon said. "I think the gap can be narrowed by about two (percentage points) once the market gains stability." 

 The corporate bond yield closed Tuesday's session at 10.42 percent while the overnight interbank call rate, the short-term benchmark, was up five basis points at 4.65 percent. 

 Asked about the government's foreign exchange market policy, Chon said: "It is not desirable for the exchange rate to change rapidly and the government will take various measures, including smoothing operations." 

 Under terms for the 1997 bailout package arranged by the International Monetary Fund, South Korea pledged not to directly intervene in the local foreign exchange market but was given the right to conduct "smoothing operations" to stabilise the market. 

 Summarising recent economic trends, the central bank governor said the average unemployment rate for the last quarter of calendar 1999 was estimated to have risen to 5.0 percent from 4.4 percent for the previous quarter. 

 A central bank report distributed at the session showed the number of unemployed stood at an estimated 1.09 million in the October-December period, up from 971,000 in the third quarter. 

 The unemployment average for 1999 is estimated at 6.4 percent with 1.37 million unemployed, compared with 6.8 percent and 1.46 million for 1998. 

 Chon reaffirmed the central bank's forecasts for 2000, including 3.1 percent growth in the consumer price index, the main inflation indicator, up from 0.8 percent for 1999. 

 This year's gross domestic product is forecast to grow by 7.2 percent on year, following growth of a projected 10.2 percent for last year, he said.
