title: FOCUS - S.Korean economic planners target bond yields.
text:
SEOUL, Jan 19 (Reuters) - South Korea's top economic planners on Wednesday said long-term interest rates were too high and that cheaper funds were needed to ensure stable economic growth. 

 The finance minister and the central bank governor said the three-year corporate bond yield - the benchmark long-term interest rate - was inappropriately high. 

 The comments buoyed the domestic bond market and fuelled speculation that authorities would soon announce steps to increase demand for bonds and drive down yields. 

 The corporate bond yield was 10.42 percent on Tuesday. 

 "Generally speaking, although there are some destabilising factors seen for the early part of the year, I expect market interest rates to begin stabilising from the middle of the year," Bank of Korea governor Chon Chol-hwan said. 

 Speaking at a business breakfast hosted by the Korea Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Chon said the gap between the overnight call rate and the corporate bond yield was too large. 

 "The current gap represents two to three (percentage points of) risk premiums and inflation expectations," Chon said. 

 "I think the gap can be narrowed by about two (percentage points) once the market gains stability." 

 The corporate bond yield closed two basis points lower at 10.42 percent, sharply higher than a 52-week low of 7.23 percent set in April last year. The overnight interbank call rate was up a slight two basis points at 4.67 percent as of 0735 GMT. 

 Finance Minister Lee Hun-jai, who took the post last week, said separately on Wednesday that local companies would be unable to withstand long-term interest rates of over 10 percent and that the rates must be stabilised below 10 percent. 

 "I think maintaining long-term interest rates below 10 percent is a key policy in aiming to stabilise the economy," said Lee, who had led financial and corporate restructuring over the past two years as head of the financial regulator. 

 DUSTING OFF THE WELCOME MAT 

 Bond traders said there was speculation the government might soon introduce a plan to exempt foreign investors from taxes on capital gains and interest earned on domestic government bonds. 

 "Local investors such as investment trusts and banks do not have the (additional) purchasing power to push down the bond yields," said one senior trader at Hyundai Securities. 

 "This has led some in the market to speculate that the government will try to lure a more active participation from offshore-based investors by giving them benefits such as tax exemptions," he added. 

 Finance ministry officials were not available for comment. 

 South Korea lifted most regulations on foreign investment in the domestic bond market in late 1997 in an effort to bring in foreign funds and ease a foreign exchange shortage. 

 But foreign investment has been lukewarm on Korean bonds, partly because of complicated trading and tax practices and because most Korean issues are rated below investment grade. 

 Asked for a view on the local currency, Chon read a prepared note summarising the finance ministry's stand. 

 "It is not desirable for the exchange rate to change rapidly and the government will take various measures, including smoothing operations," Chon said. 

 Under the terms of a 1997 bailout package arranged by the International Monetary Fund, South Korea agreed not to directly intervene in the foreign exchange market but was given the right to conduct "smoothing operations" to stabilise the market. 

 South Korea fears the won's rapid appreciation could hurt exports, which have yet to fully recover their momentum, by depriving exporters of price advantages. 

 The comment, if not new, helped boost demand for the greenback from offshore players as Chon's remarks reminded them of the strong government intention to intervene. 

 The won ended the day's trading at 1,132.5 per dollar, compared with Tuesday's closing rate of 1,127.0 per dollar, after ranging from 1,126.0 to 1,132.0. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 2000.

title: Asia Markets-Nikkei rallies as Wall St steadies.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 17 (Reuters) - Reassurance over the tame 

 nature of U.S. inflation lifted many Asian markets on Monday, 

 though Hong Kong and the Philippines were weighed down by 

 lingering interest rate fears. 

     Most markets drew their strength from a record closing high 


in the Dow Jones industrial index	    and fresh gains in the
technology-laden Nasdaq composite index	     on Friday, after



key U.S. inflation data for December came in lower than



expected.



    CPI rose 0.2 percent, compared to expectations for an



average 0.3 percent increase according to a recent Reuters poll.



    That fuelled buying in Japan's Nikkei 225	    , pushing



it to its highest close in two and a half years.



    Laggard Malaysian stocks, meanwhile, stole the limelight



with gains of more than four percent.



The bright mood in stocks rubbed off onto most regional


currencies, forcing the monetary authorities in South Korea to


intervene and Taiwan's central bank to remain vigilant against



sharp upward pressure.



Singapore stocks bucked the regional up-trend, shedding



more than two percent as fund managers banked profits and some



re-weighted their portfolios, shifting money into markets like



Malaysia.



FUND NEWS BOLSTERS TAIEX



Plans to launch a T$500 billion (US$16.2 billion) stock



stabilisation fund to absorb potential shocks to Taiwan shares



and a further loosening of restrictions for foreign investors



lifted the TAIEX to a 28-month closing high.



The index ended 2.1 percent higher, with local brokers



anticipating a rise to 9,500 or 10,000 sometime soon despite



likely bouts of profit-taking along the way.



    Buying was focused more on traditional industrial sectors



than on recently high-flying technology counters, dealers said.



    Taiwan's parliament approved a cabinet proposal to set up a



stabilisation fund at the weekend, aimed at keeping the stock



market on an even keel in case relations with China



deteriorated.



Although this could avert tremors like those last year when



souring relations caused Taiwan stocks to dive 14 percent, some



analysts were sceptical of the political motives behind the



move.



"As an institutional investor, I would be sceptical as to



whether this is positive...I would obviously question the



motives for the government to invest in their own stock market,"



Robert Penaloza, investment manager at Aberdeen Asset



Management, told Reuters Television.



"The government should perhaps stick to liberalisation



measures that they're looking to implement...like allowing



foreigners to list their shares into the market or even enabling



them to buy more shares in state-owned banks," he said.



The island's financial regulator also moved to ease listing



rules for foreign firms to improve the market's international



profile. Foreign firms can now list a minimum 20 million shares



locally instead of 30 million and they only need to show annual



profit growth of six percent instead of eight percent



previously.



KOREA POLICY SEEN UNCHANGED



South Korea's ministry of finance, led by newly appointed



minister Lee Hun-jai, announced its economic targets for 2000



and indicated no change in economic policy.



    It said it expected the economy to expand around six



percent in 2000 after growing an estimated 10 percent in 1999.



    It also said it would aim to stabilise long-term interest



rates below 10 percent this year and focus on containing



inflation under three percent.



    The country's current account surplus was expected to total



$12 billion in 2000, compared with an estimated $26 billion



surplus for 1999, it said.



    The won firmed to its highest level since late 1997 early



in the day as foreign funds extended their recent stock



shopping spree but the central bank took it off its intraday



high.



The bank's renewed efforts to temper the speed of its rise



were somewhat mixed, with the won ending the day at 1,121 -



its strongest finish versus the dollar since November 1997.


Interventionist ways were also set to continue in the



domestic bond market.



    The top manager of the country's bond market stabilisation



fund, Paik Kyung-Ho, said the fund would continue intervening in



the market until February 8, when investors in Daewoo Group



 bond funds can redeem up to 95 percent of their money



compared to 80 percent now.

title: ANALYSIS - Asia  FX intervention , old habits die hard.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 12 (Reuters) - Asian currency markets are facing more intervention this year, with many governments unwilling to leave domestic currency values to the forces of supply and demand despite signs of solid economic recovery. 

Foreign exchange analysts say that in light of rising inflationary pressures such intervention may cause more problems than it resolves, and question whether in the long run it can be successful in stopping currency gains that reflect economic fundamentals. 

 Recent interventions by South Korea and Taiwan show the reluctance of some Asian governments to stay away from the forex markets, analysts say. 

 "They are likely to continue with their King Canute policy," said Marshall Gittler, head of the global currency risk group at Bank of America in Hong Kong, referring to a Viking king of old who thought he was powerful enough to hold back the tide. 

 OLD HABITS DIE HARD...IF THEY DIE AT ALL 

 The Bank of Korea jumped into the market on the first trading day of 2000 to rein in the won as it surged to its highest level in two years on the back of a strong tide of capital inflows. 

 It has been curbing the won's rise although most analysts believe the currency is undervalued. The latest Citibank forecast said the won should rise to 1,050 per dollar by the second quarter and 1,000 in the fourth. 

 Dealers are on a sustained won intervention vigil, especially after President Kim Dae-jung said in a New Year message that Korea's usable foreign reserves would rise to $100 billion by the end of 2000, around 35 percent up on their end-1999 level. 

 IT'S NOT JUST SOUTH KOREA 

 Elsewhere, the Central Bank of China, Taiwan's central bank, was also in the market last week to curb the local dollar's rise. 

 And there were rumours the central bank of Singapore, one of the region's most efficient economies, stepped in to stem the domestic currency's gains. 

 There was no official denial of intervention but Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong was quoted as saying Singapore has never depended on a weak currency to stay competitive. 

 JAPAN LEADS INTERVENTION BINGE 

 The most glaring example of government intervention in Asia would of course be the Bank of Japan, which has intervened in currency markets some 14 times since June to check the rising yen. 

 The most recent intervention on January 4 - Japan's first trading day of the new year - took the dollar from around 101.46 yen to highs of around 103.17 yen. 

 The dollar has since strengthened to above 105 yen, taking some heat out of the yen's extended rise, at least for now. 

 Japanese finance officials issue almost daily warnings about the economic risks of an excessively strong yen, but analysts have increasingly begun to question their arguments - as well as their success rate. 

 Given that dollar/yen once rose above 160 in April 1990 and fell as low as 79.70 in May 1995, last year's 101-125 range looks fairly stable. 

 And if the strong yen merely reflects a higher assessment of Japan's economy, it should not be causing such concern. 

 Deutsche Bank argues Japanese macroeconomic variables have historically been strongest in years following a yen rise, which is in some ways equivalent to a tax cut. 

 "Japanese corporate profits are decidedly better when the yen is strong," the bank said in a report. 

 "Corporate profits on average rose by 11 percent during 

  years when the yen strengthened against the dollar...and fell 

  by five percent in years when the yen was weak," it said. 

INTERVENTION COULD WORK, BUT... 

 Analysts said Asian governments' desire to control their currency markets was not entirely unjustified, given that the aim was to stave off volatility and support the key exports sector. 

 But sometimes the line between effective and useless intervention could be very thin. Badly executed intervention can distort the market and raise false expectations. 

 "In theory, intervention does have some benefits. Currencies tend to overshoot and companies cannot handle such volatility," said Supavud Saicheua, head of economics and strategies at Merrill Lynch in Bangkok. 

 But he added that governments might not know where best to draw that line in the sand. 

 "Before the crisis, the Bank of Thailand thought the baht should be at 25 to the dollar and kept defending it at that level," he said. 

 "The result was disastrous." 

 SOMETHING HAS TO GIVE 

 The bottom line is that Asian governments cannot expect to have the best of all worlds: a strong economic recovery and subsequent capital inflows do not gel with a policy of keeping the currency soft and interest rates low. 

 To deliberately keep currencies weak to boost exports might not be a viable option at this juncture and may actually be unnecessary, given that much depends on global demand. 

 "Intervention can work short-term," said Chan Chia Lin, head of research at ABN AMRO Bank in Singapore. 

 "It can give you the best of both worlds - weak currencies and low interest rates. But given the vigour of the recovery, it might not be viable," she said. 

 "Export demand is being driven more by the economic recovery and global demand rather than having competitive currencies."

title: Korea won closes lower, reined in by  intervention .
text:
SEOUL, Dec 9 (Reuters) - South Korea's won	    -2 weakened against the dollar on Thursday, sent back into the 1,130s by direct dollar buying by central bank and government verbal intervention as well as short dollar covering by banks, dealers said.



Trade was light as most players were concerned over direct dollar sales by the Bank of Korea, they said.


 The won ended the day at 1,130.1 compared with Wednesday's close of 1,126.0. 

 It opened at 1,127.0 and ranged between 1,125.0 and 1,135.0. 

 "Trades were mostly inactive for the day as strong early intervention by the central bank kept players out of the market with no noticeable orders spotted," said a dealer at a domestic bank. 

 Before the opening bell, the Ministry of Finance and Economy made comments they would act on the won's rise to prevent export competitiveness from deteriorating. 

 With the market shrugging off those remarks, the Bank of Korea came into the market and bought dollars aimed at showing the authorities' strong intention to stem the won's rise, dealers said. 

 "While the won's rise was checked for the day, the market is still dollar-heavy as a number of domestic firms are lined up for dollar sales," said another dealer at a foreign bank. 

 He said the authorities do not have much room to step into the market directly not only because of inflationary risks but also a lack of the local unit. 

 "They are saying they are going to issue forex bonds to secure the won but for now that looks hazy as the government is still preoccupied with preventing interest rates from getting out of hand," he said. 

 In the afternoon, the finance ministry pointed out that the state-run Korea Asset Management Corp (KAMCO) is ready to take over foreign currency-denominated bad loans from banks. 

 It said to do so, KAMCO could secure dollars from the domestic forex market. 

 Speculative players in the offshore market were also on the sidelines, dealers said. 

 On Friday, the won/dollar pair is seen moving in a similar range, they said. 


In late trade, the won/yen rate stood at 10.94/96 compared to 10.94/95 late Wednesday, while the Japanese unit was at 103.05/08	  versus the dollar, compared to 102.78/81 late Wednesday.



The six-month non-deliverable forward won stood at 1,131/33 as of 0700 GMT versus 1,128/30 late Wednesday.



The one-year non-deliverable forward won was quoted at 1,138/40 versus 1,136/38. ((Kim Kyoung-Wha, Seoul Newsroom +822-727-5647, fax +822-727-5666, seoul.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: INTERVIEW - S.Korea bond fund says to cap yields.
text:
SEOUL, Nov 29 (Reuters) - South Korea's Bond Market Stabilisation Fund will continue to intervene in the local debt market aiming to prevent benchmark three-year bond yields from rising from current levels, a senior fund official said on Monday. 

 "The fund will ensure that the three-year government and corporate bond yields do not rise from current levels before the year's end," the fund's chief manager Paik Kyung-ho told Reuters in a telephone interview. 

 Paik also said he expected bond yields to begin drifting lower next year if the local currency's appreciation against the dollar continues and if international oil prices decline. 

 "We are expecting the market to turn bullish next year with the market's long-term interest rates declining," he said. 

 Paik's comments come less than a week after the stabilisation fund intervened last Wednesday to push down the benchmark three-year treasury bond yield to 8.60 percent from 9.04 percent. 

 Bond yields had steadily risen as investors shunned the longer-dated three-year issues on expectations the country's rapid economic recovery will lead to inflationary pressure next year. 

 Government officials led by the Ministry of Finance and Economy have played down the threat of inflationary pressure rising next year and said they would take measures to ensure long-term interest rates stay stable. 

 Uncertainty over the direction of long-term rates and the fear of further intervention by the stabilisation fund have nearly paralysed the local bond market, locking the benchmark yield at 8.60 percent since the fund intervened last Wednesday. 

 Market players have also said the stabilisation fund's intervention suppression of the benchmark three-year yield has distorted the country's yield curve with the three-year yield falling below those of one-and two-year assets. 

 Last Friday, the benchmark yield closed at 8.60 percent while the the 364-day issue closed at 8.65 percent and two-year Monetary Stabilisation Bonds ended at 9.01 percent. 

 But Paik said the fund's role was to stabilise the benchmark yield and that other market players should take on the responsibility of resolving the distorted yield curve.

title: ANALYSIS - Korea under fire over won  intervention .
text:
SEOUL, Nov 17 (Reuters) - The South Korean government is under fire over its efforts to sap the strength of its currency, as it tries to steer a course toward an export-led recovery while heading off inflationary pressures, analysts said on Wednesday. 

 The central Bank of Korea insists it is just smoothing out volatile trade and is not trying to dictate market trends. 

 Whatever the case, the irrepressible won was back on its robust course Tuesday, closing at 1,177.8 compared with Monday's close of 1,182, despite heavy government intervention. 

 Its strength is largely a result of foreign investors piling into the stock market, analysts said. Some $1.5 billion has flowed into the market so far this month from abroad. 

 WON SEEN UNDERVALUED WITH INFLATION 

 Many analysts say the won is undervalued given the current strength of the economic recovery and potential inflationary pressures building up in the economy. 

 "The Bank of Korea must let the won go higher to absorb inflationary pressure that is expected to intensify next year," said an economist at Samsung Research Institute. 

 But Hannuri Securities economist Lee Chong-won said the government wanted a weaker won to achieve its $25-billion trade surplus target for this year. In January to October, South Korea posted a $19 billion trade surplus year-on-year. 

 The intervention looks clumsy to some. 

 "The government seems to be forgetting hard lessons that it learned over the financial crisis and returning to old practices of attempting to put the exchange rate under its control," said an economist at LG Economic Research. 

 RESERVES HAVE RISEN 10 TIMES 

 Two years ago, the central bank squandered its foreign exchange reserves in a futile effort to prop up the downward spiralling won during the "Asian Contagion" currency crisis. 

 Seoul was forced to turn to the International Monetary Fund for a $58.35 billion bail-out when its reserves dipped to below $6 billion in early December 1997. 

 But now reserves have risen by more than 10 times to $68.4 billion as of November 15. The finance ministry said on Tuesday reserves might top $70 billion in November. Dealers construed that to mean the authorities plan to stay in the market. 

 Extensive dollar purchases by state banks, ranging between $100 million and $300 million per day this month, are the main factor shoring up the dollar for now, dealers analysts said. 

 The government is taking a multi-pronged approach to beating down the won. It will issue 5 trillion ($4.2 billion) in won-denominated bonds this month, the proceeds of which will be used to buy dollars. It is also moving forward a year-end deadline for banks to provision for foreign currency loan losses. 

 NOT A FULLY CONVERTIBLE CURRENCY A central bank official said the government was just trying to keep an embryonic market on an even keel. The won is not a fully convertible currency and the market is not that liquid. 

 "Since the local market has not fully ripened, authorities need to meddle to help the market find an equilibrium in demand and supply," said the official. 

 Dollar demand will pick up in the next few months because banks will need $4 billion to pay back foreign currency loans due by April 15, the official said. 

 Domestic financial institutions also have to set aside about $1.4-1.5 billion in foreign currency loan loss reserves against possible losses to the Daewoo Group, he added. 

South Korea intervenes by instructing the Bank of Korea as well as state-run banks, including Korea Development Bank and Export-Import Bank of Korea, to purchase currencies. 

 The Bank must tell the IMF when it intervenes under their agreement. So far, the IMF has not objected, the official said. 

 Steve Xu, regional economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Hong Kong, said the government should stop intervening. "It might work today or tomorrow or next week. It's not going to work in the end," he said. 

 "With the election coming up, the government seems preoccupied with sustaining exports and economic recovery." 

 South Korea will hold a general election in April.

title: ASIA  FOREX  - Mixed as yen slips in cautious trade.
text:
0155 GMT - Asian regional currencies were mixed in early 

 trade, with the dollar higher against the yen amid 

 short-covering ahead of the weekend. 

     Traders in Tokyo said the yen still had a firm bias as 

 investors remained keen to buy the Japanese currency. 

     But the market was cautious about pushing it up 

 aggressively ahead of a weekend meeting of deputy finance 

 ministers and central bankers of the 14 Manila Framework member 

 countries in Singapore. 

 Jitters over possible intervention by the Bank of Japan to 

 tame the yen swirled around the market overnight but the fears 

 were spurred by a stream of vague rumours. 

 *** The rupiah was holding steady despite news Indonesia's 

central bank had found evidence of crimes in the Bank Bali 

 scandal . 

Central bank deputy governor Subarjo Joyosumarto told 

 reporters after a meeting with police officials on Thursday 

 that a controversial interbank loan had not been recorded in 

 the bank's financial reports. 

     The findings have been passed to the police for 

 investigation. 

     Fresh violence between supporters and opponents of 

 independence in East Timor is another factor that could 

 pressure the rupiah. 

     At least three people were killed in violent clashes on 

 Thursday, casting a shadow over the troubled territory's final 

 day of campaigning for a U.N.-organised referendum on 

 independence, due on Monday. 

 *** The peso was little changed in pre-weekend trade. 

 All eyes are on a weekly meeting of the central bank's 

 Monetary Board amid expectations of a hike in bank reserve 

 requirements. 

 The peso is teetering at nine-month lows due to the 

 narrower spreads between domestic and U.S. interest rates, 

 exacerbated by the Federal Reserve rate hike on Tuesday. 

Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said on Thursday 

 he might have to raise bank reserve requirements if domestic 

 Treasury bill yields fail to rise at Monday's auction. 

 Philippine production indexes showed mixed results in June, 

 with value up 2.3 percent on a year earlier and volume down 1.1 

 percent. 

 The government is due to release second quarter GDP data 

 around 0230 GMT. Socio-economic Planning Secretary Felipe 

 Medalla said on Thursday the economy may have grown 3.0 percent 

 on the year in the second quarter. 

     *** Hong Kong is also due to report second quarter GDP 

 numbers at around 0800 GMT. 

     A Reuters poll of 11 economists produced an average 

 forecast for a 1.2 percent contraction in the second quarter 

 from a year earlier. 

     The government on Thursday reported a significant 

 turnaround in trade performance, with total exports in July 

 rising 3.0 percent year-on-year and July imports up 3.7 

 percent. 

 They were the first year-on-year rises in both categories 

 since early 1998. Chief government economist K.Y. Tang said 

 they supported his forecast that second quarter GDP would be 

 flat from a year ago, or at least contract at a slower rate 

 than in the year to the first quarter. 

     July month-on-month increases in exports and imports came 

 in at 10.9 percent and 10.4 percent respectively. 

     *** South Korea's won headed lower as fears of government 

intervention continue to pervade the market. 

     A meeting between Daewoo and foreign creditors, originally 

 set for Friday, has been delayed. A Daewoo spokesman told 

 Reuters that both sides needed more time to include Thursday's 

 new debt workout programme in their negotiation plans. 

     The spokesman thought it unlikely that the meeting would 

 take place anytime this week. 

     Daewoo's creditors decided on Thursday to put the embattled 

 conglomerate's 12 core companies under a workout programme, 

 freezing debt payments temporarily while creditors take over 

 managerial control and discuss debt rescheduling. 

 The government will support the process through a series 

 of 

 measures, which include guaranteeing the discounting of 

 commercial paper issued by Daewoo firms. 

 *** Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said on 

 Thursday that the ringgit would remain pegged at 3.80 to the 

 dollar, but added that he did not know if the peg would 

 continue for another year. 

     The central bank also said the present system of capital 

 gains taxes of foreign portfolio investments would remain. 

     The first anniversary of capital controls imposed in 

 Malaysia to protect the economy from speculators falls on 

 Monday.

title: ASIA  FOREX  - Regionals end firmer, yen gains ground.
text:
0930 GMT - The Asian regional currencies were firmer in 

 late business with the yen getting to its highest level since 

 mid-February. 

 The markets are watchful ahead of the second half of U.S. 

 Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins 

 testimony before the Senate Banking Committee. 

 The Fed has said that Greenspan's speech, scheduled for 

 1400 GMT, would mostly be a rehash of the previous week's 

 comments. Market analysts saw this as an attempt to calm 

 financial markets. 

 *** The rupiah gained as the market remains uncertain about 

 the political backdrop. 

 But the authorities are still trying to talk it up with 

 top economics minister Ginandjar Kartasasmita saying 6,000 would be a 

 good level. 

 "At the present moment, a value of around 6,500 is 

 comfortable," he said. "There is room for improvement. Around 

 6,000 would be a good figure for us." 

 But he also said there would be no intervention to get the 

 rupiah to 6,000. 

 Ginandjar is in Paris meeting with international donors. 

 Bank Indonesia governor Syahril Sabirin said the interest 

 rate on one-month central bank certificates will fall less than 

 one percentage point at the weekly auction scheduled for later. 

 Separately, Indonesia's net foreign reserves rose to $16.15 

 billion on July 23 from $16.11 billion on July 15. 

 *** South Korea's won was firmer despite ongoing verbal 

intervention from the government and dollar purchases by 

 state-run banks. 

 Dealers said state-run banks mopped up nearly $400 million 

 on Wednesday and it seemed the government was resolved to keep 

 dollar/won above 1,200. 

 Finance Minister Kang Bong-kyun said creditors will 

 eventually liquidate $8.3 billion in collateral put up by 

 Daewoo Group in return for four trillion won in emergency 

 loans. 

 Creditors are expected to whittle down the chaebol's 22 

 affiliates to just two firms and sell most of the rest. 

 This followed the government's move on Tuesday to leave the 

 fate of the embattled conglomerate squarely in its creditors' 

 hands. 

 In other news, June's current account surplus was reported 

 at $2.46 billion, down from $3.39 billion a year ago but up 

 from $1.99 billion in May 1999. 

 Exports in June rose 10.6 percent year-on-year to $12.78 

 billion, and imports spiked 31.2 percent to $9.85 billion. 

 From January to June 1999, exports rose 0.7 percent to 

 $67.58 billion year-on-year, and imports rose 14.4 percent to 

 $52.50 billion. 

 *** The Singapore dollar firmed, but gains were limited 

 amid rumours of central bank intervention on Tuesday when the 

currency rose to six-month highs. 

Central bank chief Lee Hsien Loong told Reuters Television 

 that the country's growth forecast for the year will be 

 upgraded following better-than-expected performance in the 

 second quarter. 

 The revised forecast will be announced on August 9, 

 Singapore's National Day holiday. 

 Lee also said the central bank was "very comfortable" with 

 the level of the Sing dollar on a trade-weighted basis.

title: S.Korea Won Dn Early; Local Bks Buy Dlrs To Up Provisions
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--The South Korean won is down early Thursday against the U.S. dollar as local banks buy the U.S. currency in an apparent effort to increase their bad loan provisions, traders say. 

 Around 0059 GMT (8:59 p.m. Wednesday EDT), the dollar was trading at 1,176.40 won, up from Wednesday's closing level of KRW1,173. 

 The dollar appeared well supported early Thursday as local banks buy dollars in an apparent effort to increase their dollar reserves for potential bad loans, traders said. The U.S. currency is also being supported by the selling of local stocks by foreign investors, traders said. 

 In addition, the market remains vigilant of the government's determination to slow the won's recent rise, traders said. The Bank of Korea, South Korea's central bank, has been intervening recently in the local currency market to support the U.S. currency in a bid to protect Korean exporters. However, no direct intervention was seen early Thursday, they said. 

 "The government's intention to raise the dollar rate is so strong," said a Seoul market watcher. 

 Traders expect the dollar to trade Thursday between KRW1,172 and KRW1,180.

title: Asian govts watch nervously as  currencies  climb.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 2 (Reuters) - Following Asia's bitter two-year experience with slumping currencies and ballooning overseas debt, governments in the region should now be breathing a sigh of relief that exchange rates are improving. 

 But the upturn in Asian currencies is worrying regional governments anxious to protect fledgling export recoveries. 

 Central banks hold little hope of turning back the tide of cash flooding into their markets. The most they can aim to do is merely slow the flow. 

 Japan is the most blatant case of a government finding it impossible to stand aside and watch a rising currency savage export earnings. 

 Its repeated dollar buying and verbal onslaughts since the release of unexpectedly strong first quarter data have kept the yen from firming beyond 118.00 to the dollar. 

 The central banks of Korea and Taiwan - Japan's major export rivals - have also been spotted buying dollars in the market to counter sharp rises in Korea's won and the Taiwan dollar. 

 While Thailand's central bank and finance ministry have denied wanting to manipulate the exchange rate to benefit exporters, the government has halved its 1999 export growth forecast to 2.1 percent. 

 And with Deputy Prime Minister Supachai Panitchpakdi saying unchecked rallies in the baht could hurt exports, many dealers suspect Thailand may seek to keep a lid on the currency. 

 But analysts say regional central banks are unlikely to do anything more than merely slow the pace of appreciation. 

 "A lot of Asian policymakers still remember the result of currency manipulations in the past. Central banks are so scared now that they are really committed to a more flexible exchange rate regime," said Quah Hong Chye, strategist at HypoVereinsbank. 

 "I don't think they are trying to manipulate their currencies to alter the direction. They are just intervening to reduce the speed and volatility of the movement," he said. 

 The Bank of Korea has been less than coy about its intentions, frequently expressing disapproval with the won's sharp rise and buying dollars through state banks as well as directly in the local currency market. 

 But with the economy growing an unexpectedly robust 4.6 percent year-on-year in the first quarter and the stock market revisiting mid-1996 highs, the central bank has had to live with a stronger won. 

 "The Korean economy is fundamentally recovering so they have to let it appreciate. But had they not intervened, we would have been at 1,150 (won per dollar) months ago," said Quah. 

 The won was trading at around 1,167 to the dollar on Friday. 

 The International Monetary Fund, which arranged a near $60 billion bailout package for South Korea in late 1997, has endorsed the central bank's interventions as aimed at smoothing moves in the currency, not weakening it. 

 Despite all the official fretting, Korean exports reached a record monthly high of $12.98 billion in June, suggesting the won's strength is not putting too much strain on trade. 

 "There are renewed inflows coming back into the country and to have that stall the export recovery is certainly the last thing they would want to see," said an analyst at a U.S. investment house. 

 "But on the other hand, there isn't really a country whose currency is appreciating in isolation so there isn't a loss of relative competitiveness," he said. 

 Much of the caution about a premature currency appreciation is rooted in the knowledge that a major external shock could still trip up the Asian recovery. 

 "Things are improving certainly, but it doesn't mean they couldn't get worse if the U.S. goes in for a hard landing, or if the Japanese economy doesn't pick up as people expect," said Thio Chin Loo, strategist at Paribas. 

 "So all things considered, it's probably a fair policy to expect them to keep their currencies stable in this economic environment," she added.

title: Korea won ends little lower, exporters limit loss.
text:
SEOUL, June 30 (Reuters) - The South Korean won	  closed slightly weaker against the dollar on Wednesday mainly due to the central bank's intervention, but export deals limited the won's further decline.



Dealers said the Bank of Korea bought about $100 million to $150 million in early trade. But the bank declined to confirm the action.


 The won closed at 1,157.6, compared with Tuesday's close of 1,157.0. It opened at 1,157.5 and ranged between 1,156.0 and 1,162.5. 

 "The central bank's dollar purchases lifted the dollar trading level above 1,160 won, but export deals were lined up at that level," said a local bank dealer. 

 Dollar sales by offshore players also pulled the dollar lower, dealers said. 

 A foreign bank dealer said local banks placed strong bids to buy dollars. 

 "It shows that the local banks had a psychological pressure to follow the government's move to stabilise the currency market," he said. 

 On Tuesday, assistant governor of the central bank urged local bank directors that the banks set aside foreign exchange loan-loss provisions in their positions, a move which would soak up at least $2 billion from the market. 

 The currency market largely ignored the inflation data, as the market concentrated on other factors like exporter deals and government intervention, traders said. 

South Korea's finance ministry said on Wednesday the inflation rate, gauged by the consumer price index (CPI), was an average of 0.6 percent for the six months of this year, the lowest six-month figure since 1965 when South Korea began to keep records on inflation. 

 The six-month non-deliverable forward (NDF) won was quoted at 1,160/63 won, while the one-year stood at 1,165/67.

title: Asian  Currencies  Drift Lower; Mkts Wind Dn At Month-End
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Most Asian currencies drifted lower against the U.S. dollar in thin end of the month trading Tuesday. 

 Activity was dominated by position adjustments as regional markets entered what one foreign exchange broker in Singapore described as the "twighlight zone" ahead of the end of the half-year and an expected increase in U.S. interest rates. 

 Despite the fall, market sentiment toward regional currencies remains broadly positive. Traders and investors alike continue to strongly favor the South Korean won, whose drop Tuesday was impelled largely by U.S. dollar purchases said to have been executed on behalf of South Korea's central bank. 

 Although repeated interventions by the Bank of Korea in recent sessions have successfully supported the U.S. dollar above KRW1,150, dealers and analysts agree that it is only a matter of time before the U.S. currency renews its slide. 

 "The market trend is clear, said Lian Chia Liang," foreign exchange and interest rate analyst at Merrill Lynch in Singapore. "Over the course of the second half of the year the won will move towards KRW1,100" against the U.S. dollar. 

 According to Lian, real effective exchange rate calculations indicate that a fair value for the won is currently around KRW900 to the dollar. 

 Although he does not believe the nominal exchange rate will approach that level in the short- to medium-term, Lian says that powerful underlying forces will continue to strengthen the South Korean currency, despite the government's continued efforts to absorb dollars from the foreign exchange market. 

 "Government policy may slow the pace of the won's appreciation somewhat, but I doubt very much if we will see the won back at KRW1,200" to the dollar, Lian said. 

 At the end of local dealings Tuesday, the U.S. dollar closed at KRW1,157.00, up from KRW1,156.20 the previous day.

title: S.Korea bank officials to meet over  forex  market.
text:
SEOUL, June 28 (Reuters) - South Korea said on Monday it would discuss the foreign exchange market trend with local bank directors in a meeting early on June 29. 

 The central Bank of Korea said its assistant governor Yoon Kwi-sup would meet managing directors at international divisions of local banks at 1030 KST (0130 GMT) to discuss the general movement of the currency market. 

 "We are expecting comments about controlling the supply and demand (of the dollar)," said a central bank official. 

 He did not elaborate. 

South Korea's central bank has intervened in the foreign exchange market several times in the past two weeks to slow the won's rise against the dollar. 

 The won recently strengthened on dollar supplies from exporter deals and on news that credit rating agency Fitch IBCA had upgraded South Korea's sovereign ratings. 

 South Korea is concerned the won's appreciation will hurt its export competitiveness and its economic recovery.

title: S.Korea won opens almost flat, eyes on govt moves.
text:
SEOUL, June 25 (Reuters) - The South Korean won	  opened barely changed against the dollar on Friday, and traders said they would continue to watch for verbal intervention by government officals or dollar purchases by the central bank.



The won opened at 1,158.0, compared with Thursday's close of 1,157.9.

 "Players would be cautious in trading because of a possible intervention by the government, but the dollar won't be able to escape from pressure to fall," said a foreign bank dealer. 

 Another dealer said: "The government will feel burdened to absorb dollars today because the market is heavy with the greenback." 

 Dealers said the commerce minister's comment on the exchange rate had little impact on the market as verbal comments by government officials had lost their market-moving power. 

 "The government would do its best so that the won/dollar rate does not hurt exports," said minister Chung Duck-koo at a breakfast meeting. 

 The dollar rose on Thursday on news that Fitch IBCA upgraded Korea's sovereign ratings and on comments by IMF's Hubert Neiss. 

 Neiss said South Korea's intervention in the currency market was not aimed at weakening the won, but at smoothing the won's movement. 

 Dealers said the dollar would move between 1,155 and 1,160.

title: ASIA MARKETS-Stocks stirred, not shaken by Wall St.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 25 (Reuters) - An overnight drop on Wall 

 Street took the shine off Asian stocks on Friday, though South 

 Korean and Thai markets were comforted by credit-rating 

 upgrades. 

     THAILAND BACK AT INVESTMENT GRADE 

     Fitch IBCA put Thailand back on investment grade, citing a 

 marked improvement in external debt and the liquidity 

 situation. 

     It raised Thailand's long-term foreign currency rating to 

 BBB minus from BB plus and its short-term rating to F3 from B. 

     The news was well received by Thai stock and currency

 markets, especially after Moody's Investors Services said this 

 week that Thai banks remained heavily insolvent. 

     But the government said the Moody's report was outdated and 

 failed to take into account Thailand's bigger banks, which have 

 been recapitalised. 

     Thailand's annual budget, now before parliament, forecasts 

 one percent growth this year and three percent for 2000, with 

 inflation seen at just 0.5 percent this year and three percent 

 next. 

 Deputy Finance Minister Pisit Leeatham said Thailand was 

 happy with the level of the baht, which strengthened sharply 

 this week after the central bank said it would not intervene to 

 curb its rise. 

 But in a sign that competitiveness was a source of concern, 

 Deputy Prime Minister Supachai Panitchpakdi said the baht would 

 be too strong for exports if it reached 35 to the dollar. 

 KOSPI HOLDS UP, WON HEADS FOR 1,150 

 Seoul stocks managed a slightly firmer finish despite some 

 profit-taking after Wall Street's fall. 

     But traders said sentiment was lifted by Fitch IBCA's move 

 to upgrade South Korea's sovereign ratings on Thursday. 

     Fitch raised the long-term foreign currency rating to BBB 

 from BBB-, citing the strong reassertion of South Korea's 

 traditional economic fundamentals. 

     The won gained from exporter dollar sales, but its rise was 

 held in check by fears of central bank intervention after the 

 commerce ministry said South Korea would try to keep won-dollar 

 movements from hurting exports. But analysts said the won 

 remained on a longer-term uptrend and the central bank's dollar 

 buying was increasingly being viewed as an effort to smooth, 

 rather than stop its rise. 

 "The central bank is intent on keeping the won quite stable in 

 the short term," said Thio Chin Loo, strategist at Paribas. 

 "But longer term, there should be a greater appetite from 

 the authorities to allow the won to strengthen with signs of 

 economic growth and with some inflationary pressures," she told 

 Reuters Television. 

 TAIWAN SHARES SUCCUMB TO RATE FEARS 

 Taiwan stocks lost a hefty 3.76 percent on huge net selling 

 by local mutual funds and worries over a possible tightening of 

 monetary policy. 

     The market appears jittery over a possible rate rise and 

 traders reckon support at 8,200 points could be tested soon. 

     There's a gap that has yet to be filled on the daily chart 

 and it will be worth watching carefully for another gap forming 

 on the way down. This would form an island reversal top which 

 is a classic trend reversal pattern. 

     Korea's KOSPI did just this in January and didn't stop 

 falling until late February. 

     KL SHARES RISE, ECONOMIC OUTLOOK IMPROVES 

     Kuala Lumpur stocks were slightly higher, but struggling to 

 make serious headway above 800 points despite an improving 

 economic outlook. 

     Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said the economy was 

 growing well but did not revise the official 1999 GDP forecast 

 of one percent. 

     The central bank has said up to three percent growth is 

 possible but the market is more in tune with Mahathir, with the 

 latest Reuters poll seeing 1.3 percent growth this year.

title: ASIA  FOREX  - Regional firmer, rupiah bucks trend.
text:

 firmer as money continues to flow into regional financial 

 markets to profit from the preceived economic recovery.

intervention, not only by the BOJ but by some of the regional

     **** The yen firmed slightly, shrugging off Sakakibara's

 in the absence of central bank intervention as hopes run high 

 over a Japanese economic recovery. 

     *** The Korean won firmed after some good news from rating 

 agency Fitch IBCA. 

     Fitch upgraded South Korea's long-term foreign currency

 rating to BBB from BBB-, citing the strong reassertion of the 

 country's traditional economic fundamentals. 

     The international credit rating agency said in a statement 

 it had also raised the country's short-term foreign currency

 rating to F2 from F3, in recognition of the continued build-up 

 of external liquidity, which has exceeded earlier expectations. 

 A Fitch official told Reuters Television that any future 

 upgrade would depend on what happens in the corporate and 

 banking sectors. 

 *** IMF Asia Pacific director Hubert Neiss, speaking at a 

 debt conference in Hong Kong, said he believed South Korea's 

 recent direct intervention in the foreign exchange market was 

 aimed at smoothing moves in the won. 

 *** The Thai baht was steady with the authorities attacking 

 rating agency Moody's for their report which said Thai banks 

 remained heavily insolvent. 

 Kiatchai Sopasathienpong, director of the Bank of 

 Thailand's financial institutions supervision department, said 

 Moody's negative views on Thai banks were not shared by other

title: FOCUS-Korea steps in again to slow  currency 's rise.
text:
SEOUL, June 23 (Reuters) - South Korea's finance minister said the government would act to rein in the local currency's rise against the dollar, but his comments and two direct interventions on Wednesday had little impact on the won. 

 "The government won't directly intervene to meet a targeted rate," Kang Bong-kyun told a breakfast meeting. "But the government will try to fulfil its role (to stabilise the market)." 

 He did not say whether the government had a targeted won/dollar rate or what an appropriate rate might be. 

 A state-run bank dealer said the government was intensifying its efforts to slow the rise of the won because it was just 10 won from what was viewed as the government's ideal rate. 

 "We have witnessed strong interventions in January and this month when the dollar neared 1,150 won," he said. 

 The won stood at 1,162.8 against the dollar when local trading closed on Wednesday compared with Tuesday's 1,159.4. 

 From the opening bell on Wednesday, South Korea intervened verbally and physically in the currency market. 

 Dealers said the central Bank of Korea bought about $350 million, including a $50 million purchase, before the close. 

 Two senior finance ministry officials said the government would act to stop the won's appreciation. 

 "The government will take effective measures to defend the dollar against the won," said Kim Yong-duk, director-general of the international finance bureau at the ministry. 

 But the series of interventions did not reverse the trend of the won substantially. 

 "Market players have already tested the government's verbal interventions which were powerless," said Lee Chang-young, a dealer at Kookmin Bank. 

 "We do not see the intervention as having any lasting effect as market sentiment remains very bullish on the Korean won," Catherine Tan, managing analyst for Asian currencies at Thomson Global Markets, told Reuters Television. 

 "I think eventually the government is not going to win the fight against the market sentiment due to the huge influx of funds," she said. 

 The won is still 27 percent weaker than its pre-crisis level of 850 won per dollar, but South Korea is concerned that a strong won will hurt exports and stall its nascent economic recovery. 

 A stronger won makes it difficult for Korean exporters to compete internationally, especially against Japan for value-added products and Southeast Asia for cheap goods. 

 Kang said the government needed to control the dollar supply later this year by boosting foreign exchange demand. 

 On Tuesday, a senior finance ministry official said South Korea might have to increase the amount of won-denominated bonds in the second half of this year to cap the won's rise against the dollar. 

 Dealers said the government was also concerned about the country's foreign exchange reserves, mainly borrowings, and the possibility of foreign equity funds flowing out if the stock market became bearish. 

 Kang said the government might use the country's foreign exchange reserves in overseas investment and in export financing. 

 Jung Woon-gab, dealer at Arab Bank, said: "I'm not quite sure whether the government's plan will work out. My question is what the government plans to do in the short-term, like in June."

title: SKorea moves again to slow won appreciation.

 "The government won't directly intervene to meet a targeted rate. But the government will try to fulfill its role (to stabilise the local currency market)," Kang Bong-kyun said in a breakfast meeting.

 A state-run bank dealer said the government was intensifying its efforts to slow the rise of the won because it was just 10 won from what was viewed as the government's bottom line. 

 "We have witnessed strong interventions, in January and this month, when the dollar nears 1,150 won," he said. 

 The won closed at midday on Wednesday at 1,163.5, against Tuesday's close of 1,159.4. 

 From the opening bell on Wednesday, South Korea intervened verbally and physically in the currency market. 

 Dealers said the central Bank of Korea (BOK) bought an estimated $300 million and two senior finance ministry officials said the government would act to stop the won's appreciation. 

 "It is undesirable for the won to appreciate (against the dollar) when the yen continues to depreciate (versus the dollar)," said Yun Yong-ro, a director at the ministry.

 "The government will take effective measures to defend the dollar against the won," said Kim Yong-duk, director-general of the international finance bureau at the ministry.

 "The market will hardly move with indirect (verbal) interventions because the government has resorted to that too often," said Jung In-woo, a dealer at ABN-Amro Bank.

 His comment came one day after a senior finance ministry official said South Korea may increase the amount of won-denominated bonds to be issued during the second half of this year to cap the won's rise against the dollar. 

 Dealers said the government was also concerned about the nature of the nation's foreign exchange reserves, which were largely borrowings, and about the inflow of foreign equity funds which could leave suddenly if the stock market became bearish. 

 Kang said the government might use the country's foreign exchange reserves in overseas investment and in export financing such as tied-loans.

title: S.Korean won weaker by noon, govt/c.bank  intervene .

 The won stood at 1,163.5 by midday, compared with Tuesday's close of 1,159.4. It opened at 1,160.0 and ranged between 1,158.5 and 1,167.0.

 Dealers said exporter deals were lined up at 1,165.0 won and dollars continued to flow into the market. 

 They said the market has little affected by verbal interventions. 

 "Market players are not afraid of verbal interventions any more," said a foreign bank dealer. "The dollar will not rise unless there is another central bank intervention." 

South Korea's finance ministry officials said the government was closely watching the currency market and that it would take effective measures to slow the won's rise against the dollar. 

 Finance Minister Kang Bong-kyun said the government would try to stabilise the local currency market. 

 "The government won't directly intervene to meet a targeted rate but it will try to fulfill its role (to stabilise the local currency market)," Kang said. 

 A stronger won makes it difficult for the country's exporters to compete in international markets, especially against Japanese goods. The two countries compete head ot head on cars, ships and electronics. 

 Traders forecast the dollar would move between 1,160 and 1,165 won in the afternoon.

title: POLL-S.Korea won seen rising to 1,148 by end-1999.
text:
SEOUL, June 14 (Reuters) - The South Korean won is set to 

 gain ground in the coming months, lifted by the country's 

 current account surplus and a heavy inflow of foreign direct 

 and portfolio investments, a Reuters poll showed. 

     But the government, fearful its exporters may lose leverage 

 because of the weaker currency, would try to control the pace 

 of the won's appreciation. 

     A Reuters poll of 11 interbank dealers and economists 

 showed an average forecast of 1,156 won per dollar at the end 

 of September and 1,148 at the end of this year. 

     The won, which is not fully convertible, stood at 1,171.5 

 won per dollar by Monday midday. It is up nearly three percent 

 so far this year. 

     "How the government induces dollar demand is the key to 

 slowing the pace of the dollar's fall," said Kim Hee-byung, a 

 fixed income analyst at Samsung Securities. 

     "The government realises it can't reverse the trend, but it 

 will try to manipulate the market to manage the pace." 

     Kim forecast the won would rise to 1,150 by the end of 

 September. 

     The financial crisis that crippled Korea in late 1997 was 

 triggered by a dire shortage of foreign currency, but that 

 situation has since turned around. 

     South Korea recorded a current account surplus of $8.80 

 billion in the January-April period, compared with a $14.42 

 billion surplus a year earlier. Foreign direct investment plans 

 in the first five months totalled $3.48 billion, up 93.3 

 percent from $1.80 billion in the same period last year. 

 Fears of a renewed foreign exchange crisis have waned and 

 South Korea is now worried about the won's climb against the 

 dollar. 

 A finance ministry official said on Monday that the 

 ministry was closely watching the won/dollar exchange rate, and 

 the central Bank of Korea intervened on three days last week, 

 buying a combined $250 million to $260 million. 

 But analysts doubted the won's trend would be reversed. 

 "Interventions will be limited to containing the pace, not 

 the course," said a dealer at a European bank, who saw the 

 local unit at 1,050 by the year-end. 

     "A steady inflow of foreign funds, an increase in exports 

 and corporate asset sales would pull the dollar down," he said. 

     Korea, a major exporter, worries the rising won will hurt 

 its competitiveness and smother its nascent economic recovery. 

     A stronger won makes it harder for Korean exporters to 

 compete in global markets, especially against Japanese goods 

 such as cars, ships and electronics. 

     "The government will try hard to protect the country's 

 exports, but it cannot intervene in the way it did before the 

 crisis because of the agreement with the International Monetary 

 Fund," said Lee Chang-seon, an economist at LG Economic 

 Research Institute. 

 The IMF arranged a $58.35 billion rescue package in 

 December 1997 for South Korea, and most of the country's key 

 economic policy decisions are made in consultation with the 

 IMF. 

 The IMF said last week South Korea faced no restraints in 

intervening to smooth day-to-day volatility on the local 

foreign exchange market. 

     But some analysts expected calls for even more government 

 latitude. 

     "The government is likely to try to convince the IMF during 

 its next policy meeting with Korea that it needs to be able to 

intervene strongly," said Lee, who expects the won to rise to 

 1,150 by the end of 1999. 

     Korea is set to meet with IMF representatives for two weeks 

 starting from June 30 for a quarterly policy review. 

     But not everyone was bullish on the won. 

     Stephen Marvin, head of research at Jardine Fleming 

 Securities, saw the won slipping to 1,250 in the last quarter. 

     "The dollar would rise towards the end of the year as 

 foreign direct and portfolio investments shrink and a decrease 

 in the trade surplus accelerates," Marvin said.

title: S.Korea won closes weaker on yen's tumble.
text:

title: INTERVIEW-S.Korea c.bank sees 5 pct '99 GDP growth.
text:
SEOUL, June 14 (Reuters) - South Korea's 1999 gross domestic product growth should exceed five percent, and with low inflation and plenty of slack in the economy, that pace can be sustained for a while, Bank of Korea chief Chon Chol-hwan said on Monday. 

 Private consumption and investment in factory expansion and equipment have risen sharply this year, and exports have begun to pick up, the central bank governor said in an interview. 

 "Even so, inflation remains very low and there's still a lot of slack in the economy," Chon said. "This means the recovery of business activity now under way should continue for some time." 

 "These factors will act to push up GDP growth to a higher level than in the first quarter, so we are now looking at somewhere above five percent for the whole year," he said. 

 The governor's projection compares with the bank's April forecast of 3.8 percent growth. But that was before the government announced first quarter GDP rose 4.6 percent on a year earlier. The economy contracted a provisional 5.8 percent in 1998 from 1997, its worst performance on record. 

 Rising imports on the back of the recovery would likely halve the 1999 current account surplus to around $20 billion, he said. 

 And while increases in public service and utility charges, coupled with rising oil prices, may cause consumer prices to edge up in the second half, consumer price inflation for the year should be held to the two percent level, Chon said. 

 The central bank governor said South Korea would be wary about its macroeconomic policy to prepare for unexpected shocks, such as a slowdown in the global economy, a hike in U.S. interest rates or a devaluation of the Chinese yuan. 

 Chon said the government was trying to keep the surging won under control through indirect intervention, such as pre-paying foreign debt and calling in some of the $20 billion in loans the central bank extended last year to domestic banks to ease a liquidity crunch in the banking system. 

 The government is worried the robust won will hurt exports, which remain the economy's growth engine. 

 But Chon said the government first consults the International Monetary Fund if it is considering a direct intervention in the market. 

 The IMF required Seoul to adopt wide-ranging fiscal, financial and corporate reforms in exchange for a record $58.35 billion rescue package it arranged in December 1997. 

 "The government consults with the IMF before intervening in the market even for 'smoothing operations'," he said. 

South Korea's foreign exchange authorities intervened at least three times last week, buying about $250 million to $260 million to prop up the dollar, market sources said. 

 They said the central bank bought dollars shortly after the IMF's senior representative in Seoul, John Dodsworth, told Reuters it was not restraining South Korea from intervening to smooth day-to-day volatility on the local foreign exchange market. 

 "There is an agreement between the government and the IMF concerning market intervention only when it is direct intervention and not indirect intervention," Chon said. 

 But he added that the government's basic policy was to let market forces determine the exchange rate. 

 South Korea would maintain its present monetary policy of stabilising short-term interest rates at their current levels during the second half of 1999, Chon said. 

 "Market interest rates should remain stable, by and large, in the second half of the year." 

 He said the bank would maintain money supply growth as measured by M3 at around 13 percent in the second half. 

 The governor also said he felt long-term interest rates were now at the right level in view of the recovering economy. 

 "Looking at the projected GDP growth, and the expected inflation rate (of around three percent), the long-term equilibrium interest rate would come out very close to the current market rate," he said. 

 The three-year corporate bond yield closed at 8.04 percent on Monday, up two basis points for the day.

title: S.Korea says consults IMF on  forex intervention .
text:
SEOUL, June 14 (Reuters) - South Korea consults with the International Monetary Fund before directly intervening in the local foreign exchange market, its central bank governor said on Monday. 

 "The government consults with the IMF before intervening in the market even for 'smoothing operations'," Bank of Korea Governor Chon Chol-hwan told Reuters in an interview. 

South Korea's foreign exchange authorities intervened in three trading days of last week, buying approximately $250 million to $260 million to prop up the dollar against the won, market sources said. 

 The sources said the central bank bought dollars shortly after the IMF's senior representative in Seoul, John Dodsworth, told Reuters that the IMF was not restraining South Korea from intervening to smooth day-to-day volatility on the local foreign exchange market. 

 "There is an agreement between the government and the IMF concerning market intervention only when it is direct intervention and not indirect intervention," Chon said. 

 But he added that central bank and the government's basic policy is to let the exchange rate be determined freely by market forces to reflect the country's fundamentals such as the current account and movements of other major currencies. 

 "The country has adopted the free-floating exchange rate regime and the exchange rate will be determined by market forces," Chon said. 

 But he said foreign exchange authorities would indirectly intervene whenever "there is a market supply and demand disparity". 

 The authorities would properly implement indirect intervention measures such as rescheduling of external debt replayments when such disparity occur, he said. 

 Chon said the central bank is also calling in some $20 billion it had extended to domestic banks last year to ease a liquidity crisis, as a way of controlling the supply of dollars on the market. 

 The Korean won finished at 1,170 per dollar, compared to Friday's close of 1,167.6.

title: S.Korea won ends barely lower on  intervention .
text:
SEOUL, June 11 (Reuters) - South Korea won closed barely down versus the dollar on Friday as a series of government measures including a direct intervention erased earlier gains, dealers said. 

 The Bank of Korea declined to confirm its action just before the close of trade, but dealers said it was the third such intervention this week. 

 The won finished at 1,167.6, compared with Thursday's close of 1,167.0. It opened at 1,169.0 and moved between 1,165.4 and 1,172.0. 

 "Interbank operators danced to the government's tune throughout the day, while corporations had a field day making profits by unwinding their dollar holdings," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 Dealers said the central bank stepped in shortly before the closing and bought about $100 million. 

 The intervention came a little after the International Monetary Fund reaffirmed that South Korea faced no restraints in intervening to smooth day-to-day volatility on the local foreign exchange market. 

 "Since the beginning of the IMF-supported programme, there has never been any intention to constrain the authorities in their day-to-day smoothing out of volatility of the exchange rate," the IMF's chief representative in Korea John Dodsworth told Reuters. 

 The central bank has intervened on each of the past two days, buying more than $100 million on Thursday and $50 million to $60 million on Wednesday, traders said. 

 Korea is concerned the won's appreciation will hurt its export competitiveness and its nascent economic recovery. 

 A stronger won makes it difficult for the country's exporters to compete in international markets, especially against Japanese goods. The two countries compete head to head on cars, ships and electronics. 

 South Korea's finance ministry on Friday acknowledged the central bank has been repeatedly buying dollars in the local foreign exchange market to contain the won's rise. 

 "The purpose is to maintain the supply and demand, to maintain a balanced market," ministry spokeswoman Kang Yeoun-sun told Reuters Television in an interview. 

 "Over a mid-term to long-term, we'd like to maintain a healthy amount of foreign exchange reserves and also maintain a positive current account balance for 1999," Kang said. 

 "The other thing is making sure there's fairness and prudential regulation in the foreign exchange market." 

 Earlier on Friday, a finance ministry official said the government was closely monitoring the movements of dollar/yen and dollar/won and the government intended to intervene immediately if the won showed signs of appreciation. 

 Traders said escalating tensions in the naval standoff between North and South Korea on the Yellow Sea also factored into the won's weakness. 

 South Korean navy vessels on Friday shoved four North Korean patrol ships out of the South's territorial waters, in an escalation of a five-day standoff in the Yellow Sea. 

 Dealers said the won's movements next week would depend heavily on the intensity of the government intervention. 

 "But the government is unlikely to overturn the (dollar's bearish) trend," a dealer at a major domestic bank said. 

 The local dealer saw the won moving in a range of 1,165 to 1,175 for next week, while the European bank dealer gave a 1,155-1,170 range. 

 The six-month non-deliverable forward (NDF) won was quoted at 1,170/72 per dollar, while the one-year stood at 1,173/75.

title: IMF-Korea can  intervene  to smooth  forex operations .
text:
SEOUL, June 11 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund on Friday reaffirmed South Korea faced no restraints in intervening to smooth day-to-day volatility on the local foreign exchange market. 

 "Since the beginning of the IMF-supported programme, there has never been any intention to constrain the authorities in their day-to-day smoothing out of volatility of the exchange rate," the IMF's chief representative in Korea John Dodsworth told Reuters. 

 "The foreign exchange market in Korea is still developing and it is important that the authorities retain such freedom to effectively implement smoothing operations," Dodsworth said. 

 The latest quarterly memorandum on economic policies agreed between the IMF and the Korean government calls for a flexible exchange rate policy. 

 "Exchange rate policy will remain flexible and Bank of Korea intervention will be limited to smoothing operations consistent with achieving the reserve target," said the policy review. 

 Local currency dealers said the central Bank of Korea had stepped into the market on Wednesday and Thursday and bought an estimated $150 million to $160 million over the two days. 

 South Korea's finance ministry said on Friday the central bank had been repeatedly buying dollars in the local foreign exchange market to contain the won's rise. 

 "The purpose is to maintain the supply and demand, to maintain a balanced market," ministry spokeswoman Kang Yeoun-sun told Reuters Television in an interview. 

 "Over a mid-term to long-term, we'd like to maintain a healthy amount of foreign exchange reserves and also maintain a positive current account balance for 1999," Kang said. 

 "The other thing is making sure there's fairness and prudential regulation in the foreign exchange market." 

 Dodsworth underlined that market forces have to be respected in determining the underlying exchange rate trends. 

 "Of course, in determining the underlying trend of the exchange rate, market forces have to be respected and this is the only way to develop a more mature foreign exchange market," the IMF chief representative said.

title: S.Korea acknowledges  forex  market  intervention .
text:
SEOUL, June 11 (Reuters) - South Korea's finance ministry said on Friday the central bank has been repeatedly buying dollars in the local foreign exchange market to contain the won's rise. 

 "The purpose is to maintain the supply and demand, to maintain a balanced market," ministry spokeswoman Kang Yeoun-sun told Reuters Television in an interview. 

 She was responding to a question about why the central bank had been intervening in the local foreign exchange market this week. 

 "Over a mid-term to long-term, we'd like to maintain a healthy amount of foreign exchange reserves and also maintain a positive current account balance for 1999," Kang said. 

 "The other thing is making sure there's fairness and prudential regulation in the foreign exchange market." 

 Local currency dealers said the central Bank of Korea had stepped into the market on Wednesday and Thursday and bought an estimated $150 million to $160 million over the two days. 

 This is the first time a government official has confirmed the central bank intervention. In the past government officials declined to comment. 

 The government has frequently expressed concerns that the steep appreciation of the won versus the dollar could seriously hamper the country's exports because a stronger won would make South Korean exports more expensive. 

 Kang said the government was not targetting the dollar/won rate at a specific level but was aiming to keep the rate within a stable range. 

 "I'd like to say that the finance ministry is not so much concerned about the recent movements of the won/dollar rate, because there is no such thing as targetting for a specific exchange rate in our policy," she said. 

 She also said the ministry was closely watching the movements of the won versus the dollar and the yen. Japan is the main competitor to South Korea in major export markets. 

 Regarding the local stock market's recent rally to nearly three-year highs, Kang said the government might decide to sell its holdings of shares in several local banks. 


"Selling the banking shares will be determined by the market condition," she said. "When the timing is right, depending on the KOSPI's	   movement, then the government will sell the banking shares."



Asked whether the government will be more tempted to sell the shares if the Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) continues to rally strongly, Kang said: "Right".



But she denied that the share sale was designed to pull down the stock market.



"It's wrong to intervene in the market," she said. "It's not necessarily for the purpose of moving around the KOSPI."

title: ASIA MARKETS - Investors sidelined by uncertainty.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 11 (Reuters) - Asian shares and currencies

 were mixed on Friday, although Japan's euphoria over strong GDP 

 data lent some support. 


    The dollar/yen	    volatility was seen limiting activity



in regional currency markets, as investors waited for it to



settle.



    The dollar was still bearish against the yen by late trade,



but dealers said caution over possible Bank of Japan (BOJ)


intervention was limiting dollar sales.



    Hong Kong shares	    firmed more than one percent, in
line with Japan's benchmark Nikkei average	    , which



finished 0.56 percent higher at 17,198.55.



    SOUTH KOREAN SHARES AND WON CLOSE LOWER AFTER FLUCTUATIONS



    South Korea's won	    inched slightly lower against the



dollar on Friday as a series of government measures erased



earlier gains.



    Dealers said the central bank stepped in shortly before the



closing and bought about $100 million.



    The intervention came after a comment by an IMF official who



told Reuters that South Korea faced no restraints in intervening


to smooth day-to-day volatility on the local foreign exchange


market.



The central bank has intervened on each of the past two



days, buying more than $100 million on Thursday and $50 million



to $60 million on Wednesday, reflecting their concern that a



strong won would hurt exports, thereby hindering a nascent



recovery.



But Andrew Dermot Fung, regional treasury economist at



Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore, said he thought the


central bank was more worried with the pace of the won's rise,



rather than the currency's strength itself.



"There's this really strong view that as the economy



strengthens, so will the won, and inflows are gong to keep



coming back as both Korea and the rest of the region improves,"



he said.



"So it's not a case of Korea's central bank and the MOFE



(Ministry of Finance and Economy) standing in front of a train



and saying stop. In fact it's more like them saying the pace is



a bit excessive, so we'll slow it down so that the impact on



exports will be less," he said.



South Korean shares closed lower after a MOFE spokeswoman



told Reuters Television that the stock market's further rally



might lead the government to sell its shares of local commercial



banks.



"Selling the banking shares will be determined by the market



condition," spokeswoman Kang Yeoun-sun said. "When the timing is



right, depending on the KOSPI's movement, then the government



will sell the banking shares."



PHILIPPINES CENTRAL BANK TO CUT KEY OVERNIGHT RATES



The Philippine central bank said it would cut its key



overnight rates by 12.5 basis points each on Monday. The cuts



would bring down the overnight borrowing rate to 9.5 percent and



the overnight lending to 11.5 percent.



The move, aimed at spurring banks to lend and boost economic



recovery, would be the 17th cut this year in overnight rates for



a total of 387.5 basis points.



TAIWAN DOLLAR POSTS FOUR-MONTH HIGH



The Taiwan dollar	  posted its fifth consecutive gain,



notching a four-month closing high as the weakening U.S. dollar



overseas showed few signs of a recovery.



Turnover was active at $497.5 million on the main market.

rise in yen and other regionals. It also pledged to respect

attention moved to the slowness of vote-counting.

title: S. Korea Won Up Early; Extends Wed Gains On Yen's Rise
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--The South Korean won is up early Thursday against the U.S. dollar, extending its sharp gains from Wednesday on the continued strength in the yen and amid the absence of significant dollar-buying by state-run banks, traders said. 

 After slipping momentarily to as low as 1,159 won (KRW) shortly after the opening of trading, at 0103 GMT (9:03 p.m. Wednesday EDT) the dollar was trading at KRW1,160, down from Wednesday's closing level of KRW1,165.50. That reflected a 13-won tumble from Tuesday's close and was the dollar's lowest finish against the Korean currency since Jan. 20, when it closed at the same level. 

 The won/dollar exchange rate often tracks movements in the yen/dollar rate, as South Korea directly competes with Japan in roughly half of its exports. 

 The yen climbed against the dollar during Wednesday's New York trading session as expectations grew that Japan's first-quarter gross domestic product figures will reflect stronger growth than originally expected. Japan's GDP data are scheduled to be released Thursday at 0630 GMT. 

 At 0100 GMT, the dollar was trading at Y119.00, up slightly from Y118.98 late Wednesday in New York late Wednesday but down from Y119.40 late Wednesday in Tokyo. 

 Despite comments Thursday by South Korean government officials that they are concerned about the won's sharp rise against the dollar, state-run banks weren't active dollar buyers early Thursday, traders said. Rumors circulated in the local currency market late Wednesday that the Bank of Korea, South Korea's central bank, was intervening directly to support the U.S. currency. Traders said that if the government fails Thursday to support the dollar directly or indirectly, the U.S. currency could test the KRW1,150 level. 

 The volatility in the dollar's levels versus the won leaves traders leery of trying to project a precise trading range for Thursday. The U.S. currency is expected to remain Thursday within a broad range of KRW1,150 to KRW1,170.
