title: ANALYSIS-S.Korea powerless to stop won climb.
text:
SEOUL, June 10 (Reuters) - Despite repeated interventions by the central bank, South Korea appears powerless to stop the steady appreciation of the won because of International Monetary Fund restraints, analysts said on Thursday. 

 After months of trying to boost the currency following a brush with sovereign default in late 1997, South Korea is now worried it is climbing too fast against the dollar. 

 The central Bank of Korea intervened for the second day in a row on Thursday to buy an estimated $100 million, ending the won's six-day rising streak. 

 But analysts said the trend would not be reversed. 

 The won finished at 1,167.0 on Thursday, compared with Wednesday's close of 1,165.5. It has risen 1.7 percent since June 1 and 3.2 percent since the start of the year. 

 Korea, a major exporter, is concerned the rising won will hurt its competitiveness and stall its nascent economic recovery. 

 A stronger won makes it difficult for the country's exporters to compete in international markets, especially against Japanese goods. The two countries compete head to head on cars, ships and electronics. 

 Dealers said the unit will strengthen further because players doubted the government's ability to reverse the won's bullish trend in the face of a heavy inflow of foreign direct and portfolio investments. 

 An official at the commerce ministry confirmed South Korea will continue to seek foreign direct investment despite concerns of a conflict with government efforts to curb rapid appreciation of the won. 

 The won was around 850 to the dollar before the country began sliding into Asia's financial crisis in July 1997. 

 "This does not mean the broad trend has been reversed," said a dealer at a major domestic bank. "It would be difficult for the government to intervene like this everyday." 

 The $100 million purchase was almost double Wednesday's dollar-buying intervention, which dealers estimated at $50 million to $60 million. 

 "It's hard for the government to (intervene in a big way) because they'd need to consult the International Monetary Fund," said a dealer at a French bank. 

 The IMF arranged a $58.35 billion rescue package in December 1997 for South Korea and most of the country's key economic policy decisions are made in consultation with the IMF. 

 The IMF has said the government should only intervene to smooth foreign exchange trading. 

 "The government is likely to try to convince the IMF during its next policy meeting with Korea that it needs to be able to intervene strongly," said Lee Chang-seon, an economist at LG Economic Research Institute. 

 Korea is set to meet with IMF representatives for two weeks starting from June 30 for a quarterly policy review. 

 Dealers said the bank last intervened between May 25 and May 31, buying $10 million to $20 million daily, but that the market had missed the intervention at the time because of the small transaction volume. Central bank officials refused to discuss the bank's trading activities. 

 The financial crisis was driven by a severe shortage of foreign currency but that situation has been reversed. 

 South Korea posted a current account surplus of $8.80 billion in January-April against a $14.42 billion surplus a year earlier. Foreign direct investment plans in the first five months totalled $3.48 billion, up 93.3 percent from $1.80 billion in the same period last year. 

 The dollar also has been pressured recently by growing optimism over Japan's economic outlook. The dollar fell to 117.89/99 yen at 0715 GMT against 119.07/17 in late New York trade on Wednesday. 

 An assistant central bank governor said on Tuesday Korea could easily halt the won's rise by buying dollars to build up reserves after Korea repays IMF loans in the second half. 

 Korea said in April it would buy $4.6 billion in the local market to keep the won from appreciating too much. 

 "How the government induces dollar demand is the key to slowing the pace of the dollar's fall," said Kim Hee-byung, a fixed income analyst at Samsung Securities. 

 "The government realises it can't reverse the trend but it will try to manipulate the market to manage the pace."

title: EMERGING MARKET  FX -Holding up, marking time.
text:
LONDON, June 9 (Reuters) - Emerging market currencies held firm on Wednesday as the dollar steadied after big drops against the euro and yen, but the surge in U.S. long bond yields to a six percent high kept alive fears of a U.S. interest rate hike. 

 Major central European currencies were little moved after making substantial headway on Tuesday, although the Slovak crown was slightly weaker ahead of a 300 million euro bond issue expected later in the day. 

 Most Asian currencies were largely unchanged on late New York levels although at least two central banks, in Taiwan and South Korea, were reported to have intervened to curb local currency gains made on the back of the stronger yen. 

 The won earlier reached around 1,161 to the dollar and remained up on the day despite dollar buying by the Bank of Korea, traders said. The central bank declined to confirm the intervention. 

 The Taiwan dollar held around three-month highs against the U.S. dollar. 

 But the Indonesian rupiah, which surged on Monday and Tuesday on a wave of cheer over the peaceful turnout to the country's first real democratic elections in 44 years, shed some of its gloss, falling back through 7,700 to the dollar. 

 Some analysts said the slow pace of the vote count, which has prompted opposition parties to voice fears of possible tampering, was weighing on the market. 

 Others were more upbeat. 

 "This is just a cooling-off period - some reflection, some profit-taking," said Jake Moore, emerging market currency analyst at Barclays Capital in London. 

 With less than four percent of votes counted by 0915 GMT, early results showed two major opposition parties had a strong lead over the ruling Golkar party. 

 "Near term, markets are likely to become more cautious as delays in vote counting and reporting will dampen sentiment," analysts at Standard Chartered said in a note to clients. 

 "Dollar/rupiah is expected to edge back towards 7,900 before a move to 7,500 is seen." 

 Emerging Asian currencies showed no immediate reaction to a Chinese state radio report that the country was cutting its benchmark interest rate to 2.25 percent from 3.78 percent. 

 In Europe the Polish zloty, Czech crown and Hungarian forint barely budged. The forint remained at the top of its trading band, 2.25 percent above basket parity, while the zloty stuck around its four-week high of 2.86 percent above parity. 

 The zloty faced tough resistance at three percent above the mid-point, but capital inflows from privatisations such as the $1 billion sale of Polish bank Pekao SA and higher growth expectations in Germany could lift the currency further, analysts said. 

 The rand also held steady after the South African Reserve bank sanctioned a further small decline in its repo rate to 15.375 percent from 15.406 percent, bolstering hopes that commercial banks will soon ease their prime lending rates. 

 Analysts said the currency was likely to ease further in the medium term, possibly towards 6.50 to the dollar by the end of the year, because of a continuing inflation differential between South Africa and the major industrial economies. 

 "It's slightly undervalued, but that undervaluation should probably persist because the latest figures show exports are not yet picking up," analyst Jean-Francois Mercier of Salomon Smith Barney told Reuters Television. 

 Analysts said the overnight rise in U.S. long bond yields increased nervousness over the possibility the U.S. Federal Reserve would raise interest rates later this month, which could squeeze capital flows to emerging markets. 

 But the currency impact would be seen mainly in Latin America later in the day, they added, as that region was likely to feel the greatest pinch from higher U.S. rates.

title: S.Korea won turns weaker by midday on  intervention .
text:
SEOUL, May 26 (Reuters) - South Korea's won	  stood turned weaker by midday on Wednesday after a state bank's intervention sparked dollar short-covering.



The won ended the morning at 1,189.9 against Tuesday's 1,187.0 close. It opened at 1,186.0 and ranged from 1,184.3 to 1,193.0.


 Dealers said the Export-Import Bank of Korea's bids had massed at the 1,190 won level, briefly pushing the dollar up to 1,193.0 won near the close of the morning. 

 "The bank is believed to have placed orders at up to the 1,192 won level but it's unclear whether the strong (dollar) sentiment could be sustained because there are many corporate sellers waiting there," said a foreign bank dealer. 


The yen	  extended its gains against the dollar but failed to provide a lasting lift to the won although the yen's strength overnight caused the won to open stronger.



The yen was quoted at 121.77/80 at midday, compared with 122.71/74 late on Tuesday in Tokyo.



Traders showed no immediate reaction to the news that Korea Telecom Corp  raised $2.49 billion through an American Depositary Receipt sale.



The government has said it would keep the proceeds from flowing into the local foreign exchange market and finance ministry officials reaffirmed the stance on Wednesday.



They said part of the money would be purchased by the central Bank of Korea and that the remaining amount would be used by Korea Telecom's overseas operations.



Remarks by the central bank governor released early on Wednesday morning were generally ignored. Bank of Korea Governor Chon Chol-hwan said in a speech to a forum that the foreign exchange rate should be left to market forces.



He reaffirmed the interest rate policy would continue to be geared towards supporting the economic recovery, indicating that there would be no swift rebound in local interest rates.



"A correlation between the foreign exchange level and local interest rates is not apparent at the moment. The foreign exchange rate should be decided by the market's supply and demand factors," Chon said.



In the non-deliverable forward trading, the six-month won was quoted at 1,194/97 at midday versus 1,191/94 in the morning and the one-year won stood at 1,200/03 versus 1,196.5/99.5.

title: Asian  Currencies  -3:  Intervention  Rumors Rife In Mkts
text:
Against the Singapore currency, the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.6998, up from S$1.6984 in late Asian trading Tuesday. 

 While regional currencies have seen marked appreciation, the Singapore dollar has seen less upward pressure because it is being used to fund regional carry trades. 

 "The interest rates are so low in Singapore that people are going short Singapore dollars to fund purchases in baht, rupiah or (Philippine) peso - currencies with higher yields," a trader at a Japanese bank in Singapore said. "Without this element, the Singapore dollar would be much stronger." 

 Traders also said rumors abound that the Monetary Authority of Singapore has been actively intervening in the market through local banks, in an effort to keep the U.S. dollar at or near S$1.70. 

 The U.S. dollar was also trading at 36.7350 Thai baht, unchanged from late Asian trading Tuesday. Despite the inactivity in the market, traders said central bank intervention - as in Singapore and South Korea - has become a fact of life in Thailand. 

 "Governments are concerned that their currencies don't strengthen too quickly, especially as funds pour into their domestic stock markets," said a currency strategist at a U.S. investment house. 

 The Bank of Thailand is thought to be using a number of foreign banks in Singapore as a quiet avenue for buying U.S. dollars. "It's a lucrative business for the foreign banks. They keep their mouths shut and get to keep tabs on what one of the largest players in the market is doing," said a trader at a U.S. bank. "Big advantage." 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the U.S. dollar was trading at 37.585 pesos, down from PHP37.610 late Tuesday. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency was at NT$32.732, down from NT$32.735 Tuesday. 

 The South Korean won was at 1205.2 to the dollar, weaker than KRW1197.5 late Tuesday.

title: ASIA  FOREX -Regionals lose early shine as yen dips.
text:
0900 GMT - Asian currencies were mostly lower in late 

 trading having lost an early firmer bias as the dollar picked 

 up to above the 115 level. 

     Dollar/yen recovered to its highest level since February 1 

 after a Wall Street Journal article reported that the U.S. was 

 urging Japan to ease monetary policy. 

     Among the regionals the rupiah and peso bucked the trend. 

     *** The rupiah moved up after comments from both IMF's Asia 

 Pacific Director Hubert Neiss and Indonesia's own Minister of 

 Industry and Trade Rahardi Ramelan, although it failed to break 

 the 8,500 level. 

 Both officials said the currency could appreciate further 

 while the Trade Minister said it may head toward 7,500 to the 

 dollar, although he added that strength beyond 7,000 is 

 undesirable due to an impact on exports. 

     Hopes for the next IMF disbursement and talk of a possible 

central bank support also gave the rupiah a lift. 

     *** In Manila, the peso rebounded on a surge in corporate 

 demand for the currency. 

     Traders said some of the corporate inflows could have come 

 from the San Miguel/Nestle deal. 

     Around $300 million in inflows were expected from the sale 

 of San Miguel's stake in Nestle Philippines. Those gains 

 completely wiped out earlier fears of a possible central bank

intervention. 

 *** The Thai baht was little changed. Hopes of a possible 

 easing of reserve requirements were dashed after the Bank of 

 Thailand announced that it had not discuss such a plan in a 

 meeting with commercial banks earlier today. 

 The central bank also said it wanted to see lower lending 

 rates although it would leave market forces to determine those 

 levels. 

     *** In Taiwan and South Korea, there was talk of government 

intervention. 

     The Taiwan dollar was little changed when the central back 

 stepped in to prop up the market and stop further losses. 

     Dealers say the central bank sold dollars to boost market 

 confidence, after poor economic growth figures on Monday. 

     Meanwhile, dealers say persistent dollar buying by Korean 

 state banks failed to keep the won from sliding.

title: S.Korea won opens flat on  intervention  fears.
text:
SEOUL, Feb 2 (Reuters) - Fears of intervention weighed down South Korea's currency market at the opening of trade on Tuesday, with the won-dollar rate stuck in tight-ranged trade, dealers said. 

 The won stood at Monday's close of 1,174.5 per dollar at 0047 GMT. It opened at 1,175.0 and moved between 1,173.0 and 1,175.0. 

 "It looks obvious the market has more dollar supplies than demand," said a local bank dealer. "But the central bank seems poised to buy dollars whenever the dollar nears the 1,170 floor." 

 Dealers said the won-dollar rate would range from 1,172 to 1,178 throughout the day. 

 The market is still pressured by heavy dollar holdings by exporters and fund inflows for investment in the local stock market, they said. 

 The six-month non-deliverable forward won was quoted at 1,186/1,191 per dollar, while the one-year won stood at 1,193/1,203. 

 The dollar was quoted at 114.90/95 yen in Tokyo, compared to 115.60/70 yen late on Monday.

title: S.Korea won weaker by midday on  intervention .
text:
SEOUL, Jan 21 (Reuters) - South Korea's won ended Thursday's morning trade weaker against the dollar after state-controlled banks intervened and bought dollars, dealers said. 

 They said Kookmin Bank bought a large amount of dollars early in the morning after the central bank asked the bank to try to halt the won's rise against the U.S. unit. 

 After opening at 1,170.0, the won fell to 1,185.0 after Kookmin bought dollars but officials at Kookmin Bank denied the intervention talk. 

 The won stood at 1,174.0 per dollar by lunch break from Wednesday's 1,165.5 close. 

 "Kookmin bought dollars heavily early in the morning to support the U.S. unit against the won," said a domestic bank dealer who asked not to be identified. 

 The dealer gave no further details. 

 Dollar buying by Korea Electric Power Corp  also helped bring the won down in the morning, dealers said. 

 They said such dollar buying forces emerged after President Kim Dae-jung said on Wednesday he wanted the won/dollar level to remain at about 1,200 won because of concerns about how a stronger currency would impact exports. 

 "The dollar buying seems to be aimed at controlling the speed of the won's rise," said another local bank dealer. 

 Dealers forecast the won would remain in a 1,170-1,185 range in the afternoon. 

 ((Nick Yon, Seoul newsroom, +822 727 5644, fax +822 727 5666, seoul.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: S.Korea c.bank  intervenes  to support dlr-dealers.
text:
SEOUL, Jan 8 (Reuters) - South Korea's central bank intervened in the local foreign exchange market in Friday's morning trading session to keep the dollar from sliding further against the won, dealers said. 

 The won was trading 1,162 per dollar at 0225 GMT after opening at 1,161 and moving between 1,150 and 1,170. 

 "The government's intentions are clear it would not allow the (dollar's) fall to continue and it has begun to take measures in earnest," said a foreign bank dealer. 

 Government officals refused to comment on the central banks' intervention. 

 "The government's official position on intervention is always NCND (neither confirm nor deny)," a finance ministry official said. 

 The won has continued to gain against the dollar since late 1997 when it reached a low of 1,995 per dollar, mostly on corporate dollar sales and dollar inflows from foreign investors. 

 The government has raised concerns a strong won could hurt South Korea's exports, which compete mainly with Japan's exports, and dampen its efforts for economic recovery. 

 ((Nick Yon, Seoul newsroom, +822 727 5644, fax +822 727 5666, seoul.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: SKorea won opens lower on  intervention , KAMCO talk.
text:
SEOUL, Dec 16 (Reuters) - South Korea's won opened weaker on Wednesday on market talk that local banks were stocking up on dollars to accommodate the sale of their non-performing foreign currency assets to a government agency, dealers said. 

 The Korean won opened at 1215.0 per dollar against Tuesday's 1,211.5 close. 

 "Aside from the KAMCO rumours, traders remain wary of possible intervention by the central bank," said a dealer at HSBC Bank. 

 State-run Korea Asset Management Corp (KAMCO) earlier this year agreed to purchase in won some non-performing foreign currency assets from local banks. 

 "Rumours that the purchases would begin before the end of this year are gaining credibility," said a foreign bank dealer. 

 Dealers said banks would need to buy dollars on the inter-bank market to accommodate the asset sales. They said the demand would reach some $700 million to $800 million. 

 Trading in the won was expected to be bound within the 1,205 to 1,215 range in the absence of new factors affecting the market, dealers said.

title: S.Korea won ends stronger amid  intervention  fears.
text:
SEOUL, Dec 7 (Reuters) - The South Korean won closed stronger against the dollar on Monday but its upside remained limited because of persistent concerns the central bank might step into the market, dealers said. 

 They said a new credit rating assignment by Moody's Investors Service on won-denominated state bonds provided a psychological boost to the local currency. 

 The won closed at 1,208.0, compared with Friday's finish of 1,214.0. After opening at 1,210.0, it moved in a 1,211.0-1,204.0 range. 

 "The dollar has continued to fall by 10 won every day," said a foreign bank dealer. "But intervention fears and the yen/dollar movement erased early losses." 

 The dollar was slightly higher against the yen in late Tokyo but operators were reluctant to buy dollars aggressively as the U.S. unit failed to recover convincingly last Friday despite stronger-than-expected U.S. payroll data, dealers said. 

 Earlier the dollar slipped as low as 118.23 yen but rebounded to 118.86/96 at 0614 GMT. 

 A local bank dealer said many believed the dollar looked cheap versus the won but have hesitated to actively buy dollars, given the persistent supply of the U.S. unit. 

 Dealers said the market hailed the Moody's decision as it was believed to be the first step before upgrading South Korea's foreign currency-denominated sovereign bonds. 

 Moody's Investors Service assigned a Baa1 rating to the won-denominated bonds of South Korea. Baa1 is two notches above the lowest investment grade. 

 Dealers said aggressive foreign buying in the local stock market, bolstered by Moody's rating announcement, would provide a stimulus to prop up the won against the dollar. 

 The stock market soared by more than four percent with foreign net buying amounting to 30.67 billion won worth. 

 Dealers said market attention focused on whether the 1,200 won support level would be breached. 

 "The dollar is likely to touch 1,180 won this week," said the local bank dealer. 

 But dealers said concerns about export growth, the key factor to boost South Korea's economoy, would invite intervention and limit any freefall on the dollar. 

 Reflecting cautiousness, trading volume remained weak at $477.2 million. ((Yeom Yoon-jeong, Seoul Newsroom +822 727 5647, fax +822 727 5666, seoul.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: SKorea exchange rate headed right way - BOK gov.
text:
SEOUL, Nov 4 (Reuters) - South Korea's central bank is not intervening in the foreign exchange market but the won is moving in the right direction, Bank of Korea Governor Chon Chol-hwan said on Wednesday. 

 "The Bank of Korea is not intervening in any way on the for. 

 "But the exchange rate is moving in the right direction," he added. 

 Responding to questions, Chon said he expected the South Korean economy to bottom out by the middle of next year "at the latest and head into recovery mode" as long as the external environment remained stable. 

 "The government does not expect a yuan devaluation," Chon said. 

 South Korea has not set any targets for the won/dollar rate or interest rates, he said. 

 "Since the outbreak of the crisis we have decided to let the markets determine everything," he said. 

 But the government was following some guidelines, including lowering interest rates as long as that did not jeopardise the foreign exchange rate, Chon said. 

 South Korea also was keeping an eye on interest rate differentials between Korea and other countries and on capital flows, he said. 

 ((Reuters newsroom +82-2-727-5640, seoul.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: ASIA MARKETS - Regionals firm as yen regains poise.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 28 (Reuters) - Asian currencies ended mostly firmer after a mixed day on Tuesday tracking the fortunes of the yen with Korean won still taking its own, more volatile road. 

 News from Tokyo that former Prime Minister Kiichi Miyazawa is likely to be the new finance minister gave the yen some strength after early weakness and the Asian currencies followed suit, though again activity is said to be light. 

 KOREAN WON SEES WILD SWINGS ON DAY 

 The won took a dramatic turn on Tuesday after rallying for several weeks against the dollar and pushing through 1,200 per dollar at one point to a high of 1185, it ended around 1,257 amid talk that a central bank intervention was imminent, dealers said. 

 "Strong bargain hunting and short-covering bids emerged after comments by an IMF official about a possible intervention and on the belief the dollar has hit its bottom," said a Korea Exchange Bank dealer. 

 Talks of a possible intervention were already circulating but got a critical boost when a senior International Monetary Fund official said outright an intervention was possible. 

 The IMF's Asia-Pacific department director Hubert Neiss told Reuters Television that there now was scope for central bank intervention in the foreign exchange market. 

 He said with South Korea's foreign exchange reserves rebuilt to about $36 billion, "there is a possibility of careful, judicious (central bank) intervention, at least to smooth out day-to-day erratic movements". 

 Neiss also said South Korea had "turned the corner" in its balance of payments crisis, but that the appreciation of the won was raising concern. 

 He said there now was scope for the government to lower interest rates and for "judicious" central bank intervention to smooth erratic day-to-day movements in the foreign exchange market. 

 "Korea has turned the corner as far as the balance of payments crisis, the foreign exchange crisis, is concerned and has now entered the restructuring phase in full," he said. 

 He added that with South Korea's foreign exchange reserves rebuilt to about $36 billion, "there is a possibility of careful, judicious (central bank) intervention, at least to smooth out day-to-day erratic movements". 

 This morning the Koreans released a new set of targets with the IMF. 

 These include a revision in the GDP forecast to a contraction of four percent. But the budget deficit target has been eased to four percent of GDP from 1.75 percent and new inflation and current account forecasts were set. 

 The economic target agreement means the Korean can expect another tranche of IMF money due in around mid-August. 

 IMF SEES 10,000 RUPIAH PER DLR STILL POSSIBLE 

 Neiss said on Tuesday an exchange rate of around 10,000 rupiah against the dollar was a "reasonable assumption" by the end of the current fiscal year next March. 

 He said the IMF and Indonesia had assumed in the government's economic programme that the rupiah would average 10,600 to the dollar during the fiscal year. He said this meant the rate would be around 10,000 towards the end of the fiscal year. 

 "I think this is still a reasonable assumption, or a possible assumption, and...prospects are now more favourable for a recovery of the rupiah because there will be ample inflows of foreign official money," he told Reuters Television in an interview. 

 RINGGIT SOFTER, KL SHARES DOWN ON ECONOMIC GLOOM 

 The ringgit was again looking softer and Kuala Lumpur shares hit a nine-year low as markets reacted to the shelving of plans to raise $2.0 billion dollars from the international bond market. 

 The lack of this funding has raised serious doubts about a scheme to shore up ailing banks, which are suffering under the weight of non-performing loans. 

 Today finance minister Anwar Ibrahim said the government was planning a series of more comprehensive measures to deal with the economic downturn later this week. 

 He didn't give any other details or an exact timing though, though speculation centres on another SRR cut. Bank Negara last cut bank reserve requirements to eight from 10 percent on July 1. 

 Worries about the economic outlook are not really moving the ringgit, which has traded in a range around 4.15 all week, but is having a big impact on the stock market. 

 The KLSE hit a fresh nine year low this morning, so below even the worst of last years Asian crisis. It broke through 400, bottomed out at around 399.23 and then recovered to be 402.30 by the mid-session break. 

 STATE OF THE UNION FAILS TO HELP MANILA MARKETS 

 In Manila worries about the economic outlook there have been taking a toll on the Peso today. This follows the first state of the nation address by the new president Joseph Estrada last night who painted a fairly poor economic picture and outlined few concrete proposals to deal with the problem. 

 Manila shares ended down nearly two percent today.

title: FOCUS-Korea won takes U-turn on  intervention  fears.
text:
SEOUL, July 28 (Reuters) - South Korea's won on Tuesday ended a rally which had lasted several weeks amid a flurry of rumours a central bank intervention was imminent to boost the dollar, dealers said. 

 The won finished at 1,257 per dollar, about six percent off the year high of 1,185 reached in the morning, after the dollar gained support from bargain hunting and short-covering. 

 The closing rate was also down from Monday's 1,209 close. 

 "Strong bargain hunting and short-covering bids emerged after comments by an IMF official about a possible intervention and on the belief that the dollar has hit its bottom," said a Korea Exchange Bank dealer. 

 Rumours of a possible intervention were already circulating but got a critical boost when a senior International Monetary Fund official said outright an intervention was possible. 

 IMF Asia-Pacific Department Director Hubert Neiss told Reuters Television there now was scope for central bank intervention in the foreign exchange market. 

 He said with South Korea's foreign exchange reserves rebuilt to about $36 billion, "there is a possibility of careful, judicious (central bank) intervention, at least to smooth out day-to-day erratic movements". 

 He said the foreign exchange situation in South Korea had made rapid progress, adding: "Indeed, the exchange rate has appreciated at a pace that has now raised concern." 

 Dealers said intervention fears would keep discouraging dollar sellers for the time being but forecast the dollar's upside would be limited by still heavy dollar positions. 

 "Many people still think the dollar's downward trend will not easily change unless the market's heavy dollar positions become lighter," said a Korea Exchange Bank dealer. 

 The won's year high of 1,185 reached on Tuesday represented a 68 percent gain in its value against the dollar since the won hit a record low of 1,995 in late December. 

 South Korea's foreign exchange reserves fell to only about $8.87 billion by the end of last year after the central bank failed in its bid to defend its plunging currency. 

 Then came the IMF, which in December arranged a record-breaking $58.35 billion rescue package for what was the world's 11th-largest economy. 

 Together with aid loan payouts, rising current account surpluses and extension of maturities on South Korean financial institutions' short-term debt owed to international lenders also helped South Korea rebuild its foreign exchange reserves 

 Active asset sales by South Korean companies to foreigners and a $4 billion overseas sovereign bond issue have also brought a flood of dollars into what was a dollar-hungry market. 

 South Korea said earlier on Tuesday it had agreed with the IMF to raise the usable foreign exchange reserves forecast to $43 billion at the end of this year from $41 billion. 

 The won's sharp appreciation, also attributed to an extremely low dollar demand in line with plunging imports, is of particular concern to exporters. 

 A stronger won would make South Korean exports more expensive even without changes in won prices, depriving their products of comparative price competitiveness. 

 The won's appreciation was also in contrast with the weakening value of Japan's yen and currencies of other South Korean competitors in exports against the dollar. ((Seoul Newsroom, +822 727 5646, fax +822 727 5666, seoul.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Korea won surges, overrides  intervention  fear.
text:
SEOUL, July 27 (Reuters) - South Korea's won hit a fresh year high against the dollar on Monday morning as steady dollar inflows overrode intervention fears, dealers said. 

 The won ended the morning at 1,216 to the dollar after hitting a year high of 1,215. It opened at Friday's close of 1,245, which was a session low. 

 Dealers said talk of possible government intervention failed to stop the won's rally, undesirable for South Korea, which is struggling to boost exports. 

 "There's little possibility for the trend to turn around in the short run as the market is so heavy with dollars, while there is no demand," a Korea Exchange Bank dealer said. 

 "Right now nothing but interventions can turn around the trend, but traders would not move until they actually see (dollar) bids coming in," said another dealer. 

 The won's strength has been underpinned by growing current account surpluses and foreign exchange reserves and active asset or stake sales by local companies. 

 At the same time, the market has shrugged off recent comments by government officials about possible interventions and what dealers said were interventions by state-run institutions in the market. 

 An official at the Bank of Korea said the bank had decided to absorb $273.16 million to be brought in by Commerzbank AG of Germany to pay for a 32.39 percent stake in Korea Exchange Bank early this week. 

 The official was confirming a report by the Maeil Business Newspaper that said the central bank had decided to absorb the money to prevent the payment from flooding the market. 

 He said the bank was following regulations that require it to swap dollars brought in by local branches of foreign financial institutions into won currency. 

 The German bank will become the second-largest shareholder in the Korean bank, with the government continuing to hold the biggest stake, of 33.62 percent. 

 Dealers said various indirect intervention efforts by the government were noticed in the market but not independently confirmed. 

 Although the central bank has been reluctant to directly step into the market, dealers said state-run banks and corporations have been buying more dollars on the market than usual. 

 "It's a known secret on the market that government authorities have been buying dollars under the government's instruction," said a dealer. 

 The rally of the won, which has gained more than 60 percent against the U.S. dollar since touching its record low of 1,995 late in December, is particularly unsettling for exporters. 

 A stronger won while the Japanese yen remains weak against the greenback makes South Korean exports expensive even without price changes in terms of won. 

 The two neighbouring countries compete head-to-head in major export markets for products ranging from electronic goods and computer chips to ships and automobiles. 

 Dealers and analysts both at home and abroad see the won's rally to be temporary now that the country's trade balance is expected to worsen in coming months in line with shrinking exports. 

 But there is no consensus on how long the rally will last or where the currency will hit bottom. 

 South Korea accepted a rescue package totalling a record $58.35 billion from the International Monetary Fund in December in exchange for painful economic reforms.

title: EMERGING MARKETS  FX -Won firms on direct investment.
text:
LONDON, July 27 (Reuter) - The South Korean won surged to around a year high on Monday as direct investment by foreign corporates sucked dollars into the economy. 

 Most other emerging markets currencies were little changed, with the rouble holding steady despite Russian debt prices hitting record lows. 

 The won was at 1,208 bid to the dollar at 1145 GMT, some five percent stronger than London's Friday close of 1,273. It earlier ended the day in Seoul at 1,209 after hitting a year high of 1,208. 

 "There's no demand really for dollars, no domestic demand for imports. But money is coming in from foreigners - corporates paying for companies or units of companies," said Paul McNamara, emerging markets economist at Julius Baer Investments in London. 

 Corporate restructuring in response to South Korea's financial crisis has resulted in a stream of equity stakes and company assets coming onto the market. 

 McNamara said South Korea's stiff market regulation meant dollar inflows from this direct investment were not being counterbalanced by portfolio outflows, hoisting the won to stronger levels than domestic demand would suggest. 

 An analyst at a U.S. bank in London, who asked not to be named, said South Korean fundamentals were also underpinning the won. 

 "Korea has just firmed incredibly," he said. "They're sticking to what the IMF wants, and taking a reasonably hard line against labour unrest." 

 Analysts were keeping an open mind on the possibility of central bank intervention to stem the won's rise, which threatens South Korea's competitiveness as it fights to boost exports, but said there was currently no word of such action. 

 "There's going to be official displeasure (at the stronger won) but there's not a great deal they can do about it," the U.S. analyst said. 

 He said one alternative to market intervention - lowering interest rates - could be counterproductive by acting as a signal of economic confidence, which could in turn attract investment and lift the currency. 

 The rouble, which weakened on Friday on the back of a cut in the benchmark refinancing rate to 60 percent from 80 percent, was stable at 6.272 bid to the dollar at 1145 GMT, virtually unchanged from Friday's London close of 6.26. 


The currency weathered the negative mood driving down Russian bonds, with benchmark PRINs		  slipping 2-3/4 from Friday's close in New York to 41-1/8 bid, just above record lows of 40-1/2 earlier on Monday.



McNamara said the free market in PRINs meant prices adjusted quickly to driving forces, notably a current glut of Russian paper. Trading in the rouble was less flexible in comparison, and the rescue package agreed with the International Monetary Fund was lending credibility to the Russian central bank.



"The rouble is defensible at these levels," he said.



Other analysts said the market was looking for a slight rouble weakening to around 6.30.



The ringgit also held steady, with analysts saying the market had foreseen the cuts in Malaysia's credit rating late last week by both Moody's Investors Service and Standard & Poor's.



"The downgrade was already priced into the market," McNamara said. "There's nobody left to sell it."



The ringgit was at 4.14 to the dollar at 1145 GMT, against 4.143 late on Friday in London. Analysts saw some further weakening, with support around 4.20.



Other emerging markets currencies were little moved, staying within tight ranges.

title: Korea won ends slightly lower on  intervention  woes.

 The won closed at 1,291 per dollar from Monday's close of 1,289. It opened at 1,292 and ranged from 1,287 to 1,293. 

 "Trading was dull because of possible central bank intervention," said a domestic bank dealer. 

 Dealers forecast narrow-ranged trading on Wednesday in the absence of fresh factors.

title: FOCUS-S.Korea's won capped by  intervention  talk.
text:
SEOUL, July 16 (Reuters) - South Korea's won retreated from its new yearly high on Thursday after the finance minister said the government may intervene to keep the currency from becoming overvalued against the U.S. dollar. 

 The won closed at 1,283 to the dollar against Wednesday's 1,282 finish, after touching an intra-year high of 1,265. It hit a low of 1,288. 

 Dealers said the won, whose upsurge has spurred concerns over the country's export outlook, was unlikely to trend weaker against the dollar over the minister's remarks but would move in narrow ranges. 

 They said the won's recent strength was due to an unusually low demand for dollars, which is unlikely to change in the near future. 

 "The government is closely watching the foreign exchange market with concern and may intervene if the market is in serious problems," Finance and Economy Minister Lee Kyu-sung told reporters. 

 The won has gained more than 50 percent versus the dollar since hitting a record low of 1,995 in late December. 

 The surge has been underpinned by growing current account surpluses and foreign exchange reserves, which late last year, had plunged below a level equivalent to a month of imports. 

 On Thursday, the central Bank of Korea said the country's usable foreign exchange reserves stood at $38.09 billion as of July 15, up from $37.04 billion at the end of June. 

 At the end of December, the country's usable foreign exchange reserves stood at $8.87 billion after the central bank poured dollars into the market in a failed attempt to defend its then plunging currency. 

 Dollars have streamed into the country with disbursements from an international aid package, a $4.0-billion overseas sovereign bond issue and a spate of major asset sales to foreigners by indebted Korean companies. 

 The extension of maturities on nearly $22 billion in short-term debt by international banks in March has also considerably eased the demand for dollars in the local market, analysts said. 

 Finance minister Lee said the government's stand would be to "neither confirm nor deny" intervention rumours. His remarks reversed comments made on Monday when he said there would be no intervention, even if the won rose above 1,300. 

 Lee said it was not appropriate for the government to "give signals on every movement in the exchange rate", indicating that a lack of comment would not exclude the possibility of an immediate intervention. 

 The currency's upsurge has raised concerns that the strong won could endanger the nation's efforts to overcome its worst economic crisis in decades through exports. A stronger currency would make the country's exports more expensive. 

 The won's strength is a big concern as the Japanese yen has weakened against the dollar this year. South Korea and Japan compete in major export markets for products ranging from electronic goods to automobiles and ships. 

 The financial crisis forced South Korea to accept a rescue package of $58.35 billion from the International Monetary Fund in December in exchange for painful economic reforms. ((Seoul Newsroom, +822 727 5646, fax +822 727 5666, seoul.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Asia Crisis At A Glance: Indonesia Signs Fourth IMF Letter
text:
-- Indonesia's government signed a fourth letter of intent with the IMF, paving the way for resumption of funding for its crippled economy. The agreement forecast a rupiah rate of IDR10,000 to the dollar by year-end, and predicted GDP will fall more than 10%, with 80% inflation, in the current fiscal year. The central bank will keep high interest rates and recapitalize, merge or close troubled banks. 

 The Asian Development Bank approved a $1.5 billion loan to reform Indonesia's financial sector. [*R/IO] 

 -- The dollar rose to Y141.65, its highest level since joint intervention June 17, before falling on worries of possible intervention. At 0815 GMT, it was at Y140.79, down from Y141.23 late Wednesday in New York. U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Summers repeated that the U.S. will intervene in foreign exchange markets if necessary. [*R/JA] 

 -- South Korea will auction bankrupt Kia Motors and Hanbo Steel, government officials said. The move is the latest in efforts to restructure the economy under the terms of a $58.35 billion IMF bailout. 

 The Financial Supervisory Commission said four or five troubled Korean commercial banks will merge with stronger ones through the purchase and assumptions method. [*R/SK] 

 -- The Bank of Japan will maintain its easy monetary policy, keeping its official discount rate at 0.5% and overnight call money rates below 0.5%. [*R/JA] 

 -- Japan posted a merchandise trade surplus of Y222.60 billion in the first 10 days of June, up 53.6%. [*R/JA]

title: Emerging market  forex  - Won, rupiah on skids again.
text:
LONDON, Dec 9 (Reuters) - Sharp drops in the South Korean won and the Indonesian rupiah led emerging Asian currencies lower on Tuesday despite some talk that the Indonesian central bank had intervened in London. 

 Growing concerns about South Korea's financial woes and overnight rumours about President Suharto's health led to the steep declines in both currencies, analysts said. 

 One market specialist in London said the Indonesian central bank had been intervening to prop up its ailing currency, but other dealers discounted the talk saying the rupiah showed no signs of recovery. 

 Both the won and the rupiah set new record lows as the Asian crisis showed no signs of abating. 

 The won plummeted to a new historic low of 1,465.7 per dollar bid, down from Monday's levels of 1,342.4 and the rupiah sank to a new record low in London of 4,640 to the dollar, from 4,156 on Monday. 

 "Overnight rumours of Suharto's health pushed the rupiah down," said Gerry Celaya, senior director at American Express Bank in London. 

 "They were more or less dispelled by the government  but again the currency has remained weak and it is still well above 4,500 so it's pretty much an overnight decline of nine percent," he added. 

 Bearish sentiment continued to drag down the Korean won as dealers questioned the credibility of the government and its commitment to implement reforms demanded by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) as part of its $57 billion rescue package. 

 The South Korean government is set to hold presidential elections on December 18. 

 The won was pulled even lower following news on Monday that Korea's useable foreign exchange reserves fell to just $6.0 billion on December 2 from $22.5 billion on October 31. 

 In the text of the IMF agreement distributed by the country's Finance Ministry earlier on Tuesday, the IMF said South Korea's policy response to rapid deterioration of its external financing situation at the end of October was "piecemeal" and it had waited until November 21 to approach the Fund. 

 Dealers said they expected the won to reach the 1,500  psychological level. 

 "At the moment it seems like it is very much a one way market," said Celaya. 

 "Everyone is looking at 1,500 level as some sort of psychological resistance level and more or less the last barrier (before) 2,000 but I don't really think we will see it get there, but obviously that is the risk," he added. 

 The drop in the won and the rupiah weighed on other Asian currencies, pulling the Thai baht in offshore markets down to 42.65 from 41.50 on Monday. 

 In contrast, analysts said emerging European currencies held up rather well. 

 "Despite further deep uncertainty in emerging Asia, we actually see a much calmer environment in major east European countries," said David Simmons, head of research for central and eastern Europe at Citibank. 

 "In particular, we continue to see dollar/rouble trading significantly stronger," he added.

title: South Korea Unveils Measures Designed To Stem Financial Downturn
text:
SEOUL -(Dow Jones)- Determined to save its economy without turning to the International Monetary Fund, the South Korean government announced Wednesday a sweeping set of financial support measures aimed at stemming the country's deepening financial crisis. 

 Although a step in the right direction, analysts and economists say the measures are too little too late, as IMF support appears the only way to restore foreign and domestic confidence in the local economy. 

 The government also softened its stance on requesting IMF support, but said it's confident it can bail itself out of the troubles before asking the organization for a helping hand. 

 Blamed for accelerating the country's financial woes, Kang Kyong-shik was dismissed from his position as Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy Wednesday. He was replaced by Minister of Trade Industry and Energy Lim Chang-ryul. 

 Lim immediately announced several much-anticipated measures aimed at reviving financial markets and the financial industry. Key measures include widening the currency trading band for the won to 10% from 2.25% above or below the day's average rate; boosting the government's bad debt fund to 10 trillion won from 3.5 trillion won; opening the country's $200 billion bond market to foreign investors; encouraging mergers and acquisitions among troubled merchant banks and banks, and allowing the central bank to borrow $10 billion from foreign financial institutions. 

 Analysts said the measures are bold, but may be too late. "The measures are a step in the right direction, but they just aren't enough," says Chi Lo, regional economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Singapore. "The measures aren't strong enough to install foreign investors' confidence in the resolve of the government to restructure the financial industry." 

 Market experts also say thing's aren't expected to improve for the hard-hit South Korean currency, with the won expected to plunge Thursday to the bottom its widened trading band, or 10% below the market average rate. The local currency has plunged to its daily permissble low for the past three days, closing Wednesday at 1035.50 won to the dollar, compared with 1012.80 won Tuesday. 

 Lo and others say the only way to regain foreign and domestic confidence in the local economy is for the South Korean government to buckle down and ask the IMF for support. 

 Meanwhile, newly chosen Finance Minister Lim indicated that South Korea could appeal for help to the U.S. and Japan. He urged both countries to cooperate with Korea's efforts to resolve its financial troubles, but didn't specify whether Korea had asked the two countries directly for support. He also didn't say whether the government plans to ask them for financial support. 

 Local newspaper reports, though denied by the Japanese and Korean governments, said South Korea is planning to ask the Bank of Japan for $20 billion to $30 billion in emergency funds. However, analysts said the Bank of Japan, facing its own financial strains, isn't in a position to help Korea. 

 Lim noted that as the world's 11th largest country, if South Korea's financial ills worsen, troubles will spread to the U.S. and Japan. "To the U.S., South Korea's its fifth-largest export country," Lim said, stressing the large influence Korea has on the U.S.'s economic stability. 

 Meanwhile, comments from the new finance ministry head indicated the government has eased its former hard-lined stance against turning to the IMF for support. "South Korea can solve (its financial crisis) if international financial institutions cooperate," said Lim. "But, if necessary, (South Korea) can consider request for IMF aid." 

 As for the reshuffling of key government officials, analysts say they doubt that alone will encourage investors. 

 "On the one hand, Kang Kyong-shik was hated by the business community so replacing him might boost some confidence," said a head of research at local brokerage house. "But on the other hand, Lim won't really change things from when things were run by Kang." 

 The research head added that the measures announced by Lim were basically devised by former finance minister Kang. He and other agree that Kang was used as a scapegoat for the country's economic ills, and removing him does little to restore confidence. 

 Kang is widely blamed for accelerating South Korea's financial woes with his actions in the Kia Group affair. He first announced the government wouldn't intervene to support the troubled group, South Korea's eighth largest congolmerate. But he eventually had to bail out the company with a state takeover by Korea Development Bank, as the crisis widened and affected other companies. 

 In addition to Kang's dismissal, Chief Presidential Economic Adviser Kim In-ho was fired and replaced by Kim Young-suk, chief of Korea's Custom's Administration. 

 Analysts say the market has already factored in the financial support measures and resignation of Kang, therefore any lasting recovery in stock prices or fall in interest rates aren't expected. Shares ended 7.93 points higher at 502.59 on the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index on anticipation of the measures, which were announced after the stock market's close. 

 Interest rates, measured by yields on three-year corporate bonds, rose 0.35 percentage point to a new 28-month high of 14%, on continued worries about liquidity problems. 

 Although the government increased its fund meant to absorb non-performing debt held by local financial institutions, analysts still worry whether the fund is sufficient. 

 Lim said banks are suffering from bad loans totaling 28.53 trillion won as of the end of September, while merchant banks are buried under around four trillion won in nonperforming debt during the same period. 

 The country's total foreign debts, meanwhile, are expected to reach $110 billion by the end of the year, about half of which are short-term debts. 

 Lo said foreign-exchange borrowing by the country's merchant banks reached $20 billion at the end of October. Of the total, $3.2 billion is short-term debts, which have been paid within a year. Analysts worry that as short-term debt matures, jittery foreign investors won't be willing to roll over their loans to Korean borrowers, which would trigger a massive credit crunch in the economy.

title: Review:Won's Fall Spotlights Korea Econ Weakness,Fuels Fears
text:
By Charles S. Lee 

 SEOUL (AP-Dow Jones)--South Koreans are calling it 'the four-digit era.' On Monday, the won closed at 999 to the U.S. dollar, pushing the rate that ordinary Koreans pay for dollars at banks to more than 1,000 for the first time ever. Local newspaper headlines heralded the new epoch curtly: '$1=W1,000.' 

 Although the currency recovered a bit in subsequent days, the implications of its slide are stark. South Korea's economy is staggering through its most bruising slump in years, and there's a growing fear that it may become the next domino to fall to the financial turmoil shaking its Southeast Asian neighbours. If that happened, the consequences would reverberate not only through Asia but also around the globe, reports the latest edition of the Far Eastern Economic Review published Thursday. 

 South Korea is the world's 11th-biggest economy and its 12th-largest trading power. Its companies play a significant role in strategic industries from semi-conductors to cars to steel, and foreign bankers and investors are far more exposed to its troubles than they are to those of Thailand and Indonesia, both now under emergency care by the International Monetary Fund. A South Korean economic crash would certainly open a new, far more dangerous, chapter in the Asian confidence crisis, and one that could encompass its neighbours in Northeast Asia. 

 'Clearly, the market has taken the view that the Asian crisis isn't over,' says Steven Xu, a regional economist for Standard Chartered Bank in Hong Kong. 'Korea is undermining everyone.' 

 The won recovered slightly by early Thursday on dollar-selling intervention by South Korea's central bank: the dollar was trading at 987.60 won, down from 988.80 won at Wednesday's close.

title: Analysts demand disclosure as Korea crisis looms.
text:
HONG KONG, Nov 12 (Reuters) - Analysts are calling for improved disclosure from South Korea on its dollar-denominated debts amid mounting concern over the state of the economy. 

 South Korea, the world's eleventh largest economy in terms of gross domestic product, faces rapidly rising servicing costs on a mountain of U.S.-dollar denominated corporate debt. The won's recent slide against the U.S. dollar has further swollen those debts. 

 The Bank of Korea intervened again on Wednesday to defend the won from falling through the key 1,000 level against the U.S. dollar. The won was trading at about 988.80 to the dollar at midday. 

 "The problem is disclosure. It's not great," said an analyst who requested anonymity. 

 "Too much of this is conjecture. Everybody knows they have a really bad debt problem, but it's guess work at the moment as to how bad things are," he said. 

 The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU), considered by some Asian brokers to be the most reliable source of information on South Korean debt, estimates that the country's external debt burden will rise to US$151 billion by the end of 1997 from 1996 levels of US$137 billion. 

 Short-term debt due to mature within one year amounts to US$77 billion of the 1997 total, the EIU said in figures compiled for its fourth-quarter country risk report. 

 This short-term debt figure, the focus of much of the concern surrounding South Korea's economic condition, compares with the central Bank of Korea's figure of US$67 billion released last week. 

 One broker estimates more than US$30 billion in short-term paper will mature before the end of the year -- but these figures are, once again, unconfirmed. 

 There is, however, mounting evidence that South Korean corporations are being forced to roll over maturing long-term debt in short-term paper at sharply higher rates following downgrades from international rating agencies. 

 Spreads against comparable U.S. treasury bonds have blown out to more than 320 basis points on the Korean Development Bank (KDB) bond due 2006, considered a benchmark for South Korean debt. The spread was about 100 basis points in June. 

 The EIU said nearly all of the external debt was corporate and denominated in U.S. dollars. This implies heavy risk for corporations without a natural hedge against the declining won through exporting revenue denominated in U.S. dollars. 

 "With the won going through the floor, U.S. dollar repayments will become that much more expensive," a source said. 

 But even the EIU figures are subject to caution. 

 Short-term debt figures depend upon information from the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), of which South Korea is a member. But the longer-term figures are harder to quantify given that South Korea stopped appearing before the World Bank in 1994. 

 One undeniable fact is that South Korea's debt burden has risen sharply over the past couple of years. A recent SBC Warburg report said South Korea's external debt had risen to current levels from US$108 billion in 1995, US$81.5 billion in 1994, US$64 billion in 1993 and US$60 billion in 1992. 

 "A lot of it comes from expansion earlier on in the decade, the government-sponsored expansion to get market share, to beat the Japanese and get themselves out of recession," another analyst said. 

 "And as you're aware, the government in Korea tells companies what to do and tells banks to lend their money and without credit screening they got themselves into a mess." 

 Financial market players also want to know the condition of the Bank of Korea's foreign exchange reserves following reports they had dwindled far below official estimates of US$30.5 billion due to currency forward commitments to defend the won. 

 Analysts said the won market was more restrictive than Thailand's foreign exchange market was before the baht fell to speculators in July. Heavy forward positions taken by the Thai central bank to defend the baht devastated reserves and forced the country to seek aid from the International Monetary Fund. 

South Korea has admitted intervening in the spot foreign exchange markets on the won's behalf, but many analysts believe the Bank of Korea has also stepped into the U.S.-dollar denominated, non-deliverable forward (NDF) market, which operates mostly offshore. 

 "The view is they've been intervening in the NDFs," the first analyst said. "And their reserves haven't gone down over the last two months.... 

 "But all of this is very, very hard to determine."

title: Currency  woes push down Singapore stocks.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Asia's bumpy road to recovery and the worsening health of the South Korean won returned to trample the Singapore stock market and other regional bourses on Friday. 

 "Nearly every major stock market in Asia fell. People are very nervous and talking of a second wave of selling in Hong Kong soon. All these because the region remains fragile, currencies weak and maybe this is really the beginning," said a dealer with a local house. 

 After opening at 1,691.82, the Straits Times Industrials Index ended at 1,671.25, down 19.28 points or 1.14 percent. 

 On Friday, the won posted another record-low close of 979.9 despite two central bank dollar-selling intervention to boost the currency, fuelling fears South Korea might be the next candidate for the International Monetary Fund aid. 

 The won's fall sent some Asian currencies reeling and regional stock markets in Tokyo, Hong Kong and Taiwan tumbling. 

 Property counters led the drop in Singapore's stock market, with the index plunging 21.50 points, or 4.95 percent, to 412.85. 

 Sharp drops were noted in property heavyweights. First Capital tumbled 90 cents to S$2.86, City Development shed 40 cents to S$7.05 and Singapore Land dropped 32 cents to S$4.28. 

 Dealers said the property companies were hit after reports that bids for a well-located residential site in Singapore were 25 to 30 percent below expectations. 

 Real estate firm Colliers Jardine called it the weakest tender in years. 

 Share trading in electronic parts distributor Electronic Resources Ltd was suspended pending a company announcement. 

 Dealers said the company could be a takeover target of U.S.-listed Ingram Micro Inc, the world's biggest computer wholesale distributor. 

 Ingram was rumoured to be keen on securing 24 percent stake in ERL at S$2.10 per share. 

 Selective electronic shares bucked the market downtrend. 

 Led by a S$1.10 rise in multimedia Creative Technology to S$44.30, the SES electronic index rose 0.42 percent to 140.36. 

 "The outlook for the electronic sector is bright ahead of the year-end festive demand. Creative is expected to do well in terms of its order book," said one dealer.

title: FOCUS-S.Korean won hits low despite  intervention .
text:
SEOUL, Sept 19 (Reuter) - South Korea's currency closed at a record low on Friday despite repeated dollar sales by the central bank, and analysts predicted worse lay in store for the won. 

 "There are no (dollar) sellers, only buyers. Exporters prefer to hold dollars rather than selling at the current level," said a dealer at a U.S. bank. 

 On Friday the won closed at 913.80 to the dollar against Thursday's close of 909.60. 

 The won's fall also contributed to a slide in the Seoul stock market. 

 Namuh Rhee, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities, said: "The trade deficit and the dollar's international trends are the main factors moving the won, and for now, the won's bottom is seen at around 930." 

 Dealers said the Bank of Korea sold about $400 million in the local interbank market on Friday to cushion the won's fall, which they attributed to a rush for import settlements. 

 A large backlog of import deals had built up during a five-day holiday that lasted through Wednesday, they said. 

 Besides the dollar's strength, the South Korean currency has also been pressured by dollar shortages at local financial institutions as a result of this year's string of corporate failures and debt defaults. 

 The won's plunge hammered the Seoul stock market, pushing the Korean Composite Stock Price Index down 1.74 percent or 12.23 points to 689.16. 

 "The won's fall discourages foreign investors in local stocks and this in turn worries local investors," said Park Byung-moon, head of research at LG Securities. 

 "Foreign investors have already been losing interest in Asian markets following the currency crisis in several Asian countries," he said, referring to slide of currencies in Thailand, the Philippines and Malaysia. 

 A weakening currency usually leads to improved price competitiveness of the country's exports, but analysts say it takes time for the benefits to flow. 

 "Investors are worried about the lack of evidence that the weakening won really would boost exports," said Park. "Instead, they are concerned that the weakening won will only end up expanding foreign exchange losses of companies." 

 For the first eight months of this year, South Korea ran up a current account deficit of $11.1 billion, slightly down from a $12.15 billion shortfall a year earlier. 

 Last year, the current account deficit rose to a record $23.72 billion from $8.95 billion in 1995. 

 The won has been depreciating against the U.S. unit for more than a year. It fell 8.2 percent against the dollar last year, and has dropped 7.6 percent so far this year.

 "People are still bearish on the baht, but they're a bit cautious at the moment because the Thai Prime Minister has a few options," said a senior dealer at a Singapore bank. 

 He said investors would react negatively if Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh decided to dissolve parliament and call a snap election. 

 "If he calls for fresh elections, it would be negative for the baht because more money would be wasted," he said. 

 Worries over Chavalit calling a snap election surfaced after public opinion forced him to endorse a new draft constitution. A final vote on the draft will be held on September 27 following a three-day no-confidence debate. 

 The dealer said the baht's weakness should be limited to 35.25 to the dollar in offshore markets, or 35.75 at worst. 

 It was at 34.75/85 at 0500 GMT against 34.45/34.55 late on Thursday. The onshore rate was 35.65/80 against 35.40/35.60. 

 The baht could also face renewed selling if the Bank of Thailand's end-August forex reserves showed a significant drop from the August 14 level of $27.9 billion, dealers said. 

 Foreign minister Thanong Bidaya told parliament last month Thailand's forward swap contracts, taken to defend the baht from a speculative onslaught in mid-May, could deplete reserves by $6-$14 billion over the following year. 

 In Malaysia, the ringgit extended its overnight losses in thin trade as players continued to focus on stock market weakness. 

 The ringgit was at 2.9530/80 to the dollar while the Kuala Lumpur stock index was down 0.03 percent to 833.92 at midday. 

 Dealers said the market wanted to see more action on the measures announced by Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim on Wednesday to curb Malaysia's current account deficit and growth. 

 Anwar said several multi-billion construction projects, would be delayed to slow growth and reduce imports. 

 "People are looking for more details of the plan. Right now, all eyes are on the October 17 budget (for 1998)," a dealer at a European bank in Singapore said. 

 "They will really have to show that they are going to be restrained about growth. Until the budget, I don't see the ringgit recovering very substantially," he said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah and Singapore dollar tracked the ringgit's decline, but dealers said trade was lacklustre and there were no signs of large flows. 

 "It's much calmer now. It's not like before when once you got hit, the next offer was 40 or 50 points away. You see now a lot more stability in the market," a local bank dealer in Jakarta said. 

 Spot rupiah was at 2,940/47 against an opening 2,950/60. 

 The Singapore dollar was at 1.5127/37 to the U.S. dollar. 

 But the Philippine peso was still haunted by worries that President Fidel Ramos may try to change the constitution to allow him a second term in office. 

 Dealers said the peso's decline was being cushioned by exporter dollar sales amid a dearth of fresh news. 

 In South Korea, fears of central bank intervention kept the won on a tight leash between 908.30 and 909.00 to the dollar. 

 Dealers said upward pressure on the dollar would be dampened by the central bank's planned injection of $500 million into the banking system to ease tightening liquidity ahead of the Chusok thanksgiving holidays next week.

title: S.Korea declares intention to stabilise  currency .
text:
SEOUL, Aug 27 (Reuter) - Repeated intervention by South Korea's central bank over the past two days has barely contained the won's slide against the dollar, but the finance ministry on Wednesday said it would not allow the won to fall sharply. 

 The statement had little impact on trading. Dealers said the government was more interested in managing the pace of won depreciation than in reversing the downward trend. 

 The won closed Wednesday's trading at 902.80 against the dollar, down from Tuesday's close of 900.50. 

 Dealers and analysts said the government believed there was more room for the local currency to weaken. The won has fallen about seven percent against the dollar so far this year, on top of an 8.2 percent decline in 1996. 

 "The government may be well aware the downward trend itself cannot be turned around, and today's announcement is seen to be aimed at slowing the speed," said a domestic bank dealer. 

 He said the finance ministry signalled its stance on Monday when it said it would expand the individual limit on foreign stock ownership to 26 percent from the current 23 percent. 

 "If the ministry wanted to reverse the won's direction, it would have taken a more aggressive policy to bring in dollars," he said, adding that government officials had earlier considered raising the limit to 28 percent. 

 A finance ministry official said the won's rate was within an appropriate range and that the government would try to stabilise the currency. 

 "The won is believed to be within an appropriate range when taking into account dollar demand and supply, the dollar's trends abroad and the price competitiveness of our exports," Won Bong-hee, director general of the ministry's financial policy division, told a news conference. 

 "In the future the government will keep the won's rate stable by actively countering steep changes on temporary demand and supply factors or speculative factors," Won said. 

 The currency continued to fall this week and hit a historic low of 909.50 on Tuesday before several Bank of Korea interventions pushed it to a higher close at 900.50. 

 Dealers said the central bank poured more than a billion dollars into the interbank market on Monday and Tuesday, during which the won tumbled by 1.1 percent. 

 "The government seems to just want to stop the won's plunge from dealing an additional blow to the business community already hit by corporate troubles," said a Citibank dealer. 

 "The government is indicating that it would no longer tolerate speculation that the dollar would pass 905 won days later and then 910 very soon after that," said another foreign bank dealer. 

 The won has been pressured by the greenback's strength in international markets and most recently was hit by dollar shortages at domestic banks. 

 South Korean merchant banks and other financial institutions have had difficulty securing dollars as foreign lenders have been reluctant to offer loans in the aftermath of this year's string of corporate failures and huge debt defaults. 

 A cheaper won would contribute to boosting the international price competitiveness of South Korean products by making them cheaper even if the won-denominated prices were kept unchanged. 

 But steep depreciation of the currency would deter foreign investment in domestic equities and industries for fear of losses in terms of the dollar value. 

 Corporate earnings were also expected to be damaged by the won's steep depreciation because companies have to pay more on their dollar-denominated debts.

title: S.Korea won tumbles despite repeated  intervention .
text:
SEOUL, Aug 25 (Reuter) - South Korea's won currency hit new lows against the dollar on Monday before recovering slightly after the central Bank of Korea stepped into the market four times to stem the fall. 

 In a highly unusual move, the Bank of Korea announced early in the morning it would sell dollars in the interbank market to ease the local currency's decline. 

 The central bank announcement came after the won fell to an all-time low 902.50 against the dollar. 

 The won rebounded on the rare statement by the bank, but only temporarily. 

 At the midday break, the won stood at 903.50, after hitting an all-time low of 907.80 earlier in the day. The won closed at 899.50 on Friday. 

 In the early afternoon, the central bank sold dollars for 904 won in its fourth intervention. 

 The Bank of Korea offered to sell dollars at 923 won in six-month forward trade at about mid-morning, dealers said. 

 Minutes later, it stepped in again, this time offering to sell dollars at 944 won in one-year forward trade, they said. 

 Dealers said the won was pressured by strong dollar demand in line with the continued dollar shortages at merchant banks. 

 Local financial institutions have been struggling to secure dollars in the aftermath of this year's string of corporate debt defaults that affected credit ratings of South Korean banks. 

 Stock investors reacted negatively to the won's sharp fall. 

 The composite index, which had opened higher on hopes for a government package to stabilise financial markets, closed for the lunch break barely higher at 743.43, up 0.85 points. 

 The won has been depreciating against the U.S. unit for more than a year. 

 It fell 8.2 percent against the dollar last year, and 6.6 percent so far this year. 

 The won's daily movement is limited to a 2.25 percent trading band. Its limited convertibility makes it less susceptible than fully convertible currencies to speculation. 

 Dealers said the won was expected to further weaken in the afternoon unless the government announced fresh steps to counter the currency's drop. 

 "Dollar demand was so strong that announcement of the intervention plan hardly affected the trading sentiment," said a foreign bank dealer.

title: S.Korea won tumbles as  central bank intervenes .
text:
SEOUL, Aug 25 (Reuter) - South Korea's currency tumbled to a new low against the U.S. dollar on Monday even though the central bank warned speculators it would step in to stem the fall -- and then did so five times. 

 Analysts were divided on the reasons for the won's dive. 

 One said it was a "self-fulfilling prophecy" of jittery corporate treasurers. Another blamed an expected widening of South Korea's August trade deficit. 

 But analysts agreed that the won, which is not pegged to the dollar and not fully convertible, was not under a serious speculative attack similar to an assault that has battered Southeast Asian currencies. 

 The won closed on Monday at 904.60 against the dollar, compared to Friday's close of 899.50 won. 

 In a highly unusual move, the Bank of Korea announced early in Monday morning trading it would sell dollars in the interbank market to stem the local currency's decline. 

 The rare announcement came after the won fell to a new low of 902.50, but its impact was only temporary. At the midday break, the won stood at 903.50. 

 Steve Marvin, head of research at Ssangyong Securities, said the won's dive was a response to a rash of corporate failures. 

 Corporate treasurers of firms whose imports feed South Korea's export industries have become jittery about monthly import settlements, he said. 

 "These guys have concluded the won is going to go down further. In a sense their worries are triggering early buying or stockpiling of dollars. They know they're going to need dollars. In a sense it's a self-fulfilling prophecy," Marvin said. 

 Graham Courtney, director of Asian economics at SBC Warburg in Tokyo, blamed South Korea's August trade deficit, which he forecast would be "very, very big," though exports recently have been increasing and imports have slowed. 

 "There is extra downward pressure on the won coming from what looks to be a particularly bad deficit," Courtney said. 

 Traders seem to disagree with recent central bank statements that a won/dollar rate of 900 was reasonable, he said. 

 "Frankly, if the trade thinks the rate should be higher, why should the central bank defend at 900? I think the Bank of Korea is now thinking it should move to a more defensible level, and fundamentally, 905-910 is much more defensible," he said. 

 The won is less susceptible than some currencies to attack. Its daily movement is limited to a 2.25 percent trading band. 

 "Restrictions on won trading make it a less appetising target," Marvin said. "There's not that comfort zone of currencies linked to the dollar," 

 The won has been depreciating against the U.S. unit for more than a year, falling 8.2 percent against the dollar last year, and more than six percent so far this year. 

 Dealers said the Bank of Korea intervened in the market three times during the morning trading session. 

 It sold dollars at 923 won in six-month forward trade at about mid-morning, then stepped in again minutes later to sell dollars at 944 won in one-year forward trade, they said. 

 In late morning, the Bank of Korea entered the market for a third time and sold dollars at about 903.00 in spot trade. 

 The fourth intervention came in early afternoon when the central bank sold dollars for 904 won in spot trading. 

 Near the close of trading, the Bank of Korea stepped in for the fifth time, selling dollars at 904.40-904.80 in spot trade. At the same time, the bank sold dollars at 907.50 in one-month forward and 916 in three-month forward trade.

title: Central bank  moves to slow rise of South Korea won.
text:
SEOUL, Aug 1 (Reuter) - South Korea's central bank intervened on Tuesday for the fourth consecutive session to halt a rise in the won against the dollar and dealers said they expected more bank buying of the U.S. currency. 

 The won, which ended on Tuesday at 757.50 to the dollar, has risen 4.12 percent against the U.S. currency since the end of last year. The dollar had been hovering in a 756-757 range in the past week, a three-and-half-year low against the won. 

 "It is the first time for the central bank to intervene for four days in a row," said a local bank dealer. "Its dollar support is expected to continue." 

 Many dealers had forcast a year-end dollar/won rate at 730-740 but a growing number of them now put it at around 750. 

 Dealers said the central bank, the Bank of Korea (BOK), stepped into the foreign exchange market twice on Monday and twice on Tuesday. 

 "It is really rare. We are really surprised," said another domestic bank dealer. 

 "We have no comment on the market talk about intervention. But it is our principle to let the won/dollar move according to the market situation," said Kim Sung-min of BOK's foreign exchange division. 

 BOK officials normally deny interventions. 

 But Kim Joon-il, of state think-tank Korea Development Institute (KDI), said: "I believe the central bank could not stand idly by when the won rises sharply, considering price competitiveness of our export products." 

 Kim said he believed 760 was a proper won/dollar level for exporters to maintain their profits in overseas markets. 

 The won/dollar rate is allowed to move one percent away from the mid-rate calculated daily based on the weighted average of the previous day's interbank spot trade. 

 The won has risen despite a growing trade deficit because of overseas dollar borrowings to finance corporate investment and official infrastructure projects. 

 South Korea's customs-cleared trade deficit was $7.68 billion in the first seven months of this year, up from $4.38 billion in the same 1994 period.
