title: Emerging  FX -Asia higher, shrug off  intervention  jitters
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 1 (Reuters) - Sustained capital inflows sent Asian currencies higher on Friday as the U.S. dollar weakened globally, with the Thai baht <THB=> leading the rally amid signs of easing market concern about central bank intervention.  

Underscoring solid fundamentals buoying most regional currencies, South Korea said on Friday the country's exports in November grew a faster-than-expected 19.8 percent to a monthly record from a year earlier, maintaining surprising strength.  

"The risk appetite is still very good and there is no sign that any growth slowdown is impacting inflows into the region at the moment, and the dollar is softer," said James Malcolm, currency strategist at Deutsche Bank.  

"So strong inflows plus a soft dollar, even with central banks intervening, means the trend remains in place," he said.  

Renewed strength in most Asian currencies in recent weeks has triggered a wave of verbal and actual intervention by regional central banks to cap further currency appreciation.  

"Looking ahead, renewed interests for short dollar positions should place dollar/Asia on track to end this week with another decline," currency strategists Claudio Piron and Yen Ping Ho at JPMorgan wrote in a research note.  

Thio Chin Loo, currency analyst at BNP Paribas, said she remained bullish about the near-term strength of Asian currencies, with the latest gains helped by dollar weakness.  

The dollar hit a 14-year low against sterling <GBP=> on Friday and a new 20-month trough versus the euro <EUR=> as the U.S. currency suffered from expectations a weakening economy will prompt the Federal Reserve to cut interest rates next year.  

BEST PERFORMERS  

The Thai baht and Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> were Friday's best performers, with the baht gaining more than two thirds of a percent to 35.71 per dollar, its strongest level in eight years.  

The Bank of Thailand has been intervening both verbally and through actual dollar buying this week, traders said.  

Callum Henderson, head of currency strategy at Standard Chartered Bank, said the baht, which has gained about 15 percent so far this year, was also supported as political uncertainty after a military coup in September eased.  

"People took another look at Thailand and said okay, inflation has peaked, growth is set to accelerate so quite a few investors who were underweight Thailand have come back in the past few months," he said.  

The latest Reuters poll on positioning in Asian currencies suggests investors stepped up long positions in the Thai baht and remained bullish on the South Korean won and Singapore dollar.  

The ringgit strengthened to about 3.5915 per dollar, up about 0.75 percent from levels traded late on Thursday. A trader said the ringgit's unusually sharp gains were largely due to technical selling of the dollar.  

The South Korean won <KRW=>, underpinned by third-quarter gross domestic product data that was revised upward, rose to as high as 927.1 per dollar, gaining moderately but still off a nine-year high this week of 925.  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> firmed as high as 32.25 per U.S. dollar, hitting its highest level in about 4-½ months, while the Singapore dollar <SGD=> briefly hit 1.5372 against the U.S. dollar, matching a nine-year high set on Thursday. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR; Change on the day at 0728 GMT

title: UPDATE 3-S.Korea's Oct factory output lifts rate outlook
text:
(Recasts with output data, analysts, markets)  

SEOUL, Nov 29 (Reuters) - South Korean factory output grew unexpectedly for a third consecutive month in October, data showed on Wednesday, strengthening the chance the central bank will lift interest rates next year.  

The industrial output index in October rose a seasonally adjusted 2.6 percent from the previous month, compared with the median 0.8 percent drop forecast in a Reuters poll and following a revised 3.1 percent gain in September.  

Government bond prices gave up their early gains to turn weaker as the data, together with a separate government indicator suggesting an upbeat economic outlook, improved the prospect of a rise in interest rates.  

Investors have said the central bank could lift interest rates early next year, if local housing prices kept growing despite a series of government steps and as long as Asia's third-largest economy stayed on a sustained growth track.  

"The market's focus has recently been shifting toward an increasing probability of a rate increase and today's production data reinforced the probability even further," said Kong Dong-rak, a fixed-income analyst at SK Securities.  

Industrial output in October rose 4.6 percent from a year earlier, data from the National Statistical Office showed, below a 5.8 percent gain forecast in the Reuters survey.  

But the effect of slower annual growth was outweighed by strong monthly growth and the statistics agency's separate data showing the economy's outlook had improved in October.  

The agency said its leading composite index -- compiled from 10 types of indicators about the future -- rose 4.5 percent in October from a year earlier, accelerating from a 4.1 percent rise in September. It releases only the growth rates.  

SOFTER U.S. ECONOMY, FIRMER WON  

Treasury bond December futures <KTBc1> gave up more than an earlier gain of 13 ticks to close down four ticks at 108.67.  

Analysts said South Korean exports were expected to fare better next year than many had earlier predicted as the effect of a slowing U.S. economy would be offset by robust economies elsewhere, such as Europe and China.  

"The figures showed South Korea's economy is in very good shape, led by strong exports, and that U.S. and global economies are healthy," said Oh Suk-tae, an economist at Citigroup. "The Bank of Korea may consider raising interest rates, given the bubble in South Korea's property market."  

Analysts do not expect the Bank of Korea to raise interest rates at its Dec. 7 policy meeting after its surprise upgrade in required cash reserve ratios announced on Nov. 23.  

The commerce ministry was also optimistic about exports, as it said on Wednesday that this year's shipments abroad would probably total about $326 billion, up 14.6 percent from 2005 and above a target set at $318 billion. [ID:nSEO150476]  

Analysts said the firmer won would not have a big impact on South Korea's exports, unlike in recent years, although the stronger currency will hurt profitability at export industries.  

But the firmer won has hit the current account surplus, which plunged to a seasonally adjusted $1.97 billion for the first 10 months of this year from $14.12 billion a year earlier, the central bank said earlier on Wednesday. [ID:nSEO184210]  

The won <KRW=> has gained more than 8 percent this year to hit its strongest levels in more than nine years against both the dollar and the yen this month. It has since fallen back slightly.  

Dealers had said South Korea carried out heavy dollar-buying intervention this month to contain the won's strength, including about an estimated $1 billion purchase on Wednesday alone.  

(Additional reporting by Lee Soo-jung and Cheon Jong-woo)

title: UPDATE 2-S.Korea Oct c/a surplus hits 5-mth high
text:
(Updates with central bank official, won)  

 SEOUL, Nov 29 (Reuters) - South Korea recorded its biggest current account surplus for five months in October, central bank data showed on Wednesday, underlining the government's difficulty in curbing the won's strength.  

 However, given expectations that the current account surplus will deteriorate next year, the broad measure of trade flows is unlikely to offer the currency support longer term.  

 "The trade surplus will probably be sustained next year but the overall current account balance will worsen due to (a) growing deficit in the services account," said Park Yong-il, senior FX trader at DBS Bank's Seoul branch.  

 October's current account surplus was a seasonally adjusted $723 million, the biggest since a $1.19 billion surplus in May and swelling from a revised $426 million surplus in September, the Bank of Korea said.  

 South Korea, Asia's third-biggest economy, has become more dependent on exports for growth this year as domestic demand has cooled.  

 But at the same time authorities are battling to control the won's strength to keep exports competitive as the currency has risen to nine-year highs against the dollar and the yen.  

 The won was up 0.1 percent on the day against the dollar, showing little reaction to the data, partly because of expectations the current account will weaken next year, a trend that is already underway.  

 The current account surplus for the first 10 months of this year plunged to a seasonally adjusted $1.97 billion from a $14.12 billion surplus a year earlier, the Bank of Korea data showed.  

 The surplus has been eroded by higher global energy prices and increased spending by Koreans abroad due to the won's strength.  

 The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said in a report on Tuesday it expected a current account surplus equivalent to 0.3 percent of gross domestic product this year to swing by 2008 to a deficit of 0.4 percent of GDP.  

 The jump in the current account in October was mostly generated by a rise in the merchandise trade surplus to $2.71 billion from a revised $2.13 billion surplus in September, offsetting a slightly expanded deficit in services.  

 The won has gained more than 8 percent this year and earlier this month hit its strongest bid level in more than nine years against both the dollar and the yen <JPYKRW=>.  

 It has since fallen back slightly in what dealers said was heavy government currency intervention.  

 A senior central bank official said South Korea would achieve a $4 billion current account surplus in 2006 "without much difficulty".  

 However, that would still show a sharp drop from a $16.56 billion surplus in 2005.  

 Jeong Sam-yong, head of the Bank of Korea's international balance of payments team, said the unadjusted current account surplus in November would be similar to the $1.73 billion surplus recorded for October.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia rallies, central banks watch closely
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 23 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rallied on Thursday, with the Singapore dollar hitting a nine-year high and the Philippine peso touching a 4-1/2-year peak, in reaction to a broad sell-off in the U.S. currency overnight.  

Renewed strength in local currencies triggered a wave of comments from officials. South Korea warned against won strength and the Thai central bank said it may relax its capital controls further to help ease upward pressure on the baht.  

Central bank intervention to curb currency strength was suspected in South Korea and India.  

Trade was generally subdued with U.S. and Japanese markets closed for a holiday. But with the dollar taking a beating overnight as investors adjusted positions ahead of the break, Asia's currency markets held their firm tone.  

"Over the last few weeks we have seen bouts of intervention on some currencies, while some central banks have said they are not concerned about currency strength," said Callum Henderson, head of currency strategy at Standard Chartered Bank.  

"But the bias is for further Asian currency strength and we have had a major move in the dollar in the last 24 hours, albeit on thin liquidity."  

The Philippine peso <PHP=> rose to 44.66 to the dollar, its highest level in about 4-½ years, while the Singapore dollar <SGD=> extended Wednesday's gains to a new nine-year high of about 1.5520 per U.S. dollar.  

The Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> rose to 7.8575 per dollar, the strongest since its July 2005 revaluation, while the Japanese yen <JPY=> was at 116.58 per dollar, up about 0.75 percent from late Wednesday's levels in Asia.  

SPOTLIGHT ON WON  

The South Korean won <KRW=> added as much as 0.5 percent to about 929.20 per dollar -- its highest in just over 1-½ weeks.  

It was supported by a South Korean central bank decision on Thursday to raise reserve requirements on short-term deposits.  

The chief foreign exchange official at South Korea's central bank warned the bank would take steps whenever necessary to stabilise the currency market, adding the won had overshot fair value.  

"It is more a case of the authorities wanting not only just to stem won strength because of concerns about exporters but also because it is starting to detect that speculative flows are behind won gains," said Bank of America currency strategist Christy Tan.  

The won by some measures was still at record highs, raising concerns about export competitiveness, Tan said.  

The won gapped higher at Thursday's opening -- a sign of market strength, according to technical analysts.  

In Singapore, dealers said they did not suspect the central bank of intervening to cap gains in the Singapore dollar despite market wariness in early trade about such action.  

A trader in Manila said it also appeared that the Philippine central bank had stayed away from the market as weakness in local stocks helped limit the peso's rally.  

"I don't think they (the central bank) have been in the market," he said. "One reason for the peso high is the major U.S. dollar sell-off overnight, but there is some weakness in the stock market, so the factors are balancing out."  

Elsewhere, Miranda Goeltom, Bank Indonesia's senior deputy governor, said the current exchange rate of the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> was still conducive for the country's exports and imports. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0753 GMT

title: POLL-Markets further increase Asian  FX  long positions
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 15 (Reuters) - Currency markets raised their long positions on the Singapore dollar and South Korean won and remained bullish on the Indonesian rupiah and Thai baht in the past couple of weeks, undeterred by sporadic central bank intervention, a Reuters poll shows.  

The twice-monthly survey asked 15 currency strategists to estimate how the market is positioned in four Asian currencies against the U.S. dollar.  

It measures estimates on the net long or short position in a currency on a scale of minus 3 to plus 3. A score of plus 3 indicates the market is significantly long on dollars.  

The findings of the survey conducted on Nov. 14 are as follows:  

-- SOUTH KOREAN WON <KRW=>:  

The average positioning was minus 1.33, indicating the market had increased its short dollar positions versus the won in early November, having reversed a long dollar position in the previous two weeks. The scores ranged between zero and minus 2 with one respondent saying the market was neutral.  

-- SINGAPORE DOLLAR <SGD=>:  

The average positioning was minus 1.77, suggesting the market has ratcheted up long Singapore dollar positions against the U.S. dollar. The scores ranged between minus 1 and minus 3.  

-- INDONESIAN RUPIAH <IDR=>:  

The average positioning was minus 0.63, implying the market had slightly pared its short dollar-long rupiah positions. Scores ranged from minus 2 to zero.  

-- THAI BAHT <THB=>:  

The average positioning score was minus 1.67, almost the same level of long baht positions as estimated in the Oct. 31 poll. Scores ranged from zero to minus 3.  

Several Asian currencies hit multi-month or multi-year highs versus the dollar this week, underpinned by foreign equity investment flows into Asia, softer U.S. economic data and talk that China was diversifying its estimated $1 trillion in currency reserves.  

Central banks in South Korea, India and Thailand were suspected of having intervened to check the gains in their currencies.  

"Widespread U.S. dollar underperformance, coupled with steady gains in the yuan, has supported Asian regionals on a broad basis," said Sue Trinh, a currency strategist at RBC Capital Markets.  

"We are seeing modest consolidation today after the hefty intervention especially by Bank of Korea early this week but, on a relative basis, Asia is still performing well," she said.

(Updates to close)  

SEOUL, Nov 14 (Reuters) - The South Korean won <KRW=> slid against the dollar for a second session on Tuesday, ignoring the yen's <JPY=> spurt after what dealers suspected was more dollar buying intervention by the authorities to weaken the local unit.  

South Korea purchased dollars for a second day on Tuesday after buying $1 billion on the currency market on Monday, dealers reported, worried the won's <KRW=> relentless rise to almost nine-year highs would hit the country's exports, which already face a slowing U.S. economy.  

The won settled domestic trade at 937.1 dollar, compared to the previous close of 934.8. In the prior session, the won hit a six-month high of 927.8 per dollar.

The yen rallied on Tuesday after data showed Japan's economy grew more rapidly than expected in the third quarter, keeping the Bank of Japan on track to raise interest rates in the next few months. [ID:nT121]  

Japan's gross domestic product expanded at a 2 percent annual rate in the July-September quarter, double forecasts, while growth for the previous quarter was revised up to a 1.5 percent annualised pace from 1.0 percent previously.  

On the economic front, South Korean import prices in won terms fell 1.4 percent in October from a year earlier, posting their first annual loss in one and a half years, central bank data showed on Tuesday.  

The Japanese yen <JPY=> was last quoted at 117.52/56 per dollar, from 118.14/16 in late New York trade the previous session.

title: UPDATE 2-S.Korea says missile launch won't hurt economy
text:
(Recasts after meeting ends, updates markets)  

SEOUL, July 5 (Reuters) - South Korean officials said they did not expect a missile launch by North Korea on Wednesday to have much impact on the South's economy, but they were concerned that financial markets might overreact.  

Share prices and the won fell in early trade on worries the incident could dampen investors' confidence in Asia's fourth-largest economy, already faced with growing pessimism among consumers and companies.  

North Korea launched at least six missiles, including a long-range Taepodong 2 that appeared to fail in flight, U.S. officials said. See [ID:nL0465618] for details.  

Vice Finance Minister Bahk Byong-won told reporters after a meeting of senior economic policy makers the incident could slow down an improvement in South Korea's credit rating outlook but would not lead to an immediate change in the ratings themselves.  

Bahk said participants at the meeting, including the central bank's deputy governor, had agreed to set up an emergency team to monitor financial markets before deciding whether to take measures.  

"I don't think this will have any direct influence on the overall economy, although it may hurt the sentiment of investors, and the government has no plan at present to take any specific steps," Bahk told reporters.  

"If you look back on what happened in 1998, financial markets regained stability pretty soon after some turbulence in the early days," Bahk said, referring to a North Korean missile test-launch that year that sparked falls in markets in South Korea and elsewhere in Asia.  

The won <KRW=> lost just 0.1 percent to 944.5 per dollar in morning trade and reaction was also muted on Seoul's stock market, with the KOSPI <.KS11> down 0.49 percent at 0202 GMT, having fallen 2 percent at the start.  

"The missile launch is certainly a negative factor, but the effects should be limited to the short term ... This kind of drop is the least that can be expected in the situation," said Lim Chang-gue, a fund manager at Samsung Investment Trust Management.  

Bond prices edged up, with the five-year treasury bond yield <KR5YT=RR> offered three basis points lower at 4.97 percent.  

Chin Dong-soo, the second vice finance minister in charge of international affairs, told reporters currency markets could temporarily show some instability and said the government would take steps if necessary.  

He did not elaborate, but South Korea has intervened in the local currency market in the past when the won has moved wildly, although it has loosened its grip on the market of late.  

International credit rating agencies have said military tensions with the communist North were the single most important factor hurting South Korea's ratings. The two Koreas have remained technically at war since their 1950-53 conflict.  

"The test could delay a sovereign ratings upgrade of South Korea by Moody's, since the containment of the North Korea risk was one of the agency's criteria for an upgrade," said Dominique Dwor-Frecaut, an economist at Barclays Capital in Singapore, in a research report.  

The missile launch comes at a time when data is showing consumers and companies growing more pessimistic about the economic outlook as global oil prices remain high and a recovery in domestic demand fails to pick up pace. (Additional reporting by Lee Shin-hyung)

title: Emerging Asia  FX - Intervention  as won, Sing dlr hit 8-year highs
text:
SINGAPORE, May 3 (Reuters) - The currencies of South Korea, Singapore and Malaysia hit their highest levels in more than eight years on Wednesday, prompting central bank intervention, as the U.S. dollar fell on speculation U.S. interest rates would stop rising soon.  

The won <KRW=> hit a high of 933.2 per dollar, its strongest level since October 1997.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose as high as 1.5730 per dollar, its highest since November 1997, while the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> hit 3.6049 per dollar, a level last seen in April 1998.  

Traders said central banks across the region stepped in with dollar purchases to stifle further gains in their currencies. Some central banks intervened through state lenders.  

"The state-run banks have been buying dollars aggressively," said a Singapore currency dealer at a foreign bank.  

The dealer said investors held off from bidding the Singapore dollar higher after seeing the authorities intervene at 1.5730/35 levels. The currency could retreat to levels around 1.58 before traders pushed it higher again, dealers said.  

Similar intervention was noted in South Korea, Malaysia and Thailand.  

Asian authorities are worried that stronger currencies, could hurt Asian exports to the United States, Europe and Japan, particularly when China is keeping the yuan on a tight leash.  

Data on Wednesday indicated that the South Korean authorities had been intervening in the foreign exchange market since April. The country's foreign exchange reserves jumped $5.55 billion last month to $222.89 billion, the fourth largest in the world.  

"The authorities are afraid of the pace and further appreciation of the won. That's why they came into the market to support the dollar. But the intervention is a smoothing operation -- they want to moderate the pace and not stop the trend," said Roh Sang Chil, a currency trader at Kookmin Bank in Seoul.  

Swiss bank UBS said concerns about the record U.S. current account deficit, attempts by central banks to diversify their reserves away from the dollar and expectations that the Fed may end its rate-rise cycle after another increase this month were likely to dominate currency markets.  

It expects the yen <JPY=> to strengthen to 108 per dollar in three months from about 113.25 now. The euro <EUR=> could climb to $1.3 from about $1.26 over the same period, it said.  

TAIWAN INFLOWS  

The bearish dollar outlook and a surge in foreign investment in Taiwan's stock market helped push up the Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> to a nine-month high of 31.59 per U.S. dollar.  

Foreign investors continued with their purchases of Taiwan stocks, picking up a net T$11.7 billion worth on Wednesday. They bought T$170 billion worth in April, the highest monthly total since December.  

The Philippine peso <PHP=> jumped more than half a percent to 51.32 per dollar, its strongest level in two weeks.  

The currency had tumbled to an eight-week low last week on concern about record high oil prices and the likely impact on the country's fiscal deficit but some analysts reasoned that strong remittances from overseas Filipino workers were likely to offset the outflow of dollars caused by soaring crude oil import costs. New York oil futures <CLc1> traded close to $75 per barrel, near last week's record high of $75.35.

title: UPDATE: Korea Keeps Pressure On KRW; Bonds Rally
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--The South Korean authorities Wednesday continued to put pressure on the won through verbal and actual intervention, and warned bond issuance could be increased to support dollar-buying efforts.  

The moves, following through on Tuesday's dollar-buying and tough talk, pushed the dollar a little higher against the won, but sent government bonds rallying as market expectations grow for the Bank of Korea to keep the call rate unchanged next month.  

The benchmark five-year treasury bond yield, which started the day's session higher at 5.14%, fell to finish at 5.06%. The dollar, meanwhile, ended at KRW946.5, up from Tuesday's close of KRW945.0.  

According to traders, the government was suspected to have bought about $500 million worth of dollars against the won early in the morning, about the same amount at Tuesday's intervention.  

Later, South Korea's Minister of Planning and Budget Byeon Yang-Kyoon said the government may consider increasing its ceiling on treasury bond issues for foreign exchange market stabilization.  

"The sharp fall in the (dollar-won) foreign exchange rate and rise in international oil prices have reached a serious level, and should be dealt with," Byeon said.  

"Financial authorities don't like to see an increase in foreign exchange market stabilization bond issues because it burdens the fiscal budget, but the government can raise the ceiling on foreign exchange stabilization bond issues next year" from its current likely level of KRW10 trillion, said Byeon.  

The government's ceiling on treasury issuance for foreign exchange purposes has been set at KRW11 trillion for this year.  

Although the news is potentially bearish for bonds, the market didn't react much as traders considered any increase would not be immediate.  

Instead, reported comments by Bank of Korea Governor Lee Seongtae at a closed-door meeting bolstered the bond market. According to Yonhap Infomax, Lee said, "It is doubtful that (exporting) companies can endure (the dollar-won exchange rate) at such a level."  

"The market is thinking that if companies are having such a hard time, it will be difficult for the Bank of Korea to consider tightening the call rate soon," said a trader at a local securities firm.  

Indeed, "market players are betting highly on the BOK holding the policy interest rate steady (in May)," said a trader at a local bank.  

The next central bank monetary policy committee meeting is scheduled to take place May 11. The overnight call rate target is now at 4.00%.  

Although the authorities seem intent on pushing the won down further, Korea's robust economy continues to support a stronger currency. For instance, Citigroup economist Oh Suktae expects the dollar to move back to KRW940 in the next few weeks, and for five-year treasurys to yield 5.20%.  

Kwon Tae-Kyun, director general of the Ministry of Finance and Economy's international finance bureau, told Dow Jones Newswires Tuesday the won's rise should slow even though the Japanese yen is strengthening sharply.  

As the won has risen 7.6% against the U.S. unit so far this year versus a relatively steady yen during the same period, "this is not the time for the won to be tracking the yen" up, Kwon said.  

Instead, he said, "the dollar/won level should take this opportunity to recover when the dollar/yen is dropping, so that the yen/won cross rate can regain above 8.5."  

At 0600 GMT, the yen was at KRW8.2300, slightly down from Tuesday's KRW8.2483, as the dollar recovered to above Y115.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Stall near highs, Korean  intervention  seen
text:
SINGAPORE, April 25 (Reuters) - Suspected intervention by central banks in South Korea and Singapore on Tuesday and a pause in the Japanese yen's rally led to a slight retreat in the won, Singapore dollar and other Asian currencies.  

The won, Sing dollar, Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah had hit fresh multi-year highs in early trade after European Central Bank President Jean-Claude Trichet called for an adjustment in Asian exchange rates, echoing statements from the Group of Seven nations and the International Monetary Fund.  

The won <KRW=> climbed to a fresh 8-1/2-year high near 936 per dollar overnight and was underpinned by data showing faster-than-expected first-quarter economic growth.  

It slipped later and shed more than half a percent after the Bank of Korea's suspected dollar-buying intervention.  

"With the big move in dollar/yen over, the fears of intervention has bubbled to the surface again and we may see a short squeeze in Asia," said Ben Simpfendorfer, a regional economist with The Royal Bank of Scotland in Hong Kong.  

Although loss of momentum in the Asian currencies had stalled the Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP>, the support from continuing equity inflows would eventually push the currency to 31.50 per U.S. dollar, Simpfendorfer said.  

The Taiwan dollar rose to 31.86 per U.S. dollar, its highest in more than 3 months, but then pulled back to 31.97/99.  

Traders said the Asian rally was also undermined by the yuan's failure to strengthen despite renewed pressure from Western policy-makers for China to play a greater role in the adjustment of global trade imbalances.  

China's central bank fixed the central point of the yuan's trading band for Tuesday at 8.0160 per dollar, weaker than Monday's close at 8.0150. It later rose marginally to 8.0120.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> retained some gains but retreated to levels around 1.5880/85 per U.S. dollar from the overnight high of 1.5850, its strongest level in nearly 8 years.  

The Thai baht <THB=> was briefly quoted at a 6-year high of 37.48 per dollar, before it followed the regional trend.  

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> pulled back to levels around 8,800 from around 8,780 per dollar, its strongest level since May 2004.  

The Philippine peso <PHP=> remained an exception to the wider trend in Asia, undermined by concerns over the country's fiscal position. It continued falling and hit a 2-month low of 51.90 per dollar. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0800 GMT

title: S.Korea  FX  reserves rise amid  intervention  talk
text:
SEOUL, April 18 (Reuters) - South Korea's foreign exchange reserves rose $1.21 billion during the first half of April, central bank data showed on Tuesday, amid talk the authorities had bought dollars in a bid to contain a rising won <KRW=>.  

The Bank of Korea said in a statement the reserves, which rank fourth in the world after China, Japan and Taiwan, rose to $218.55 billion by April 15 from $217.34 billion at the end of March due to investment gains.  

An official refused to comment on talk among dealers that the authorities actively intervened in the local currency market early this month, when the won rallied to its highest in eight years and a half against the dollar.  

Central banks usually do not comment on intervention.  

South Korea often admits to "smoothing operations", which it says are aimed at keeping the won from moving due to speculative trading, but would not say whether authorities are targeting a particular rate.  

The won gained 2.4 percent against the dollar during the first five trading days in April before falling back slightly. It is now trading up about 6 percent so far this year.  

Policy makers are worried a firmer won could hurt exports, although government and central bank officials have recently appeared to be showing more tolerance over the won's strength.  

Rhee Yeung-kyun, an assistant governor at the Bank of Korea, said on Monday a firmer won has had little impact on exports so far, with exporters such as ship builders maintaining good orders.  

South Korea, Asia's fourth-largest economy, is home to global suppliers of microchips, mobile phones and ships such as Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. , LG Electronics Inc. and Hyundai Heavy Industries Co. .  

Meanwhile, the central bank official said the Bank of Korea might stop releasing mid-month figures from as early as May, in line with previous comments by the finance ministry.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Korean won, Taiwan dollar shine
text:
SINGAPORE, April 6 (Reuters) - The South Korean won rose to its highest level in 8-½ years on Thursday and the Taiwan dollar pushed higher as well on the back of strong foreign demand for local equities.  

Other Asian currencies were little changed and largely ignored a softer tone in the Japanese yen <JPY=>. Markets in Thailand and India were closed for a holiday.  

The won <KRW=><KRW=KFTC> rose as far as 951.6 per dollar, up about 0.6 percent from Wednesday's close in local trade and the strongest level since October 1997.  

Vice Finance Minister Bahk Byong-won said on Thursday that South Korea would be prepared to intervene in the currency market if there were abnormal signs such as speculative trading.  

But dealers said firm demand for local shares, optimism about the economy and a feeling that U.S. interest rates may not rise much further meant that further gains in the won were likely.  

"Won strength has picked up since the end of March. This has coincided with broad dollar weakness, but it is also because of inflows and expectations for more rate hikes in Korea when the U.S. is unlikely to lift rates too much further," said Jan Lambregts, head of Asia-Pacific research at Rabobank.  

"We are looking for dollar/won to come off substantially."  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> added half a percent to 32.30 per U.S. dollar from Tuesday's domestic close. Taiwan's financial markets were closed on Wednesday for a holiday.  

A rally in Taiwan's key stock index <.TWII> lifted expectations of foreign demand for local shares.

Analysts said expectations of a pick-up in the pace of appreciation in the Chinese yuan <CNY=CFX> also bolstered regional currencies.

title: S.Korea c.bank faces 2006 net loss on  FX  policy
text:
SEOUL, March 6 (Reuters) - South Korea's central bank is likely to suffer a third consecutive yearly loss in 2006 on costs related to heavy foreign-exchange intervention, an official at the Bank of Korea said on Monday.  

The central bank reported a 1.87 trillion won ($1.93 billion) net loss in the year ended Dec. 31, 2005 after losing 150.22 billion won in 2004, when it recorded its first loss in 10 years, said the official.  

"Increased costs related to monetary stabilisation bonds and the dollar/won exchange rate's drop were the main causes for the loss last year," said the official, who declined to be named.  

Monetary stabilisation bonds (MSBs), issued to absorb liquidity partly due to dollar-buying intervention, jumped 9 percent to an outstanding 155.2 trillion won at the end of 2005 from a year earlier, he said.  

South Korea intervened in the local currency market heavily between late 2003 and early 2005 to keep the won <KRW=> down against the dollar due to fears that a strong local currency would hurt exports, the main driver of growth in Asia's fourth-largest economy in recent years.  

It would not be possible to slash quickly the outstanding amount of MSBs this year and the central bank would probably suffer another net loss, the official said.  

The central bank, which manages the world's fourth-largest foreign exchange reserves valued at $215.95 billion at the end of February, also lost out on the value of its reserves in won terms because of the domestic currency's rise against the dollar last year.  

The currency gained 11.8 percent on average against the dollar in 2005 from the previous year.  

The Bank of Korea has more than sufficient internal reserves to cover the losses, but the deficit sparked calls from politicians and the media for the central bank to reduce intervention in currency markets from the middle of 2005. ($1=970.9 Won)

title: S.Korea  FX  reserves down in Feb on euro, swap

SEOUL, March 3 (Reuters) - South Korean foreign exchange reserves fell $983 million, or 0.45 percent, in February due to a weaker euro <EUR=> and a currency swap with the state pension agency, the central bank said on Friday.  

The country's foreign reserves, the fourth-largest in the world, fell to $215.95 billion by the end of February from $216.93 billion a month earlier, the Bank of Korea said in a statement, marking the first monthly fall since June 2005.  

The euro's 2 percent drop against the dollar reduced the dollar value of euro assets, while the central bank also conducted a dollar-won swap with the National Pension Service, a Bank of Korea official said.  

"We had some gains from investment of the reserves but the euro's weakness and a currency swap with the pension agency more than offset the gains," the official said.  

The official would not disclose the size of the swap deal, through which the central bank can absorb won liquidity from the financial system without issuing bonds.  

A breakdown of a country's reserves by currency is usually kept secret as it could influence specific financial markets.  

Changes in South Korean reserves, behind only Japan, China and Taiwan in size, are closely watched in the currency market because big moves could indicate active intervention by authorities in the market, analysts say.

title: UPDATE 1-Sth Korea optimistic on growth, plays down won risk
text:
(Recasts after news conference, adds details)  

SEOUL, Feb 23 (Reuters) - Accelerating domestic demand means South Korea's 2006 economic growth target of 5 percent is achievable despite the risks from a firmer won and higher oil prices, Finance Minister Han Duck-soo said on Thursday.  

Han also said annual growth in exports would return to a double-digit rate in February after plunging far below 10 percent to the slowest pace in nearly three years in January.  

Speaking at his ministry's weekly media conference, he said the impact of the won's <KRW=> value on exports was less than it once had been, underlining the government's recent attitude of showing more tolerance on the currency's short-term movements.  

Han said growth in domestic demand was accelerating, with recent indicators of private consumption, the most important element in domestic demand, pointing to continued expansion.  

"Taking into account the recent trend, we don't expect any big difficulty in achieving growth of around 5 percent," said Han. South Korea's economy grew 4 percent in 2005.  

The central bank has raised its target interest rate three times in five months, most recently on Feb. 9, to head off the risk of inflation rising as the economy gathered strength.  

January exports rose 3.8 percent from a year earlier, the slowest pace in nearly three years.  

Economists were wary of reading too much into the data because it was distorted by the Lunar New Year holidays, which had fallen on February in 2005, and Han said exports were robust.  

"We still view exports as maintaining a sound momentum because exports are expected to recover at a double-digit growth rate in February with the daily average exports staying above $1 billion," Han said.  

South Korea is home to global suppliers of chips, cars, ships and mobile phones such as Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. , Hyundai Motor Co. , Hyundai Heavy Industries Co. and LG Electronics Inc. .  

The won has gained about 4 percent against the dollar so far this year on top of a 12 percent gain on average in 2005, prompting officials from the commerce ministry to criticise the finance ministry and the central bank as being too complacent.  

South Korea has stayed away from massive intervention in the currency market since early last year, after criticism from politicians and media about the costs paid for capping the won's strength in the previous few years.

title: S.Korea foreign reserves edge down by mid-Feb
text:
SEOUL, Feb 17 (Reuters) - South Korean foreign exchange reserves edged lower during the first 15 days of February due to the dollar's rise against major currencies over the period, the central bank said on Friday.  

The country's foreign exchange reserves, which are the world's fourth largest, fell to $216.38 billion by Feb. 15 from $216.93 billion at the end of January, the Bank of Korea said in a statement.  

A firmer dollar cuts the value of assets held in other currencies when converted into the U.S. unit. The euro <EUR=> fell 1.5 percent against the dollar, while the yen <JPY=> was barely changed over the period, according to Reuters data.  

"The decline was due to a reduced dollar-converted value of assets held in euro and other currencies after these currencies weakened," the central bank said.  

The Bank of Korea does not release a breakdown of currencies in its portfolio.  

The data is closely watched because a sharp rise in reserves can indicate dollar-buying intervention in the currency market by the authorities seeking to influence the won <KRW=>.  

South Korean authorities have purchased more than $1 billion per day on occasions when the won rose sharply, according to dealers, although neither the government nor the central bank generally comment on intervention.  

The won lost 1 percent during the first 15 days of February against the U.S. dollar, indicating authorities may have refrained from intervening actively in the market over the period.

title: Weak dollar forces Asia's hand on  intervention
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 8 (Reuters) - Just when a large stockpile of foreign currency reserves and strong domestic demand was finally weaning Asia off its currency-weakening intervention habit, weakness in the U.S. dollar has thrown a spanner in the works.  

Central bank data showed Asia's reserves, excluding China's, jumped in January by $29 billion, more than in any month in the past year, as a weaker U.S. dollar and portfolio inflows forced central banks to intervene to hold their currencies down.  

South Korea's $6.5 billion growth in reserves in January was the highest since December 2004, Singapore's $3.55 billion increase was the biggest since April last year and the Philippines reported its largest monthly gain in reserves on record, taking total Asian reserves to just over $2.7 trillion.  

 The figures were evidence of the overwhelming flows the region has received, giving central banks little choice but to absorb some of them and temper the rise in their currencies.  

 Even with the intervention, the Korean won <KRW=> rose nearly 5 percent in January, the Thai baht <THB=> rose 5 percent and the Singapore dollar <SGD=> 2 percent.  

 "January was clearly a month of enormous pressure on Asian currencies to appreciate. I would have been surprised if Asian central banks hadn't intervened," said Merrill Lynch's head of Asian currency strategy, Simon Flint.  

 It could be a sign of how 2006 will shape up on the currency policy front.  

 Asia's reserves grew by just $251 billion in 2005, compared with $538 billion in 2004 and $473 billion in 2003, as Japan stopped buying dollars and other regional central banks grew less obsessed with export-driven growth and more tolerant of currency gains.  

 Besides, the dollar was rising through most of 2005.  

 But, with U.S. rates probably close to a peak, the dollar started 2006 on a weak footing. If that trend persists and strong growth in the United States and elsewhere leads to higher Asian trade surpluses and portfolio investment in Asian markets, the region's reserves could very well surge, as they did in 2003 and 2004, analysts say.  

 "A number of countries, Korea in particular, are trying to move away from intervention policy," Flint said.  

 "They intend to intervene less. It's just that the market conditions dictate that they continue to intervene significantly."  

 STRONGER CURRENCIES

 Asia has a number of reasons to intervene less and let its currencies rise faster, the main one being the still high cost of the oil the region imports.  

 Also, analysts believe China and Malaysia are allowing a faster pace of appreciation in the yuan and ringgit than immediately after they unlinked the two from the dollar in July 2005.  

 Growth is more broad-based, with consumption and investment demand picking up and reducing Asia's reliance on exports. Japan's deflationary pressures have abated.  

 Moreover, rates in the United States may peak just as Asia steps up monetary tightening. That means the cost of issuing paper to absorb the local currency released in dollar-buying intervention, known as sterilisation, could mount just as returns on dollar assets stop rising.  

 "The current environment of increased inflation risk should prompt Asian countries to be more willing to accept domestic currency strength. So should ongoing, albeit modest, yuan appreciation," said Jan Lambregts, head of Asia-Pacific research at Rabobank.  

Intervention therefore should not be as big a factor in the currency market as in 2003 and 2004, Lambregts said in a note.  

 "At the same time, there's some early evidence of Asian countries falling back on bad intervention habits in the face of the U.S. dollar's weak start to the year that warrants monitoring," he wrote.  (For a table detailing Asian countries' reserves, click on [nSP89186])

title: UPDATE 2-S.Korea vows to  intervene  to smooth won rise
text:
(Adds Lotte source, updates market in paragraphs 9-12)  

SEOUL, Feb 7 (Reuters) - South Korea pledged on Tuesday to intervene to smooth a rally in the won <KRW=>, which the finance ministry says poses a growing risk to the country's economic growth along with high oil prices.  

Vice Finance Minister Kwon Tae-shin said the government was obliged to intervene when the foreign exchange market moved rapidly. He was speaking hours after another official at the ministry said the government might take stabilising measures.  

Kwon also told a television programme the country's monetary policy should be maintained because of lingering risks facing Asia's fourth-largest economy, such as the firmer won and weak investment.  

The remarks came as data showed producer prices grew by their fastest annual pace in nine months in January, two days before the central bank reviews interest rates.  

"The government is obliged to stabilise the market if the exchange rate shows an excessive volatility," Kwon, who was a deputy minister in charge of foreign exchange policy between 2003 and 2004, said during the television programme.  

A stronger won helps cap domestic inflation by cushioning higher global oil prices, but surprisingly slow growth in January exports has renewed worries about the more direct impact of the won's strength on economic growth.  

"The won's rise is due to the solid economic performance and healthy exports. But the government will conduct smoothing operations if the market is tilted to one side," Kwon said.  

Kwon Tae-kyun, head of the ministry's international finance bureau, told Reuters early on Tuesday the government would take measures when necessary to cap the won's rise, a remark that was followed by what traders suspected was dollar-buying intervention.  

LOTTE IPO MONEY  

As the voices of concern swirled, a source at South Korea's Lotte Shopping Co. told Reuters later it did not plan to bring in all the proceeds from its overseas initial public offering so as not to influence the currency market.  

The remark came as the won has been strongly supported by expectations for a heavy dollar supply from the department store chain's $3.54 billion IPO, as 80 percent of the shares offered were sold abroad.  

"We have sufficient time to exchange the proceeds as we have no immediate demand for money, so we will manage the process in such a manner as not to impact the foreign exchange market," said the source by telephone.  

The won rose to hit an eight-year high of 957 per dollar on Feb. 1, before falling back slightly to 967.8 by the close of domestic trade on Tuesday, up 4.5 percent from the end of 2005.  

But on interest rate policy, Vice Minister Kwon made clear that should be decided by the central bank.  

Analysts were evenly split on whether the central bank would raise interest rates or leave them unchanged at its Thursday policy meeting, but all agreed the rates would increase once or twice in the next six months, a Reuters poll showed on Monday.  

Central bank data underlined rising inflation pressures, as the producer price index rose 2.1 percent in January from a year earlier, the fastest annual gain in nine months.  

Other data from the National Statistical Office showed annual growth in consumption spending per South Korean household accelerated in the fourth quarter from the third, in line with growing household income.  

Both the finance ministry and the central bank have forecast South Korea's economic growth will accelerate to 5 percent this year from 4 percent in 2005, driven by recovering domestic demand and underpinned by resilient exports. (Additional reporting by Lee Shin-hyung, Lee Soo-jung)

title: RPT-ANALYSIS-Asia  FX  rally may resume on growth optimism
text:
(Repeats item that first ran on Thursday)  

SINGAPORE, Feb 2 (Reuters) - Asian currencies have paused after a breathless run-up in January, but analysts said on Thursday the rally would soon resume given the strength of investment inflows into the region's markets.  

Currencies of Thailand, the Philippines, Indonesia and South Korea, among the world's best performers against the dollar so far this year, still rank among the top picks in Asia, they said.  

However, the Singapore dollar and the Taiwan dollar might struggle for gains in coming months.  

The strategists' call came even as the dollar struck a seven-week high against the yen <JPY=> as markets bet U.S. short-term rates would peak at 5 percent, instead of 4.25-4.5 percent predicted late last year.  

"On balance the story remains positive for Asian currencies," wrote Shahab Jalinoos, currency strategist at ABN AMRO Bank.  

"Equity flow data continue to show net inflows into the region, while the drop in oil prices overnight lowers the threat posed by perhaps the most obvious risk factor likely to derail Asia -- energy prices."  

Equity inflows have enabled Asian currencies to counter the dollar's strength against the yen and euro <EUR=>, pushing some of them to their highest levels in years as they overcome sporadic dollar-buying intervention by local central banks.  

More than $3 billion in foreign investment has flown into Thai stocks <.SETI>, $2.3 billion into South Korean stocks, $1.2 billion into Taiwan <.TWII> and $820 million into India <.BSESN> since the start of the year.  

At the same time dealers said authorities in South Korea, Thailand, Singapore and Taiwan have bought billions of dollars to stall gains in their currencies to support exports.  

In a sign of intervention, South Korea's foreign exchange reserves jumped $6.54 billion in January, marking their biggest monthly gain in 14 months.  

SINGAPORE ROADBLOCK  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=>, in particular, faces a road-block from local authorities as the currency may have hit the top end of a band used by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) to guide the trade-weighted exchange rate, analysts said.  

"As such, we would not push for much more aggressive gains over the short-term," Swiss bank UBS said in a report.  

"However, we still think that the Singapore dollar will perform well on a medium-term view given the potential for the MAS to adopt a more aggressive tightening bias should the strong data continue."  

Indeed, the region could see more investment inflows since economists are upgading their growth forecasts for most Asian countries on the back of stronger exports and growing domestic consumption.  

The improved outlook has already stoked investors' appetite for taking on higher risks. Many have borrowed low-interest bearing yen to buy Asian stocks, bonds and currencies.  

"This reflects the fact that low-yielding yen is currently a global funding currency in a risk-loving environment, while Asian currencies are beneficiaries of risk-seeking global capital seeking returns in their asset markets," Jalinoos wrote.  

The quest for higher returns is reflected in the increased purchase of foreign bonds by Japanese investors, tired of getting low returns on local debt.  

In contrast, Korean investors have focused domestically, driving Seoul's benchmark stock index <.KS11> to record highs and leaving little for them to invest overseas.  

This contrast is one of the reasons the won rose to an eight-year high of about 8.14 per yen <JPYKRW=R> this week.  

The yen might strengthen in the medium term, if the Bank of Japan tightens monetary policy later in the year, Sean Callow, currency strategist at Westpac Banking, said in a report. "But short-term, Korean won should find buyers on dips on crosses including (vs) the yen, particularly if the Bank of Korea hikes (rates) again at the Feb. 9 meeting, as seems likely," he said.  

Rising rates, against a backdrop of persistently strong growth and inflationary pressures, would support high-yielding currencies such as the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=>, Philippine peso <PHP=> and Thai baht <THB=>, analysts said.

"Asia may be a leveraged play on global growth, but in many ways so is the U.S., with the most active major central bank and high average growth rates."  

Yetsenga expects a clearer indication once the latest U.S. non-farm payrolls data is out on Friday and incoming Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke delivers testimony before Congress on Feb. 15.  

If the jobs data is weak, Yetsenga sees the dollar weakening against Asian currencies.

title: ANALYSIS-Asia  FX  rally may resume on growth optimism
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 2 (Reuters) - Asian currencies have paused after a breathless run-up in January, but analysts said on Thursday the rally would soon resume given the strength of investment inflows into the region's markets.  

Currencies of Thailand, the Philippines, Indonesia and South Korea, among the world's best performers against the dollar so far this year, still rank among the top picks in Asia, they said.  

However, the Singapore dollar and the Taiwan dollar might struggle for gains in coming months.  

The strategists' call came even as the dollar struck a seven-week high against the yen <JPY=> as markets bet U.S. short-term rates would peak at 5 percent, instead of 4.25-4.5 percent predicted late last year.  

"On balance the story remains positive for Asian currencies," wrote Shahab Jalinoos, currency strategist at ABN AMRO Bank.  

"Equity flow data continue to show net inflows into the region, while the drop in oil prices overnight lowers the threat posed by perhaps the most obvious risk factor likely to derail Asia -- energy prices."  

Equity inflows have enabled Asian currencies to counter the dollar's strength against the yen and euro <EUR=>, pushing some of them to their highest levels in years as they overcome sporadic dollar-buying intervention by local central banks.  

More than $3 billion in foreign investment has flown into Thai stocks <.SETI>, $2.3 billion into South Korean stocks, $1.2 billion into Taiwan <.TWII> and $820 million into India <.BSESN> since the start of the year.  

At the same time dealers said authorities in South Korea, Thailand, Singapore and Taiwan have bought billions of dollars to stall gains in their currencies to support exports.  

In a sign of intervention, South Korea's foreign exchange reserves jumped $6.54 billion in January, marking their biggest monthly gain in 14 months.  

SINGAPORE ROADBLOCK  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=>, in particular, faces a road-block from local authorities as the currency may have hit the top end of a band used by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) to guide the trade-weighted exchange rate, analysts said.  

"As such, we would not push for much more aggressive gains over the short-term," Swiss bank UBS said in a report.  

"However, we still think that the Singapore dollar will perform well on a medium-term view given the potential for the MAS to adopt a more aggressive tightening bias should the strong data continue."  

Indeed, the region could see more investment inflows since economists are upgading their growth forecasts for most Asian countries on the back of stronger exports and growing domestic consumption.  

The improved outlook has already stoked investors' appetite for taking on higher risks. Many have borrowed low-interest bearing yen to buy Asian stocks, bonds and currencies.  

"This reflects the fact that low-yielding yen is currently a global funding currency in a risk-loving environment, while Asian currencies are beneficiaries of risk-seeking global capital seeking returns in their asset markets," Jalinoos wrote.  

The quest for higher returns is reflected in the increased purchase of foreign bonds by Japanese investors, tired of getting low returns on local debt.  

In contrast, Korean investors have focused domestically, driving Seoul's benchmark stock index <.KS11> to record highs and leaving little for them to invest overseas.  

This contrast is one of the reasons the won rose to an eight-year high of about 8.14 per yen <JPYKRW=R> this week.  

The yen might strengthen in the medium term, if the Bank of Japan tightens monetary policy later in the year, Sean Callow, currency strategist at Westpac Banking, said in a report. "But short-term, Korean won should find buyers on dips on crosses including (vs) the yen, particularly if the Bank of Korea hikes (rates) again at the Feb. 9 meeting, as seems likely," he said.

"The key issue for Asian FX is whether Asia, or the U.S. dollar, is rewarded for this growth performance," wrote Richard Yetsenga, Asian currency strategist at HSBC in Hong Kong.

title: S Korea Govt Aide: FX  Mkt  Intervention  Unavoidable-Report
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--A senior official from South Korea's Ministry of Finance and Economy said Tuesday that intervention in the foreign exchange market is unavoidable, reported online news provider edaily.  

"The foreign exchange market has a 'zero-sum game' structure, but it has the tendency to go one-sided because of a small group of participants... That's why the government has to intervene," Kwon Tae-Kyun, director-general of the Ministry of Finance and Economy's international finance bureau, was quoted as saying. [ 31-01-06 0539GMT ]  

"There are about 56 participants in the local foreign exchange market, and about 20-30 are active participants, so they all know who bought at what level... this is how the forex market differs from the equity market," edaily reported Kwon as saying.  

"These participants conduct short-term day trading, ignoring government's policy on liberalizing forex trading or its mid- to long-term forex market measures."  

Kwon said in the edaily that stability in the local currency is important, regardless of what level it is at, because Asian countries have now begun to discuss the introduction of a joint currency, like the euro.  

The local media has quoted Kwon as saying the joint currency will be implemented in 10 to 15 years.  

-By Seoul Bureau; Dow Jones Newswires; 822-732-2165; djnews.seoul@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 1-INTERVIEW-S.Korean ratings could rise despite N.Korea
text:
(Adds quotes, details)  

SEOUL, Jan 26 (Reuters) - South Korea's credit ratings could be raised even before the North Korean nuclear crisis is resolved, if the South makes progress on structural economic reforms, an S&P official said on Thursday.  

Takahira Ogawa, a credit analyst at Standard & Poor's Ratings Services, also told Reuters in a telephone interview that the South Korean government's suspected resumption of intervention in the currency market would not affect its ratings.  

The agency raised the country's long-term foreign currency rating by one notch to A in July last year, citing increased flexibility in foreign exchange policy along with an improved financial industry.  

It has since said that North Korea's nuclear ambitions remained the key constraint on the South's ratings.  

"Still, there is a chance (of an upgrade) even if the North Korean situation doesn't change that much," Ogawa said.  

"If the government could achieve or facilitate an environment in which the private sector can ensure more market-oriented competition, then perhaps we have a good chance of seeing higher ratings for Korea," he added.  

Talks involving the two Koreas, the United States, China, Russia and Japan produced an agreement in September last year on dismantling the North's nuclear programmes but follow-up talks have since hit snags.  

The July upgrade, the first for South Korea in three years, put the country's ratings at five notches above investment grade and above China and Malaysia at A-minus.  

Moody's Investors Service has an A3 rating on South Korea while Fitch Ratings puts it at A-plus.  

INTERVENTION

The South Korean authorities are believed to have intervened massively to cap the won <KRW=> <KRW=KFTC>, which has jumped since December to hit eight-year highs against the U.S. dollar.  

South Korea's foreign exchange reserves soared by $4.27 billion in the first 15 days of January, a rise attributed by analysts mainly to intervention.  

"This year they started to do it again, but until then, they were quite patient," Ogawa said of the suspected intervention.  

"At this stage I still think their stance is changing," he added, meaning he believed the authorities, even if they intervened, would not do so as heavily as they did two years ago.  

Ogawa also said a possible slowdown in the U.S. economy could be the biggest risk to economic growth in South Korea this year, more so than won strength or high oil prices.  

"I think a slowdown in the U.S. or the global economy could be the strongest factor," he said.  

"(South Korea is) less vulnerable to fluctuations in the foreign exchange rate, in part because companies like Samsung, Hyundai Motor and so on started to establish or have already completely established their brand image," he added.  

South Korea is Asia's fourth-largest economy and home to Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. , the world's largest maker of computer memory chips and the second biggest producer of flat screens, as well as car maker Hyundai Motor Co. Ltd. .  

Commenting on a domestic controversy about tax increases, Ogawa said steep tax rises would put a significant dent in consumer sentiment, which is recovering from a protracted slump.  

"If the government tries to move ahead with substantial tax increases, that could hurt sentiment in the economy more than, for example, one more round of interest rate increases by the Bank of Korea," he said.  

President Roh Moo-hyun said on Wednesday he would not seek to increase taxes sharply, a comment made in response to suspicions the government wanted to raise taxes to fund welfare spending.  

The Bank of Korea raised interest rates twice in the fourth quarter of 2005 to head off inflation and economists expect the central bank to lift borrowing costs further this year.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Won hits 8-year high, rupiah and baht surge
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 26 (Reuters) - The South Korean won hit an eight-year-high on Thursday while the Indonesian rupiah and Thai baht rose to their strongest levels since last March as the improving economic outlook in Asia boosted demand for stocks.  

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> strengthened beyond 1.62 per dollar to a 10-1/2-month high in overnight trading, nearly hitting its highest level since 1998, but caution over central bank intervention led it to pull back during Asian trading hours.  

 The Thai baht <THB=> jumped as much as 1.1 percent to 38.8 per dollar.  

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> edged towards a 2-1/2-year high of 52.25 per dollar hit on Jan. 9.  

 The gains in Asian currencies contrasted with a decline in the yen <JPY=> against the dollar and indicated investors' appetite for taking risks in emerging markets, where growth is likely to outperform the developed countries.  

 Investors have flocked to Asian stock markets this year on optimism that the region would grow in 2006 at a faster pace than previously anticipated thanks to an upturn in exports and a revival in domestic consumption.  

 "There's been strong inflows into the region this month," said James Malcolm, Asian currency strategist at Deutsche Bank.  "It's not just speculative money. There's a large amount of money going into places like Korea based on strong fundamentals. Growth is good, inflation pressures are certainly there."  

 Reuters polls of Asia's 10 biggest economies outside Japan released on Wednesday showed that economists had upgraded their growth forecasts for all countries except Taiwan and Malaysia since the previous poll conducted in October.  

 Malcolm said China and Malaysia were likely to let their currencies appreciate at a faster pace starting in February or March, which would also tend to push up other Asian currencies.  

 "We're particularly positive on the peso, reasonably positive on Korea and positive on Taiwan and Thailand," he said.  

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR  

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> touched 1.6172 per dollar in overnight trade but then fell back to levels weaker than 1.62.  A breach of 1.6162 per dollar would take the currency to its strongest level since October 1998.  

 Some dealers suggested that the central bank was trying to keep the currency weaker than the 1.62-per-dollar level.  

 "They're checking around prices, so everybody's being cautious in bidding it higher," said a Singapore currency dealer.  

 "I think the market is oversold (on dollars) so there will be a slight correction."  

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore conducts monetary policy by guiding the Singapore dollar's trade-weighted exchange rate within an undisclosed band.  

 Malcolm said the Singapore currency would be allowed to move higher if other major currencies strengthened.  

 "They're not trying to draw a line in the sand," he said.  

 But, as of now, the Singapore dollar was expensive, compared with the currencies of its trade partners, he said.  

 Dealers reported dollar-buying intervention in South Korea which forced the won to retreat from its eight-year high of 965.9 per dollar.  The Indonesian rupiah strengthened to its highest level since March 3, 2005 at 9,285 per dollar, dealers said.  

 The currency has rallied from a four-year low of 11,750 per dollar in August as the central bank pushed up key interest rates to 12.75 percent to curb inflationary pressures.  

 Dealers in Jakarta said that the interest rates paid on local bonds, among the highest in Asia, were attracting foreign investors. Money has also been flowing into Jakarta stocks.  

 "It's related to stock and debt inflows," said one dealer in the Indonesian capital. "We suspect Singapore banks are actively selling dollar-rupiah." CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Edge down, rally on hold for now
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 17 (Reuters) - Asian currencies eased on Tuesday, hurt by a slowdown in foreign buying of local stocks and a view that an early 2006 rally in the regionals against the U.S. dollar had got ahead of itself.  

 A perception that U.S. interest rates are close to reaching a peak has bolstered Asian currencies since the start of the year. But dealers said with little new leads to drive regional currencies higher, some profit-taking had now set in.  

 "Our short-term positioning indicators suggest the gains in Asian currencies are overstretched and that more positive news would be needed for the rally to continue," said Shahab Jalinoos, senior currency strategist at ABN AMRO. "Equity inflows were one factor but it looks like these are easing off as well."  

 The Taiwan dollar <TWD=> and Thai baht <THB=> both shed about half a percent against the U.S. dollar, while the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> fell about 1 percent to 9,550 per dollar -- its softest level in more than a week.  

 The yen also <JPY=> hit is lowest level in more than a week,  weighing on Asian currencies, although it had recovered some ground by late Asian trade.  

 Foreign buying in Asian equity markets has eased in the past week, denting the appeal of regional currencies, analysts said.  

 Indonesia's benchmark stock index <.JKSE> fell as much as 2.5 percent on Tuesday, while data from Nomura International showed heavy foreign selling of Indian and Korean equities in the past week.  

 "There has been profit-taking in equity markets in Asia in recent sessions and there have been signs of a slowdown in foreign buying," said Craig Chan, a currency strategist at the Royal Bank of Scotland in Hong Kong.  

 Some traders, however, said Asian equity markets were likely to perform well over the next few months, and that should bode well for regional currencies.  

 "The overall fundamental story is still positive for Asia and over the long term we should see money flowing into the equity markets," one trader in Singapore said.  

 DATA LIFTS SING DOLLAR  

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> hit a session high at 1.6303 per U.S. dollar, paring earlier falls, after the government said growth in non-oil exports would not be curbed by currency strength and data showed a sharp rise in exports.  

 Singapore's non-oil exports rose 18 percent in December from November on a seasonally adjusted basis, much higher than the 1.0 percent increase forecast by analysts.  

 "There are definitely some flows coming in after the data," a trader said. "The Singapore dollar has strengthened since the end of last year and this is in line with the central bank's view of a gradual appreciation of the currency. The economy is doing better and this does justify a stronger Sing dollar."  

 The South Korean won <KRW=><KRW=KFTC> weakened as much as 0.8 percent from Monday's domestic close to 990.3 per dollar, moving further away from last week's 8-year high at about 973.8.  

 Dealers said they remained wary about possible dollar-buying intervention to curb recent won strength, especially after foreign exchange reserve figures suggested the authorities had been intervening in the market.  

South Korea's foreign exchange reserves rose $4.27 billion in the first 15 days of January, central bank data on Tuesday showed. It was the biggest gain in South Korea's foreign reserves for a half-month period since a $4.66 billion rise in the first half of March 2005, an official at the Bank of Korea said. title: Emerging Asia  FX -Hitting new highs after a pause
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 12 (Reuters) - Asian currencies hit fresh multi-month highs against the dollar on Thursday as traders bet that the U.S. currency had further to fall after a brief consolidation early this week.  

 Hawkish comments from the Swiss central bank, expectations that the European Central Bank would sound a hawkish note at a meeting later in the day and anxiety ahead of U.S. trade data all weighed on the dollar. It has already shed about 2.5 percent in trade-weighted terms <=USD> this month.  

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose to its highest level in nearly 10 months at about 1.6220 per U.S. dollar, and the Thai baht <THB=> rose to about 39.38 per dollar, its highest since May 2005.  

 The South Korean won <KRW=><KRW=KFTC> strengthened more than one percent from Wednesday's domestic close to 973.8 per dollar, its strongest level since November 1997.  

 The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> also added more than one percent to its strongest level in almost 10 months, while the Taiwan dollar <TW1D=TP> firmed to 31.831 per U.S. dollar -- its highest level since early August.  

 "There's been a lot of appreciation against the dollar but, the way these currencies are managed, I doubt there's been much trade-weighted appreciation," said Tim Condon, head of research at ING in Singapore.  

 Callum Henderson, head of currency strategy at Standard Chartered Bank, said that while there had been a huge move in currency markets at the start of 2006, similar rapid moves in the early weeks of the past three years had not been sustained.  

 "We will see some degree of consolidation. However, we are very much in the camp that believes in medium-term dollar weakness so any consolidation will be a further opportunity to offload more dollars," he said.  

 WATCHFUL CENTRAL BANKS  

 The Thai baht's rise versus the dollar has made it a "bit too strong" and its appreciation should require central bank action, Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakul said on Thursday. "No one has confirmed central bank intervention but everybody is talking about it," said a trader in Bangkok. "The central bank is worried that a strong baht is not good for exports so intervention would not be a surprise."  

 So far this month, South Korea has warned against won strength, while Taiwan has intervened in the market to curb Taiwan dollar strength.  

 Analysts said that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had been less aggressive than expected in its intervention to cap Sing dollar gains and this had encouraged some investors to push the currency higher.  

 The Sing dollar has risen nearly 3 percent in the past three weeks.  

 "The entire street seems to be short Sing dollar against the basket," said a local trader.  

 He said the U.S. dollar's weakness, driven by the view that U.S. monetary tightening was close to an end, had left those betting against the Sing dollar in the red and led to short-covering.  

 "And with MAS intervening only in bits and pieces, it is making life for those Sing dollar shorts pretty miserable."  

 The MAS's chief monetary policy tool is the currency, which it manages within an undisclosed trade-weighted band against a basket of currencies.  CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0825 GMT

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Regional  currencies  rise to multi-month highs
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 4 (Reuters) - Asia's currency markets enjoyed another day of stellar gains on Wednesday as the minutes from the last Federal Reserve meeting fuelled talk that the U.S. central bank is almost done with lifting interest rates.  

Most regional currencies, in a rally led by the Japanese yen <JPY=>, hit multi-month highs against the dollar.  

The South Korean <KRW=> <KRW=KFTC> strengthened past the psychologically important 1,000 mark to hit an 8-month high at 997.9 per dollar.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> hit a 4-½ month peak at 1.6461 per dollar, the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> set its highest level in almost a month at about 9,635 per dollar and the Taiwan dollar rose as much as one percent in local markets to hit a 4-month high of 32.33 per U.S. dollar.  

The minutes of the Fed's Dec. 13 meeting, released on Tuesday, showed the central bank's top officials believed the number of additional rate increases would not be large although its future action would depend on economic data.  

Asian currencies had already started the new year on a strong footing, helped by a view that the U.S. monetary tightening that bolstered the dollar last year was unlikely to last much longer.  

Analysts said the minutes and data on Tuesday showing a drop in the U.S. Institute for Supply Management's factory index gave the rally in Asian currencies fresh momentum.  

"People are looking at what the big trade of this year will be and there are enough houses saying the dollar will have a poor year," said Westpac senior currency strategist Sean Callow.  

"So people are either putting on new positions or receptive to news confirming their suspicions -- such as the ISM data."  

The sharp rise in regional currencies raised the spectre of central bank intervention.  

A dealer in Singapore said the market was wary of intervention to curb the Singapore dollar's sharp gains but had so far seen no signs of such action.  

South Korea's central bank was suspected of intervening in the market on Tuesday to cap the won's strength. A central bank official said on Wednesday that the won's latest rise was the result of an excessive reaction to the Fed minutes.  

"The market is unlikely to be afraid of the threat of intervention from Korea," said Callow. "Korean authorities are aware that they are unlikely to stem the tide of a broad trend in the currency market."  

MORE THAN JUST A DOLLAR STORY  

The Philippine peso <PHP=> gained more than half a percent from Tuesday's close in local markets to a fresh 2-½ year peak of 52.37 per dollar, while the Thai baht <THB=> strengthened to 40.50 -- its strongest level against the dollar in 7 months.  

Dealers said besides a soft tone in the U.S. dollar, investors were also responding to strong local equity markets, brighter economic data and favourable technical patterns.  

"There was strong (dollar) support in the 40.70/85 area and this has been broken," said a trader in Bangkok, referring to the baht. "We have also seen heavy offshore selling of dollar/baht this morning."  

The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> rose and the yuan, traded in offshore derivative markets <CNYNDFOR=>, was pulled higher in line with the regional currency strength.  

Six-month non-deliverable forwards moved to price the yuan at 7.8675 per dollar, compared with 7.8730 late on Tuesday. The one-year contract priced the yuan at 7.7200 against the dollar from 7.7350 late the previous session.  

"The move in the NDFs is consistent with the move in the spot market and with the forecasts for a decline in the dollar in the months ahead," Callow said. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0818 GMT

Benign inflation data means the central bank would probably hold interest rates steady for a second consecutive month at its Dec. 8 policy meeting, dealers said, helping snap three days of gains for the local unit.
