title: Yen tumbles to 20-year low on BOJ index
text:
TOKYO, Nov 21 (Reuters) - The yen hit a 20-year low against the currencies of major trading partners in early November on a Bank of Japan index, underscoring weakness that should help spur a recovery from deflation in Japan's economy.  

The BOJ's real effective exchange rate index, which gauges the yen's trade-weighted and inflation-adjusted performance, fell to 106.2 by Nov. 17, its lowest since October 1985. The index was updated on Monday.  

The low level reflects the yen's broad slide against a variety of currencies but also nearly eight years of deflation, which has made Japanese goods cheaper compared with those of countries where prices have been rising.  

Such a drop in the yen should make Japanese exports more attractive and buttress an economic rebound increasingly being helped by consumer and business spending. Japan's exports hit a record 5.925 trillion yen ($49.72 billion) in September.  

"The main significance is the impact on export competitiveness," said Richard Jerram, chief economist at Macquarie Securities Japan. "There's quite nice support for the economic recovery coming from the exchange rate."  

The yen has suffered as more than four years of near zero short-term interest rates has prompted many Japanese investors to put cash to work in higher-yielding foreign bonds this year, driving the currency to a two-year low versus the dollar.  

Against other currencies the yen has fared even worse, tumbling to seven-year lows against the British pound, Australian dollar and South Korean won this week, as well as an eight-year nadir against the New Zealand dollar on Monday.  

The Ministry of Finance's once massive yen-selling intervention is also seen as a factor behind the currency's woes after the government flooded markets with yen to prevent a sharp appreciation that could exacerbate deflation.  

The MOF sold 35 trillion yen in the 15 months to March 2004 but has since stayed out of the market. With no intervention on Monday the MOF will have gone its longest without intervening since records began to be kept in 1991.  

The yen's depreciation has been enough to prompt South Korea to threaten intervention, with Vice Finance Minister Kwon Tae-shin telling Reuters on Monday that Seoul is worried about the won's rise and will act if it is deemed excessive.  

Tohru Umemoto, chief currency strategist at Barclays Capital in Tokyo, said in a recent report that the level of the yen index means Japanese manufacturers are enjoying their best comparative price advantage since the Plaza Accord of 1985.  

The Plaza Accord was an agreement between Japan, the United States, France, Britain and the then West Germany that included coordinated currency intervention to weaken the dollar and help reduce the U.S. trade deficit, particularly with Japan.  

Two decades later the focus has swung to the record U.S. trade deficit, partly driven by Chinese exports and Beijing's policy of keeping the yuan's value tied closely to the dollar.  

In late Tokyo trade on Monday, the yen hovered around 119.40 per dollar <JPY=>, not far from its weakest since August 2003, and a long way from a five-year peak near 101.65 hit in January.

Some analysts say the yen's weakness also reflects the sheer amount of carry trades in the currency market, where speculators and investors borrow yen at nearly no cost and sell it to buy other currencies for their higher yields.

title: S.Korea worried about yen, but no  intervention  seen
text:
SEOUL, Nov 2 (Reuters) - South Korea is likely to avoid a new round of currency intervention to curb the strength of the won, which hit a seven-year high against the yen on Wednesday, for fear of fanning inflation, analysts said.  

Finance ministry and central bank officials have expressed concerns about the won's strength but dealers do not expect any massive intervention to follow the rhetoric.  

A weaker currency could mean a rise in import costs, which could increase the pressure on the central bank to boost interest rates again.  

"The finance ministry apparently doesn't like to see interest rates raised aggressively and so must be concerned about inflation," said Oh Suk-tae, an economist at Citibank.  

South Korean and Japanese exporters are major competitors in many markets, such as for autos and technology.  

The won gained 13 percent against the yen <JPYKRW=R> this year to hit 8.89 per yen on Wednesday, its strongest since August 1998. It has gained 5.6 percent in last two months alone.  

Rhee Gwang-ju, head of the Bank of Korea's international department, told Reuters on Wednesday the won had gained too much against the yen but would now reverse the trend.  

"(We) expect the bullish sentiment for the won to reverse to reflect the dollar's strength against major currencies," he said, echoing a similar comment on Tuesday by the finance ministry's head of the international finance bureau, Kwon Tae-kyun.  

Traders, including Park Yong-il, senior foreign exchange trader at DBS Bank's Seoul branch, shrugged off the comments.  

"If they meant to step in, they should have done it today," he said.  

The won's rise against the yen would make South Korean products more expensive relative to competing Japanese ones, even in dollar markets, although analysts said the impact may not be that great since importers also look at other factors, such as quality, rather than just price.  

"The government may want to smooth out the rise but the possibility is low because they know well the exchange rate is not very important in exports any longer," said Park.  

The yen/won rate is based on each currency's value against the dollar. The won's rise against the yen has been the result of its slower depreciation against the dollar compared with the yen.  

So far this year, the yen has skidded more than 12 percent against the dollar, while the won has fallen less than 1 percent.  

"I think the government's foreign exchange policy has been to stay away," said Oh. "The won is strong not only against the yen but against many currencies. But I don't think the government can do something about this."  

FINANCE MINISTRY LESS HAWKISH  

The finance ministry decides when to intervene and the central bank acts on its behalf in the foreign exchange market.  

Hawkish finance ministry officials successfully kept the won flat versus the dollar in 2003 despite the yen's <JPY=> 11 percent rise and the euro's <EUR=> 20 percent increase against the U.S. currency.  

But the won snapped back against the dollar, yen and euro last year. Despite the currency gyrations, exports have remained surprisingly resilient this year.  

South Korea's inflation has been relatively benign this year, largely the result of the won's strength last year which has helped offset the soaring import cost of crude oil -- the main factor fuelling inflation world wide.  

The finance ministry now appears concerned a weaker won would fan inflation, in turn forcing the central bank to raise interest rates and dampen a nascent revival in consumer spending, analysts said.  

"I think the finance ministry doesn't want to create a situation in which the central bank will have to raise interest rates," said Citibank's Oh.  

The central bank raised interest rates last month by a quarter percentage point from a record low of 3.25 percent for the first time in more than three years, citing future inflation pressure as a result of recovering domestic demand.  

The annual inflation rate remains low at below 3 percent, but persistently high global oil prices and a pick-up in domestic demand could fuel price pressures in coming months, analysts say.

Rhee Gwang-ju, director general at the Bank of Korea's international department, said in an interview he doubted the won's levels would have a serious impact on inflation.  

"Over the next quarter, for instance, it is difficult to find any factors for a strengthening won," Rhee said, adding the trade surplus could drastically shrink in line with recovering domestic demand.  

"There clearly is some upward pressure (on inflation) from the foreign exchange rate but I don't think the impact will be serious," he said.  

Inflation was 2.7 percent in September, the highest since June.  

The won weakened slightly against the dollar after Rhee's comments. Analysts said the fact Rhee did not talk up the won suggested he saw no reason for the current weakening trend against the dollar to change.

The won's levels are critical for South Korea's exporters, which have provided the main economic growth for the country in recent years.  

But like many other Asian countries, Korea has taken a major hit on its import bill as crude prices soared, undermining the country's trade surplus, the won's levels and raising concerns about imported inflation.

Rhee brushed off concerns about the strength of the won against the yen, a cross rate closely monitored since Korea and Japan compete in similar export markets, such as for computer chips, ships, autos and steel.

title: TABLE-Asia ex-China reserves dip $4.6 bln in May
text:
SINGAPORE, June 9 (Reuters) - Asian holdings of foreign exchange reserves excluding China fell $4.6 billion in May, central bank figures show, a fall which currency analysts said reflected a rally in the dollar against the euro <EUR=>.   

Including China's holdings as at the end of March -- it has not released figures for April and May -- Asian central banks hold $2.53 trillion in foreign exchange reserves.   

Analysts expect the net change in Asian reserves during May would be positive if China's reserves were included, suspecting that the speculation of a yuan revaluation led to inflows of foreign money into the country in April and May.   

They said the fall in reserves for other economies was mostly due to the U.S. dollar's gains against the euro and other major currencies in May, driven by a strengthening U.S. economy, the euro zone's economic woes and uncertainty that culminated in French and Dutch voters rejecting a new EU constitution.   

The euro fell almost 4.5 percent against the dollar in May. With an estimated 20 percent share of world reserves, the euro's fall would have caused revaluation losses for reserve-holders.   

Japan, Indonesia and India suffered the biggest falls in reserves in dollar terms, each losing over $1 billion in May.   

The region's reserves have grown by $83.5 billion so far in 2005. The largest foreign flows have been into China, Malaysia, South Korea and Taiwan, although dollar-buying intervention by central banks has been far lower than in 2004, analysts say.   

Asia ex-Japan's reserves increased by $173 billion in the last quarter of 2004, which analysts said was a record quarterly jump. China's reserves alone rose over $95 billion in the final quarter of 2004 to a record $609.9 billion.   

Amidst the euro's descent and the steep rise in U.S. Treasury prices since March, there has been renewed talk about whether Asian central banks are diversifying their dollar holdings.   

Over 60 percent of global central bank reserves were held in dollar assets at the end of 2003, IMF figures show.   

Some traders believe the euro's decline has been exacerbated by talk Asian central banks may be less inclined to buy the weakening currency. Others felt this was an opportune time for euro-buying by the central banks.   

"What would make logical sense in terms of currency allocation is to be buying the euro when it comes off like this," said James Malcolm, currency strategist with Deutsche Bank in Singapore.   

"But that is not the way it seems to work in practice."   

Besides fitting in with their longer term investment mandates, such central bank buying could help restrain the volatility in the euro and in U.S. Treasuries, he said. Latest foreign exchange reserve holdings:

title: S Korea Won Ends Lower; Suspected Govt  Intervention
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--The South Korean won ended lower against the U.S. dollar Friday on short-covering triggered by suspected dollar buying by authorities.  

The dollar closed at KRW1,002.5, up from KRW1,001.7 Thursday, after trading between KRW998.9 and KRW1,003.5.  

The U.S unit opened at KRW1,000.5 on offshore dollar selling and later extended its losses on export settlements.  

The dollar/won stayed above KRW999 on import settlements, but the pair recovered sharply on dollar short-covering in the last hour on suspected intervention as the central bankers of South Korea, China and Japan discussed ways to strengthen ties on the sidelines of an international conference on monetary policies.  

The Bank of Korea said the dollar/won trading volume was $3.80 billion, up from $2.71 billion Thursday and $2.10 billion Wednesday. The volume is usually around $4 billion on normal trading days.  

"But the market was thin throughout the week, and when you consider that, the BOK is suspected of having bought quite a lot (of dollars)," said a trader at a foreign bank.  

BOK Governor Park Seung, Bank of Japan Governor Toshihiko Fukui and People's Bank of China Governor Zhou Xiaochuan met for an hour after signing a currency swap pact at the conference in Seoul.  

Despite high expectations for some discussions on a change in the Chinese currency regime, the three governors intentionally skipped foreign exchange-related talk, "as the topic is sensitive now and we have the more urgent task of strengthening ties," Park told Dow Jones Newswires.  

Zhou declined to talk to reporters, but in his opening address to the conference he suggested Beijing's reforms will be gradual and careful in respect to the economic developments in the country as it transforms to a market economy from a centralized one. He didn't mention the yuan.  

His comments - a reiteration of what senior Chinese officials have been saying as the U.S. pressures it to revalue the yuan - will likely further damp speculation about the imminent strengthening in the Chinese and other Asian currencies.  

Traders said they expect the dollar to trade between KRW998 and KRW1,005 Monday.  

"The central bank again showed that it can act swiftly to defend KRW1,000, so the local pair won't fall sharply below KRW1,000, but offshore players have been selling heavily around KRW1,002-3," said the foreign bank trader.  

In the options market, volatility implied by one-month at-the-money options edged down to 6.4%/6.8% from 6.5%/6.9% Thursday.  

"There were more sellers in the shorter-term vols, but more bids in six months and longer as players want to hedge against possible risk in case there is the yuan revaluation," said an options trader at a foreign bank.  

The one-month delta risk reversal, which indicates market bias, was in favor of dollar puts/won calls at 0.1%/0.5%, relatively unchanged from Thursday as the spot trade remained in a boxed range. [ 27-05-05 0749GMT ]  

South Korean government bond prices closed sharply lower after the finance minister expressed concern over a possible bubble forming in the real-estate sector.  

Yields on three-year treasurys rose eight basis points to close at 3.70%, while the five-year treasurys gained seven basis points to 3.84%. The 10-year treasury yield added six basis points to end at 4.33%.  

"Although inflation has been successfully managed, the Korean economy has seen a substantial increase in housing prices," Minister of Finance and Economy Han Duck-Soo told a lunch meeting with participants of an international conference hosted by the Bank of Korea.  

"I'm aware of the debate on whether monetary policy should respond to an asset bubble. I hope to gain an answer (to that issue)", Han said.  

A trader at a local brokerage firm said Han's comment "strongly suggests that there won't be further easing in monetary policy, while opening up a possibility for tightening."  

Han's comments also hurt the futures market. The June contract plunged 24 ticks to 111.94 as foreigners took profits as well.  

Market participants expect the three-year treasury yield to trade in a range of 3.67%-3.77% next week.  

"If the industrial output data come out within expectations, the bond market will remain relatively predictable," said the trader.  

The National Statistical Office is scheduled to issue April industrial production data at 2230 GMT Sunday.  

The average of 10 economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires was that industrial output fell 0.2% on month after seasonal adjustment, swinging from a 3.8% gain in March, because export growth weakened and private consumption remained depressed. On year, output likely rose 4.7% in April compared with a 4.8% gain in March.

title: DJ S Korea Ctrl Bank Gov Rules Out  Currency Intervention  -FT
text:
NEW YORK, May 18, 2005 (ODC via Comtex) --  

South Korea's central bank won't intervene any further in foreign exchange markets, the governor of the Bank of Korea said Wednesday, according to an article on the Web site of the Financial Times.  

"I believe that we now have sufficient reserves to secure our sovereign credibility, so I do not anticipate increasing the amount of foreign reserves further," Park Seung told the FT. South Korea's foreign currency reserves stand at $206 billion, the fourth-largest in the world.  

Park told the newspaper: "We now need to take more consideration of profitability, and I think we're at a stage where we need to manage our reserves in a more useful way."  

Although he made no explicit comment on the won, Park's remarks imply that South Korea is now unwilling to undertake the intervention required to stem its currency's rise, the FT said.  

Park said he didn't envision changing the currency mix of the country's reserves, about two-thirds of which is thought to be in dollar-denominated assets, the newspaper reports.  

With Japan, China and South Korea - which together hold at least a third of the world's central bank foreign exchange reserves - each likely to suffer if one moves first to lessen their exposure to the dollar, some economists believe there is scope for more regional cooperation.  

Park told the FT: "I think that the economic cooperation of these three nations and the cooperation of their central banks is necessary to promote the growth and development of the global economy."  

But the banks were working together only to maintain financial stability and weren't doing anything that might "affect" international markets, he told the newspaper.  

Regarding adjustments to China's currency, Park told the FT that "I think that is China's job, (but) China is smart enough to deal with this issue to help adjust the imbalances within the global economy and stabilize the regional economy."  

Of greater concern to Park were the U.S.'s current account and budget deficits, which Asian central banks have largely been funding. The deficits "will aggravate the global imbalances and undermine global economic growth," Park said to the newspaper. "I think there is a need for the U.S. to dissolve these twin deficits for the benefit of the U.S. economy, the world economy and the Korean economy."

title: UPDATE 1-S.Korea has no plan to alter  FX  reserves - c.bank
text:
(Updates with quotes and details)  

SEOUL, May 19 (Reuters) - South Korean authorities have no plan to either increase or decrease foreign exchange reserves, a central bank official told Reuters on Thursday, in comments aimed at clarifying the country's stance on the sensitive issue.  

Rhee Gwang-ju, the head of the central bank's international affairs bureau, also said by telephone that authorities were ready to take action if the domestic currency market showed signs of instability.  

The comments came after the Financial Times quoted central bank governor Park Seung as saying he did not anticipate the country would increase the amount of its foreign exchange reserves.  

"The Financial Times report carrying an interview with the governor was not correct. In case speculative money flows into the country based on reports that are different from facts, we will take firm action," the central bank said in a later statement.  

The report helped push the dollar down against the yen to a session low of 106.76 yen <JPY=> in New York as dealers interpreted it to mean that there could be less dollar-buying intervention from Asian monetary authorities in the future.  

The won <KRW=> <KRW=KFTC> opened domestic trade firmer at 999.5 per dollar, breaching the psychologically-important 1,000 mark. It traded at 1,001.7 at 0023 GMT, up 0.35 percent.  

"The governor's remarks meant that the country has a scope of flexibility on the reserve front but was not intended to hint that the authorities would not need to increase reserves or not intervene in the currency market," Rhee said.  

"We do not have a plan to artificially increase or decrease reserves," he added.  

Financial markets are especially sensitive to even the slightest hint of central bank diversification out of dollar-denominated assets, particularly given intense speculation that China will soon make its exchange rate regime more flexible.  

Most analysts expect other Asian currencies to appreciate against the dollar once China allows the yuan to strengthen.  

"I believe that we now have sufficient reserves to secure our sovereign credibility, so I do not anticipate increasing the amount of foreign reserves further," the Financial Times quoted the central bank governor as saying.  

"We now need to take more consideration of profitability, and I think we're at a stage where we need to manage our reserves in a more useful way," he added.  

Separately, Park told Reuters in an interview with Reuters on Wednesday that there were no immediate plans to change the currency composition of the country's huge foreign exchange reserves.  

At around $207 billion, South Korea's currency reserves are the fourth-largest in the world.  

The Bank of Korea also took issue with part of the Financial Times report that said South Korea would not intervene any further in the foreign exchange markets and said in a statement that the governor had been "misinterpreted".  

"The central bank will take action if the foreign exchange market turns unstable", the statement added.

title: UPDATE 1- South Korea FX  reserves hit record on  intervention .
text:
SEOUL, March 17 (Reuters) - South Korea's foreign exchange reserves rose $4.66 billion in the first 15 days of March to a new record, boosted by massive government currency intervention to cap a soaring won, the central bank said on Thursday.  

The Bank of Korea also announced in a separate statement it planned to increase its fund management team by around a half as part of efforts to boost returns on the country's reserves, the world's fourth largest.  

South Korea's reserves grew 2.3 percent to $206.82 billion as of March 15 from $202.16 billion at the end of February, the central bank said in a statement.  

The central bank made a rare acknowledgement that dollar-buying intervention by authorities aimed at containing a surge in the won was behind the increase.  

"In addition to increased foreign currency assets resulting from the process of stabilising the forex market, the conversion value of existing reserves in euro and other currencies has risen because of a weakening U.S. dollar," it said.  

The central bank's explicit reference to intervention appeared aimed at showing its determination to try and quell what it has called speculative trading driving up the won, dealers said.  

Dealers in Seoul estimated some $3 billion of the increased reserves came from direct purchases by authorities in the market to cap the won, after the local unit soared to a seven-year high against the U.S. currency late last week.  

The reserves, which fell to less than $4 billion during the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis, have jumped 16 percent since the end of October when the won currency started rising sharply.   


The won            , a star performer in Asia with a 15 percent gain in
2004, has risen another 3 percent against the U.S. dollar over the year
to date.
  

MORE MANAGERS  

The central bank said in another statement it wanted to raise the number of fund mangers as part of efforts to make the management of its reserves more profitable, a goal officials at the bank have been pursuing since reserves have kept growing.  

The statement followed a central bank report in late February that it would diversify its reserves into high yielding paper and a greater variety of currencies, though it later clarified the plan did not mean it would sell dollars to buy other currencies.  

"We have been making efforts to increase profitability from foreign exchange reserves by investing them in wider areas, at the same time keeping in mind securing liquidity and stability of those assets," it said.  

The central bank said it would increase the number of forex asset managers to over 100 from the current 66.  

"At a time where forex reserves are marking $200 billion, the Bank of Korea is seeking to revamp the management organisation and personnel of the reserves," the central bank said.  

A time-frame for the new appointments would be set in April, Won Jong-seok, an official at the central bank's foreign exchange management division, told Reuters by telephone.  

He said the central bank's returns on reserves were already relatively higher than those at other central banks and yields on global bonds, thanks to the upgrading of its reserves management systems and recruitment of professional managers.  

South Korea's finance ministry also plans to launch a separate government agency later this year to invest an initial $20 billion of the country's reserves, targeting more aggressive investment returns.

title: UPDATE 2-S.Korea plays down Asia  FX  impact of yuan reform.
text:
SEOUL, March 17 (Reuters) - South Korea's central bank said on Thursday Asian currencies, notably the won and Taiwan dollar, were unlikely to rise much more against the U.S. dollar, even if China revalued its currency.  

The remarks appeared to be another attempt by South Korean authorities to quell speculation in the won, which has risen sharply along with some other Asian currencies partly in expectation China will relax controls over the yuan, dealers said.  

Several Asian countries have intervened heavily in markets to curb the strength of their currencies, leaving their central banks with record foreign exchange reserves.  

"Even if the yuan appreciates following the increased flexibility in the yuan system, it will not have a big impact on improving the trade balances (with) Asian countries and therefore will not likely play a role in sparking a follow-up appreciation of currencies in these countries," the Bank of Korea said in a report on international economic affairs.  

China and other Asian countries have come under pressure from the United States and Europe to allow their currencies to appreciate to address global current account imbalances.  

On Wednesday, the United States said its 2004 current account deficit hit a record equal to more than 6 percent of gross domestic product.  

China, with the world's fastest growing major economy, has faced most criticism to relax its currency controls that limit the yuan's movement to a razor-thin 8.276-8.28 per dollar.  

Beijing has resisted, saying reforms will be gradual.  

WON'T BE TOLERATED  

The Bank of Korea said the won and Taiwan dollar have already appreciated considerably on the prospect of a yuan revaluation.  

"Even if the flexibility of the yuan is heightened, the scope of its appreciation is very likely to be limited within tolerable ranges due to possible intervention by the People's Bank of China," it said, referring to China's central bank.  

The won and the Taiwan dollar have risen 14 percent and 9 percent, respectively, against the U.S. dollar in the last five months.  

"Moreover, the scope of appreciation in Asian currencies will likely be limited because each country is expected to intervene in the market when the appreciation pressure builds up on yen and other currencies after the yuan's appreciation," it said.  

Asian central banks have close to $2.5 trillion in foreign exchange reserves in their coffers as a result of intervention to sap the strength of their currencies.  

South Korea's reserves rose $4.66 billion in the first half of March to more than $200 billion, while Taiwan's reserves were $247 billion at the end of February.  

Foreign exchange dealers in Seoul were sceptical of the central bank's view, at least in the case of the won.  

"The won has appreciated a lot from its 2001 level but there is still some room for the won to go up further once the yuan is revalued," said Park Yong-il, senior FX dealer at DBS Bank's Seoul branch. "The remarks appear partly aimed at preventing a yuan revaluation from sparking a panic situation."  

The won has gained 32 percent since the end of 2001 against the U.S. dollar, while the Taiwan dollar is up 12.6 percent.  

Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao said on Monday Beijing could spring a surprise on markets in deciding when and how it reformed the yuan, a comment seen as a warning to speculators trying to profit from a rise in the currency.

SEOUL (Dow Jones)--South Korea's foreign exchange reserves climbed $4.65 billion in the first half of March to a record $206.82 billion due to intervention by the authorities to curb the won's rise, the Bank of Korea said Thursday.

title: S.Korea bonds flat by mid-morning, won moves eyed.
text:
SEOUL, March 11 (Reuters) - South Korean government bond prices were flat by mid-morning on Friday, as investors sat tight to study the next direction of the market after the central bank held interest rates steady and amid a volatile currency market.   

Investors could sell bonds if the benchmark three-year yield fell close to 4.0 percent and amid caution after the central bank sold 6 trillion won ($6 billion) worth of monetary stabilisation bonds via window sales in the morning, dealers said.    


By 0142 GMT, the yield on three-year treasury bonds             was
offered flat at 4.08 percent. The five-year treasury bond yield
   was offered up one basis point at 4.31 percent, dealers said.
   

"Sentiment was helped after the central bank governor said the bank will maintain a low interest rate policy, but bond investors are being pressured by the three-year yield level," a bond analyst said.   

Debt sentiment firmed up after Bank of Korea Governor Park Seung said on Thursday the central bank would keep rate policy supportive of a smooth economic recovery. But he also expressed more optimism about the prospects for South Korea's economy, Asia's third largest.   

Fears about bond supply eased somewhat after a senior finance ministry official said on Thursday the government had enough funds for its operations in the foreign exchange market, allaying fears of a heavy treasuries issuance to fund intervention efforts. But the South Korea won's movements are still being closely monitored by the debt market. Currency dealers said the government interevened to the tune of $2 billion on Thursday to curb the won's strength.   

On the supply front, the Bank of Korea held window sales to sell 2 trillion won in 140-day MSBs at a yield of 3.55 percent, 1.5 trillion won in 364-day paper at 3.85 percent and 2.5 trillion won in 546-day MSBs at 3.98 percent.   

On the Korea Futures Exchange, the key March contract for three-year treasuries fell one tick to 110.76.   

On the local stock market, the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index rose 1.94 percent. ($1=1000.2 Won).

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Taiwan dlr sets new 4-1/2-year high, baht falls.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, March 3 (Reuters) - The Taiwan dollar reached
its strongest level in over 4-1/2-years on Thursday after signs
of easing tensions with China and a strong economy lifted
foreigners' demand for the island's shares over the past month.
    The Taiwan dollar gained as much as a fifth of a percent to
30.82 per dollar, its strongest since July 2000, before ending
the day at 30.86. Foreigners pumped a net T$136 billion into
local stocks since the start of February but turned net sellers
for the second time in a month on Thursday.
    The Thai baht fell a third of a percent on concern the
central bank's decision on Wednesday to raise interest rates to
ward off inflation could slow growth and discourage foreign
investors who have driven a four-month stock rally.
    In Taiwan, the equity inflows since February helped the
Taiwan dollar overcome central bank intervention in the past
week aimed at stalling the gains.
  


 The inflows also helped the
currency emerge as the top performer in Asia this year.
 
    "It's got a lot to do with the turnaround in the technology
sector," said Song Seng Wun, economist at GK Goh Securities.
    "Also, if you don't have any quarrels with the mainland
then it helps," he said, referring to improving ties since
China allowed direct flights from Taiwan in February.
    Signs of a revival in domestic consumer demand helped push
  

up the South Korean won to about 1,006 per dollar. The gains  

were capped by concerns about won-selling intervention by the  

Bank of Korea.  

South Korea foreign exchange reserves climbed 1.2 percent  

in February to a record $202.16 billion. The pace of  

accumulation quickened from January after authorities appeared  

to step up their dollar buying to keep the won competitive  

against rivals.  

The won has surged almost 10 percent against the yen since  

the end of October. The currency has lost ground since it hit a  

seven-year high of 998.1 per dollar last week.  

BAHT STUMBLES

hit a one-month low because of the central bank rate rise and  

oil prices touching a four-month high.  

"Foreign equity inflows have been phenomenal in the past  

four months," said Danny Suwanapruti, a currency analyst at

sharp reversal in the inflows."  

Song said some investors saw the Bank of Thailand's move as

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Won pares back gains - rupee up after budget.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Feb 28 (Reuters) - The South Korean won pared
early sharp gains on Monday on concerns about central bankintervention and month-end dollar buying by importers after
surging on economic data.
    The won jumped three-quarters of a percent to 1,001 per
dollar after industrial production for January beat
expectations and encouraged foreign investors to buy more local
stocks.
 
    The won ended local trading a fifth of a percent higher at
1,006 per dollar.
    The Thai baht gained a quarter of a percent on expectations
the central bank could raise benchmark interest rates on
Wednesday.
    The Indian rupee gained a fifth of a percent after the
  

finance minister presented the country's budget for 2005/2006,  

cutting corporate taxes and taking steps to boost growth in  

infrastructure and rural areas.  

The won was lifted earlier on Monday by data which showed  

South Korea's factory output rose a faster-than-expected 3.1  

percent in January from December.  

Signs of a revival in the domestic economy attracted  

overseas investors to its stock markets this month, pushing its  

benchmark stock index to a five-year high on Monday. Foreign  

investors have bought a net 2.32 trillion won in shares so far  

this year.   


 
    "We see end-March won at 1,000 (per dollar) and end-June at
990," said Christy Tan, an analyst at 4CAST Ltd. in Singapore.
    Yet, analysts said intervention concerns may keep the won
  

from breaching the 1,000 won per dollar barrier in the near  

term. South Korea could sell more bonds to fund intervention

in the currency markets to stem the won's rise, Irene Cheung,  

head of Asian currency strategy at ABN AMRO Bank in Singapore,  

said in a report.  

The South Korean data was followed by statistics from  

Japan which showed industrial production rose a

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Down as China, G7 expectations pared.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Jan 31 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were pushed
lower on Monday as markets scaled back their expectations for
an imminent Chinese yuan revaluation and for the upcoming Group
of Seven nations' meeting to put more pressure on the region.
    That happened after fresh comments from Chinese top
officials suggested they were in no hurry to reform the yuan
regime, and the U.S. dollar found support ahead of key data and
a Federal Reserve  policy meeting.
    Traders braced for a volatile week that will end with the
Group of Seven nations' meeting in London on Friday and
Saturday and could see U.S. rates raised by another 25 basis
points.
    U.S. Treasury Undersecretary John Taylor added to the
pressure on regionals with his remarks that there was no need
for the dollar to crash and that the G7 statement would not be
different from the one issued last year in Florida.
  


 Officials
from China, India and other emerging economies have been
invited to talks with the seven industrialised nations.
 
    The Korean won fell from near Friday's 7-year high of 1,023
a dollar to around 1,026.
    The Singapore dollar fell about a quarter percent to 1.64 a
dollar and then trimmed losses. The Thai baht and Indonesian
rupiah were down.
    There was talk of intervention in Singapore and in the
  

Philippines, where the peso barely moved after its rapid 2.3  

percent gains in 3 weeks, helped by a 12 percent rally in  

stocks  

Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist with UBS, said even if  

the G7 called on Asia to share in the adjustment of the massive  

U.S. trade deficit by letting currencies rise, the region would  

not oblige readily.  

"Even if the rhetoric is stepped up on level to  

burden-sharing, I believe it will not be very significant for  

currency moves."  

"What is central for Asian authorities is that economic  

growth in most areas is clearly off the peak. They will  

continue to intervene to protect against sharp appreciation in  

their currencies, thereby trying to keep exports competitive,"  

he said.  

The Philippines released data on Monday showing annual  

gross domestic product grew 6.1 percent in 2004, the quickest  

pace in 15 years. But growth in the last quarter of 2004 was  

disappointing, and analysts warned the currency market was  

probably overestimating potential investment inflows and  

remittances.  

DOLLAR SUPPORTED  

Meanwhile, the see-sawing on the prospects of China  

revaluing its virtually pegged yuan continued, with China's  

deputy central bank governor Li Ruogu dashing expectations by  

saying China did not have the capacity to address global  

economic imbalances and was not willing or able to do it.  

The premium on one-year yuan in non-deliverable forwards  

was down to 3,850 points, pricing in 4.9 percent gains,  

compared with 5.6 percent on Friday.  

Global oil prices fell, with U.S. oil below $47 a barrel,  

after OPEC producers left output unchanged and Iraq's election  

passed without disruption to oil exports.   


 
    "The dollar will bounce this week," said Claudio Piron,
currency strategist with JP Morgan.
    "Oil prices are lower and that should help the dollar. The
Fed FOMC will be delivering 25 basis points and positioning in
Asia is very aggressive," he said.
    YEN-WON CROSS
    Piron said the north Asian currencies would suffer, but
that markets would be divided on whether to buy the won against
the yen. The yen-won cross rate showed the yen at 9.89 won.
    Markets have been torn between the urge to buy the yen-won
  

cross below the 10 mark - which they believe is the highest  

level for the won Korean authorities can tolerate - and the  

belief that South Korea will not intervene heavily, since the  

government is running out of bonds to offset the intervention.  

Traders waited for data on foreign exchange reserves from  

Korea for evidence of intervention in January and confirmation  

of their view that Korea intervened less in order to stabilise  

its bond markets.  

The finance ministry's announcement on Friday that it would  

issue 5 trillion won in fiscal bonds in February, however,  

frustrated some won bulls. That came after Korea said it would  

cut down on the amount of treasuries issued in February.

text:

plunged on Monday, hit by concerns about an increase in debt
supplies from the finance ministry and the central bank.

surging won currency.
    The central bank has to refinance some 12 trillion won worth

investors more anxious about purchasing bonds.
    "The market is spooked by concerns about overall supply
conditions, holding investors back from trading," said an analyst
at a local investment trust company.
   


    "But I think the yield has reached the level of overshooting
and could stabilise ahead of the Lunar New Year holidays," he
added.
    The yield on three-year treasury bonds
jumped 12 basis points to close at 4.06 percent, its highest
since Aug. 9 last year when it hit 4.08 percent.

trading partners is expected to follow suit.
    Traders added many players settled their long-positions on

title: INTERVIEW: Korea Keen To Establish Euro Bond Benchmark
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The South Korean government is considering issuing in euros for its next international bond to help establish a pricing benchmark for the growing number of local firms keen to issue in the single currency.  

Speaking to Dow Jones Newswires on the sidelines of a recent Citigroup investor conference in Hong Kong, Yeo Kwon Yoon, director of the international finance bureau within South Korea's Ministry of Finance and Economy, said, "These days, there are many Korean companies or banks that want to go to the euro market."  

"There is some demand to make a benchmark in the euro market as well as the dollar market."  

The government said late last year that it was considering denominating its 2005 global bond in the single European currency, following a high-profile EUR1 billion bond sale by the Chinese government. China attracted hefty demand for the bond and priced it through comparable U.S. dollar-denominated paper.  

Size-wise, issuance this year will be the same as in 2004 and in 2003 with the National Assembly having given approval for the Korean government to sell $1 billion equivalent in international bonds this year.  

No decision has been made on the structure and terms of the proposed bond, but Yoon said that "our mandate is just the amount. We have a free hand in which currency to issue."  

Yoon said that a number of investment banks have been pitching proposals to issue in euros. The ministry will submit its issuance plan for this year to the president in mid February, slightly later than expected.  

Market conditions currently favor issuance in euros, but Yoon said that could change very quickly.  

Among Korean banks and companies seeking to issue in euros is state-run Korean Development Bank which is preparing a EUR500 million issue via ABN Amro and Deutsche Bank. KDB is set to sell the bond next week, having set its preferred price earlier Friday while meeting international investors.  

Euro-denominated bonds were also among the ideas submitted last week to the Korea Exchange Bank which is expected to come to the market later this quarter.  


 
   Domestic Issuance Still On Track 
   

Also on the cards is a long-dated $300 million deal from Shinhan Bank, suggesting that a Korea sovereign sale may not be in the offing until closer to mid year at the earliest.  

The Korean government last tapped the international bond market last September with a $1 billion bond that attracted over $3 billion in orders. Priced at 85 basis points over U.S. Treasurys, it is currently trading around 72 basis points over U.S. government debt.  

Yoon said the amount the government raises through the international bond markets would not be affected by its fund-raising domestically since each is fixed separately.  

The government recently cut issuance of treasurys for next month to barely a third of January's as yields, particularly at the middle to longer end, soared after the Bank of Korea kept its policy interest rate unchanged two weeks ago. There were expectations the central bank would cut rates to stimulate the fragile economy.  

Yoon said that despite the cut in supply next month, the government will still likely sell a planned KRW59.4 trillion in domestic bonds this year.  

The ministry and the Bank of Korea agree the recent rise in yields was "groundless," and stemmed mainly from January's hefty supply, he said. What concerned the two was the speed of the increase. "In one to two weeks, the bond yield went up 50 basis points. That is too fast," he said. "If the fluctuation in yields isn't sharp, there is not much concern for the ministry."  

As such, he forecast the government would continue to sell around KRW5 trillion in bonds each month in a continued effort to expand fiscal policy to boost domestic demand.  

Yoon noted that while credit card volumes and department store sales were improving they were "still very weak."  

The Bank of Korea is an alternative buyer of government bonds should the government not want to sell to the market proper.  

Last week, the central bank said it would buy KRW1 trillion of treasurys to stabilize the market.  

News of the cut in February bond sales sent the won higher against the U.S. dollar as the market reckons the government's ability to intervene on the foreign exchange markets to suppress won strength may have diminished.  

Yoon shrugged off any long-term won appreciation, however, saying a one-month decrease in bond issuance wouldn't have any sustained impact.  

South Korea, like many Asian countries, has been intervening to suppress the value of the domestic currency in order to keep exports competitive.  


 
   -By Karen Lane, Dow Jones Newswires; 65 6415 4043; karen.lane@dowjones.com

title: S.Korea won ends lower,  intervention  fears weigh.
text:
SEOUL, Jan 4 (Reuters) - The South Korean won ended a shade
lower on Tuesday, weighed down by fears about possible government
dollar-buying intervention, but losses were capped as many
players saw the U.S. currency's weakness extending into 2005.
 
    The won                   settled in domestic trade at
1,038.7 per dollar, compared with Monday's close of 1,038.1.
    Warnings by a finance ministry official that the government
  

would increase, if necessary, the ceiling on bond issuances to  

fund intervention in the local currency market had little impact,  

dealers said.  

"The cautious mood dominated the market," said a currency

trader. "Investors are holding onto the view that the dollar's  

weakness will continue but intervention fears halted any brave  

attempts to place sizable won-buying orders."  

Choi Joong-kyung, head of the finance ministry's  

international finance bureau, told Reuters in an interview that  

the won's recent gains against the dollar appeared excessive  

given a sluggish domestic economy.  

"The won's recent rises have been rather excessive even if we  

take into account the global trend of a softer dollar that became  

more pronounced since last October," Choi said.  

"If there is a justification, the government will push ahead  

to increase the ceiling on treasury bond issues to finance  

foreign exchange operations," he added.  

The government plans to sell 5 trillion won in treasury bonds  

for foreign exchange market operations in January alone, a record  

monthly issuance for such a purpose.  

A central bank data released on Tuesday showed the country's  

foreign exchange reserves rose 3.4 percent in December to a  

record high as dealers pointed to further intervention by

title: South Korea's  FX  policy - running against the global tide?
text:
SEOUL, Dec 17 (Reuters) - South Korea is ready to spend trillions more won next year to control its currency and try to keep its stuttering economy growing, a policy analysts say is an expensive failure that has cost $15 billion this year.   

 The won has risen 12.6 percent against the dollar so far in 2004, hitting a 7-year high this month, despite official intervention based on fears a surging won would derail exports.   

 The finance ministry is positioning for another big year of buying dollars in 2005, yet analysts say South Korea cannot stand in the way of a widespread decline in the U.S. dollar caused by Washington's large budget and current account deficits.   

 "The effect on exports from the won's value is getting increasingly limited now, and the dollar's weakness is now taking place globally and on a wider scope than before," said Lim Ji-won, an economist at JP Morgan Chase.   

 On Friday, the central bank released figures showing foreign exchange reserves had risen $3.4 billion in the first half of December, citing "smoothing operations" in the won as a factor.   

 Reserves now stand at at a record $196 billion, the fourth largest in the world, having almost doubled in three years.   

 The finance ministry could claim success in 2003, when heavy intervention helped the won stay flat against the dollar, the main currency for South Korean exports.   

 In contrast, Japan - a trade competitor and another to heavily intervene in the forex market to manage its currency - saw its yen gain 11 percent in 2003.   

 But in 2004 the competitive edge has been eroded. The yen has risen just 2.7 percent, taking the relative values of the two currencies back to where they were two years ago at just over 10 won per yen.   

 $300 A HEAD   

 Opposition politicians say the ministry - which wants to raise treasury bonds worth 21.9 trillion won ($20.6 billion) next year to fund forexoperations - has merely delayed the won's rise through a policy that some analysts estimate has cost more than $300 per person in South Korea this year alone.   

 "Its massive intervention has proved a failure as we now see the fast appreciation to a level before the massive intervention began," said Oh Suk-tae, an economist at Citigroup. "The effect of its intervention will from now be very limited."   

 The finance ministry is determined to foster exports as they are the main driver of growth in South Korea, with consumers still loath to open their wallets after a credit bubble burst two years ago.   

 There are also fears that the attempt to limit the won's rise has fuelled inflation, by exposing South Korea to high energy and commodity prices. Inflation hit 3.8 percent in the year through October, although the rate eased back to 3.3 percent in November.   

 While the government can print won as it likes, Oh estimates it has cost the government at least $15 billion to carry its huge foreign exchange reserves, which are mostly in dollars.   

 Analysts say a weaker won may have helped exporters win orders when the global economy was buoyant but demand for South Korea's high-tech goods has cooled and the impact has waned.   

 UNDETERRED   

 Government officials are also debating whether they can really keep a cap on the won. Facing criticism from the central bank, finance ministry official Choi Joong-kyung broke months of silence this week to argue currency policy was an important tool to support exports.   

 "The exchange rate is and will continue to be an important macroeconomic policy tool," Choi, the head of the ministry's international bureau and an influential foreign exchange policy maker, told reporters.   

 It was a direct challenge to an assistant governor at the Bank of Korea, Rhee Yeung-kyun, who told a seminar on Monday foreign exchange rates should not be a policy tool to support local firms and the government could not be expected to keep the exchange rates at a certain level.   

 Next year's limit on bond issuance for foreign exchange operations is 16 percent higher than the 18.8 trillion issued this year. Dealers said some of the extra will be used to square forex positions taken this year.   

 They wonder when the finance ministry will tire of its dollar buying and realise it can not hold back the tide.   

 "The dollar's drop is a global pattern now and the ministry won't try to run counter the trend," said Chung In-woo, executive FX trader at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi's Seoul branch. data. (US$1=1,061 won) (Additional reporting by Cheon Jong-woo).

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Won weakens on  intervention  fears.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Dec 17 (Reuters) - The South Korean won weakened
on Friday as indications of increased dollar-buying
intervention by the South Korean central bank and
better-than-expected U.S. current account data helped the
dollar.
    The won        lost a quarter of a percent to 1,059 per
dollar after the Bank of Korea said it had carried out
"smoothing operations" in the won market in the first half of
December, boosting the country's foreign exchange reserves by
$3.4 billion.
    Analysts said the central banks of South Korea, Singapore
and India had stepped up dollar-buying intervention since
November to slow an Asian currency rally triggered by concerns
that a record U.S. current account deficit would hurt the
dollar.
 
    Stronger currencies make Asian exports, a key source of
growth in the region, less competitive in the United States.
  


    "With domestic demand still fragile (in South Korea),
expect such smoothing' behaviour to persist if the won renews
its strong appreciation trend," ABN AMRO Bank said in a report.
    The won has led the rally in Asian currencies since the
  

start of October and is Asia's best performing currency this  

year, having gained almost 13 percent. It hit a seven-year high  

near 1,037 per dollar on December 6, but has since lost ground.  

It has fallen one percent since the end of November.  

The Taiwan dollar has gained 5 percent and the  

Singapore dollar strengthened 3.2 percent as the yen has  

appreciated 2.6 percent this year.  

Data showing the U.S. current account deficit was narrower  

than expected in the third quarter, even though at a record  

high, helped ease some concerns about the dollar.  

"Taken collectively, the data suggests that the financing  

of the current account deficit was not a major problem in the  

third quarter, in the context of solid but not spectacular  

official inflows," said Alan Ruskin, an analyst at 4CAST, in a  

report.  

"The bad quarters, in contrast, see the dollar under marked  

pressure, and the current account and financial account data  

for the fourth quarter is likely to provide a far less  

encouraging picture longer-term," he said.  

The third-quarter data came a day after U.S. Treasury  

figures showed net inflows into the United States in October  

were not enough to cover that month's record $55.5 billion  

trade deficit.  

TAIWAN DOLLAR, BAHT  

The Taiwan dollar and the Thai baht are expected to lead  

another Asian rally against a weakening dollar because of the  

strength of their economies and greater central bank tolerance  

for currency strength, JP Morgan said in a report.  

Improving labour markets in South Korea, Hong Kong and  

Singapore and increased foreign equity investment in South  

Korea, Taiwan and Thailand would support currencies, JP Morgan  

said.  

The baht weakened a quarter of a percent to 39.25 per  

dollar, paring gains made on Thursday after a surprise 25 basis  

point interest rate rise by the Bank of Thailand.  

The Indonesian rupiah lost half a percent on renewed  

concerns about a drop in foreign direct investment and higher  

fuel subsidies which have widened the budget deficit.  

On Thursday, Japan's trade minister, Shoichi Nakagawa, said  

Indonesia needed to tackle corruption and improve law  

enforcement if it wanted Japanese investment to return.

title: S.Korea fin min official rebuffs c.bank  FX  comment.
text:
SEOUL, Dec 15 (Reuters) - A senior South Korean finance ministry official said on Wednesday the foreign exchange rate was still an important policy tool, rejecting recent comments by a central bank official about the exchange rate policy.  

Choi Joong-kyung, head of the ministry's international bureau, reiterated his earlier view that the government might intervene in the market if necessary.  

"The exchange rate is and will continue to be an important macroeconomic policy tool," said Choi, when asked to comment by reporters. "The government will intervene when necessary."  

An assistant governor at the Bank of Korea, Rhee Yeung-kyun, told a seminar on Monday foreign exchange rates could not be a policy tool to support local companies and that companies should not expect the government to keep the rate at a certain level.   


Those remarks came as a surge in the won currency             against
the U.S. dollar threatened South Korea's export-driven economy amid
cooling demand from its key markets.
  

Economists and dealers have said that South Korea's heavy market intervention late last year had kept its currency undervalued compared with those in rival countries.  

But the won has gained 12 percent against the U.S. dollar so far this year, outperforming other currencies, like the Japanese yen , which has advanced 2 percent, and the euro , which has gained 6 percent against the dollar.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Retreat alongside yen as US dlr rebounds.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Dec 9 (Reuters) - Asian currencies retreated
further from recent multi-year highs on Thursday, following the
Japanese yen, as the U.S. dollar extended a corrective rebound
against major currencies.
    The dollar's recovery this week, which some see as a pause
in a longer-term decline, has been helped by several factors,
including increased verbal intervention from the Japanese and
European authorities.
    A decision by high-yielders, Australia and Canada, to hold
interest rates steady and the weight of positions stacked
against the dollar in recent months also led to the dollar
buying.
    Within Asia, the Korean won, which had outperformed in the
rally, has suffered the biggest losses this week, shedding
nearly 2 percent from seven-year highs. It was quoted around
1,057 a dollar, some 20 won off that peak.
    The Singapore dollar, Indian rupee and the Taiwan dollar
have also dropped a percent each this week.
  


 The yen has fallen
over two percent from 5-year highs.
    The worries of a sovereign ratings downgrade dragged down
the Philippine peso and rupiah selling by oil importers kept
the Indonesian currency around 9,180 a dollar, near two-month
lows.
    Jimmy Koh, head of research at United Overseas Bank in
Singapore, said expectations that China will revalue its yuan
sometime next year underpinned the regionals, based on the view
that a firmer yuan will make Asian authorities more tolerant of
gains.
    Chinese yuan non-deliverable forwards showed markets have
pared expectations of a near-term change in the tightly managed
yuan, after China's key annual economic policy meeting at the
weekend failed to provide clues on yuan policy.
 
    But one-year NDFs still priced in an appreciation of over
five percent from current levels around 8.278 yuan per dollar.
    INTERVENTION FEARS HAUNT
    Markets fear Asian central banks will use the momentum of
the dollar rebound to intervene and push their currencies down

title: S Korea Won Ends Lower On Yen Slide, Govt  Intervention
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--The South Korean won finished lower Friday following the dollar's recovery from a five-year low against the yen Thursday. Authorities' purchases also helped the greenback sustain its gains despite continued selling by exporters, market participants said.  

The dollar ended at 1,045.5 won, up from its close of KRW1,041.5 Thursday, the lowest since Nov. 19, 1997. It traded from KRW1,044.1 to KRW1,048.0 intraday.  

The U.S. unit remained in positive territory all day, starting off as high as KRW1,048 after it regained above the Y103 level overnight on short covering on speculation that U.S. nonfarm payrolls data due later Friday might be stronger than expected.  

But the dollar's fall against the South Korean currency wasn't as dramatic as the yen, with players hesitant to build dollar-long positions against the won for fear of spurring more speculative selling by exporters.  

At 0740 GMT, the dollar was at Y103.97, up sharply from a low of Y101.86 in Japan a day earlier.  

"It wasn't that there were many buyers in the market, but more of less selling by exporters ahead of the U.S. payrolls data," said a dealer at a foreign bank.  

Buying of dollars by South Korean authorities persisted throughout the day to absorb the dollar supplies from exporters and sustain the U.S. unit's rising momentum.  

"Authorities must have sighed in relief. If not for the (decline of the) yen, we could have seen the break of the 1,040 level today," a local bank dealer said.  

The won has repeatedly hit seven-year highs this week. The local unit has risen despite repeated warnings from government officials, including President Roh Moo-Hyun, that they will act - possibly jointly with Japan - to slow the won's gains to lessen the negative impact on South Korea's export-reliant economy.  

"These warnings and interventionist comments failed to stir the market because authorities' actions won't be able to match the strong words due to limited (intervention) funds left," another local dealer said.  

Earlier Friday, the government said it will issue an additional KRW1 trillion in three-year treasurys Monday to stabilize the currency market. Including the new issue, the government would have issued a total of KRW18 trillion in treasurys earmarked for forex operations this year, leaving just KRW800 billion in its intervention budget for the full year.  

U.S. nonfarm payrolls data for November are expected to show the economy added 218,000 new jobs, according to a Dow Jones Newswires survey of economists. The U.S. economy created 337,000 new jobs in the previous month.  

If the data are better than expected, the dollar could rally to 105.0 against the yen, and above 1,050 versus the won, traders said.  

Investors largely kept to the sidelines in the options market on the belief that the 1,040-1,050 range would prevail in the near term.  

The volatility implied by one-month at-the-money dollar/won options was 8.9%/9.6%, hardly changed from the previous day.  

"The options market is usually quiet in December. Without a spot price break of 1,030, this year won't be an exception," said an options dealer at a foreign bank.  

The one-month delta risk reversal - which indicates market bias - still favored dollar puts/won calls at 1.4%/1.9%, a tad lower than 1.5%/2.0% a day earlier.  

Traders expect the dollar to trade between KRW1,040.0 and KRW1,050.0 in the spot market Monday. [ 03-12-04 0757GMT ]  

South Korean treasurys ended mostly flat Friday due to continued pressure from the tight spread between the overnight call rate target and the three-year government bond yield, said market participants.  

The three- and five-year treasury yields finished unchanged at 3.29% and 3.43%, respectively.  

"The narrow spread between the policy rate and the three-year treasury yield pressured the market, while players were losing confidence over (the likelihood of) an additional rate cut" when the monetary policy committee meets Thursday, said Kim Nam-Soo, a fund manager at Kyobo Investment Trust.  

The news of the extra KRW1 trillion three-year treasury issue by the Ministry of Finance and Economy Monday to raise funds for currency market operations had little impact on bonds.  

Including this additional issue, the finance ministry is slated to issue a total of KRW2.08 trillion in treasurys Monday.  

"The market had already expected the news, so no one was surprised by the announcement," said Yang Jin-Mo, an analyst at SK Securities.  

"Rather, the government's plan to offer more bonds for currency market action eased uncertainty over excessive supply. So the market will keep to the sidelines until the BOK decides on the policy rate Thursday," said Kim at Kyobo.  

Analysts expect the widely traded three-year treasury yield to range between 3.28% and 3.31% Monday.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Baht, Sing dollar lead decline.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Dec 3 (Reuters) - The Thai baht lost almost 1
percent on Friday as Asian currencies declined on growing
expectations that central banks would sell their currencies to
stem a rally that could hurt the region's exporters.
    The baht        weakened from a seven-month high against
the dollar to about 39.48 per dollar. The Singapore dollar
 , the Taiwan dollar  and the Indonesian rupiah
  lost more than half a percent each, following a 1.5
percent drop in the yen.
    Central bankers and government officials in South Korea
and
 Japan have issued repeated warnings they may intervene to stem
a two-month rally in their currencies which they say have
become overvalued compared with economic fundamentals.
    "Central banks across Asia will be wary of speculative
attacks on their currencies," said Lian Chia Chiang, an
economist at JP Morgan Chase in Singapore.
    Still, Lian does not expect the dollar's weakening trend to
reverse anytime soon.
  


 JP Morgan expects the baht to appreciate
to 39 per dollar by the end of the year and to 37 per dollar by
September next year.
    The baht has underperformed most other Asian currencies
this year, partly on concerns about violence in its southern
region. The currency has gained 0.4 percent this year, compared
with a 14 percent surge in the South Korean won
  and a near 4 percent gain in the yen.
 
    Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devaluka said on
Friday the baht was still competitive for exports.
    Lian said the strength of Thailand's economy -- which he
  

expects to grow 5 percent in 2005 compared with 6 percent  

growth this year - and a broadly weakening dollar will help  

boost the baht's value next year.  

U.S. DOLLAR RESILIENCE  

The north Asian currencies and the Singapore dollar took a  

beating after South Korean President Roh Moo-hyun said in  

London on Thursday that the government was ready to guard  

against excessive currency moves and aims to coordinate such  

measures with other governments.  

Data released Thursday showed the South Korean central bank

had intervened in the currency market in November, although the  

Bank of Japan has stayed away from the markets since March.  

Song Seng Wun, economist at Singapore-based G.K. Goh  

Securities said both central banks may use thin trading in the  

upcoming Christmas and year-end holiday season to sell their  

currencies and reverse the two-month rally that took the won to  

a seven-year high and the yen to a five-year high this week.  

The dollar could also get support from the recovery in the  

U.S. economy which has forced the U.S. Federal Reserve to raise  

benchmark rates this year. Most analysts expect the Fed to  

raise rates once more at a meeting this month.  

Some traders who sold the dollar this month on concerns  

about the widening U.S. current account and budget deficits  

reversed their bets ahead of the release of U.S. non-farm  

payrolls data later on Friday.  

The U.S. economy created 180,000 non-farm jobs in November,  

after 337,000 jobs created in October, according to the median  

of a Reuters poll of economists. "There's a bit more  

resilience to the U.S. economy than many people think," said  

Song.  

Song said expectations for stronger U.S. data and fears of  

Asian central bank intervention would stall the dollar's slide  

in the shorter term, although the longer-term forecast was for  

a further decline in the U.S. currency.

title: Emerging Asia  FX - Currencies  weaken on  intervention  fear.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Dec 3 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar and the
Thai baht weakened more than half a percent on Friday, leading
declines in Asia as authorities increased warnings they might
sell their currencies to stem a two-month rally.
    The Singapore dollar       , which hit a six-year high
against the dollar on Wednesday, traded at about 1.6422 per
dollar. The baht  weakened to 39.37 per dollar, paring
gains that took it to a seven-month high on Thursday.
    South Korea must be ready to prevent excessive gains in its
currency and work with other countries to stem sharp currency
moves that hurt exporters, President Roh Moo-hyun said at a
press briefing in London on Thursday.
    The won        surged 14 percent this year to a seven-year
high on Thursday, leading gains in Asian currencies against a
broadly weakening dollar.
    Roh's comments resonated among other Asian officials,
particularly in Japan, who may be preparing to intervene,
analysts said.
  


    "The authorities may be signalling that enough is enough,"
said Song Seng Wun, economist at G.K. Goh Securities in
Singapore.
    "With the holiday season coming up, and liquidity low, they
may think that this is the best time to intervene because they
don't want to waste too much ammunition."
 
    South Korea has already intervened by buying dollars with
won last month, data showed this week.
    UBS expects more intervention from the Bank of Korea as
authorities seek to protect the country's biggest companies
which are also the country's largest exporters.
    The won        weakened 0.3 percent on Friday to about
1,044.30 per dollar. The Taiwan dollar  lost half a
percent to about 32.15 per dollar.
    "Considering that the Korean domestic economy is not
exactly humming along it's not surprising that the authorities
should be whining about the won's gains," said Song.
    JAPAN INTERVENTION
    UBS also expects the Bank of Japan to start dollar-buying
intervention, for the first time since March, this month, to
stall the yen.
    The yen        plunged 1.3 percent to about 103.33 per
dollar on Friday, coming off a five-year high reached on
Thursday.
    The Christmas and year-end holiday season reduces trading,
  

making it easier for Asian central banks to reverse the rally  

in their currencies by selling relatively light amounts of  

currency, analysts said  

Worries that Asian central banks might slow down the  

purchase of U.S. treasuries to fund the U.S. deficit were eased  

by data on Thursday showing foreign central banks turned net  

buyers of U.S. Treasuries in the week ending Dec. 1.  

Asian central banks, packing the world's largest foreign  

currency reserves, have some of the biggest holdings of U.S.  

treasuries.  

Speculation that some might cut purchases of U.S.  

government debt to shift to euro assets was partly responsible  

for the dollar's decline against Asian currencies, analysts  

said.  

Dealers expect the dollar to weaken longer term, but say  

the currency could find some support short term on the strength  

of the U.S. economy as reflected by rate increases by the U.S.  

Federal Reserve this year.

title: =DJ INTERVIEW/BOK Bd Member: Inflation Tamer, Growth To Slow
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--A member of the Bank of Korea's monetary policy committee Wednesday said inflationary pressures have eased while economic growth is expected to decelerate next year, comments likely to boost mounting expectations for an interest-rate cut.  

Kim Tae-Dong also told Dow Jones Newswires that the Bank's surprise rate cuts in August and November have boosted the economy, countering arguments by private economists that the moves have been ineffective.  

Earlier Wednesday, South Korean treasury prices surged to new highs on renewed expectations for further interest-rate cuts, after the consumer price index showed November inflation was softer than expected.  

'At the time of the November rate decision, oil prices had declined while the foreign exchange rate (of the dollar to the Korean won) had plunged, helping inflation. The foreign exchange rate has gone even further down since then, while oil prices have maintained similar levels,' said Kim, whose four-year term as a committee member ends in 2006.  

At the same time, economic growth is expected to be 'close' to the 5% potential growth rate this year, but fall short of that rate by 1 percentage point next year, he said, echoing remarks Tuesday by Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hun-Jai.  

The government has pinned its hopes on attaining 5% growth this year - the level at which Korea's economy is considered able to expand in the long run without triggering excessive inflation. But many investment banks forecast that the South Korean economy will grow at the 4% level this year before expanding at the 3% level next year, triggering possible job losses and a prolonged slowdown.  

Kim said his foremost concern is stabilizing inflation, while economic growth is secondary. He said he is confident that core inflation won't break the 2.5%-3.5% target band set for 2004-2006. This year, core inflation is likely to reach 3.0%, he said.  

Kim said the Bank of Korea's interest-rate cuts in August and November have been effective, countering market sentiment that their impact on the economy has been muted. The Bank of Korea defied market expectations, and bucked a global tightening trend, when it twice eased rates by 25 basis points, to a record low 3.25%.  

Kim said monetary easing rarely has any impact on capital investment in any country, so lack of impact there isn't unique to Korea. As for reviving private spending, he said large household debt has weakened the impact on consumption, but lower rates will nudge consumers to spend once South Korea's debt overhang eases.  

Kim, however, also blamed government intervention in the foreign exchange market for reducing the impact of the rate cuts.  

In an open economy, the local currency should decline after a monetary easing, boosting exports, but market forces weren't fully functioning because of the government's intervention, and the dollar fell, he said.  

'But the foreign exchange rate would have fallen even more if there had been no monetary easing,' he added.  

On criticism that the Bank of Korea doesn't give sufficient signals to the market before its rate decisions, Kim said the market isn't diligent enough in watching for the BOK's signals.  

'Just look at the BOK's rate cut pattern; look at when the second rate cut occurred after the first cut. If there was no rate cut two months after the first cut, what's the probability that there would have been a rate cut in the following month?' he said. Last year, the Bank of Korea cut interest rates by quarter points each in May and July.  

In October, BOK Governor Park Seung berated the bond market for betting heavily in favor of a rate cut, calling it 'overheated' and in need of 'more training.' These comments led the market to wrongly assume that the central bank would shelve its easing bias until 2005.  

As for the government, which has openly called for more interest-rate cuts to revive the economy, Kim said the government needs to be 'more aggressive' with fiscal policy. However, he recommended tax cuts rather than increased spending.  

Under current circumstances, when national transparency is quite low, there's a possibility that government money won't flow into high-productivity investments, he said.  

Asked whether he generally favors higher or lower interest rates, Kim said, 'I can't say whether I'm hawkish or dovish, that's for you to decide, but I argued for a rate cut between February and April 2003, six to one before monetary easing in May,' he said.  

-By In Kyung Kim, Dow Jones Newswires; 822-732-2165; in-kyung.kim@dowjones.com
