title: INTERVIEW-Asia must share  FX  pain with euro - OECD's Cotis.
text:
PARIS, Nov 30 (Reuters) - The euro zone has paid its share of the economic bill for the slide in the dollar and Asia must now do so by letting its currencies rise versus the greenback, OECD chief economist Jean-Philippe Cotis says.  

In an interview with Reuters, Cotis said that the European Central Bank should avoid raising interest rates, probably until 2006, to help the 12-nation euro area economy weather a surge in world oil prices and the impact of a sharp drop in the dollar.  

Cotis's recommendations to Asia come at a time of renewed market fears that Japan, South Korea or other Asian countries may intervene to keep their currencies from rising too much on the grounds that their exports and growth are threatened.  

"It's an anomoly to ask the weakspot of the world economy to do all the (currency) appreciation," Cotis, who presented the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development's report on the economy of the 30-country OECD on Tuesday, said.  

"The fact that some Asian currencies seem to be appreciating also alongside the euro is for us a good beginning, a sign of a better readjustment of current account imbalances," he said, making it clear he hoped Asia would steer clear of intervention this time round and let currencies in the region appreciate.  

The euro has surged to records against the dollar in recent days as markets sign up to the idea that Washington is not unhappy with a dollar slide that could help U.S. exports and trim a record U.S. trade deficit regarded as unsustainable.  

Cotis said further rises could be very damaging for the euro zone but he hoped he had detected signs of greater willingness in Asia to let currencies there rise too, sharing the burden this imposes by making their exports relatively more costly.   


Governments in countries such as Japan and South Korea have watched the
yen  and won       soar to four-and-a-half and seven-year highs
respectively in recent days but refrained from past practice of
intervening in the markets to drive their money back down in value and
thereby protect their exports.
  

Cotis declined to venture an estimate of what level might be excessive for the euro's rise against the dollar - it soared above $1.33 last week - preferring to stress the need for an orderly adjustment where all regions helped absorb the change.  

ECB RATES ON HOLD THROUGH 2005?  

Not so long ago markets were convinced that an interest rate rise from the ECB was as good as inevitable in 2005, but that was before the oil price spike, dollar slide and news of poor growth in the third quarter in the euro zone. "Should the appreciation of the euro get out of proportion - and knowing that the recovery so far has been export driven and there's little domestic momentum in the recovery - I guess there'd be a case for relaxation (of ECB rates)," Cotis said.  

"But I don't think we are there yet. There is a strong case for not tightening and the option of relaxing is in case of a catastrophic outcome on the exchange rate side."  

He highlighted that the recent surge in the euro and Asian currencies followed another bout of dollar weakness in early 2004, a time when the euro zone bore much of the brunt as Asian countries resisted with dollar-buying intervention.  

"Now we seem to be moving towards a pattern of better shared adjustment worldwide with the Koren won appreciating, the yen appreciating, (although) the Chinese renmimbi is still missing from the list," he said.  

"What we need is a worldwide effort to cure a worldwide problem. Basically allowing an appreciation is in the best long-term interests of the Asian economies."  

The twice-yearly OECD report that he presented cut growth forecasts for the eurozone to 1.8 percent for 2004 from 2.0 percent and to 1.9 percent in 2005 from 2.4 percent.  

The OECD tweaked the U.S. growth forecast marginally upwards to 4.4 percent for this year and lowered it to 3.3 percent from 3.7 percent for next year, and cut Japan's growth outlook to 4.0 percent from 4.4 this year and to 2.1 from 2.8 for 2005.  

LIVING WITH DEARER OIL  

Cotis put most of the changes down to the same thing, a surge in world oil prices to more than $50 a barrel in the third quarter of 2004, leaving them around 50 percent higher than at the start of the year.  

"Should oil prices stabilise, growth is going to accelerate. If it stops there, at current prices, I don't see that this would stand in the way of a continued recovery."  

In the late 1990s the world's oil consuming countries were keen to see the price of a barrel of oil remain around $25, but they could now live with a price of $40 or more, he said, as long as there was stability and no surges of the recent kind. The OECD includes all the world's rich industrialised economies as well as emerging market economies such as Turkey, Mexico and eastern European countries which have just joined the European Union.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Weaken on data,  intervention  fears.

By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Nov 30 (Reuters) - Asian currencies weakened on
Tuesday after disappointing economic data from Japan and
comments from Asian leaders calling for concerted action to
stall a two-month rally in their currencies.
    The Taiwan dollar lost about 0.4 percent in early deals to
32.28 per dollar. The South Korean won shed 0.1 percent to
about 1,048 per dollar.
    Last week, the Taiwan dollar had climbed to its strongest
level in four years while the won had appreciated to a
seven-year high.
    The rally stalled on Monday due to worries about likely
central bank interventions across Asia. South Korea's
presidential office said on Monday that the leaders of Japan,
China and South Korea agreed on the sidelines of the
Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Laos
on the need for stable exchange rates.
    Meanwhile, industrial production data from South Korea and
Japan disappointed markets.
  


 Japanese data showed industrial
output unexpectedly fell 1.6 percent in October from a month
earlier. On Monday, South Korea said industrial output fell 0.9
percent in October.
    "The weak Japanese and Korean data are making people
conclude that the U.S. economy is cyclically the strongest
now," said Simon Flint, a currency strategist at Bank of
America in Singapore.
    Some traders and investors, who had bid up the won and
other Asian currencies this month on concerns about prolonged
weakness in the dollar, probably rewound their bets after the
agreement among Asian leaders that the rally in their
currencies was overdone, Flint said.
    "The talk about that meeting may have had an impact on the
market," he said. "The decline in the dollar has been arrested
for the time being."
    Further data from Japan, including gross domestic product
figures and the Tankan survey due early next month, is likely
to reconfirm that the Japanese economy may be slowing.
    Bank of America still expects the dollar to weaken to 100
yen by the end of the year, from around 103.15 on Tuesday, and
to $1.35 per euro, from $1.325 on Tuesday, because of the
widening U.S. current account deficits.
    Traders are looking for further clues on whether Asian
central banks are curtailing purchases of U.S. treasury bills
and other dollar assets in their foreign currency reserve
holdings.
    A Chinese economic adviser said last week U.S. government
data showed that China, which holds the world's second-largest
foreign currency reserves, reduced its dollar holdings.
    Many other Asian central banks could reduce their dollar
holdings if the dollar weakness persists and that could lead to
further dollar weakness in the longer term, Flint said.
    "I don't think this question is going to go away soon,"
Flint said. "There's enough structural themes pointing to a
dollar weakness in the longer term." CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Won, Taiwan dollar weaken on  intervention .
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Nov 29 (Reuters) - Asian currencies weakened on
Monday, led by the South Korean won and the Taiwan dollar,
after state-run banks stepped in to buy dollars to curb a rally
that drove regionals to multi-year highs last week.
    The South Korean won lost as much as 0.6 percent against
the dollar to 1,053 per dollar in local trades on suspected
central bank intervention, before recovering most of its lost
ground. The Taiwan dollar weakened 0.3 percent to 32.205 per
dollar.
    Government officials in Japan and South Korea have
threatened to intervene over the past month to stem the
dollar's broad-based slide that drove the won to a 7-year high
and the Taiwan dollar to a 4-year high last week.
    South Korea is particularly hurt by the weaker dollar
because the won has appreciated 10 percent in the past three
months to outperform other Asian currencies.
  


 
    The currency gained 1 percent on Friday as the rally
triggered sales of dollar receipts by the country's exporters.
    "The Korean central bank needed to calm down the markets
for the shorter term," said Mark Cranfield, head of treasury
and capital markets at Landesbank Baden-Wuerttemberg.
    "Trading was frantic and truly became reckless last week. I
wouldn't be surprised if the Bank of Japan was in the market
too."
    The won also came under pressure after data showed South
  

Korea's industrial production fell a seasonally adjusted 0.9  

percent in October from the month earlier. Analysts in a  

Reuters poll had expected a median rise of 0.7 percent.  

While South Korea's current account surplus has tripled in  

the first 10 months of this year, export growth has slowed  

since the second quarter, dragging on the outlook for the  

economy already weakened by a slump in domestic consumer  

demand.  

CHINA FACTOR  

The Singapore dollar traded at about 1.6385/90, close to a  

6-year high.  

Other Asian currencies were weighed down by Chinese Premier  

Wen Jiabao's statements on Sunday signalling the country was in  

no rush to revalue the yuan.  

Jiabao said China needed a stable economy and a healthy  

financial system before making changes to the yuan's peg to the  

dollar.  

Speculation that China might soon relax controls over its  

currency and allow the yuan to trade in a broader band had  

fuelled the rally in Asian currencies.  

"I think you can believe (Premier Wen)," said Cranfield.  

"The bottomline is that China would do only what's important  

for them. It'll never do what the rest of the world wants them  

to do."  

Cranfield said the dollar was likely to continue on its  

weakening trend against most major currencies in the longer  

term.  

Since the start of this year, the dollar has weakened  

almost 14 percent against the won, nearly 6 percent against the  

Taiwan dollar and over 4 percent against the yen as U.S.  

officials voiced concerns about the country's widening current  

account deficit.  

Several U.S. Federal Reserve officials have argued that the  

shortfall could be met by a drop in the value of the dollar  

against the currencies of major trading partners of the U.S..

title: S.Korea won flat early amid  intervention  worries.
text:
0030 GMT - South Korea's won             little changed against the
dollar in early domestic trade, anchored by worries about renewed
government intervention.
  

 - The won at 1,065.2 per dollar, against its previous local close of 1,065.3. On Monday, the won ended off session highs on suspected central bank intervention after touching its strongest level since late 1997 at 1,060.0 at one point.   

 - "Almost everyone thinks the dollar's downward trend will continue, but intervention is an immediate concern," said a dealer at a local bank. "Dollars are still coming in."   

 - The yen  also little changed against the U.S. currency in early Asian trade, quoted at 103.14/18 versus 103.15 late in New York.   

 - Dealers concerned about aggressive intervention after Finance Minister Lee Hun-jai made a rare request on Monday to the central bank to take a stronger role in controlling the won's rise, according to a government source.

title: DJ AWSJ(11/23) Bank Of S Korea Steps In To Slow Surge Of Won
text:
Nov 22, 2004 (ODC via COMTEX) --  

(From THE ASIAN WALL STREET JOURNAL)  

By Donald Greenlees SEOUL -- South Korea's central bank intervened in foreign-exchange markets to slow the appreciation of the won against the dollar, as concern mounted over the impact a stronger currency would have on exports, the main driver of the country's economy. Yesterday's intervention was the second in less than two weeks by the Bank of Korea after it aggressively bought dollars on Nov. 10, traders said. In spite of that previous intervention, the won continued to strengthen, reaching a seven-year high against the dollar last week. A currency dealer at a Seoul bank estimated that authorities yesterday purchased roughly $500 million to $600 million of the U.S. currency to bolster its value following a meeting between Finance Minister Lee Hun Jai and Park Seung, the central bank governor, to discuss measures to curb the won's rapid strengthening. Government officials are concerned the strong won will hurt exports of memory chips, consumer electronics, household appliances and automobiles, which are the mainstays of South Korea's economic growth, amid weak domestic consumption. A strong won will increase the dollar prices of exports, potentially reducing demand for them in the U.S. and elsewhere. Those same fears about a strong won pushed down shares of export-oriented manufacturing companies on the Korea Stock Exchange yesterday. The main index fell 17.04 points, or 2%, to close at 849.99. Markets elsewhere in Asia dropped on currency concerns. In Japan, the Nikkei 225 Stock Average slid 2.1%, while in Taiwan, the benchmark index was down 3.1%. After opening at 1,068.70 won per dollar, the South Korean currency strengthened to end the day at 1,065.30 per dollar, despite the central-bank intervention in the afternoon. Dealers said the relatively small size of the intervention suggested that the bank was trying to slow the rate of the won's ascent rather than prevent further strengthening. The head of the Bank of Korea's foreign-exchange market team, Oh Jae Kwon, said he couldn't comment on "whether the government intervened or not." In his meeting with the central-bank governor, Mr. Lee urged the bank to be "bolder and more aggressive" in its foreign-exchange policy, according to a senior official at the Ministry of Finance and Economy quoted by Dow Jones Newswires. The official said Mr. Lee suggested the bank print won to buy up dollars in the foreign-exchange market. Despite the two interventions this month, economic analysts predict the Bank of Korea will intervene more firmly only if central banks in Japan and Taiwan also choose to come into the market to buy dollars. "My sense is that they don't have the appetite to intervene unless they can coordinate it with other central banks in the region," said Michael Spencer, chief economist for Asia at Deutsche Bank in Hong Kong. The strength of the won, with the dangers that poses to Korean exports and economic growth, appears to be replacing inflation as the Korean government's major concern. Mr. Spencer predicted that the won's performance would prompt the Bank of Korea to make another quarter-percentage-point cut in interest rates by early 2005. This could help take some of the pressure off exporters, which might start to see profit margins squeezed in their results for the current quarter or the first three months of 2005. --- Seah Park contributed to this article.

title: S.Korea won ends off 7-yr high,  intervention  cited.
text:
SEOUL, Nov 22 (Reuters) - South Korea's won  closed local trade higher against the dollar on Monday, but pared its gains on suspected intervention, after hitting a fresh seven-year high earlier during the session, dealers said.   

 The won  closed local trade up 0.3 percent on the day at 1,065.3 per dollar, after paring some of its early gains on what dealers said was selling on behalf of the authorities.   

 The selling, which briefly pushed the won below Friday's local close of 1,068.7 in the afternoon, followed a rare request by the finance minister for the central bank to intervene more strongly in the market.   

 Dealers said a flood of dollars were still awaiting to hit the market and the impact of any intervention was only likely to slow the won's rise as long as the dollar's global weakness persists.   

 "Intervention was not very strong today. The dollar/won won't turn up unless the dollar/yen rose to somewhere above 105," said Jung In-woo, executive FX trader at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi's Seoul branch.   

 The yen  stood at 103.27/30 per dollar at 0733 GMT, down slightly on the day but still in sight of the 102.70 hit in New York on Friday, the highest level since March 2000. The yen is closely watched by dealers in Seoul, given the strong competition between the two neighbours in export markets.   

 "Exporters appeared hasty to sell dollars while importers preferred to wait a little more," Jung said, indicating that exporters still had a lot of dollars to sell.   

 EXPORTS ALREADY SLOWING   

 The strength of the won, which has gained 6 percent this month against the dollar and 12 percent so far this year, also sent the local stock market  tumbling about 2 percent.   

 Earlier on Monday, Finance Minister Lee Hun-jai asked the central bank chief, Park Seung, to take a stronger stance to cap the won's rise, according to a government source.   

 "He asked Governor Park that the central bank take bolder and more aggressive counter measures," the source said by telephone, adding that this could include the central bank using its right to print money.   

 In non-deliverable forward trading, the one-month won was quoted at 1,066.0/7.0 late on Monday, against 1,069.5/70.5 late on Friday, according to Prebon Yamane Asia Pacific. Three-month won rose to 1,067.4/8.4, from 1,070.9/1.9.   

 The rare meeting between Lee and the governor of the Bank of Korea came as the won's rally raised concerns about the export-dependent economy being damaged as slowing exports combine with a persistent slump in local demand.   

 The Bank of Korea has taken the leading role in controlling the won's rise since the finance ministry was criticised last month in parliament for keeping the won undervalued.   

 The amount of money the ministry can mobilise to fund intervention has also been limited by parliament.   

 The rising won has added to concerns about Chinese demand for exports after Beijing raised interest rates for the first time in nine years to step up a drive to cool its economy.   

 China is the largest market for South Korean exports, soaking up a fifth of its total shipments abroad.   

 Last week the finance minister all but abandoned a long-standing target of 5 percent economic growth this year, saying the chance of meeting the forecast was extremely slim.   


The firmer won also hit export-reliant manufacturers on the Seoul stock
market. Chipmaker Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd.  fell 3.1 percent and
automaker Hyundai Motor Co.             lost 2.4 percent. (Additional
reporting by Lee Shin-hyung and Cheon Jong-woo).
